— Linear Algebra —
31

Vectors

Concept

A vector is an ordered list of numbers representing a point or a direction in space. In AI, everything becomes a vector: a planet's features [mass, radius, orbital_period], a sentence's meaning, a user's behavior. Embeddings — the currency of modern AI — are just vectors, and "similar meaning" becomes "small angle between vectors." Once data is a vector, geometry becomes your toolkit: distance, angle, projection.

  • Magnitude: the vector's length — np.linalg.norm(v). Often normalized away so only direction matters.
  • Direction: where it points — for embeddings, this is what carries the meaning.
  • Dimensions: a 3-feature planet lives in 3-D; an OpenAI embedding lives in 1536-D. Same math, more axes.
Two embedding vectors: the angle between them measures how related the meanings are.
Example 
import numpy as np

flare = np.array([0.8, 0.3, 0.1])   # embedding of "solar flare"
cme   = np.array([0.7, 0.4, 0.2])   # embedding of "CME event"

cos = flare @ cme / (np.linalg.norm(flare) * np.linalg.norm(cme))
print(f"similarity: {cos:.3f}")   # close to 1 → related concepts
Real scenario — space-weather semantic search

Your Mission Control RAG embeds every DONKI space-weather report as a vector. When a user asks "any sun eruptions this week?", the query vector lands near "solar flare" report vectors even though the words differ — that geometric closeness IS the retrieval. Every downstream trick (reranking, hybrid search) is just refining which vectors count as "near".

32

Matrices

Concept

A matrix is a grid of numbers that acts as a transformation: multiply a vector by a matrix and the vector gets rotated, stretched, sheared, or projected into a different space. That's the real mental model — not "a table of numbers" but "a machine that moves vectors." Every neural-network layer's weights are a matrix doing exactly this: the layer takes your 4-feature planet vector and transforms it into a new representation where the next layer's job is easier.

  • An m×n matrix maps n-dimensional vectors to m-dimensional ones — it can change dimensionality.
  • The columns of a matrix tell you where the basis vectors land — the whole transformation follows from that.
  • Rotation, scaling, projection: all just special patterns of numbers in the grid.
A matrix is a transformation: the unit grid goes in, a rotated/stretched grid comes out.
Example 
import numpy as np

theta = np.deg2rad(45)
R = np.array([[np.cos(theta), -np.sin(theta)],
              [np.sin(theta),  np.cos(theta)]])   # 2×2 rotation matrix

probe = np.array([1.0, 0.0])    # probe position on the x-axis
print(R @ probe)                # [0.707 0.707] → rotated 45°
Real scenario — every layer of your exoplanet classifier

Your tabular exoplanet classifier's first Dense layer holds a 12×64 weight matrix. Each forward pass, a planet's 12 features get multiplied by it — rotated and stretched into a 64-dimensional space where "planet" and "false positive" are easier to separate. Training is nothing more than nudging the numbers in that grid.

33

Matrix multiplication

Concept

Rows of the left times columns of the right: each cell of the result is one dot product between a row of A and a column of B. An (m×n) matrix times an (n×p) matrix gives an (m×p) result — and the inner dimensions must match, because a row of length n can only be dotted with a column of length n. This one operation is what GPUs spend their lives doing: a transformer forward pass is a long chain of matrix multiplications, and "FLOPs" mostly counts these.

  • Shape rule: (m,n) @ (n,p) → (m,p) — read it left to right, the n's cancel.
  • Not commutative: A @ B ≠ B @ A in general — order is meaning.
  • Cost is O(m·n·p) multiplications — why model size × sequence length dominates your GPU bill.
One highlighted row of A meets one highlighted column of B to produce one cell of C.
Example 
import numpy as np

planets = np.random.rand(3, 4)   # 3 planets × 4 features   (m×n)
weights = np.random.rand(4, 2)   # 4 features → 2 hidden units (n×p)

hidden = planets @ weights       # (3×4)·(4×2) → (3×2)
print(hidden.shape)              # (3, 2)

bad = np.random.rand(5, 2)
planets @ bad                    # ValueError: shapes (3,4) and (5,2)
                                 # — the inner 4 and 5 don't match
Real scenario — the shape-mismatch crash you WILL hit

Wiring your light-curve CNN's flattened output into the dense head, you'll hit mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied — the classic inner-dimension mismatch. Reading shapes like (batch, 3197) @ (3197, 64) fluently is how you debug it in seconds instead of an hour. Batched inference is the same trick: stack 256 light curves as rows and one matmul scores them all.

34

Dot product

Concept

Multiply element-wise and sum: a·b = a₁b₁ + a₂b₂ + … — one number measuring how aligned two vectors are. Positive means pointing the same general way, zero means orthogonal (no relationship along these axes), negative means opposed. This is the raw score inside both attention (query · key = "how much should this token attend to that one") and vector search (query · document = relevance).

  • Geometric identity: a·b = |a||b|cos(θ) — alignment scaled by lengths.
  • In NumPy: a @ b or np.dot(a, b).
Key distinction

Dot product vs cosine similarity: cosine is just the dot product after normalizing both vectors to length 1 — pure angle, lengths ignored. Vector DBs let you pick either; if your embeddings are already normalized (many are), they rank identically.

The sign of a dot product: same direction, no relation, opposite direction.
Example 
import numpy as np

v_sat   = np.array([7.5, 0.0])    # satellite velocity, km/s
v_along = np.array([3.0, 0.0])    # thrust along the orbit
v_ortho = np.array([0.0, 3.0])    # thrust perpendicular
v_retro = np.array([-3.0, 0.0])   # retrograde burn

for name, u in [("along", v_along), ("ortho", v_ortho), ("retro", v_retro)]:
    print(name, v_sat @ u)         # 22.5 · 0.0 · -22.5
Real scenario — the score behind every retrieval

When Mission Control RAG retrieves the top-50 mission-log chunks for a query, the vector DB is computing your query embedding's dot product against millions of stored chunk embeddings and sorting. And inside the LLM answering with those chunks, attention heads are computing query·key dot products between every token pair. Two layers of the same operation, one interview answer.

35

Eigenvalues

Concept

Most vectors get knocked off their direction when a matrix transforms them. But for special directions, the matrix acts as pure scaling: Av = λv — the output is the same vector, just stretched or shrunk. The eigenvalue λ is that scaling factor, and the set of eigenvalues summarizes what a transformation fundamentally does: which directions it amplifies (|λ| > 1), which it dampens (|λ| < 1), which it flips (λ < 0).

  • Read Av = λv as: "along direction v, the matrix A is just multiplication by the number λ."
  • Big eigenvalue spread (condition number) = a hard optimization landscape — connects to topic 43.
Along an eigen-direction, the whole matrix collapses to a single number: λ.
Example 
import numpy as np

A = np.array([[3.0, 1.0],
              [0.0, 2.0]])
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(A)

for lam, v in zip(vals, vecs.T):
    print(np.allclose(A @ v, lam * v))   # True, True — Av = λv holds
print(vals)                              # [3. 2.] — the pure scale factors
Real scenario — how many telemetry channels really matter

Your satellite streams 64 telemetry channels into Kafka, but they're heavily correlated. Compute the covariance matrix's eigenvalues and you'll typically see 3–4 large ones and a long tail of near-zeros: the spacecraft's state effectively lives in a 4-dimensional subspace. That single eigenvalue spectrum tells you how much you can compress before the anomaly detector loses signal.

36

Eigenvectors

Concept

The eigenvectors are the special directions from the previous rung — the vectors whose direction survives the transformation (only their length changes, by factor λ). Where eigenvalues tell you "how much", eigenvectors tell you "along which axes". The flagship application: PCA's principal components are exactly the eigenvectors of the data's covariance matrix — the directions along which your data varies most, ranked by their eigenvalues.

  • Eigenvector 1 (largest λ): the single direction that captures the most variance.
  • Eigenvectors of a symmetric matrix (like covariance) are orthogonal — they form a new axis system for your data.
PCA: the covariance matrix's eigenvectors are the natural axes of the data cloud.
Example 
import numpy as np

# correlated orbital measurements: 500 samples, 2 features
X = np.random.randn(500, 2) @ np.array([[3.0, 0.0], [1.0, 0.5]])
X -= X.mean(axis=0)                 # center the cloud

cov = np.cov(X.T)                    # 2×2 covariance matrix
vals, vecs = np.linalg.eig(cov)
pc1 = vecs[:, np.argmax(vals)]       # direction of most variance
print(pc1)                           # PCA's first principal component
Real scenario — visualizing your embedding space

To sanity-check Mission Control RAG's embeddings, you'll project 1536-D chunk vectors down to 2-D with PCA and plot them: propulsion reports should cluster away from crew-log chunks. Those two plot axes ARE the top-2 eigenvectors of the embedding covariance. If the clusters smear together, your chunking — not your retriever — is usually the problem.

37

Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

Concept

Any matrix — square or not — factors into rotation × scaling × rotation: A = UΣVᵀ. U and V are rotations (orthogonal matrices); Σ is diagonal, holding the singular values in decreasing order — how strongly A stretches along each of its natural axes. The killer property: keeping only the top-k singular values gives the best possible rank-k approximation of A. That is the exact intuition behind LoRA: a weight update can be well-approximated by a low-rank matrix, so you train two skinny matrices instead of the full grid.

  • Eigendecomposition needs a square matrix; SVD works on anything — it's the workhorse.
  • Singular values decay fast in real data → most matrices are "secretly low-rank".
SVD factors any matrix; truncating Σ after the top-k values compresses it optimally.
Example 
import numpy as np

T = np.random.randn(200, 64)      # 200 timesteps × 64 telemetry channels
U, S, Vt = np.linalg.svd(T, full_matrices=False)

k = 5                              # keep only the 5 strongest directions
T_k = U[:, :k] * S[:k] @ Vt[:k, :] # best rank-5 approximation of T

err = np.linalg.norm(T - T_k) / np.linalg.norm(T)
print(f"rank-{k} reconstruction error: {err:.1%}")
Real scenario — the interview bridge to LoRA

When you fine-tune a model for mission-log summarization with LoRA, you're betting that the needed weight change ΔW (say 4096×4096) is approximately rank-16 — so you train B (4096×16) and A (16×4096) instead: 0.8% of the parameters. "Why does that work?" is a favorite interview question, and "singular values of real-world updates decay fast, and SVD says top-k is the optimal truncation" is the answer.

— Calculus for Training —
38

Derivatives

Concept

The derivative is the instantaneous rate of change — the slope of a function at a point. Zoom in far enough on any smooth curve and it looks like a straight line; the derivative is that line's slope. This is the single most important idea in this volume, because all of training is "compute the slope of the loss, walk downhill". If the derivative of loss with respect to a weight is positive, decreasing the weight decreases the loss — so you decrease it.

  • Notation: f′(x) or df/dx — "how fast does f change if I nudge x?"
  • Numerical check: (f(x+h) − f(x)) / h for tiny h — how autograd is unit-tested.
  • f′(x) = 0 marks flat spots: minima, maxima, saddle points — where training wants to land.
The derivative at a point is the slope of the tangent line touching the curve there.
Example 
def f(x):
    return x ** 2          # e.g. atmospheric drag vs probe velocity

x = 3.0
for h in [1e-1, 1e-3, 1e-6]:
    slope = (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
    print(f"h={h:.0e}  slope ≈ {slope:.6f}")   # converges on 6.0 = 2x
Real scenario — gradient checking your custom loss

You write a custom weighted loss for the exoplanet classifier (transits are rare, so false negatives cost more). Before trusting autograd through it, you verify with exactly the snippet above: nudge one weight by h, watch the loss change, compare to what .backward() reported. A mismatch means your loss has a non-differentiable kink or a detached tensor — caught in minutes, not after a wasted training run.

39

Partial derivatives

Concept

When a function has several inputs, a partial derivative is the slope with respect to one variable while all others hold still: ∂f/∂x asks "if I nudge only x, how does f respond?" Loss functions in ML take millions or billions of parameters as input; training asks for the loss's partial derivative with respect to every single one — each weight gets its own private answer to "which way should I move?"

  • Symbol ∂ ("del") instead of d signals: other variables are frozen.
  • Computing one partial = ordinary 1-D differentiation with the other variables treated as constants.
On a loss surface (contour view), each partial derivative is the slope along one axis only.
Example 
def loss(w, b):                      # tiny model: radius = w·mass + b
    pred = w * 2.0 + b               # one planet, mass = 2.0
    return (pred - 1.4) ** 2         # true radius 1.4

h = 1e-6
dw = (loss(3 + h, 1) - loss(3, 1)) / h   # ∂loss/∂w — b held still
db = (loss(3, 1 + h) - loss(3, 1)) / h   # ∂loss/∂b — w held still
print(dw, db)                              # 22.4, 11.2 — each knob's own slope
Real scenario — what .backward() actually returns

Your light-curve CNN has ~400k parameters. One call to loss.backward() fills every parameter's .grad with exactly its partial derivative — 400k separate "hold everything else still" slopes, computed in one backward sweep. When you later inspect param.grad.norm() per layer to debug vanishing gradients, you're reading statistics over these partials.

40

Chain rule

Concept

The derivative of nested functions multiplies through the layers: d/dx f(g(x)) = f′(g(x)) · g′(x). Rates of change compose by multiplication — if u changes 2× as fast as x, and y changes 3× as fast as u, then y changes 6× as fast as x. A neural network is nothing but deeply nested functions: loss(softmax(W₃·relu(W₂·relu(W₁·x)))). This one rule, applied backward through the network layer by layer, IS backpropagation.

  • Each layer contributes one local derivative factor; the gradient at any depth is the product of everything above it.
  • Long chains of small factors → vanishing gradients; of large factors → exploding gradients. Both are chain-rule arithmetic.
Forward computes values left-to-right; backward multiplies local derivatives right-to-left.
Example 
import numpy as np

def f(x):
    return np.sin(x ** 2)            # nested: sin ∘ square

def f_prime(x):                       # chain rule, by hand
    return np.cos(x ** 2) * 2 * x     # outer′(inner) · inner′

x, h = 1.3, 1e-7
numeric = (f(x + h) - f(x)) / h
print(np.isclose(f_prime(x), numeric))   # True — the rule holds
Real scenario — why your deep CNN wouldn't train

First version of your light-curve CNN: 12 conv layers, sigmoid activations, loss frozen after epoch 2. Diagnosis via the chain rule: sigmoid's derivative maxes out at 0.25, and 0.25 multiplied through 12 layers is ~6e-8 — the early layers' gradients had vanished. Swapping to ReLU (derivative 1 for active units) and adding skip connections fixed it. That entire debugging story is chain-rule arithmetic.

41

Gradients

Concept

The gradient ∇f stacks all the partial derivatives into one vector — and that vector points in the direction of steepest increase of the function. So training steps in the opposite direction: w ← w − η·∇loss, where η is the learning rate. "Gradient descent" is literally just that sentence, repeated until the loss stops improving.

  • Gradient = vector of partials: ∇f = [∂f/∂x, ∂f/∂y, …] — direction AND steepness (its norm).
  • η too small: crawling. η too large: overshooting the valley and diverging. The classic first hyperparameter.
  • SGD = same walk, but each step estimates ∇ from a mini-batch instead of the full dataset.
Gradient descent: repeatedly step against the gradient until the bowl's flat bottom.
Example 
import numpy as np

pos = np.array([3.0, 4.0])       # start high on the loss bowl
lr = 0.1
for step in range(25):
    grad = 2 * pos               # ∇f for f(x,y) = x² + y²
    pos -= lr * grad             # walk downhill

print(pos)                       # ≈ [0.011 0.015] — near the minimum
Real scenario — the loss curve you stare at every day

Every TensorBoard loss curve for your exoplanet classifier is a trace of this walk. Loss exploding to NaN after a few steps? Learning rate too high — the step overshot the valley wall. Loss plateauing early? Possibly too low, or stuck on a flat region. When you reach for a scheduler (cosine decay, warmup), you're just modulating η along this exact descent path.

42

Jacobian

Concept

When a function maps vectors to vectors (n inputs → m outputs), one number can't describe its slope. The Jacobian is the m×n matrix of every output's partial derivative with respect to every input — row i answers "how does output i respond to each input?" It's the bookkeeping structure that makes backprop through whole layers coherent: each layer's local derivative is a Jacobian, and the chain rule becomes Jacobian matrix multiplication.

  • Shape: outputs × inputs. A layer mapping 64 → 32 features has a 32×64 Jacobian.
  • The Jacobian is also the best linear approximation of the function near a point — "locally, every smooth map is a matrix."
A 2-in, 2-out function has a 2×2 Jacobian: all four input→output sensitivities.
Example 
import numpy as np

def orbit_xy(r, theta):               # polar orbit coords → cartesian
    return np.array([r * np.cos(theta), r * np.sin(theta)])

r, th, h = 7000.0, 0.6, 1e-6          # LEO radius (km), true anomaly
J = np.column_stack([
    (orbit_xy(r + h, th) - orbit_xy(r, th)) / h,   # column 1: ∂(x,y)/∂r
    (orbit_xy(r, th + h) - orbit_xy(r, th)) / h,   # column 2: ∂(x,y)/∂θ
])
print(J)   # [[cosθ, -r·sinθ], [sinθ, r·cosθ]] — matches the analytic Jacobian
Real scenario — error bars through a coordinate change

Your Orbital Research Agent gets an asteroid's position from the NEO API in range-and-angle form, with measurement uncertainty. To report uncertainty in x/y map coordinates, you propagate it through the polar→cartesian transform using exactly this Jacobian (Σ_xy ≈ J Σ_rθ Jᵀ). Same object, different hat: inside PyTorch, every layer's backward pass is a Jacobian-times-vector product.

43

Hessian

Concept

The Hessian is the matrix of second derivatives — the curvature of the loss surface. Where the gradient says "which way is down", the Hessian says what shape the terrain is: a bowl (all eigenvalues positive — a minimum), a dome (all negative — a maximum), or a saddle point (mixed signs — down in one direction, up in another). It also explains why optimizers like Adam adapt step sizes per direction: when curvature is steep one way and shallow another, a single global learning rate is always wrong for one of them.

  • Shape: n×n for n parameters — why you never materialize it for a billion-parameter model.
  • Condition number = largest/smallest eigenvalue; big ratio = elongated valley = slow, zig-zagging SGD.
Contours of two bowls: round (easy for SGD) vs elongated (needs per-direction steps).
Example 
import numpy as np

# f(x, y) = x² + 3y² — an elongated loss valley
H = np.array([[2.0, 0.0],    # ∂²f/∂x² = 2
              [0.0, 6.0]])   # ∂²f/∂y² = 6 → 3× steeper in y

vals = np.linalg.eigvalsh(H)
print(vals)              # [2. 6.] — curvature per principal direction
print(vals[1] / vals[0]) # 3.0 condition ratio: one global lr can't fit both
Real scenario — why you default to Adam

Training the exoplanet classifier with plain SGD, the loss zig-zags: raw flux features and engineered ratio features have wildly different scales, so the loss valley is a long, thin trench — a high condition number Hessian. Adam's per-parameter step scaling (a cheap diagonal-curvature stand-in) walks straight down the trench. When someone asks "why Adam over SGD?", this picture is the answer.

— Probability —
44

Bayes theorem

Concept

P(A|B) = P(B|A) · P(A) / P(B): flip a conditional probability around using prior knowledge. It's the mental model for updating beliefs with evidence: start with a prior (how common is A at all?), observe evidence B, and get the posterior (how likely is A now?). Its most famous lesson is the base-rate fallacy: when A is rare, even a very accurate test produces mostly false positives — the tiny prior dominates.

  • Prior P(A): belief before evidence. Likelihood P(B|A): how well the evidence fits. Posterior P(A|B): belief after.
  • Naive Bayes classifiers, spam filters, and medical-test intuition are all this one equation.
Area view of 10,000 surveyed stars: the false-positive strip dwarfs the true-positive box.
Example 
# transit survey: 1% of stars host a detectable planet
p_planet = 0.01
p_signal_given_planet = 0.95    # detector sensitivity
p_signal_given_none   = 0.05    # false-alarm rate

p_signal = (p_signal_given_planet * p_planet
            + p_signal_given_none * (1 - p_planet))
posterior = p_signal_given_planet * p_planet / p_signal
print(f"P(planet | signal) = {posterior:.1%}")   # 16.1% — not 95%!
Real scenario — reading your classifier's precision honestly

Your exoplanet classifier reports 95% recall and a 5% false-positive rate — sounds shippable. But true transits are ~1% of candidate light curves, so Bayes says only ~16% of its alerts are real planets. That's why you'll tune the decision threshold on precision at the actual base rate, not on accuracy — and why the astronomer reviewing your alert queue will thank you.

45

Conditional probability

Concept

P(A|B) is the probability of A once you know B happened — you've shrunk the universe to only the B cases and re-measured A inside it: P(A|B) = P(A∩B) / P(B). This "shrink the universe, renormalize" move is the heart of probabilistic reasoning, and everything in probabilistic ML is conditional on something: a language model computes P(next token | all previous tokens); your classifier computes P(planet | features).

  • Conditioning ≠ causation: P(A|B) can be high because B causes A, A causes B, or something causes both.
  • If P(A|B) = P(A), knowing B told you nothing — that's the definition of independence.
Given B, only the blue region exists; P(A|B) is the overlap's share of it.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)

d1 = rng.integers(1, 7, 100_000)     # two dice, 100k rolls
d2 = rng.integers(1, 7, 100_000)

given = d1 == 3                       # shrink the universe: first die = 3
p = np.mean(d1[given] + d2[given] == 8)   # P(sum = 8 | d1 = 3)
print(f"{p:.4f}  vs analytic 1/6 = {1/6:.4f}")
Real scenario — space-weather odds, conditioned on evidence

Your Orbital Research Agent pulls DONKI flare events and answers "what are the chances of a geomagnetic storm this weekend?" The honest computation is conditional: P(storm | an M-class flare was just observed) is far higher than the unconditional base rate. Get the conditioning wrong — or let the agent quote the marginal when evidence exists — and the answer is confidently useless.

46

Random variables

Concept

A random variable is a variable whose value is the numeric outcome of a random process — it's the bridge between real-world randomness and math you can compute with. Flip 10 coins: "the number of heads" is a random variable X taking values 0–10. Random variables come in two flavors: discrete (countable outcomes — dice, event counts) and continuous (any value in a range — heights, temperatures, noise voltages).

  • The random variable is the mapping from outcomes to numbers — not the number itself.
  • Once something is a random variable, it earns a distribution, a mean, a variance — the next three topics.
A random variable maps messy outcomes to numbers — which then have a distribution.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(1)

# X = flares detected in a 10-day window, p = 0.5 per day
detections = rng.random((10_000, 10)) < 0.5
X = detections.sum(axis=1)          # 10,000 samples of the random variable

vals, counts = np.unique(X, return_counts=True)
print(dict(zip(vals, counts / 10_000)))   # X's empirical distribution
Real scenario — modeling asteroid traffic

Your Orbital Research Agent summarizes NEO close approaches per week. "Close approaches next week" is a random variable — you don't know its value, but you can characterize it (roughly Poisson) from historical API data. That framing is what lets the agent say "12 next week would be unusually high (top 5%)" instead of just printing a number with no context.

47

Probability distributions

Concept

A distribution is the full description of a random variable: which values are how likely. For discrete variables it's a pmf (probability mass function — a bar per value, bars sum to 1); for continuous ones a pdf (probability density function — a curve where area, not height, is probability); and the cdf (cumulative) answers "what fraction falls at or below x?" This vocabulary is everywhere in AI: a softmax output is a pmf over classes, sampling temperature reshapes that pmf, and a language model is a distribution over next tokens.

Three views of "which values, how often": mass per value, density, and cumulative share.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(2)

uniform  = rng.uniform(0, 1, 10_000)        # sensor jitter: flat pdf
normal   = rng.normal(0, 1, 10_000)         # thermal noise: bell pdf
binomial = rng.binomial(10, 0.3, 10_000)    # detections per 10 passes: pmf

for name, x in [("uniform", uniform), ("normal", normal), ("binomial", binomial)]:
    print(f"{name:9s} mean={x.mean():.2f}  var={x.var():.2f}")
Real scenario — temperature is distribution surgery

When Mission Control RAG's answer generator runs at temperature=0.2, you're sharpening the model's next-token pmf so probability mass piles onto the top few tokens — good for factual answers about mission logs. At temperature=1.2 the pmf flattens and tail tokens get sampled — good for brainstorming, terrible for citing telemetry values. Same model, different distribution.

48

Gaussian distribution

Concept

The bell curve, defined entirely by two numbers: mean μ (where it's centered) and standard deviation σ (how spread out). Its superpower is the Central Limit Theorem: sum (or average) many small independent effects — whatever their individual distributions — and the result tends toward a Gaussian. That's why it shows up everywhere: measurement noise, sensor error, aggregated returns. And it's why weight initialization and noise models default to it in deep learning.

  • Notation: X ~ N(μ, σ²). Standard normal: μ=0, σ=1.
  • CLT is the reason "average of many measurements" is such a trustworthy quantity.
Same mean, two spreads: μ places the bell, σ widens it — that's the entire parameterization.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(3)

# CLT: average 1,000 UNIFORM noise readings; repeat 10,000 times
means = rng.uniform(0, 1, (10_000, 1_000)).mean(axis=1)

print(f"μ ≈ {means.mean():.3f}")    # 0.500
print(f"σ ≈ {means.std():.4f}")     # ≈ 0.0091 = 1/√(12·1000)
# histogram `means` and a bell curve appears — from flat ingredients
Real scenario — the noise model in your telemetry pipeline

Each satellite temperature reading aggregates thousands of tiny physical effects, so its noise is near-Gaussian — which is exactly why your Kafka-stream anomaly detector models each channel as N(μ, σ²) and flags residuals beyond 3σ. Same distribution on the training side: your CNN's initial weights are drawn from a scaled Gaussian (He init) so activations neither vanish nor explode at layer 1.

49

Bernoulli distribution

Concept

A single yes/no trial with success probability p — the atom of discrete probability. One coin flip, one transit-or-not observation, one user click. Mean is p, variance is p(1−p) (maximal uncertainty at p=0.5, zero at the extremes). Its direct AI significance: a logistic-regression (or any sigmoid) output IS the p of a Bernoulli — the model says "this light curve is a planet with p=0.83", and binary cross-entropy loss is just the Bernoulli log-likelihood, negated.

  • Stack n independent Bernoulli(p) trials and count successes → the Binomial(n, p) distribution.
  • The label y ∈ {0, 1} in binary classification is modeled as Bernoulli(p(x)).
The whole distribution: two bars. Every binary classifier's output parameterizes it.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(4)

p = 0.3                              # P(transit dip in one observation)
trials = rng.random(10_000) < p      # 10,000 Bernoulli(0.3) draws

print(trials.mean())                 # ≈ 0.30 — mean = p
print(trials.var())                  # ≈ 0.21 — variance = p(1−p)
Real scenario — what your classifier's 0.83 actually means

Your exoplanet classifier's sigmoid says 0.83 for a candidate: it's claiming the label is Bernoulli(0.83). That claim is testable — collect all predictions near 0.8 and check that ~80% are actually planets. When they aren't, the model is miscalibrated, and you fix it with temperature scaling before anyone uses those probabilities to rank telescope follow-up time.

— Statistics —
50

Mean

Concept

The arithmetic average — sum divided by count — is the balance point of the data: put the values on a seesaw and the mean is where the fulcrum balances. It's the workhorse summary statistic, but its weakness is the whole reason the next rung exists: a single outlier drags it arbitrarily far, because every value pulls on it with force proportional to its distance.

  • The mean minimizes squared distance to all points — which is why MSE-trained models predict means.
  • Great for symmetric, well-behaved data; misleading for skewed data (salaries, latencies, planet masses).
The mean is a balance point: one extreme value shifts the fulcrum far from the crowd.
Example 
import numpy as np

# ten rocky-planet masses (Earth masses)
masses = np.array([0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 0.95, 1.05, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 0.85])
print(masses.mean())                   # 0.965 — a fair "typical planet"

with_giant = np.append(masses, 317.8)  # one Jupiter sneaks into the sample
print(with_giant.mean())               # 29.77 — "typical" is now nonsense
Real scenario — the latency dashboard that lies

Your FastAPI RAG endpoint's mean latency reads 1.4s — looks fine. But one query per hundred triggers a cold reranker load and takes 30s, and those few calls drag the mean up while most users see 0.9s. Mean-only dashboards hide exactly the pain your users feel (or hide that most users are fine). This is why the next topic exists — and why you'll report percentiles.

51

Median

Concept

The middle value when sorted — half the data below, half above. Because it only cares about position in the sorted order, not magnitude, it's robust to outliers where the mean is not: a billionaire joining the room barely moves the median salary but wrecks the mean. When someone says "average", ask which one — for skewed data the choice changes the story completely.

  • Median = 50th percentile = p50; the same idea generalizes to p95, p99 — the language of latency SLOs.
  • The median minimizes absolute distance to all points (the mean minimizes squared).
The median is defined by sorted position, so extreme values can't drag it.
Example 
import numpy as np

masses = np.array([0.8, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 0.95, 1.05, 0.9, 1.0, 1.1, 0.85])
with_giant = np.append(masses, 317.8)   # same billionaire trick, planet edition

print(np.median(masses))       # 0.975
print(np.median(with_giant))   # 1.0   — barely moved
print(with_giant.mean())       # 29.77 — the mean exploded (topic 50)
Real scenario — report p50/p95, not mean

After topic 50's dashboard lie, you switch the FastAPI metrics to median and p95: "p50 = 0.9s, p95 = 2.1s" tells the true story — typical users are fast, the reranker cold-start tail is the problem to fix. Same move in your RAGAS evals: one catastrophically bad answer shouldn't sink the median faithfulness score, but it will sink the mean — check both and you learn more.

52

Variance

Concept

Variance is the average squared distance from the mean — how spread out the data is. Squaring does two jobs: it kills the sign (deviations below and above both count) and it punishes big deviations disproportionately. The price: variance lives in squared units (km² for km data), which is why its square root — the standard deviation — is what you usually quote.

Key distinction

The n vs n−1 gotcha: dividing by n gives population variance; dividing by n−1 (ddof=1) gives sample variance, which corrects the bias from estimating the mean from the same sample. NumPy defaults to n (ddof=0), pandas defaults to n−1 — a classic source of "why don't our numbers match?" between two scripts.

Each point contributes the square of its deviation — literally an area. Variance averages them.
Example 
import numpy as np

periods = np.array([88.0, 224.7, 365.2, 687.0])   # orbital periods (days)

mu = periods.mean()
by_hand = ((periods - mu) ** 2).sum() / len(periods)

print(by_hand == np.var(periods, ddof=0))   # True — population variance (÷n)
print(np.var(periods, ddof=1))              # sample variance (÷(n−1)) — larger
Real scenario — feature scaling and the ddof ambush

Standardizing exoplanet features before training means dividing by each feature's spread — and if your training script computes it with NumPy (ddof=0) while your evaluation notebook uses pandas .std() (ddof=1), your "identical" pipelines silently disagree on every scaled value. Small dataset, real skew in metrics. You'll lose an afternoon to this exactly once; after that you always pass ddof explicitly.

53

Standard deviation

Concept

The square root of variance, which puts spread back in the original units — a σ of 0.3 K on a temperature channel means what it says. For Gaussian data, σ comes with the famous 68–95–99.7 rule: about 68% of values fall within 1σ of the mean, 95% within 2σ, 99.7% within 3σ. That rule is the entire basis of "3-sigma anomaly detection": a reading beyond 3σ happens by chance only ~0.3% of the time, so it's probably not chance.

  • Z-score: (x − μ) / σ — "how many standard deviations out is this value?"
  • Standardizing features = subtract μ, divide by σ — every feature ends up in comparable units.
The 68–95–99.7 rule: for Gaussian data, σ slices the bell into predictable bands.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(5)

noise = rng.normal(0, 1, 100_000)      # telemetry noise, σ = 1

within1 = np.mean(np.abs(noise) < 1)
within2 = np.mean(np.abs(noise) < 2)
within3 = np.mean(np.abs(noise) < 3)
print(f"{within1:.1%} {within2:.1%} {within3:.1%}")   # 68.3% 95.4% 99.7%
Real scenario — the 3σ alert on your Kafka stream

Your telemetry consumer keeps a rolling μ and σ per channel and alerts when a reading's z-score passes 3. On the battery-temperature channel that fires roughly 3 times per 1,000 readings by pure chance — so you require two consecutive 3σ readings before paging anyone. Choosing that threshold IS choosing your false-alarm budget from the 68–95–99.7 table.

54

Hypothesis testing

Concept

The formal way to ask "is this difference real, or just noise?" Frame a null hypothesis H₀ ("no difference"), collect data, and compute how surprising the data would be if H₀ were true. Only if it's very surprising (below a pre-chosen threshold α, usually 0.05) do you reject the null and call the effect significant. This is the machinery behind every A/B test you'll run on models, prompts, and rerankers.

  • You never "prove" H₀ — you either reject it or fail to reject it. Absence of evidence ≠ evidence of absence.
  • Pick the test for the data: t-test for means, chi-squared for counts, Mann-Whitney when distributions are skewed.
  • Decide α and sample size before looking at results — peeking inflates false positives.
Two overlapping samples: the test asks whether the gap between means exceeds what noise explains.
Example 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(6)

old = rng.normal(1.20, 0.3, 200)   # RAG v1 answer latency (s)
new = rng.normal(1.12, 0.3, 200)   # RAG v2 — truly 0.08s faster

t, p = stats.ttest_ind(old, new)
print(f"t={t:.2f}  p={p:.4f}")     # small p → reject "no difference"
# rerun with identical means: p jumps around, mostly large
Real scenario — is the new reranker actually better?

You swap Mission Control RAG's reranker and faithfulness moves 0.81 → 0.84 on 60 eval questions. Real improvement or eval noise? Run the paired test on per-question scores before celebrating: with only 60 questions and noisy LLM-judged metrics, a 0.03 gap often fails to clear H₀. The test is what stops you from shipping (and later reverting) a coin-flip.

55

P-value

Concept

The p-value is the probability of seeing data at least this extreme if the null hypothesis were true. Small p = "hard to explain as luck." That's all it is — and misreading it is the most common statistical error in tech.

Key distinction

A p-value is NOT the probability the null is true, and 1−p is not the probability your change works. It's a statement about the data under an assumption, not about the hypothesis. And at threshold 0.05, one in twenty truly-null experiments "succeeds" by luck — run enough tests and you will manufacture discoveries. That's the multiple-comparisons problem.

The p-value is the shaded tail: how often pure chance would produce a result at least this big.
Example 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats
rng = np.random.default_rng(7)

false_alarms = 0
for _ in range(100):                    # 100 A/A tests: no real effect
    a = rng.normal(0, 1, 100)
    b = rng.normal(0, 1, 100)             # identical distributions
    if stats.ttest_ind(a, b).pvalue < 0.05:
        false_alarms += 1
print(false_alarms)                       # ≈ 5 — luck alone "succeeds"
Real scenario — the metric dashboard that always finds a win

Your RAGAS eval reports 8 metrics across 4 question categories = 32 comparisons per experiment. At α = 0.05, ~1.6 of them will look "significant" for a change that does nothing. So when the new chunking strategy shows p = 0.04 on "answer relevancy for DONKI questions" only, that's likely the lottery, not the win. Pre-register one primary metric, or correct for multiple comparisons (Bonferroni: α/32).

56

Confidence interval

Concept

A confidence interval is a range constructed so that, across repeated experiments, it captures the true value 95% of the time (for a 95% CI). It's the honest upgrade from a point estimate: "faithfulness = 0.84" hides everything; "0.84, 95% CI [0.79, 0.89]" tells you the measurement is soft. Note the subtlety: the 95% is a property of the procedure — any single interval either contains the truth or doesn't.

  • More data → narrower interval (width shrinks like 1/√n).
  • The bootstrap builds a CI with zero formulas: resample your data with replacement, recompute the statistic thousands of times, take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles.
  • Two models whose CIs overlap heavily? You probably can't tell them apart yet.
Eight experiments, eight intervals: most straddle the truth, occasionally one misses.
Example 
import numpy as np
rng = np.random.default_rng(8)

radii = rng.normal(1.6, 0.4, 60)    # 60 measured exoplanet radii (R⊕)

# bootstrap: resample with replacement, recompute the mean 10,000 times
boots = rng.choice(radii, (10_000, 60), replace=True).mean(axis=1)
lo, hi = np.percentile(boots, [2.5, 97.5])
print(f"mean = {radii.mean():.3f}   95% CI = [{lo:.3f}, {hi:.3f}]")
Real scenario — the eval number you can defend

Leadership asks if the new Mission Control RAG pipeline is better. You bootstrap per-question RAGAS scores and report: "v2 faithfulness 0.84 [0.79, 0.89] vs v1 0.81 [0.76, 0.86] — overlapping intervals; we need ~200 more eval questions to resolve a 0.03 gap." That sentence — interval, overlap, sample-size plan — is what separates measurement from vibes, in evals and in interviews.
