— Preparing the Data —
57

Feature engineering

Concept

Feature engineering is turning raw columns into signals a model can actually use. Models don't understand your domain — they only see numbers. A raw timestamp is nearly useless; hour, weekday, and is_weekend derived from it can be gold. On tabular problems, one well-crafted feature routinely beats switching to a fancier model, because you're injecting domain knowledge the model could never invent from the raw columns alone.

  • Ratios & interactions: mass / radius³ is density — physically meaningful where the raw pair isn't.
  • Time components: hour, weekday, month, days-since-event from a single timestamp.
  • Aggregations: per-group means, counts, rolling windows ("this star's average planet radius").
  • Domain flags: booleans encoding expert rules, like in_habitable_zone.
Same information, new shape: derived columns encode physics the model could never reconstruct alone.
Example 
import pandas as pd
import numpy as np

df = pd.read_csv("exoplanets.csv")  # radius_earths, mass_earths, temp_k, orbital_period

# ratios and transforms that encode physics
df["density"]    = df["mass_earths"] / df["radius_earths"]**3
df["log_period"] = np.log1p(df["orbital_period"])
df["temp_ratio"] = df["temp_k"] / 288          # vs Earth's ~288 K

# a domain flag an astronomer would ask about first
df["earthlike_size"] = df["radius_earths"].between(0.8, 1.6).astype(int)
print(df[["density", "log_period", "temp_ratio", "earthlike_size"]].head())
Real scenario — exoplanet classifier, week one

Your first exoplanet classifier on raw Archive columns plateaus at 0.81 AUC. You add density, log_period, and a temp_ratio feature — no model change at all — and jump to 0.88. The gradient-boosted upgrade you were planning would have bought you 0.02. Feature engineering bought 0.07 in an afternoon.

58

Feature selection

Concept

After engineering comes pruning. Feature selection drops columns that add noise instead of signal — every useless feature is one more dimension to overfit on, one more thing to compute at inference, one more line in the explanation you owe stakeholders. Fewer features means faster, more robust, more explainable models.

Three families, in increasing cost:

  • Filter: score each feature alone (correlation with target, mutual information) — cheap, ignores interactions.
  • Wrapper: train on subsets and keep the best (RFE) — expensive, respects interactions.
  • Embedded: let the model choose while training — tree feature_importances_, L1 coefficients pushed to zero.
Funnel the feature set: rank, keep the top slice, retrain — often with no score loss at all.
Example 
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
import pandas as pd

rf = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)

ranks = pd.Series(rf.feature_importances_, index=X_train.columns)
top5 = ranks.sort_values(ascending=False).head(5).index
print(ranks.sort_values(ascending=False).round(3))

# retrain on just the top 5 and compare
rf_small = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=300, random_state=0)
rf_small.fit(X_train[top5], y_train)
print("all:", rf.score(X_test, y_test), "top5:", rf_small.score(X_test[top5], y_test))
Real scenario — the feature that was a leak

Ranking importances on your exoplanet classifier, catalog_version lands in the top 3 — suspicious, since it says nothing about planets. It turns out confirmed planets were re-catalogued later, so version number leaks the label. Feature selection isn't just about speed: reading the importance ranking is how you catch a leak before it ships.

59

Missing value handling

Concept

Real tables have holes, and most models refuse to train on NaN. The decision is per column, not global: drop the rows (only if few and random), drop the column (if mostly empty), or impute — fill with the median (robust to outliers), the mean, or a per-group value. Fancy option: model the missing value from other columns.

The key insight interviewers fish for: missingness is often a signal itself. A missing mass_earths usually means the planet was found by the transit method, which can't weigh planets — and that correlates with everything else about it. Adding a was_missing 0/1 indicator column lets the model use that fact instead of having it papered over by the median.

Impute the value, keep the fact: a was_missing indicator preserves the signal the median erased.
Example 
from sklearn.impute import SimpleImputer

# add_indicator=True appends the was_missing 0/1 columns automatically
imp = SimpleImputer(strategy="median", add_indicator=True)
X_train_f = imp.fit_transform(X_train)   # fit on train only
X_test_f  = imp.transform(X_test)        # apply the same medians to test

print(X_train.shape, "→", X_train_f.shape)  # extra cols = missingness flags
Real scenario — missing mass is a detection-method fingerprint

In the Exoplanet Archive, mass_earths is missing for most transit-discovered planets but present for radial-velocity ones. When you add the was_missing flag, your classifier's F1 climbs — the model learns that "unweighed planet" correlates with the small, distant planets transit surveys find. Silently imputing without the flag threw that signal away.

60

Data cleaning

Concept

Data cleaning is everything you do before the data is even wrong-in-interesting-ways: deduplication, type fixes (numbers stored as strings), outlier decisions (is that 40,000 K star a typo or a real O-type?), and normalizing inconsistent categories — 'Kepler', 'KEPLER', and 'kepler ' are three categories to a model and one telescope to you. It's unsexy, and it's where most real-world model failures are born.

The professional habit: cleaning is a script, not a session. Every fix is code that logs what it changed, so the same cleaning runs identically on next month's data pull and an auditor can see exactly what happened to the raw file.

Cleaning as a reproducible pipeline stage: every fix logged, rerunnable on next month's dump.
Example 
import pandas as pd

df = pd.read_csv("exoplanets_raw.csv")
n0 = len(df)

df = df.drop_duplicates(subset="planet_name")
print(f"dropped {n0 - len(df)} duplicate rows")

# type fix: '3,050' → 3050.0
df["temp_k"] = pd.to_numeric(df["temp_k"].astype(str).str.replace(",", ""), errors="coerce")

# category normalization: 3 spellings → 1
before = df["telescope"].nunique()
df["telescope"] = df["telescope"].str.strip().str.lower()
print(f"telescope categories: {before} → {df['telescope'].nunique()}")
Real scenario — the phantom telescope

Your exoplanet classifier suddenly treats 'KEPLER' planets differently from 'Kepler' ones after a catalog merge — because one-hot encoding (item 63) made them separate columns with separate learned weights. A three-line strip().lower() fix in the cleaning script recovers more accuracy than any hyperparameter you tuned that week.

61

Normalization

Concept

Normalization (min-max scaling) squeezes a feature into [0, 1] with (x − min) / (max − min). The smallest value becomes 0, the largest becomes 1, everything else lands proportionally in between. Simple, interpretable, and exactly what you want when features must share a bounded range — pixel intensities, neural-net inputs, anything fed to a distance metric.

Its Achilles heel: one extreme outlier compresses everyone else into a corner. If orbital periods run 1–400 days and one rogue planet clocks 100,000, then after scaling the rogue sits at 1.0 and every normal planet is crushed into [0, 0.004] — the feature is effectively destroyed. Know your min and max before you trust min-max.

Min-max scaling before and after one extreme value: the outlier owns the range.
Example 
import numpy as np
from sklearn.preprocessing import MinMaxScaler

period = np.array([[3.5], [12.0], [88.0], [225.0], [400.0]])

by_hand = (period - period.min()) / (period.max() - period.min())
sklearn = MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(period)
print(np.allclose(by_hand, sklearn))          # True — same formula

# now inject a rogue 100,000-day orbit and watch the squeeze
rogue = np.vstack([period, [[100_000]]])
print(MinMaxScaler().fit_transform(rogue).round(4).ravel())
# [0. 0.0001 0.0008 0.0022 0.004 1.] — the real planets are gone
Real scenario — the rogue orbit that flattened a feature

Your exoplanet table includes one directly-imaged planet with a 100,000-day orbit. After min-max scaling, orbital_period looks constant for 99.9% of rows and your KNN baseline ignores it entirely. The fix that works here: log_period first (item 57), or standardization (next item), which doesn't hand the whole range to one point.

62

Standardization

Concept

Standardization rescales a feature to zero mean and unit variance: z = (x − mean) / std. Unlike min-max it's unbounded, but far more robust to outliers, and it's what distance-based models (KNN, K-Means, SVM) and gradient-based models want — otherwise a feature measured in thousands (temp_k) drowns out one measured in single digits (radius_earths).

The rule that separates professionals from tutorials: fit the scaler on training data only, then apply those same train-derived mean and std to the test set. Fit it on all data and the test set's statistics have leaked into training — your evaluation is quietly optimistic. An sklearn Pipeline enforces this automatically inside cross-validation.

Fit on train, transform test with the same statistics — the anti-leakage contract.
Example 
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier
from sklearn.model_selection import cross_val_score

# scaler lives INSIDE the pipeline → refit on each CV training fold only
pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=5))
scores = cross_val_score(pipe, X, y, cv=5)
print(scores.mean().round(3))

# the leaky version: StandardScaler().fit_transform(X) BEFORE the split —
# test-fold means/stds contaminate training. Never do this.
Real scenario — temp_k drowns radius_earths

Unscaled, your exoplanet features span wild ranges: temp_k in the thousands, radius_earths mostly 0.5–15. KNN's Euclidean distance is then ~99% temperature — radius might as well not exist. Wrapping StandardScaler into the pipeline lifts KNN from coin-flip to competitive, because now each feature votes on distance with equal weight.

63

One-hot encoding

Concept

Models can't do math on strings, so categorical columns must become numbers. The naive fix — kepler=1, tess=2, jwst=3 — invents a fake ordering (is JWST "three times" Kepler?). One-hot encoding avoids that: each category becomes its own 0/1 column, and exactly one is hot per row. No false ordering, and linear models get a separate learnable weight per category.

The breakdown point is high cardinality: 1,000 distinct cities means 1,000 nearly-empty columns — a sparse, memory-hungry matrix where each column carries almost no examples. That's when you reach for target encoding (replace category with its historical target mean) or learned embeddings (Volume 04's territory).

One string column fans out into one 0/1 column per category.
Example 
import pandas as pd

df = pd.DataFrame({"telescope": ["kepler", "tess", "jwst", "kepler"],
                   "radius_earths": [1.1, 2.4, 0.9, 11.2]})

encoded = pd.get_dummies(df, columns=["telescope"], dtype=int)
print(encoded.columns.tolist())
# ['radius_earths', 'telescope_jwst', 'telescope_kepler', 'telescope_tess']

# with 10,000 unique values you'd mint 10,000 near-empty columns —
# that's the cue for target encoding or embeddings instead.
Real scenario — discovery facility, 300 categories deep

One-hotting telescope (a handful of values) works great in your exoplanet classifier. But discovery_facility has 300+ observatories, most with under 5 planets — one-hot turns it into 300 columns of noise. You switch that one column to target encoding (each facility → its confirmed-planet rate) and keep one-hot for the small columns. Per-column encoding choices, not one global rule.

— Supervised Models —
64

Linear regression

Concept

Linear regression fits the line (in one dimension) or hyperplane (in many) that minimizes squared error between predictions and targets: y = w·x + b. It's a weak learner but a great teacher: the coefficients are readable ("each extra Earth radius adds 40 K to predicted temperature"), it has a closed-form solution (the normal equation — no iterative training needed), and it's the baseline every fancier model must beat before it earns its complexity.

  • Normal equation: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹Xᵀy — solve it directly, no gradient descent.
  • Residuals: the vertical gaps between points and the line; squared and summed, they're the loss.
  • If a plain line ties your deep model, ship the line.
The fitted line minimizes the sum of squared vertical gaps (residuals) to the data.
Example 
import numpy as np
from sklearn.linear_model import LinearRegression

rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
X = rng.uniform(0.2, 5, (200, 1))            # stellar flux (Earth=1)
y = 180 + 95 * X[:, 0] + rng.normal(0, 12, 200)  # temp_k with noise

# normal equation: w = (XᵀX)⁻¹ Xᵀ y  (with a bias column of ones)
Xb = np.c_[np.ones(len(X)), X]
w = np.linalg.solve(Xb.T @ Xb, Xb.T @ y)
print("normal eq :", w.round(2))               # ≈ [180, 95]

lr = LinearRegression().fit(X, y)
print("sklearn   :", lr.intercept_.round(2), lr.coef_.round(2))  # same
Real scenario — the baseline that explains itself

Before your exoplanet temperature model gets fancy, you fit linear regression on stellar_flux and orbital_period. The coefficient on flux is ~95 K per Earth-flux — a number an astronomer can sanity-check against radiative physics on a whiteboard. When XGBoost later beats it by 8%, you can say precisely what the extra complexity bought, because the baseline was legible.

65

Logistic regression

Concept

Logistic regression is a linear model pushed through a sigmoid, σ(z) = 1/(1+e⁻ᶻ), so the raw score w·x + b becomes a probability between 0 and 1. Despite the name, it's a classifier — "regression" is a historical accident. Above a threshold (default 0.5) you predict positive; below, negative.

It remains the production workhorse for tabular classification baselines: fast to train, calibrated-ish probabilities out of the box, coefficients that show which features push toward which class, and hard to overfit with a little regularization. The probability output matters as much as the label — 0.93 and 0.51 are both "positive," but you'd only wake someone up for the first.

The sigmoid maps any linear score to (0,1); the threshold turns probability into a label.
Example 
from sklearn.linear_model import LogisticRegression

# X: [temp_ratio, radius_earths, density] · y: 1 = habitable-zone candidate
clf = LogisticRegression(max_iter=1000).fit(X_train, y_train)

proba = clf.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]   # P(candidate) per planet
print(proba[:4].round(3))                 # e.g. [0.93 0.08 0.51 0.77]
print(clf.predict(X_test)[:4])            # same rows thresholded at 0.5

# which features push toward 'candidate'?
print(dict(zip(X_train.columns, clf.coef_[0].round(2))))
Real scenario — triage by probability, not label

Your exoplanet classifier feeds a follow-up queue with limited telescope time. Labels alone would treat a 0.51 and a 0.97 candidate identically; sorting by predict_proba instead means the near-certain candidates get observed first and the coin-flips wait. Logistic regression gives you that ranking for free — which is why it's still the baseline everything else must beat.

66

Decision trees

Concept

A decision tree is recursive if/else: at each node, pick the feature and threshold whose split makes the two child groups purest (measured by Gini impurity or entropy gain), then recurse into each child. Prediction is just walking a path from root to leaf — which means the model is a human-readable ruleset.

The catch: grown to full depth, a tree will happily memorize the training set — one leaf per weird example, perfect train accuracy, poor generalization. Depth limits and minimum-leaf sizes tame it, but the real move is the next three items: trees are weak alone but powerful in ensembles, which is why the forest and boosting rungs come right after.

A depth-2 tree on exoplanet features: prediction = walk the ifs from root to a leaf.
Example 
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier, export_text

tree = DecisionTreeClassifier(max_depth=3, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
print(export_text(tree, feature_names=list(X_train.columns)))
# |--- temp_k <= 350.0
# |   |--- radius_earths <= 1.8
# |   |   |--- class: candidate ...

# unlimited depth memorizes: near-perfect train, worse test
deep = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
print(deep.score(X_train, y_train), deep.score(X_test, y_test))
Real scenario — the ruleset you can show an astronomer

A domain scientist won't trust "the model said so." You hand them the export_text of your depth-3 exoplanet tree — "temp under 350 K, radius under 1.8 Earths → candidate" — and they immediately recognize it as a crude habitable-zone + rocky-planet rule. The tree's accuracy is mediocre, but it buys the trust that lets the random forest replace it.

67

Random forest

Concept

A random forest fixes the single tree's memorization problem with deliberate diversity: train many trees, each on a bootstrap sample of the rows (drawn with replacement) and considering only a random subset of features at each split. Then average their votes. Each tree still overfits — but each overfits differently, and the errors largely cancel when you average. That's variance reduction by ensembling (this technique is called bagging).

  • The reliable default for tabular data: strong out of the box with almost no tuning.
  • Parallel: trees are independent, so training scales across cores.
  • Free extras: feature_importances_ and out-of-bag error estimates.
Bagging: bootstrapped rows + random feature subsets → diverse trees → averaged vote.
Example 
from sklearn.ensemble import RandomForestClassifier
from sklearn.tree import DecisionTreeClassifier

single = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)
forest = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=200, random_state=0).fit(X_train, y_train)

print("single tree :", single.score(X_test, y_test).round(3))
print("200-tree RF :", forest.score(X_test, y_test).round(3))
# same data, same split — the forest usually wins by a clear margin
Real scenario — the exoplanet classifier's default engine

Your exoplanet classifier ships v1 on a 200-tree random forest: zero tuning beyond n_estimators, 0.90 AUC on temp_k, radius_earths, density, and log_period, trains in seconds, and feature_importances_ doubles as the explanation slide for the science team. Boosting (next three items) will fight for the last few points — the forest earned the baseline.

68

XGBoost

Concept

Where the forest builds trees in parallel and averages, gradient boosting builds them sequentially: each new tree is trained to fix the errors (residuals) of the ensemble so far, and its prediction is added with a small learning rate. Dozens to thousands of small corrections compound into a very strong model. XGBoost is the implementation that ruled tabular competitions for a decade: strong regularization built into the objective, second-order gradients, sparsity-aware splits, fast histogram training.

The knob that matters most in practice: early stopping. Watch validation loss as rounds accumulate and stop when it stops improving — the model picks its own size instead of you guessing n_estimators.

Boosting is sequential: tree N is trained on the residual errors left by trees 1…N−1.
Example 
from xgboost import XGBClassifier

clf = XGBClassifier(
    n_estimators=2000,           # generous cap — early stopping decides
    learning_rate=0.05,
    max_depth=5,
    early_stopping_rounds=50,    # stop after 50 rounds with no val gain
    eval_metric="auc",
)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train, eval_set=[(X_val, y_val)], verbose=False)
print("stopped at round:", clf.best_iteration)
print("val AUC:", clf.best_score)
Real scenario — squeezing past the forest

The random forest plateaus at 0.90 AUC on your exoplanet features. XGBoost with a 0.05 learning rate and early stopping reaches 0.93 — best_iteration lands at 412, meaning the model chose its own depth-of-correction against the validation split. Those three points matter because they translate directly into fewer wasted follow-up observations per real candidate found.

69

LightGBM

Concept

LightGBM is gradient boosting rebuilt for speed on large data. Two ideas do the heavy lifting. First, histogram binning: continuous features are pre-bucketed into ~255 bins, so finding the best split means scanning bins, not sorting raw values. Second, leaf-wise growth: instead of growing every tree level by level (as XGBoost classically did), LightGBM always splits the leaf with the biggest loss reduction — deeper, more asymmetric trees that get more accuracy per split.

The trade: leaf-wise trees can overfit small datasets, so num_leaves and min_data_in_leaf are the knobs to respect. On big tabular data, it's usually the fastest strong option — often several times quicker than XGBoost at equal accuracy.

Level-wise grows evenly; leaf-wise chases the split with the biggest loss reduction.
Example 
import time
from lightgbm import LGBMClassifier
from xgboost import XGBClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import roc_auc_score

for name, model in [("lgbm", LGBMClassifier(n_estimators=500)),
                    ("xgb ", XGBClassifier(n_estimators=500))]:
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    model.fit(X_train, y_train)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1])
    print(f"{name}: {time.perf_counter()-t0:5.1f}s  AUC={auc:.4f}")
Real scenario — the full Kepler table in seconds

When you scale the exoplanet classifier from 5,000 confirmed planets to 200,000 Kepler Objects of Interest with 40 light-curve summary features each, XGBoost takes minutes per experiment; LightGBM's histogram bins cut that to seconds at the same AUC. Faster iterations means you test five feature ideas an hour instead of one — the speed IS the accuracy, indirectly.

70

CatBoost

Concept

CatBoost is the boosting library that eats categorical features natively — you pass raw strings and name the columns; no one-hot step. Internally it uses ordered target statistics: each row's category gets encoded using the target mean of only the rows that came before it in a random ordering. That "only the past" trick prevents the row's own label from leaking into its own encoding — the classic failure of naive target encoding, and the reason CatBoost overfits less on high-cardinality columns.

  • Great defaults: often competitive with tuned XGBoost/LightGBM untouched.
  • Also uses ordered boosting and symmetric trees for extra overfitting resistance.
  • The pick when your table is full of string columns like facilities, spectral types, instrument names.
Ordered target statistics: each row's category encoding is computed from earlier rows only.
Example 
from catboost import CatBoostClassifier

# raw string columns go straight in — no get_dummies, no target-encode step
cat_cols = ["telescope", "discovery_facility", "spectral_type"]

clf = CatBoostClassifier(iterations=800, learning_rate=0.05, verbose=200)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train,
        cat_features=cat_cols,
        eval_set=(X_val, y_val))
print(clf.get_best_score())
Real scenario — 300 observatories, zero encoding code

Remember the 300-facility column that broke one-hot (item 63)? CatBoost takes discovery_facility as a raw string via cat_features and its ordered statistics handle the rare facilities gracefully — no hand-rolled target encoding to leak, no 300-column blowup. Your exoplanet pipeline loses forty lines of encoding code and gains half a point of AUC.

71

SVM

Concept

A support vector machine asks a sharper question than "find a separating boundary": find the boundary with maximum margin — the greatest distance to the nearest training points of either class. Those nearest points are the support vectors; they alone define the boundary, and every other point could be deleted without changing it. Fat margins generalize better than boundaries that graze the data.

The second idea is the kernel trick: to get a non-linear boundary, implicitly map points to a higher-dimensional space where they are linearly separable — without ever computing that mapping. The RBF kernel does this with a similarity function, turning "line" into "any smooth curved boundary." Scale your features first (item 62); SVMs are distance-based to the core.

Max-margin boundary: only the ringed support vectors matter; the dashed lines are the margin edges.
Example 
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
from sklearn.svm import SVC
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
from sklearn.pipeline import make_pipeline

X, y = make_moons(n_samples=400, noise=0.25, random_state=0)

for kernel in ("linear", "rbf"):
    pipe = make_pipeline(StandardScaler(), SVC(kernel=kernel))
    print(kernel, pipe.fit(X, y).score(X, y).round(3))
# linear ≈ 0.88 (a line can't bend around moons) · rbf ≈ 0.97
Real scenario — the curved boundary between planet families

Plotting your exoplanets in (log_period, radius_earths) space, hot Jupiters and rocky planets form two curved lobes no straight line separates. A linear SVC scores 0.84; the RBF kernel wraps a smooth boundary around each lobe and hits 0.95. Same data, same margins-maximizing machinery — the kernel just changed what "line" means.

72

KNN

Concept

K-nearest neighbors has no training step at all: to classify a point, find the k closest training points (usually Euclidean distance) and take a majority vote. The "model" is literally the training data. That makes it trivially simple, but expensive at inference (every prediction scans the dataset) and cursed by dimensionality — in high dimensions, everything is roughly equidistant from everything, and "nearest" loses meaning.

Why it matters beyond the basics: KNN is the conceptual ancestor of vector search. Retrieving the top-k most similar embeddings from a vector database is exactly a nearest-neighbor query — the same idea, industrialized with approximate indexes (HNSW, IVF) so it scales to billions of vectors.

Classify the query by majority vote among its k nearest training points.
Example 
import numpy as np
from sklearn.neighbors import KNeighborsClassifier

def knn3(X_train, y_train, q):
    dists = np.linalg.norm(X_train - q, axis=1)   # Euclidean to every row
    top3 = np.argsort(dists)[:3]                   # indices of 3 nearest
    return np.bincount(y_train[top3]).argmax()     # majority vote

mine = [knn3(X_tr, y_tr, q) for q in X_te]
skl  = KNeighborsClassifier(n_neighbors=3).fit(X_tr, y_tr).predict(X_te)
print((mine == skl).all())   # True — same votes
Real scenario — from KNN to your vector database

When Mission Control RAG answers "any solar flare anomalies last week?", the vector DB fetches the k nearest mission-log embeddings to the query embedding — a literal k-nearest-neighbor search in 1,536 dimensions. Everything you know about KNN transfers: distance metric choice, why k matters, and why at scale you swap exact search for approximate indexes. This humble classifier is the theory behind every retrieval call you make.

— Unsupervised —
73

K-Means

Concept

No labels? K-Means finds structure anyway. Pick k centroids, then loop two steps until nothing moves: assign every point to its nearest centroid, then move each centroid to the mean of its assigned points. It converges fast and runs everywhere — but you must choose k yourself, and it assumes clusters are roughly round and similar in size (it partitions space into nearest-centroid cells, which can't wrap around crescents or chains).

  • Inertia: sum of squared point-to-centroid distances — K-Means' internal loss.
  • Elbow method: plot inertia for k = 1…10; pick k where the curve stops dropping steeply.
  • Standardize features first — it's pure distance math.
Left: centroids (+) settle at cluster means. Right: the elbow in the inertia curve suggests k.
Example 
from sklearn.cluster import KMeans
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(planets[["log_period", "radius_earths", "temp_k"]])

for k in range(1, 11):
    km = KMeans(n_clusters=k, n_init="auto", random_state=0).fit(Xs)
    print(k, round(km.inertia_, 1))   # look for the elbow

labels = KMeans(n_clusters=4, n_init="auto", random_state=0).fit_predict(Xs)
Real scenario — discovering planet families without labels

You K-Means the exoplanet table on log_period, radius_earths, temp_k with k=4 and the clusters that emerge are the families astronomers already name: hot Jupiters, warm Neptunes, super-Earths, and long-period giants. Nobody told the algorithm those categories exist — the structure was in the geometry. That plot becomes slide one of your portfolio demo.

74

DBSCAN

Concept

DBSCAN clusters by density, not distance-to-centroid: a point with at least min_samples neighbors within radius eps is a core point; cores within reach of each other chain into clusters of any shape — crescents, rings, filaments. Points in sparse regions join nothing and are labeled noise (label −1). Two superpowers K-Means lacks: no k to choose, and an explicit outlier concept built in.

The cost: you tune eps and min_samples instead, and clusters with very different densities are hard to capture with a single eps. Think of DBSCAN as the complement to K-Means — reach for it when shapes are weird or when the noise points are what you actually care about.

Density chains form arbitrary shapes; isolated points are declared noise, not forced into a cluster.
Example 
from sklearn.cluster import DBSCAN, KMeans
from sklearn.datasets import make_moons
import numpy as np

X, _ = make_moons(n_samples=400, noise=0.07, random_state=0)

db = DBSCAN(eps=0.2, min_samples=5).fit(X)
print("clusters:", len(set(db.labels_)) - (1 if -1 in db.labels_ else 0))
print("noise pts:", np.sum(db.labels_ == -1))
# DBSCAN: 2 clean moons · KMeans(2) slices straight across both
Real scenario — telemetry anomalies are the noise label

On satellite telemetry snapshots (temperature, bus voltage, wheel RPM), healthy operating modes form dense blobs — station-keeping, downlink, eclipse. You run DBSCAN and ignore the clusters entirely: the −1 noise points are the deliverable, because a reading too sparse to belong to any known mode is exactly what an anomaly looks like. DBSCAN turns "weird" into a queryable label.

75

Hierarchical clustering

Concept

Hierarchical (agglomerative) clustering doesn't pick a number of clusters — it builds every clustering at once. Start with each point as its own cluster; repeatedly merge the two closest clusters until one remains. The merge history forms a dendrogram: a tree whose branch heights record how dissimilar the merged groups were. Cut the tree at any height and you get a clustering; lower cuts give many small clusters, higher cuts give few large ones.

Often the dendrogram itself is the deliverable — it shows structure at every scale simultaneously, which no single flat clustering can. The main knob is linkage: how to measure distance between clusters (ward minimizes variance and is the usual default; single chains; complete compacts).

One dendrogram, every clustering: slide the cut line to choose granularity after the fact.
Example 
from scipy.cluster.hierarchy import linkage, dendrogram, fcluster
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Z = linkage(Xs, method="ward")      # the full merge tree
dendrogram(Z, truncate_mode="level", p=5)
plt.show()

# cut at two different heights — no refit needed
coarse = fcluster(Z, t=2, criterion="maxclust")   # 2 clusters
fine   = fcluster(Z, t=6, criterion="maxclust")   # 6 clusters, same tree
Real scenario — mission-log taxonomy at every zoom level

You hierarchically cluster embeddings of 2,000 NASA mission-log chunks for Mission Control RAG. Cut high: two branches — propulsion vs. avionics. Cut lower: propulsion splits into fuel systems, thruster burns, pressure anomalies. The dendrogram becomes the navigation taxonomy for your document browser, and you never had to guess "how many topics are there?" up front.

76

PCA

Concept

Principal Component Analysis finds the directions along which your data varies the most — the eigenvectors of the covariance matrix (rung 36 returns) — and projects the data onto the top few. PC1 is the single axis capturing maximum variance; PC2 is the best axis perpendicular to it; and so on. Keep 2 components of a 64-dimensional dataset and you have the best possible 2D "shadow" of it, with explained_variance_ratio_ telling you exactly how much information the shadow retains.

  • Compression: 64 features → 10 components that keep 95% of the variance.
  • First look: the standard way to eyeball high-dimensional data in 2D.
  • Linear only: it can only rotate and project — curved structure needs t-SNE/UMAP (next two items).
PCA rotates to the axes of greatest spread, then keeps only the top ones.
Example 
from sklearn.decomposition import PCA
from sklearn.preprocessing import StandardScaler
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

Xs = StandardScaler().fit_transform(X)      # PCA needs comparable scales
pca = PCA(n_components=2)
X2 = pca.fit_transform(Xs)

print(pca.explained_variance_ratio_)        # e.g. [0.46 0.21] → 67% kept
plt.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], c=y, s=8, cmap="cool")
plt.xlabel("PC1"); plt.ylabel("PC2"); plt.show()
Real scenario — 40 light-curve stats, one scatter plot

Each Kepler light curve in your exoplanet pipeline is summarized by 40 statistical features — impossible to eyeball. PCA to 2D, color by label, and the confirmed planets form a visible ridge while false positives smear diagonally: instant evidence the features carry signal before you train anything. The explained_variance_ratio_ of [0.38, 0.19] tells you the picture shows 57% of the story.

77

t-SNE

Concept

t-SNE is a non-linear projection built for one job: revealing cluster structure. It converts distances into neighbor probabilities in high dimensions, then arranges points in 2D so that local neighborhoods are preserved — points that were close stay close. Where PCA smears curved manifolds flat, t-SNE untangles them into crisp islands.

Now the warning label, which interviewers love: in a t-SNE plot, distances between clusters mean nothing and cluster sizes mean nothing. The algorithm expands dense regions and compresses sparse ones, and different perplexity values redraw the map. Read it as "these points group together" — never as "cluster A is twice as far from B as from C."

t-SNE separates what PCA smears — but only the grouping is trustworthy, not the geometry between groups.
Example 
from sklearn.datasets import load_digits
from sklearn.manifold import TSNE
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

digits = load_digits()                      # 64-dimensional images
X2 = TSNE(n_components=2, perplexity=30,
          random_state=0).fit_transform(digits.data)

plt.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], c=digits.target, s=6, cmap="tab10")
plt.title("10 digit islands — compare with your PCA plot"); plt.show()
Real scenario — the false-positive island

t-SNE on your 40 light-curve features splits what PCA showed as one smear into distinct islands — and one island is almost entirely false positives with a signature eclipsing-binary shape. That discovery becomes a new engineered feature (item 57 again). But when a teammate measures "distance between the islands" to claim two planet classes are 'similar', you get to deliver the warning label.

78

UMAP

Concept

UMAP plays the same game as t-SNE — non-linear projection preserving local neighborhoods — but built on manifold theory, it's typically much faster, scales to hundreds of thousands of points, and preserves global structure better: the relative placement of islands is somewhat more meaningful (though still not literal distances). It also supports .transform() on new points, which t-SNE classically can't.

For an AI engineer, UMAP's killer app is eyeballing embedding spaces: project your vector database's embeddings to 2D and you can literally see whether topics form clean islands, where duplicate chunks pile up, and which queries land in no-man's-land. Key knobs: n_neighbors (small = local detail, large = global shape) and min_dist (how tightly points pack).

Projecting an embedding space to 2D: topic islands become visible, and query placement becomes debuggable.
Example 
import umap
from sentence_transformers import SentenceTransformer
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

model = SentenceTransformer("all-MiniLM-L6-v2")
emb = model.encode(headlines)               # 200 space-news headlines → 384-dim

X2 = umap.UMAP(n_neighbors=15, min_dist=0.1,
               random_state=0).fit_transform(emb)
plt.scatter(X2[:, 0], X2[:, 1], s=10)
plt.title("do topics form islands?"); plt.show()
Real scenario — debugging retrieval by looking at it

Mission Control RAG keeps retrieving irrelevant chunks for propulsion queries. You UMAP the whole vector store: the plot shows propulsion and electrical-power chunks fused into one island — your chunking split documents mid-section, blending topics. One look at a 2D map diagnosed what a week of metric-staring didn't. Re-chunk, re-embed, and the islands (and retrieval quality) separate.

— Judging the Model —
79

Accuracy

Concept

Accuracy is the fraction of predictions that were correct: (TP + TN) / total. It's the first metric everyone learns and the one most likely to lie to you. On imbalanced data it's deceptive to the point of uselessness: if 99% of rows are negative, a model that always predicts negative scores 99% accuracy while catching exactly zero positives — the entire reason the next five rungs of this ladder exist.

  • Trust it only when classes are roughly balanced and all errors cost the same.
  • Always compare against the majority-class baseline: if "always predict the biggest class" scores 0.99, your 0.99 model has learned nothing.
The lazy majority-class model: stellar accuracy, zero value on the rare class you care about.
Example 
from sklearn.dummy import DummyClassifier
from sklearn.metrics import accuracy_score, recall_score

# y_test: 990 zeros, 10 ones (habitable-zone candidates)
lazy = DummyClassifier(strategy="most_frequent").fit(X_train, y_train)
pred = lazy.predict(X_test)

print("accuracy:", accuracy_score(y_test, pred))   # 0.99 — looks amazing
print("recall  :", recall_score(y_test, pred))     # 0.00 — caught nothing
Real scenario — the 99% model that found nothing

Habitable-zone candidates are ~1% of your exoplanet table. An early stakeholder demo proudly reports "99% accuracy" — until you show the dummy baseline also scores 99% while flagging zero candidates. From that meeting on, your exoplanet classifier reports precision, recall, and AUC, and accuracy is banned from the slide deck.

80

Precision

Concept

Precision answers: of everything the model flagged positive, how much really was? precision = TP / (TP + FP). It's the metric of false-alarm cost. Optimize precision when acting on a flag is expensive or damaging: a spam filter that junks real mail, a fraud system that blocks legitimate cards, an alert queue that pages a human.

Precision looks only at the flagged pile — it says nothing about the positives you never flagged (that's recall, next item). You can make precision arbitrarily high by flagging only your single most confident case, which is exactly why precision and recall are always read together.

Precision lives entirely inside the flagged set: what share of the alarms were real.
Example 
from sklearn.metrics import precision_score, confusion_matrix

# imaginary spam filter: write out the matrix, compute by hand first
#                 predicted spam   predicted ham
# actual spam          TP=40           FN=10
# actual ham           FP=5            TN=945
tp, fp = 40, 5
print("by hand :", tp / (tp + fp))                 # 0.889

print("sklearn :", precision_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)).round(3))
Real scenario — every false alarm burns telescope hours

Each planet your classifier flags gets follow-up spectroscopy — scarce, expensive telescope time. At precision 0.70, three of every ten follow-ups are wasted on false alarms, and the observatory partners notice. You raise the decision threshold from 0.5 to 0.8: fewer flags, precision climbs to 0.92, and the follow-up queue stops burning nights on noise. The price is recall — the next item.

81

Recall

Concept

Recall answers the mirror question: of everything actually positive, how much did the model catch? recall = TP / (TP + FN). It's the metric of miss cost. Optimize recall when a missed positive is the disaster: cancer screening, safety-content filters, structural-fault detection. A screening test would rather raise ten false alarms than let one real case walk out the door — the alarms get a second look; the miss never does.

Precision and recall trade off through the decision threshold: lower it and you flag more (recall up, precision down); raise it and you flag less (precision up, recall down). Which side you favor is a product decision about which error hurts more — not a modeling decision.

Recall lives entirely inside the actual-positive set: what share of the truth you caught.
Example 
from sklearn.metrics import recall_score

# same spam-filter matrix as item 80
tp, fn = 40, 10
print("by hand :", tp / (tp + fn))                 # 0.800

# lower the threshold → flag more → recall rises, precision falls
proba = model.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
for t in (0.8, 0.5, 0.2):
    print(t, recall_score(y_test, proba >= t).round(3))
Real scenario — the first-pass screen must not miss

Your exoplanet pipeline has two stages: a cheap first-pass screen over all 200,000 KOIs, then the expensive follow-up ranker (item 80's precision game). The screen is tuned for recall 0.99 at threshold 0.2 — a missed Earth-twin here is gone forever, while its false alarms just cost the second stage some compute. Same model family, opposite threshold, because the cost of a miss is different at each stage.

82

F1 score

Concept

When you need one number that respects both precision and recall, the F1 score is their harmonic mean: F1 = 2PR / (P + R). Harmonic — not arithmetic — and that choice has teeth: the harmonic mean is dragged toward the smaller value, so a model can't buy a good F1 by maxing one metric and abandoning the other. Precision 0.9 with recall 0.3 averages to 0.6 arithmetically, but F1 says 0.45 — it punishes the imbalance hard.

  • F1 = 1 only when precision and recall are both 1; either at 0 makes F1 exactly 0.
  • Use it to compare models on imbalanced data with one scalar; use the P/R pair when the two error costs differ a lot.
  • Variants: F0.5 weights precision more, F2 weights recall more.
The harmonic mean sinks toward the weaker metric — imbalance between P and R is punished, not averaged away.
Example 
from sklearn.metrics import f1_score

p, r = 0.9, 0.3
f1 = 2 * p * r / (p + r)
print("arithmetic mean:", (p + r) / 2)   # 0.60 — flattering
print("F1 (harmonic)  :", round(f1, 3))  # 0.45 — honest

# on real predictions
print(f1_score(y_test, model.predict(X_test)).round(3))
Real scenario — one column in the model-comparison table

Your exoplanet experiment tracker compares logistic regression, random forest, XGBoost, and CatBoost across thresholds. Precision and recall each need context; F1 gives the leaderboard one honest column. The forest posts P 0.88 / R 0.61 (F1 0.72); XGBoost posts P 0.81 / R 0.79 (F1 0.80) — arithmetic averaging would have called it nearly a tie, but F1 correctly rewards the balanced model.

83

ROC-AUC

Concept

Every metric so far depends on one chosen threshold. ROC-AUC judges the model across all thresholds at once: sweep the cutoff from 1 down to 0, and at each point plot true-positive rate (recall) against false-positive rate. That trace is the ROC curve; the area under it summarizes ranking quality. AUC has a beautiful interpretation: it's the probability that a randomly chosen positive gets a higher score than a randomly chosen negative.

  • 0.5 = coin-flip ranking (the diagonal); 1.0 = every positive ranked above every negative.
  • Threshold-free: perfect for comparing models before you commit to an operating point.
  • On extreme imbalance, precision-recall AUC is often more informative — FPR barely moves when negatives dominate.
Sweep the threshold, trace TPR vs FPR: the curve hugging the top-left corner wins.
Example 
from sklearn.metrics import roc_curve, roc_auc_score
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

for name, m in [("forest", rf), ("xgboost", xgb)]:
    proba = m.predict_proba(X_test)[:, 1]
    fpr, tpr, _ = roc_curve(y_test, proba)
    auc = roc_auc_score(y_test, proba)
    plt.plot(fpr, tpr, label=f"{name} AUC={auc:.3f}")

plt.plot([0, 1], [0, 1], "--", label="chance")
plt.legend(); plt.show()
Real scenario — choosing the ranker before choosing the threshold

Your exoplanet screen (recall stage) and follow-up ranker (precision stage) will run at very different thresholds — so you select the underlying model with AUC, which ignores thresholds entirely. XGBoost's 0.93 vs the forest's 0.90 means: pick any operating point later, XGBoost ranks candidates better at all of them. One chart, two curves, decision made — then items 80–81 set the actual cutoffs.

84

Confusion matrix

Concept

The confusion matrix is the 2×2 grid every metric above is computed from: rows are the truth, columns are the prediction, and the four cells are TP (hit), FP (false alarm), FN (miss), and TN (correct rejection). Accuracy is the diagonal over the total; precision is the left column's purity; recall is the top row's coverage. Reading one fluently — including instantly spotting which error type dominates — is table stakes in any ML conversation.

The habit to build: look at the matrix before any scalar metric. Two models with identical F1 can fail in opposite directions — one drowning in false alarms, the other quietly missing positives — and only the matrix shows which. For multi-class problems it generalizes to k×k, where off-diagonal hot spots reveal exactly which classes get confused with which.

Four cells, every metric: precision reads down the predicted-positive column, recall reads across the actual-positive row.
Example 
from sklearn.metrics import confusion_matrix, ConfusionMatrixDisplay
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

cm = confusion_matrix(y_test, model.predict(X_test))
tn, fp, fn, tp = cm.ravel()      # sklearn order: [[TN, FP], [FN, TP]]
print(f"hits {tp} · misses {fn} · false alarms {fp} · correct rejects {tn}")

ConfusionMatrixDisplay(cm, display_labels=["non-hab", "candidate"]).plot(cmap="Blues")
plt.show()
Real scenario — the eval report's first figure

Every exoplanet-classifier release ships an eval report, and the confusion matrix heatmap is figure one — before AUC, before F1. In the v3 release it caught what the scalars hid: F1 was flat vs v2, but FN jumped from 8 to 19 while FP fell — the "improved" model had quietly traded misses for precision, the wrong direction for a screening tool. One glance at four cells; the rollback took a minute. Master this grid, and items 79–83 are just arithmetic on top of it.
