— Frameworks —
85

PyTorch

Concept

PyTorch is built from three ideas that stack cleanly. A tensor is a NumPy array that can live on a GPU. Autograd watches every operation you perform on tensors that have requires_grad=True and silently records a computation graph — so when you call loss.backward(), it walks that graph in reverse and fills in .grad for every parameter automatically. nn.Module packages weights and a forward() method into composable layers. That's the whole framework; everything else is convenience.

The reason PyTorch won research and then production is that the training loop is your Python code — an ordinary for loop you can print from, debug, and modify — not a black box. Every LLM you'll touch later (Volume 05 onward) is a big nn.Module trained by exactly the loop below.

  • The sacred loop: forward → loss → backward() → step() → zero_grad(). Memorize the order.
  • Forgetting zero_grad() makes gradients accumulate across steps — the classic first bug.
  • .to("cuda") moves tensors/models to GPU; model and data must be on the same device.
The PyTorch training cycle: every model you will ever train runs this exact four-beat loop.
Example 
import torch

# learn y = 2x + 1 from scratch: two parameters, the sacred loop
x = torch.linspace(0, 10, 50).unsqueeze(1)
y = 2 * x + 1

w = torch.randn(1, requires_grad=True)
b = torch.zeros(1, requires_grad=True)
opt = torch.optim.SGD([w, b], lr=0.01)

for epoch in range(200):
    loss = ((w * x + b - y) ** 2).mean()  # forward + MSE
    loss.backward()                          # autograd fills w.grad, b.grad
    opt.step()                               # w -= lr * w.grad (roughly)
    opt.zero_grad()

print(w.item(), b.item())  # → ≈2.0, ≈1.0
Real scenario — the exoplanet classifier's spine

Your exoplanet classifier — the CNN that reads Kepler light curves later in this volume — is an nn.Module trained by this exact loop. When training mysteriously plateaus at epoch 3, you'll print model.conv1.weight.grad.norm() inside the loop and discover in thirty seconds whether gradients are flowing. That debuggability is why you chose PyTorch.

86

TensorFlow

Concept

TensorFlow is Google's framework, and its personality is the opposite of PyTorch's: it wants to compile your model into a graph. Modern TF runs eagerly by default (line-by-line, like PyTorch), but decorate a function with @tf.function and TF traces it once, freezes it into an optimized dataflow graph, and reruns that graph without touching Python again — great for speed, awkward for debugging (your print() fires only during tracing).

You'll likely write PyTorch, but you must read TensorFlow fluently: an enormous amount of production ML — especially older pipelines, mobile apps (TF Lite), and serving infrastructure (TF Serving, the SavedModel format) — is TF. Interviewers also love the "eager vs graph" question because it tests whether you understand what a framework actually does.

  • Eager mode: ops execute immediately — TF 2.x default, feels like NumPy.
  • @tf.function: traces Python into a graph; Python side effects happen once, tensor ops every call.
  • SavedModel: a directory format bundling graph + weights — the deployment contract for TF Serving.
Example 
import tensorflow as tf

w = tf.Variable(0.0); b = tf.Variable(0.0)
opt = tf.keras.optimizers.SGD(learning_rate=0.01)

@tf.function   # ← everything below is traced into a graph on first call
def train_step(x, y):
    with tf.GradientTape() as tape:      # TF's autograd is explicit
        loss = tf.reduce_mean((w * x + b - y) ** 2)
    grads = tape.gradient(loss, [w, b])
    opt.apply_gradients(zip(grads, [w, b]))
    return loss

x = tf.linspace(0.0, 10.0, 50); y = 2 * x + 1
for _ in range(200): train_step(x, y)
print(w.numpy(), b.numpy())   # → ≈2.0, ≈1.0
Real scenario — inheriting a legacy cloud-mask model

A satellite-imagery team hands you their cloud-detection model as a TensorFlow SavedModel directory served by TF Serving. You don't rewrite it in PyTorch — you load it with tf.saved_model.load(), inspect its signature, and wrap it behind the same FastAPI endpoint as your PyTorch models. Reading TF fluently means the handoff takes an afternoon, not a sprint.

87

Keras

Concept

Keras is the high-level API that turns "define, compile, fit" into three declarative calls. You describe the architecture as a stack of layers, model.compile() attaches an optimizer, loss, and metrics, and model.fit() runs the entire training loop — batching, shuffling, validation splits, progress bars — that you wrote by hand in #85. Since Keras 3 it's multi-backend: the same code can run on TensorFlow, JAX, or PyTorch underneath.

The tradeoff is honest: you gain speed for standard architectures and lose sight of the loop. Use Keras when the problem is conventional and the value is iteration speed; drop to raw PyTorch when you need a custom loss, a weird sampling scheme, or gradient surgery. Knowing what fit() hides — because you built it yourself in #85 — is what separates an engineer from an API user.

define

Sequential / functional API — layers as a list or a graph.

compile

Pick optimizer, loss, metrics. No training yet — just wiring.

fit

The whole loop from #85, plus batching, validation, callbacks.

Example 
import keras
from keras import layers

# 3-layer classifier: 200 flux features → transit / no-transit
model = keras.Sequential([
    layers.Dense(64, activation="relu", input_shape=(200,)),
    layers.Dense(32, activation="relu"),
    layers.Dense(1,  activation="sigmoid"),
])
model.compile(optimizer="adam", loss="binary_crossentropy",
              metrics=["accuracy"])
model.fit(X_train, y_train, epochs=10, batch_size=32,
          validation_split=0.2)          # the whole #85 loop, one line
Real scenario — baseline in an afternoon

Before investing a week in a custom PyTorch CNN for exoplanet light curves, you spend one afternoon fitting a Keras dense network on 200 engineered flux features. It hits 89% validation accuracy — now you know the signal is learnable, you have a baseline to beat, and the week of CNN work is justified by the 6 points it must add.

— How Networks Learn —
88

Perceptron

Concept

The perceptron is one artificial neuron: multiply each input by a learned weight, add them up with a bias, and pass the sum through a hard threshold — output 1 if the sum is positive, else 0. Geometrically it draws a single straight line (a hyperplane) through input space and classifies by which side you're on. Its learning rule is beautifully simple: when it misclassifies, nudge the weights toward the correct answer; Rosenblatt proved this converges whenever a separating line exists.

Its fame comes from its failure: XOR — output 1 when inputs differ — has no separating line, so a single perceptron can literally never learn it. Minsky and Papert's 1969 proof of this froze neural-net research for a decade, and the fix (stack layers, #89) is the reason "deep" learning exists. Every interview question about "why do we need hidden layers?" is really asking about this.

The perceptron: weighted sum, threshold, output. These weights compute AND — no weights exist for XOR.
Example 
import numpy as np

X = np.array([[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,1]])
y = np.array([0, 0, 0, 1])          # AND — linearly separable
w, b, lr = np.zeros(2), 0.0, 0.1

for epoch in range(10):
    for xi, yi in zip(X, y):
        pred = int(xi @ w + b > 0)
        w += lr * (yi - pred) * xi     # the perceptron learning rule
        b += lr * (yi - pred)

print([int(xi @ w + b > 0) for xi in X])  # [0,0,0,1] ✓
# swap y for XOR = [0,1,1,0] and this loop cycles forever — no line exists
Real scenario — the anomaly flag that outgrew its threshold

Your satellite-telemetry alert starts life as a perceptron in disguise: 0.6·temp_z + 0.6·voltage_z − 1 > 0 → alert. It works until you notice the failure mode where temperature and voltage are individually normal but anomalous together in opposite directions — an XOR-shaped pattern. No reweighting fixes it. That's your cue that the alert needs a hidden layer, which is exactly topic #89.

89

Neural networks basics

Concept

A neural network is layers of perceptron-like units where the hard threshold is replaced by a smooth non-linear activation (ReLU, tanh, sigmoid), stacked so each layer's output feeds the next. The non-linearity is not decoration — it is the entire point. Compose two linear maps and you get… another linear map: W₂(W₁x) = (W₂W₁)x. A hundred linear layers collapse into one matrix. Insert a non-linearity between them and the collapse is broken: the network can now bend, fold, and warp input space.

With enough hidden units, one hidden layer can approximate any continuous function — the universal approximation theorem. That's why the same recipe (linear → activation → linear → …) classifies light curves, translates languages, and powers every LLM: it's a general-purpose function-fitting machine, and the rest of this volume is about how to fit it efficiently.

  • Width = units per layer (capacity per step); depth = number of layers (composition of steps).
  • ReLU max(0, x) is the modern default: cheap, and its gradient doesn't vanish for positive inputs.
  • Remove the activations and any network — however deep — degrades to linear regression.
Linear → non-linearity → linear. Without the tanh between them, W₂W₁ collapses into a single matrix.
Example 
import torch, torch.nn as nn

X = torch.tensor([[0.,0.],[0.,1.],[1.,0.],[1.,1.]])
y = torch.tensor([[0.],[1.],[1.],[0.]])       # XOR — the perceptron-killer

model = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(2, 3), nn.Tanh(),   # delete Tanh → never learns
                      nn.Linear(3, 1), nn.Sigmoid())
opt = torch.optim.Adam(model.parameters(), lr=0.1)

for _ in range(500):
    loss = nn.functional.binary_cross_entropy(model(X), y)
    opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

print(model(X).detach().round().squeeze())  # → [0., 1., 1., 0.] ✓
Real scenario — feature interactions in transit vetting

In your exoplanet classifier, a deep transit is planet-like only if the orbital period is stable, and a short period is fine only if the depth is shallow — the label depends on the interaction, not the individual features. Logistic regression (one linear boundary) tops out at 71%; the same features through one hidden layer with ReLU jump to 88%, because the hidden units learn the folds where the interaction lives.

90

Forward propagation

Concept

Forward propagation is the network actually computing: data enters, and each layer performs one matrix multiply, one bias add, one activation — a = activation(W·x + b) — then hands the result to the next layer. That's it. Inference is one forward pass; training is a forward pass plus a backward pass (#91). Every intimidating architecture diagram you'll ever see — ResNet, Transformer, diffusion U-Net — is just a fancier routing of this same per-layer computation.

Hand-computing one full forward pass, once, with real numbers, is the highest-value exercise in this volume. It makes tensor shapes concrete (a (2,3) weight matrix turns a 2-vector into a 3-vector), and shape errors are the single most common deep-learning bug you'll debug.

A 2-2-1 forward pass with real numbers. Data flows left to right; shapes must chain: (2)→(2)→(1).
Example 
import numpy as np

# fixed weights → verify your paper computation to 4 decimals
W1 = np.array([[0.5, -0.3], [1.0, 0.8]]); b1 = np.array([0.0, 0.0])
W2 = np.array([[1.2, -0.7]]);              b2 = np.array([0.1])

x  = np.array([1.0, 0.0])
z1 = W1 @ x + b1          # [0.5, 1.0]   — linear
h  = np.tanh(z1)          # [0.4621, 0.7616] — bend
z2 = W2 @ h + b2          # [0.1214]
y  = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-z2))
print(h.round(4), y.round(4))   # [0.4621 0.7616] [0.6303]
Real scenario — the shape bug at 2 a.m.

Your light-curve model crashes with mat1 and mat2 shapes cannot be multiplied (32×201 and 200×64). Because you've traced a forward pass by hand, you read this instantly: the batch of 32 curves has 201 flux bins but the first Linear layer expects 200 — someone changed the binning upstream in the Kafka consumer. You fix the preprocessing, not the model.

91

Backpropagation

Prerequisite

This is the chain rule from calculus (topic #40) industrialized: if L depends on ŷ, which depends on h, which depends on W₁, then ∂L/∂W₁ = ∂L/∂ŷ · ∂ŷ/∂h · ∂h/∂W₁. Backprop is nothing more — and nothing less — than organizing that multiplication so no term is ever computed twice.

Concept

Backpropagation answers the only question training ever asks: "for each of the network's million weights, if I nudged it slightly, how much would the loss change?" That number is the weight's gradient, and the naive way to get it — nudge each weight, rerun the forward pass, compare — would cost one million forward passes per step. Backprop gets every gradient in a single backward sweep, for roughly the cost of one extra forward pass. That efficiency is the entire reason deep learning is computationally possible.

The mechanism: during the forward pass, each layer caches its inputs. Then, starting from the loss, an error signal ∂L/∂output flows backward. At each layer the signal does two jobs: (1) multiplied by the cached input, it yields that layer's weight gradients — which get stored for the optimizer; (2) multiplied by the layer's weights, it becomes the error signal for the layer below — and flows on. Every layer only needs local information: its cached input, its own weights, and the signal arriving from above. No layer knows anything about the whole network — yet the chain rule guarantees the global gradients come out exactly right.

This is the crux rung of all 308 topics. Vanishing/exploding gradients (#98), why BatchNorm helps (#96), why ResNet skip connections exist (#100), what Adam consumes (#94), what LoRA computes gradients through, why long sequences blow up transformer memory — every one of these is a statement about backprop's error signal. Own this and the rest of the ladder gets easier.

  • Forward caches, backward consumes: that's why training uses far more memory than inference.
  • Each layer multiplies the incoming signal by its local derivative — a chain of factors. Many factors < 1 → signal vanishes; many > 1 → it explodes.
  • loss.backward() in PyTorch runs precisely this sweep over the recorded autograd graph.
  • Cost: one backward sweep ≈ 2× a forward pass, regardless of parameter count.
Forward flows left→right and caches inputs; the error signal flows right→left, dropping weight gradients (yellow) at each layer as it passes.
Example 
import numpy as np; import torch

# tiny net: y_hat = sigmoid(w2 · tanh(w1 · x)) — backprop by hand
w1, w2, x, y = 0.5, -0.4, 1.5, 1.0

h     = np.tanh(w1 * x)                    # forward, cache everything
y_hat = 1 / (1 + np.exp(-w2 * h))
L     = (y_hat - y) ** 2

dL_dyhat = 2 * (y_hat - y)                 # backward: chain rule, right to left
dyhat_dz = y_hat * (1 - y_hat)             # sigmoid's local derivative
dL_dw2   = dL_dyhat * dyhat_dz * h         # drop gradient for w2
dL_dh    = dL_dyhat * dyhat_dz * w2        # signal keeps flowing down…
dL_dw1   = dL_dh * (1 - h ** 2) * x        # tanh' = 1 − h², drop w1's gradient

# verify against autograd — the numbers must match exactly
tw1 = torch.tensor(w1, requires_grad=True); tw2 = torch.tensor(w2, requires_grad=True)
tl = (torch.sigmoid(tw2 * torch.tanh(tw1 * x)) - y) ** 2
tl.backward()
print(dL_dw1, tw1.grad.item())   # same number, twice ✓
print(dL_dw2, tw2.grad.item())   # same number, twice ✓
Real scenario — the NaN hunt in the exoplanet loss

You write a custom focal loss for the exoplanet classifier's brutal class imbalance (1 transit per 500 curves) and training NaNs out at step 40. Because you know backprop, you know exactly where to look: a log(p) in the loss whose local derivative 1/p explodes as p→0, injecting an infinite error signal that the backward sweep faithfully multiplies through every layer. One p.clamp(min=1e-7) fixes it. Engineers who treat loss.backward() as magic re-architect the whole model instead.

92

Gradient descent

Concept

Backprop (#91) gives you every weight's gradient — the direction of steepest loss increase. Gradient descent is the obvious response: step every weight the opposite way, w ← w − lr·∂L/∂w, and repeat until the loss stops falling. The learning rate lr scales the step, and it is the most consequential hyperparameter in all of deep learning.

Picture the loss as a valley. Too large a learning rate and you leap across the valley, land higher than you started, leap again — the loss diverges to NaN. Too small and you inch downhill for hours, possibly stalling on a flat shelf. The classic tell: loss shooting up or oscillating → cut lr by 10×; loss creeping down a fraction of a percent per epoch → raise it. Modern training wraps lr in schedules (warmup, cosine decay), but the intuition here is what those schedules are managing.

One valley, three learning rates: smooth descent (green), ping-pong divergence (orange), and a crawl (yellow).
Example 
import torch

def train(lr, steps=60):
    w = torch.tensor([8.0], requires_grad=True)
    for _ in range(steps):
        loss = (w ** 2).sum()          # a simple bowl, minimum at w=0
        loss.backward()
        with torch.no_grad(): w -= lr * w.grad
        w.grad.zero_()
    return loss.item()

for lr in [10, 0.1, 0.0001]:
    print(f"lr={lr}: final loss {train(lr):.2e}")
# lr=10 → inf (diverged) · lr=0.1 → ~0 (converged) · lr=1e-4 → 62.9 (barely moved)
Real scenario — the telemetry autoencoder that NaN'd overnight

Your anomaly-detecting autoencoder on satellite telemetry trains fine for 2 epochs, then the loss hits nan at 3 a.m. The Kafka stream delivered a burst of spikes, gradients grew, and lr=1e-2 turned a big gradient into a catastrophic leap. The fix is the standard pairing: drop to 1e-3 and add torch.nn.utils.clip_grad_norm_(model.parameters(), 1.0) so no single batch can throw the weights across the valley.

93

SGD — stochastic gradient descent

Concept

True gradient descent computes the gradient over the entire dataset before taking one step — perfectly accurate, absurdly expensive at scale. SGD instead estimates the gradient from a small random minibatch (32, 64, 256 samples), takes a slightly-wrong step, and repeats. You take thousands of cheap noisy steps instead of a few expensive perfect ones, and the total progress per unit of compute is dramatically better.

The surprise is that the noise isn't just tolerable — it helps. Noisy steps jitter the trajectory out of sharp, narrow minima (which generalize poorly) and settle it into wide, flat basins (which generalize well). This is why minibatch SGD-family optimizers train literally every modern model, and why batch size is a real hyperparameter: bigger batches = smoother but more expensive steps and less of that useful regularizing noise.

  • Epoch = one full pass over the data; with batch 32 and 90k samples that's ~2,800 steps per epoch.
  • Shuffle every epoch — otherwise the "random" batches repeat and the noise gains a pattern.
  • In PyTorch, "SGD" = torch.optim.SGD fed by a DataLoader; the loader provides the stochasticity.
Two roads to the same minimum on a loss contour map: exact-and-slow vs noisy-and-cheap. Noisy wins at scale.
Example 
import torch
from torch.utils.data import TensorDataset, DataLoader

ds = TensorDataset(flux, labels)          # 90k light curves
loader = DataLoader(ds, batch_size=32, shuffle=True)  # ← the "stochastic"
opt = torch.optim.SGD(model.parameters(), lr=0.01, momentum=0.9)

for epoch in range(5):
    for xb, yb in loader:                 # ~2,800 noisy steps per epoch
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)     # gradient from 32 samples only
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
# full-batch equivalent: ONE step per epoch, each needing all 90k forward passes
Real scenario — 90k light curves vs 16 GB of GPU

The full Kepler light-curve set doesn't fit on your GPU as one batch even if you wanted it to — 90k × 2001 flux bins is the easy part, but the activations backprop must cache (#91) scale with batch size and blow past 16 GB instantly. Minibatches of 64 make memory constant, and your loss curve's visible jitter is the healthy signature of stochasticity, not a bug.

94

Adam optimizer

Concept

Plain SGD gives every one of a million weights the same learning rate. But real networks are lopsided: some weights see huge, steady gradients; others see rare, tiny ones. Adam keeps two exponential moving averages per parameter — m, the mean of recent gradients (momentum: where have gradients been pointing?), and v, the mean of recent squared gradients (scale: how big have they been?) — and steps each weight by lr · m̂ / (√v̂ + ε). Consistently large gradients get damped; small steady ones get amplified. Every parameter effectively tunes its own learning rate.

In practice you'll use AdamW, which fixes a subtle flaw: Adam entangles L2 weight decay with its adaptive scaling, so decay strength varies per parameter. AdamW decouples the decay — applying it directly to weights, outside the adaptive machinery — and it is the default optimizer for pretraining and fine-tuning essentially every transformer and LLM you will ever touch. Default starting point: lr=3e-4, or 1e-5–5e-5 when fine-tuning pretrained models.

Adam: each gradient feeds two running averages — direction (m) and magnitude (v) — that shape a per-parameter step.
Example 
# the only line that changes vs SGD — same loop, same everything else
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.parameters(), lr=3e-4, weight_decay=0.01)

for epoch in range(5):
    for xb, yb in loader:
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()

# typical outcome on the same net: SGD lr=0.01 needs ~40 epochs to reach
# the loss AdamW hits in ~8 — per-parameter adaptation does the tuning for you
Real scenario — fine-tuning on satellite imagery, day one

Fine-tuning a pretrained ResNet on your ship-detection satellite tiles, you don't run a learning-rate search on day one — you reach for AdamW(lr=1e-4) because its per-parameter scaling tolerates the wildly different gradient magnitudes between the frozen-ish early conv layers and your freshly initialized final head. SGD could match it after careful tuning; AdamW gets you a strong baseline by lunch.

95

RMSProp

Concept

RMSProp is Adam's direct ancestor and the cleanest way to understand what "adaptive learning rate" means. It keeps just one running average per parameter — the RMS (root-mean-square) of recent gradients — and divides the learning rate by it: w ← w − lr · g / (RMS(g) + ε). Parameters whose gradients have been large get small careful steps; parameters with faint gradients get boosted ones. Geoff Hinton introduced it in a Coursera lecture (it was never formally published), and it fixed AdaGrad's fatal flaw of accumulating squared gradients forever until learning ground to a halt.

Hold the family tree in your head and optimizer questions become easy: SGD is the baseline; add a velocity term and you get momentum; divide by the gradient RMS and you get RMSProp; do both (plus bias correction for the early steps) and you get Adam (#94). You'll still meet RMSProp in the wild — classic reinforcement-learning configs (DQN) and older Keras defaults — and knowing it as "Adam minus momentum" means those codebases read instantly.

The optimizer family tree: two independent upgrades to SGD, and Adam is simply their merge.
Example 
import torch

optimizers = {
    "sgd":     lambda p: torch.optim.SGD(p, lr=0.01),
    "rmsprop": lambda p: torch.optim.RMSprop(p, lr=0.01, alpha=0.99),
    "adam":    lambda p: torch.optim.Adam(p, lr=0.01),
}
for name, make in optimizers.items():
    model = build_model(); opt = make(model.parameters())
    losses = []
    for step, (xb, yb) in enumerate(loader):
        loss = loss_fn(model(xb), yb)
        opt.zero_grad(); loss.backward(); opt.step()
        losses.append(loss.item())
    print(name, f"final={losses[-1]:.4f}")  # plot all three: one chart, one story
Real scenario — reading the old DQN station-keeping repo

You inherit a 2019 reinforcement-learning repo that trains a satellite station-keeping policy, and its config says RMSprop(lr=2.5e-4, alpha=0.95). Instead of "why not Adam?", you recognize the deliberate choice: classic DQN avoided momentum because stale velocity is poison when the data distribution shifts under the policy every few thousand steps. You keep RMSProp for the replication run — and note the reasoning in the migration doc.

96

Batch normalization

Concept

As training updates every layer simultaneously, each layer's input distribution keeps shifting under it — layer 5 is trying to learn from activations whose scale and center changed since the last step. Batch normalization stabilizes this: for each feature, normalize the activations across the current minibatch to mean 0 and variance 1, then let the network undo it where useful via two learned parameters — a scale γ and shift β. The result: layers train against a steady input distribution, you can use much higher learning rates, and deep nets converge in a fraction of the epochs.

The trap is that BatchNorm is two different functions. At training time it normalizes using this batch's statistics while quietly maintaining running averages. At inference it must use those frozen running statistics — a single satellite image has no "batch" to normalize over. model.eval() is what flips the switch; forget it and predictions wobble with whatever batch they happen to share, one of the most common production bugs in deep learning.

BatchNorm per feature: standardize over the batch, then hand control back via learned γ and β.
Example 
import torch, torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(200, 64), nn.BatchNorm1d(64), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Linear(64, 2),
)
# --- train ... then the classic bug, reproduced on purpose: ---
x = torch.randn(4, 200)              # same 4 light curves each time

model.train()                          # WRONG mode for inference
print(model(x[:2])[0])               # curve 0, batched with curve 1
print(model(x)[0])                   # curve 0, batched with 3 others → DIFFERENT!

model.eval()                           # frozen running stats
print(model(x[:2])[0] == model(x)[0])  # identical now ✓
Real scenario — the flaky exoplanet endpoint

Your FastAPI /classify endpoint returns 0.91 for a light curve when called alone, 0.78 for the same curve when it arrives in a batch of requests. Nothing "random" is on — the culprit is a missing model.eval() after loading the checkpoint: BatchNorm is normalizing each request against whatever neighbors share its batch. One line fixes it, and it goes into your model-loading checklist forever.

97

Dropout

Concept

Dropout fights overfitting with sabotage: during training, randomly zero each neuron's output with probability p (commonly 0.1–0.5), a fresh random mask every batch. No neuron can rely on any specific other neuron existing, so the network is forced to spread knowledge across redundant pathways instead of building brittle co-adapted circuits that memorize the training set.

Two framings make it stick. Ensemble view: each mask defines a different sub-network, so training samples an exponential family of networks that share weights; at inference (where dropout turns off automatically via model.eval()) you get their implicit average. Bookkeeping: PyTorch scales surviving activations by 1/(1−p) during training so the expected magnitude matches inference — that's why eval needs no correction. Like BatchNorm (#96), it behaves differently in train vs eval mode; unlike BatchNorm, forgetting eval() here makes predictions outright noisy.

Dropout: a fresh random mask each batch. Crossed neurons output zero; no circuit can depend on one neuron.
Example 
import torch.nn as nn

model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Linear(200, 256), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Dropout(0.5),          # half the hidden units vanish, per batch
    nn.Linear(256, 64), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.Dropout(0.3),
    nn.Linear(64, 2),
)
# before dropout: train acc 99.4%, val acc 82.1%  → memorizing
# after  dropout: train acc 93.0%, val acc 90.3%  → generalizing
model.eval()   # inference: dropout becomes identity — never predict in train mode
Real scenario — 600 labeled transits, 512 hidden units

Your confirmed-exoplanet training set is small — a few hundred positives — and your dense head has enough capacity to memorize every one of them, which it promptly does (train 99%, validation 82%). Dropout(0.5) on the head closes the gap to 93/90. Bonus trick for later: leaving dropout on at inference ("MC dropout") and predicting 30 times gives you a spread — a cheap uncertainty estimate for flagging borderline transit candidates for human review.

98

Weight initialization

Concept

Before any learning happens, the initial random weights decide whether learning is possible. Each layer multiplies its input by weights, so signal variance gets multiplied by a factor at every layer. Init too small and that factor is <1: after 10 layers the activations — and worse, the backprop error signal (#91) — shrink toward zero and the early layers never receive a gradient. Too large and the factor is >1: activations saturate, gradients explode, loss goes NaN at step one. All-zeros is even worse: every neuron in a layer computes the identical output and identical gradient, so they can never differentiate — the symmetry problem.

The fix is to choose the initial variance so the multiply factor is ≈1 for your activation: Xavier/Glorot init (variance ∝ 1/fan) balances signal for tanh/sigmoid; He/Kaiming init (variance ∝ 2/fan_in) compensates for ReLU killing half its inputs. PyTorch layers ship with sensible defaults — this bites you when you build custom layers, port papers, or need to explain why someone's hand-rolled 10-layer net "just doesn't train."

Gradient norms across a 10-layer stack under three inits. Only variance-matched init keeps the signal alive end to end.
Example 
import torch, torch.nn as nn

net = nn.Sequential(*[nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(256, 256), nn.ReLU())
                      for _ in range(10)])

def he_init(m):
    if isinstance(m, nn.Linear):
        nn.init.kaiming_normal_(m.weight, nonlinearity="relu")
        nn.init.zeros_(m.bias)
net.apply(he_init)

out = net(torch.randn(32, 256)); out.mean().backward()
for i, layer in enumerate(net):        # healthy: same order of magnitude
    print(f"layer {i}: grad norm {layer[0].weight.grad.norm():.4f}")
# rerun with nn.init.normal_(m.weight, std=3.0) → watch layer-1 explode
Real scenario — the ported paper that wouldn't train

You port a 12-layer light-curve encoder from a paper's pseudocode into PyTorch, but swap its tanh activations for ReLU "because ReLU is better." Training flatlines. The paper's Xavier init was matched to tanh; under ReLU, half of each layer's output is zeroed and the signal decays layer by layer until layer 1's gradients are 1e-9. Switching to kaiming_normal_ — He init, designed for exactly this — and the same architecture trains on the first try.

— Vision Architectures —
99

CNN — convolutional neural network

Concept

A dense layer on a 224×224 image needs ~150k weights per neuron and has to re-learn "bright edge" separately for every pixel position. A convolutional layer fixes both absurdities: it learns a small filter (say 3×3 = 9 weights) and slides it across the whole image, computing a dot product at each position. The output — a feature map — lights up wherever the pattern occurs. One pattern, 9 weights, detected everywhere: this weight sharing plus translation tolerance is the entire trick, and it's why CNNs made deep learning famous in 2012.

Stack the idea: early layers learn edges and blobs, middle layers combine those into textures and parts, deep layers into objects. Pooling (or strided conv) downsamples between stages so deeper filters see a wider fraction of the image — a growing receptive field. And nothing says the grid must be 2D: a Conv1d slides a filter along a time series, which is exactly how your exoplanet model reads light curves — a transit dip is the same U-shape wherever it occurs in time.

  • Channels: each layer learns many filters; 32 filters → 32 stacked feature maps.
  • Stride and padding control output size; kernel 3, padding 1, stride 1 preserves length.
  • Params for a conv layer = k_h · k_w · C_in · C_out — independent of image size.
A 3×3 filter slides across the input; each stop produces one feature-map value. Shared weights find the pattern anywhere.
Example 
import torch.nn as nn

# 1-D CNN reading raw light curves: (batch, 1 channel, 2001 flux bins)
model = nn.Sequential(
    nn.Conv1d(1, 16, kernel_size=11, padding=5), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool1d(4),                 # 2001 → 500
    nn.Conv1d(16, 32, kernel_size=11, padding=5), nn.ReLU(),
    nn.MaxPool1d(4),                 # 500 → 125
    nn.Flatten(),
    nn.Linear(32 * 125, 2),          # transit / no-transit
)
# the 16 first-layer kernels, plotted, look like little dip- and edge-detectors:
# plt.plot(model[0].weight.detach()[i, 0]) for i in range(16)
Real scenario — why Conv1d beats your feature spreadsheet

Your Keras baseline (#87) used 200 hand-engineered flux features and hit 89%. The Conv1d model reads the raw 2001-bin curve and hits 95% — because a transit dip is a local U-shaped pattern that can occur at any phase, which is precisely the inductive bias convolution encodes: same filter, every position. You didn't tell it what a transit looks like; the first-layer kernels learned dip detectors on their own.

100

ResNet

Concept

Before 2015, stacking past ~20 conv layers made networks worse — not from overfitting, but because plain deep stacks are hard to optimize: backprop's error signal (#91) degrades through every layer it must traverse. ResNet's fix is one line: add each block's input to its output — out = F(x) + x. This skip connection means the block only has to learn the residual F(x), the correction to identity, rather than re-derive the whole mapping. Learning "change nothing" becomes trivially easy (push F toward 0), so extra depth can no longer hurt.

The gradient story is the deeper reason: at the addition, backprop's signal splits and one copy flows straight through the skip, unmodified — a gradient highway from the loss back to layer 1, bypassing every multiplication that could shrink it. This idea took depth from 20 layers to 152+, and the same trick reappears as the residual stream in every transformer. Practically, ResNet-18/50 pretrained on ImageNet are the default backbones you fine-tune for any custom image task.

The residual block: learn only the correction F(x); the skip connection gives gradients an unobstructed route back.
Example 
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import models

# fine-tune ImageNet-pretrained ResNet-18: satellite tile → ship / no-ship
model = models.resnet18(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")
for p in model.parameters():
    p.requires_grad = False              # freeze the pretrained backbone

model.fc = nn.Linear(model.fc.in_features, 2)   # replace ONLY the head
opt = torch.optim.AdamW(model.fc.parameters(), lr=1e-3)
# train the head a few epochs, then optionally unfreeze layer4 with lr=1e-5
# — with 2,000 labeled tiles this reaches ~94% where training from scratch gets ~78%
Real scenario — 2,000 labels, one afternoon

You have 2,000 labeled satellite tiles for ship detection — hopeless for training a deep CNN from scratch. But ResNet-18's pretrained backbone already knows edges, textures, and shapes from ImageNet; your 2,000 labels only need to teach the final layer what "ship wake in open water" means. Freeze, replace fc, train 5 epochs: 94%. This freeze-and-replace pattern is the same mental template you'll reuse for LLM fine-tuning later.

101

VGG

Concept

VGG (2014) is historically important for proving a design principle: don't hand-craft exotic filter sizes — just stack uniform 3×3 convolutions, doubling channels as you halve resolution. Two stacked 3×3 convs see a 5×5 region, three see 7×7, with fewer parameters and more non-linearity than one big filter. That "small filters, deep and uniform" recipe became the grammar every later CNN speaks — ResNet (#100) is VGG's philosophy plus skip connections.

Know also why nobody deploys it: VGG-16 is 138M parameters, and ~124M of them sit in three dense layers bolted onto the end (the very first one, flattening 512×7×7 features into 4096 units, is ~103M alone). Modern nets replace that stack with global average pooling and a tiny head — which is most of how ResNet-18 does better with 12× fewer parameters. VGG survives as a comparison baseline and, curiously, as the standard backbone for perceptual loss in image-generation work, where its simple feature hierarchy is an asset.

Where VGG's bulk lives: the flatten-into-4096 dense layers, not the convolutions everyone remembers it for.
Example 
from torchvision import models

vgg = models.vgg16(); res = models.resnet18()
count = lambda m: sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters())

print(f"vgg16    total: {count(vgg)/1e6:6.1f}M")        # 138.4M
print(f"  conv features: {count(vgg.features)/1e6:6.1f}M")  # 14.7M
print(f"  dense head:    {count(vgg.classifier)/1e6:6.1f}M") # 123.6M ← the bulk
print(f"resnet18 total: {count(res)/1e6:6.1f}M")        # 11.7M
Real scenario — the model that won't fit the edge box

A vendor proposes a VGG-16-based cloud classifier to run on the ground-station edge server. You run the parameter count above in the review meeting: 138M params ≈ 528 MB of float32 weights before activations, on a box with 2 GB RAM shared with the Kafka consumer. You counter with ResNet-18 (45 MB) or EfficientNet-B0 (#102, 20 MB) at equal-or-better accuracy — and the numbers end the debate in five minutes.

102

EfficientNet

Concept

Given a bigger compute budget, how do you grow a CNN? Deeper (more layers)? Wider (more channels)? Higher-resolution inputs? Teams used to pick one and guess. EfficientNet's insight is that the three axes are complementary — higher resolution needs more layers for receptive field and more channels to capture the finer detail — so you should scale all three together by fixed ratios: depth ×αφ, width ×βφ, resolution ×γφ, where one knob φ sets your budget. Grid-search α, β, γ once on the small model; turn φ to get B0 through B7.

Combined with a mobile-optimized building block (MBConv, inverted residuals with squeeze-and-excitation), this delivered state-of-the-art accuracy at ~10× fewer parameters and FLOPs than rivals in 2019. That accuracy-per-FLOP framing is why you reach for it on constrained deployments: edge boxes, batch pipelines with cost ceilings, anywhere the GPU bill is a design constraint. EfficientNet-B0: 5.3M params vs ResNet-18's 11.7M, typically a couple of points more accurate.

Compound scaling: depth, width, and input resolution grow together by principled ratios, driven by a single budget knob.
Example 
import torch.nn as nn
from torchvision import models

eff = models.efficientnet_b0(weights="IMAGENET1K_V1")
eff.classifier[1] = nn.Linear(eff.classifier[1].in_features, 2)

count = lambda m: sum(p.numel() for p in m.parameters()) / 1e6
print(f"efficientnet_b0: {count(eff):.1f}M params")   # 5.3M
# vs resnet18: 11.7M — same fine-tuning recipe as #100, and on the
# ship-tile task: B0 ≈ 95.1% with less than half of ResNet-18's params
Real scenario — nightly imagery under a GPU budget

Your pipeline classifies 40,000 satellite tiles nightly on a single spot-instance T4, and the finance dashboard tracks the GPU-hours. Swapping the ResNet-50 for a fine-tuned EfficientNet-B1 keeps accuracy within 0.4 points while cutting inference FLOPs ~3× — the batch finishes in 22 minutes instead of 65, and the job fits comfortably inside the cheapest instance tier. Accuracy-per-FLOP is a business metric here, not a leaderboard vanity stat.

103

Vision Transformer (ViT)

Concept

The Vision Transformer asks a heretical question: what if we skip convolution entirely and treat an image like a sentence? Chop the image into 16×16 patches (a 224×224 image → 196 patches), flatten each patch and project it through one linear layer into an embedding — now you have 196 tokens. Add learned position embeddings (so the model knows patch order — otherwise it's a bag of patches), prepend a learnable [CLS] token to collect the global summary, and feed the sequence to a bone-standard transformer encoder. Classification head reads the [CLS] output. Done.

The tradeoff is data hunger: ViT lacks convolution's built-in locality and translation bias, so it must learn those from scratch — on ImageNet-1k alone it loses to ResNet, but pretrained on hundreds of millions of images it wins, because self-attention can relate any patch to any other in one hop. The strategic reason this tops your vision ladder: ViT is the vision half of every multimodal LLM — when GPT-4V or Claude "sees" an image, a ViT-style encoder is turning it into tokens that sit in the same sequence as the words. Learn this and Volume 05's transformer will already feel familiar.

Image-as-sentence: patches become embedded tokens, a [CLS] token joins them, and a plain transformer does the rest.
Example 
from transformers import ViTModel, ViTImageProcessor
from PIL import Image

proc  = ViTImageProcessor.from_pretrained("google/vit-base-patch16-224")
model = ViTModel.from_pretrained("google/vit-base-patch16-224")

img    = Image.open("satellite_tile.png").convert("RGB")
inputs = proc(images=img, return_tensors="pt")   # resized to 224×224

patches = model.embeddings.patch_embeddings(inputs.pixel_values)
print(patches.shape)      # torch.Size([1, 196, 768]) ← image as 196 tokens!

out = model(**inputs)
print(out.last_hidden_state.shape)   # [1, 197, 768] — 196 patches + CLS
Real scenario — asking questions of hurricane imagery

Your Orbital Research Agent pulls EONET wildfire and storm imagery, and you want "does this GOES frame show an eye wall?" answered by a multimodal model. Understanding that the model literally sees 196 patch tokens explains its real failure modes: a 10-pixel feature dissolves inside one 16×16 patch (so you tile and zoom the input), and fine spatial precision degrades (so you don't ask it for pixel coordinates). The patch grid isn't trivia — it's the debugging manual.

— Detection & Beyond —
104

YOLO — you only look once

Concept

Early detectors ran a classifier over thousands of image crops — accurate, glacial. YOLO reframes detection as a single regression problem: one forward pass of one network predicts every bounding box and class probability simultaneously. Conceptually, the image is divided into an S×S grid; each cell is responsible for objects centered inside it and emits box coordinates, an objectness score, and class scores — all as one big output tensor. Non-max suppression (#107) then deletes the duplicates.

One pass means real-time: modern versions (YOLOv8/v11 from Ultralytics) run 30–150+ FPS on a GPU and remain usable on CPUs and edge devices. The classic tradeoff — single-shot speed vs two-stage accuracy (#105) — has narrowed to near-parity, which is why YOLO is the practical default for live video, robotics, and any "detect things now" job. The Ultralytics API also made training on custom data a config-file exercise, a big part of its dominance.

YOLO's bet: detection as one dense prediction over a grid — every box, every class, one network pass.
Example 
from ultralytics import YOLO

model = YOLO("yolov8n.pt")                # nano: 3.2M params, real-time on CPU

results = model("harbor_tile.png", conf=0.4)
for box in results[0].boxes:
    cls  = results[0].names[int(box.cls)]
    print(cls, box.conf.item(), box.xyxy.tolist())  # label, score, corners

# fine-tune on your own labels (YOLO-format txt files + data.yaml):
model.train(data="ships.yaml", epochs=50, imgsz=640)
Real scenario — counting ships in this morning's pass

Your satellite-imagery service gets a new harbor scene every morning and must post ship counts to the dashboard before the 9 a.m. standup. A YOLOv8s fine-tuned on 1,500 annotated tiles chews through the 40,000-tile scene in minutes on one GPU — a two-stage detector (#105) would triple the runtime for a +1 mAP you don't need to count ships. Speed is the requirement; YOLO is the answer.

105

Faster R-CNN

Concept

Faster R-CNN is the definitive two-stage detector. Stage one: a Region Proposal Network (RPN) slides over the backbone's feature map and, at each location, scores a set of template boxes (anchors of varied size and aspect ratio) for "is there some object here?" — emitting a few hundred candidate regions. Stage two: each candidate's features are cropped and resized from the feature map (RoI pooling), and a second head classifies the region and fine-tunes its coordinates. Propose first, then examine each proposal closely.

Versus YOLO's single glance (#104), the second look costs speed (~5–20 FPS) but historically bought accuracy — especially on small, crowded objects, since stage two studies each candidate at a normalized scale instead of asking one grid cell to describe everything at once. Interview framing: two-stage = propose-then-refine, accuracy-leaning; one-stage = dense one-shot prediction, speed-leaning. It's also the chassis for Mask R-CNN (#106), so this architecture keeps paying rent.

Two stages: the RPN proposes candidate regions; a second head classifies and refines each one individually.
Example 
import torch
from torchvision.models.detection import fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn
from torchvision.io import read_image

model = fasterrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights="DEFAULT").eval()
img = read_image("launchpad.jpg") / 255.0

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model([img])[0]                # dict: boxes, labels, scores

keep = out["scores"] > 0.8
for box, label, score in zip(out["boxes"][keep],
                             out["labels"][keep], out["scores"][keep]):
    print(label.item(), f"{score:.2f}", box.round().tolist())
Real scenario — small debris in crowded frames

Counting harbor ships wanted speed, but your other job — flagging small vehicles and equipment across cluttered launch-facility imagery for an audit — wants precision on objects 12 pixels wide, offline, overnight. Here your YOLO run keeps merging adjacent trucks; Faster R-CNN's second stage, examining each proposal at normalized scale, separates them cleanly. The batch takes 3× longer and nobody cares: it runs while you sleep. Matching stage-count to the job is the actual skill.

106

Mask R-CNN

Concept

Mask R-CNN is Faster R-CNN (#105) with one addition: alongside the classify-and-refine head, each proposed region also feeds a small convolutional mask head that outputs a 28×28 per-pixel mask — which pixels inside this box belong to the object. Box detection upgraded to instance segmentation (#108): not "a ship is in this rectangle" but "these exact pixels are ship #3."

The technical fix that made it work is RoIAlign: RoI pooling snapped region coordinates to the feature grid, and those rounding errors — harmless for classification — smear per-pixel masks. RoIAlign samples features with bilinear interpolation, no rounding, keeping masks pixel-accurate. The design lesson generalizes across all of ML: a shared backbone doing the expensive understanding, plus cheap parallel task heads (box, class, mask — pose keypoints in later variants) trained jointly.

Mask R-CNN = Faster R-CNN + a parallel mask head, made pixel-accurate by RoIAlign's interpolated sampling.
Example 
import torch
from torchvision.models.detection import maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn
from torchvision.io import read_image

model = maskrcnn_resnet50_fpn(weights="DEFAULT").eval()
img = read_image("street.jpg") / 255.0

with torch.no_grad():
    out = model([img])[0]

keep  = out["scores"] > 0.8
masks = out["masks"][keep] > 0.5       # (N, 1, H, W) booleans, full image size
print(masks.shape, masks[0].sum().item(), "pixels in instance 0")
# overlay: blend each mask onto img with alpha=0.4 in its own color
Real scenario — acres, not bounding boxes

EONET flags a wildfire and your agent pulls the satellite tiles. A bounding box around an irregular, wind-stretched burn scar might be 60% healthy forest — useless for the "hectares burned" figure the report needs. Instance masks trace the actual scar boundary, so mask.sum() × area-per-pixel gives a defensible burned-area estimate per distinct fire front. When the deliverable is an area or a shape, boxes were never going to cut it.

107

Object detection — IoU, NMS, mAP

Concept

Step back from architectures: object detection the task is "localize + classify," and three model-agnostic concepts govern it. IoU (intersection over union) measures how well two boxes agree: overlap area ÷ combined area, from 0 (disjoint) to 1 (identical). A prediction "counts" as correct when its IoU with a ground-truth box clears a threshold (0.5 classically). NMS (non-max suppression) cleans up the near-duplicate boxes every detector emits around each object: keep the highest-scoring box, delete neighbors whose IoU with it exceeds a threshold, repeat.

mAP (mean average precision) is the headline score: sweep the confidence threshold to trace a precision-recall curve per class, average the area under it (AP), then average over classes — "mAP@0.5" uses IoU 0.5 as the match rule; COCO's stricter "mAP@[.5:.95]" averages over ten IoU thresholds. These three outlive any particular model — YOLOv12 or whatever ships next year will still be tuned by NMS thresholds and judged by mAP.

IoU is the geometry of "did you find it": shared area over combined area. Every detection metric builds on it.
Example 
def iou(a, b):
    """boxes as (x1, y1, x2, y2)"""
    ix1, iy1 = max(a[0], b[0]), max(a[1], b[1])
    ix2, iy2 = min(a[2], b[2]), min(a[3], b[3])
    inter = max(0, ix2 - ix1) * max(0, iy2 - iy1)   # 0 if disjoint
    area  = lambda r: (r[2] - r[0]) * (r[3] - r[1])
    return inter / (area(a) + area(b) - inter)

print(iou((0,0,10,10), (0,0,10,10)))   # 1.0  identical
print(iou((0,0,10,10), (20,20,30,30))) # 0.0  disjoint
print(iou((0,0,10,10), (2,2,8,8)))    # 0.36 full containment ≠ match!
Real scenario — the "duplicate ships" bug that wasn't the model

Your dashboard reports 23 ships in a harbor scene that plainly holds 9. The model is fine — your tiles overlap by 20% so each ship near a seam is detected twice, and per-tile NMS can't see across tiles. The fix is pure #107: merge all boxes into scene coordinates, run one global NMS pass with your iou(), count what survives. No retraining, no new model — just understanding that detection hygiene lives outside the network.

108

Image segmentation

Concept

Segmentation classifies every pixel. The output isn't a list of boxes — it's a mask the same height and width as the image, holding a class id at each position. Two flavors, and interviewers love the distinction: semantic segmentation answers "what is this pixel?" — all ships share one 'ship' label, as one undifferentiated region; instance segmentation answers "what is this pixel and which object is it part of?" — ship #1 and ship #2 get separate masks even where they touch. (Panoptic = both at once: instances for countable things, semantic for background "stuff" like water and sky.)

Architecturally, semantic segmentation nets (U-Net, DeepLab) are encoder-decoders: convolutions downsample to understand, then upsample back to full resolution to draw, with skip connections shuttling fine detail from encoder to decoder. Instance segmentation typically rides on detection (Mask R-CNN, #106). Choose by the question: "how much of the tile is cloud?" is semantic; "how many ships, and trace each hull" is instance.

Semantic: one label map, identities merged. Instance: each object owns its pixels. Pick by the question you're answering.
Example 
import torch
from torchvision.models.segmentation import deeplabv3_resnet50

model = deeplabv3_resnet50(weights="DEFAULT").eval()

with torch.no_grad():
    logits = model(batch)["out"]        # (1, 21 classes, H, W)
mask = logits.argmax(dim=1)             # (1, H, W) — a class id per pixel

total = mask.numel()
for cls in mask.unique():
    pct = 100 * (mask == cls).sum().item() / total
    print(f"class {cls.item():2d}: {pct:5.1f}% of pixels")
Real scenario — cloud fraction gates the whole pipeline

Every downstream job — ship counts, burn-scar area — is garbage on a cloudy tile, so the very first stage of your imagery pipeline is a semantic segmentation model (a small U-Net trained on cloud masks) computing cloud_pct = (mask == CLOUD).mean(). Tiles over 40% cloud are skipped, and the number is logged with each result so analysts can trust — or discount — the day's counts. Nobody asked "which cloud is which": semantic was the right flavor.

109

OCR — optical character recognition

Concept

OCR turns pixels into text in three stages: detect where text lives (boxes around words/lines), recognize the characters inside each box, and — the stage everyone underestimates — reconstruct layout: reading order, columns, table structure. Recognition is largely solved for clean print; layout is where real documents fight back. A two-column NASA report read naively becomes interleaved gibberish; a table flattened row-by-row loses which value belongs to which parameter.

Tooling tiers: Tesseract (classic, free, strong on clean scans), PaddleOCR/EasyOCR (deep-learning, better on photos and skew, layout-aware), and document-AI models (LayoutLM-family, vision-LLMs) that read text and structure jointly. For your ladder, OCR is the front door of document AI: this exact skill returns in the RAG volumes as document parsing, because a retrieval system over PDFs is only as good as the text extraction that fed it.

The OCR pipeline: detect, recognize, then rebuild layout — reading order and tables are the hard 20%.
Example 
import pytesseract
from PIL import Image

img = Image.open("mission_report_p12.png")

# words + positions + confidences — not just a text blob
data = pytesseract.image_to_data(img, output_type="dict")

rows = {}
for word, top, conf in zip(data["text"], data["top"], data["conf"]):
    if word.strip() and int(conf) > 60:
        rows.setdefault(top // 14, []).append(word)   # bucket by line

for _, words in sorted(rows.items()):
    print(" ".join(words))       # reading-order lines, ready to chunk
Real scenario — the Apollo-era scans your RAG can't read

A third of the corpus behind Mission Control RAG is scanned 1970s technical memos — image PDFs with zero embedded text, invisible to your chunker. The ingest fix is this pipeline: OCR each page, use the confidence scores to route low-quality pages to a stronger model, and preserve line structure so tables of engine parameters survive as coherent chunks. Retrieval quality over those documents is decided here, months before any embedding model sees a byte.

110

OpenCV

Concept

OpenCV (cv2) is the workhorse toolbox for classical image processing — no learning involved, just fast, battle-tested operations: resize/crop/warp, color conversions, thresholding (pixels above/below a value), Canny edge detection, contours (outlines of connected regions), morphology (erode/dilate to clean noise), and video I/O. Images are plain NumPy arrays throughout, so it composes naturally with everything else in your stack.

Its modern role is the pre- and post-processing layer around every deep model: resizing and normalizing tiles before the CNN, deskewing pages before OCR (#109), drawing YOLO's boxes on frames, turning a segmentation mask into countable contours. And sometimes it replaces the model: if bright-blob detection on a dark sky solves the problem, threshold + contours beats training a network. Two gotchas worth tattooing somewhere: cv2 loads images as BGR, not RGB — the #1 cause of "why are my model's predictions garbage" — and its coordinate convention is (x, y) while NumPy indexing is [row=y, col=x].

A classic cv2 chain: each stage is one function call, and the output is always just a NumPy array.
Example 
import cv2

img  = cv2.imread("coastal_tile.png")             # NumPy array, BGR order!
rgb  = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2RGB)       # before ANY model sees it

gray  = cv2.cvtColor(img, cv2.COLOR_BGR2GRAY)
blur  = cv2.GaussianBlur(gray, (5, 5), 0)
edges = cv2.Canny(blur, 50, 150)                 # coastline pops out

contours, _ = cv2.findContours(edges, cv2.RETR_EXTERNAL,
                               cv2.CHAIN_APPROX_SIMPLE)
big = [c for c in contours if cv2.contourArea(c) > 500]
print(f"{len(big)} large regions")   # no model, no GPU, ~5 ms
Real scenario — the 5-millisecond gate before the GPU

Before any satellite tile reaches your EfficientNet, ResNet, or YOLO, it passes through a cv2 gauntlet: BGR→RGB conversion (the bug that once cost you a full day of "mysteriously bad" predictions), resize to 224×224, and a cheap Laplacian-variance blur check that discards unusable frames in 5 ms instead of wasting GPU time. The deep models get the glory; OpenCV quietly decides what they get to see.
