— Classical NLP —
111

Tokenization

Concept

Tokenization splits text into the units a model can number. Models never see letters or words — they see integer IDs looked up in a fixed vocabulary. Modern LLMs use subword schemes like BPE (byte-pair encoding) and SentencePiece: the tokenizer is trained by repeatedly merging the most frequent character pairs, so common words end up as single tokens while rare words split into recognizable pieces. Nothing is ever "out of vocabulary" — worst case, a weird string falls apart into bytes.

This one design choice explains a surprising amount of LLM behavior: why API cost and context limits are measured in tokens (roughly ¾ of an English word each), why non-English text and code cost more tokens per character, and why models are famously bad at counting letters — they literally can't see them.

  • Vocabulary size is fixed at training time — typically 32k–256k entries.
  • Every model has its own tokenizer: token counts for the same string differ between GPT-style BPE and BERT's WordPiece.
  • A leading space is usually part of the token: " tank" and "tank" are different IDs.
Subword tokenization: "flatlined" and "LOS" shatter into pieces; frequent words survive intact. (_ marks a leading space.)
Example 
import tiktoken
from transformers import AutoTokenizer

log = "Oxygen tank 2 anomaly at 055:54:53 — telemetry flatlined."

enc = tiktoken.get_encoding("cl100k_base")      # GPT-4-family BPE
ids = enc.encode(log)
print(len(ids), [enc.decode([i]) for i in ids][:5])

bert = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")  # WordPiece
print(len(bert.tokenize(log)), bert.tokenize("flatlined"))
# counts differ — two tokenizers, two vocabularies; rare word → pieces
Real scenario — budgeting the Mission Control RAG

Before embedding 40,000 NASA mission-log chunks, you tokenize a sample with tiktoken to size the job: average chunk ≈ 420 tokens, so chunking at "500 words" would silently blow past your embedding model's 512-token limit and truncate the tail of every log — the part where the anomaly resolution usually lives. Token counts, not word counts, drive your chunker, your cost estimate, and how many reranked chunks fit into the generator's context.

112

Stemming

Concept

Stemming crudely chops suffixes off words with hand-written rules so that different forms collapse to one shape: running → run, engines → engin, studies → studi. The classic Porter stemmer (1980) knows nothing about English beyond its rule list — no dictionary, no grammar — which makes it blazingly fast and frequently wrong. The output doesn't need to be a real word; it only needs to be consistent, so that a query and a document containing different forms of the same word land on the same string.

  • Good for: search indexes, keyword matching, quick corpus statistics — recall goes up.
  • Bad for: anything user-facing — telemetri in a UI looks like a bug.
  • Over-stemming merges unrelated words (universal/university → univers); under-stemming misses forms.
Porter stemming: fast string surgery. Query "telemetry" and doc "telemetric" both become "telemetri" — and that's the whole point.
Example 
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer

stem = PorterStemmer().stem
words = ["running", "engines", "studies", "telemetry",
         "was", "pressurized", "anomalies", "communication"]

for w in words:
    print(f"{w:15s} → {stem(w)}")
# running → run          engines → engin
# studies → studi        telemetry → telemetri
# was → wa               communication → commun   ← visibly butchered
Real scenario — keyword search over Apollo transcripts

Your Mission Control RAG has a sparse-retrieval leg (BM25) next to the vector leg. Stemming its index means a query for "pressurization failures" matches logs saying "pressurized", "pressurizing", and "failure" — recall jumps with zero model cost. The stems never reach the user; they only live inside the inverted index, so "telemetri" hurts nobody.

113

Lemmatization

Concept

Lemmatization reduces a word to its true dictionary form — its lemma — using vocabulary and part-of-speech information: better → good, was → be, anomalies → anomaly. Where a stemmer does string surgery, a lemmatizer does a grammar-aware lookup: it has to know that "better" is the comparative of "good" and that "was" is a form of "be" — no suffix rule could ever discover that. The price is speed and the need for a language model of the pipeline sort (a tagger), which is why lemmatization usually rides inside a tool like spaCy.

Key distinction

Stemming = fast, rule-based, output may not be a word — fine for indexes. Lemmatization = slower, dictionary + POS-informed, output is always a real word — required the moment a human will read the result, or when you're counting "how often does anomaly occur" and want anomalies to count too.

Same inputs, two philosophies: chopped strings vs. true base forms. "better → good" is impossible for any suffix rule.
Example 
import spacy
from nltk.stem import PorterStemmer

nlp  = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
stem = PorterStemmer().stem

doc = nlp("The crews were better prepared for the anomalies.")
for t in doc:
    if t.is_alpha:
        print(f"{t.text:10s} stem: {stem(t.text):10s} lemma: {t.lemma_}")
# crews     stem: crew      lemma: crew    — both fine
# were      stem: were      lemma: be      — only the lemma knows grammar
# anomalies stem: anomali   lemma: anomaly — diff the two columns
Real scenario — normalizing entities in mission summaries

Your report generator counts topic frequencies across a week of DONKI space-weather logs to build a "top recurring issues" panel. Lemmatizing first means "flares", "flare", and "flaring" all tally under flare, and the panel prints the real word — where a stemmed "flar" would look broken in the dashboard your team actually reads.

114

N-grams

Concept

An n-gram is a contiguous run of n tokens: unigrams (1), bigrams (2), trigrams (3). Sliding a window across text and counting what falls inside it is the pre-neural way to capture local context — "New York" behaves nothing like "new" plus "york", and the bigram sees that where single words can't.

N-grams also carry a piece of history you should recognize: n-gram language models predicted the next word from the previous n−1 words using counted frequencies. That is exactly GPT's objective — predict the next token — just with a lookup table instead of a neural network. The table approach died of sparsity (most 5-word sequences have never occurred even once in all recorded text), and that failure is precisely what neural language models fixed.

  • Still useful today for keyword features, collocation mining, and quick corpus analysis.
  • CountVectorizer(ngram_range=(1,2)) gives classical classifiers phrase awareness cheaply.
Bigram extraction: the sliding window turns free text into countable phrase units.
Example 
from collections import Counter
import re

log    = open("apollo13_transcript.txt").read().lower()
tokens = re.findall(r"[a-z0-9']+", log)

bigrams  = Counter(zip(tokens, tokens[1:]))
trigrams = Counter(zip(tokens, tokens[1:], tokens[2:]))

print(bigrams.most_common(5))
# [(('main', 'bus'), 41), (('o2', 'tank'), 38), ...]
print(trigrams.most_common(3))
# [(('main', 'bus', 'undervolt'), 17), ...]  ← phrases, not words
Real scenario — mining DONKI alerts for phrase vocabulary

Before designing chunking for Mission Control RAG, you run bigram counts over a year of DONKI space-weather alerts. "coronal mass", "mass ejection", "radio blackout", and "proton event" dominate — telling you these must never be split across chunk boundaries, and giving you a phrase list for the BM25 leg so "coronal mass ejection" is matched as a unit rather than three unrelated words.

115

TF-IDF

Concept

TF-IDF weights a term by how often it appears in this document (term frequency) times how rare it is across all documents (inverse document frequency, a log of the ratio). Words that appear everywhere — "the", "system", "reported" — get an IDF near zero and fade out; words distinctive to a document — "cryogenic", "hypergolic" — pop. Each document becomes a huge sparse vector (one dimension per vocabulary word, almost all zeros), and similarity between documents is the cosine between their vectors.

This is the sparse-retrieval baseline that neural embeddings must beat — and its tuned descendant BM25 is still the standard keyword leg in hybrid RAG search. Build the intuition here; it pays off directly in the RAG block.

Frequency alone would crown "the". Multiplying by rarity hands the vector to the words that identify the document.
Example 
from sklearn.feature_extraction.text import TfidfVectorizer
from sklearn.metrics.pairwise import cosine_similarity

docs = [
    "Cryogenic oxygen tank pressure anomaly during transearth coast.",
    "Oxygen tank two failed; crew moved to the lunar module.",
    "Routine stationkeeping burn completed, all systems nominal.",
]
vec = TfidfVectorizer(stop_words="english")
X   = vec.fit_transform(docs)          # sparse matrix: docs × vocab

print(cosine_similarity(X).round(2))
# docs 0 and 1 score highest — both about the tank; doc 2 is a stranger
Real scenario — the sparse leg of hybrid retrieval

A user asks Mission Control RAG about "hypergolic propellant leak procedures". Dense embeddings retrieve conceptually similar chunks, but "hypergolic" is exactly the kind of rare, high-IDF term where sparse retrieval shines — the TF-IDF/BM25 leg nails the three documents that actually contain the word, and your hybrid fusion merges both lists. When an eval shows dense-only retrieval missing jargon queries, this is the fix.

116

Word2Vec

Concept

Word2Vec (2013) learns a dense vector for every word by giving a tiny network a fake job: skip-gram predicts the context words around a center word (CBOW does the reverse). The predictions are thrown away — the point is the side effect. Because "flare" and "CME" keep appearing in the same kinds of sentences, the training pressure pushes their vectors together. Meaning emerges from co-occurrence: the distributional hypothesis made computable.

The famous result: vector arithmetic captures relations — king − man + woman ≈ queen. This started the embedding era. Its key limitation prepares you for BERT: Word2Vec is static — one vector per word, so "dock" the maneuver and "dock" the harbor structure share a single point in space.

The fake task (predict neighbors) exists only to force the real product: a geometry where related words are close.
Example 
from gensim.models import Word2Vec

sentences = [line.lower().split() for line in open("mission_logs.txt")]
model = Word2Vec(sentences, vector_size=100, window=5,
                 min_count=3, sg=1, epochs=20)   # sg=1 → skip-gram

for word in ["flare", "scrub", "apogee"]:
    print(word, "→", model.wv.most_similar(word, topn=3))
# flare → [('x-class', 0.81), ('cme', 0.77), ('blackout', 0.74)]
# sanity-check the space: do the neighbors make domain sense?
Real scenario — why your RAG retrieval works at all

Every embedding model in Mission Control RAG is a descendant of this idea. When a user's query "sun eruptions this week" retrieves DONKI chunks about "X-class flares" despite sharing zero words, that is distributional semantics doing the work. Training a small Word2Vec on your own mission-log corpus is also a fast diagnostic: if most_similar("scrub") returns launch-delay vocabulary, your corpus has enough signal for domain fine-tuning later.

117

FastText

Concept

FastText (Facebook, 2016) is Word2Vec rebuilt from character n-grams: each word's vector is the sum of vectors for its 3–6 character pieces, like <an, ano, nom, oma, mal, aly> for "anomaly" (the angle brackets mark word boundaries). Because meaning is assembled from pieces, a misspelling or a word never seen in training still gets a sensible vector — it shares most of its pieces with the correct form. Word2Vec, holding one vector per whole word, can only throw a KeyError.

  • Shines on morphology-rich languages (Tamil, Finnish, German compounds) where word forms explode.
  • Also ships a brutally fast text classifier — still a respectable baseline before reaching for a transformer.
Vectors built from pieces: unseen words are just new sums over mostly-seen n-grams.
Example 
from gensim.models import FastText, Word2Vec

sents = [l.lower().split() for l in open("mission_logs.txt")]
ft  = FastText(sents, vector_size=100, min_count=3)
w2v = Word2Vec(sents, vector_size=100, min_count=3)

print(ft.wv["transformerish"][:4])   # made-up word — still a vector
try:
    w2v.wv["transformerish"]
except KeyError:
    print("Word2Vec: KeyError — never saw this exact string")
Real scenario — typo-proof search over crew annotations

Astronaut and controller notes in your telemetry-annotation store are full of typos and ad-hoc jargon ("telemetrry", "PGNCS-y behavior", callsign shorthand). A FastText index over those notes still lands "telemetrry dropouts" next to real telemetry-dropout entries because the character pieces overlap — the same query kills a Word2Vec-based index dead with a KeyError on the misspelled token.

118

GloVe

Concept

GloVe (Stanford, 2014) reaches the same destination as Word2Vec by a different road: instead of sliding a window and predicting locally, it first counts a global co-occurrence matrix — how often every word appears near every other word across the whole corpus — then fits vectors so that dot products reproduce the log of those counts. Local prediction vs. global counting; both encode the same distributional signal.

In practice, what mattered was distribution of a different kind: pretrained GloVe files (trained on Wikipedia, Common Crawl) were the standard download for years — the first taste most engineers got of "someone else's compute, my task". Like Word2Vec, GloVe vectors are static: one vector per word, context-blind.

GloVe: vectors fit directly to the global co-occurrence table, rather than learned from local window predictions.
Example 
import gensim.downloader as api

glove = api.load("glove-wiki-gigaword-100")     # ~128 MB, cached locally

print(glove.most_similar(positive=["king", "woman"],
                         negative=["man"], topn=1))
# [('queen', 0.77)] — the classic analogy
print(glove.similarity("astronaut", "cosmonaut"))  # high — same job
print(glove.most_similar(positive=["mars", "moon"],
                         negative=["earth"], topn=3))  # your own analogy
Real scenario — the zero-cost embedding baseline

Before paying for API embeddings in the exoplanet-literature search tool, you baseline with pretrained GloVe: average the vectors of each abstract's words and retrieve by cosine. It's crude — word order and context vanish — but it's free, instant, and gives you a floor. When your paid sentence-embedding model only beats mean-GloVe by two points of recall@10 on your eval set, that's a finding worth escalating before the invoice grows.

— The Attention Revolution —
119

Attention

Concept

Pre-2014 sequence models had a bottleneck: the encoder had to compress an entire input sentence into one fixed-size vector, and the decoder had to reconstruct everything from it. Long inputs degraded badly — imagine summarizing a full mission log from a single 512-number snapshot. Attention (Bahdanau et al., 2014) removed the bottleneck: at every output step, let the decoder look back at all input positions and take a weighted average, with weights the model learns to compute on the fly.

The mechanism is three lines of math: score the current query against every stored input vector (a dot product), softmax the scores into weights that sum to 1, and return the weighted sum as the context. It's a differentiable, soft lookup — "which parts of the input matter for what I'm producing right now?" — and because it's differentiable, the model learns where to look by backpropagation. This is the idea that unlocked everything after 2017.

Thicker line = larger learned weight. The output step reads a weighted blend of ALL inputs — no bottleneck vector.
Example 
import numpy as np

def softmax(x): return np.exp(x - x.max()) / np.exp(x - x.max()).sum()

# memory: 3 encoder states, 4-dim each
mem = np.array([[1., 0, 0, 1], [0, 1., 1, 0], [1., 1, 0, 0]])
q   = np.array([1., 0, 0, 0.9])     # what the decoder needs right now

scores  = mem @ q                    # relevance of each state to q
weights = softmax(scores)            # [0.82 0.05 0.13] — sums to 1
context = weights @ mem              # weighted blend, not a bottleneck
print(weights.round(2), context.round(2))  # mostly state 0 — as it should be
Real scenario — why long mission logs stopped being a problem

When Mission Control RAG's generator writes "the anomaly began at GET 055:54" it is attending — at that exact decoding step — to the two retrieved chunks containing the timestamp, nearly ignoring the other six in context. Attention is why stuffing eight reranked chunks into the prompt works at all: the model doesn't average them into mush, it looks up the right one per output token.

120

Self-attention

Concept

Self-attention turns attention inward: the sequence attends to itself. Every token computes attention weights over every other token (itself included) and rebuilds its own representation as a weighted blend of the whole sequence — in one parallel step. The word "it" in "the tank vented because it failed" pulls most of its new vector from "tank", resolving the reference; every other token does the same trick simultaneously for whatever relation it needs.

This replaced recurrence entirely. An RNN passes information along the sequence one step at a time — position 1 reaches position 400 through 399 handoffs, degrading along the way, and nothing parallelizes. Self-attention gives every pair of tokens a direct connection at distance one, and the whole thing is a couple of matrix multiplications — exactly what GPUs devour. The price: cost grows as O(n²) in sequence length, which is why context length is the eternal battleground.

Key distinction

Attention (119) in the original sense connects two sequences: decoder queries look at encoder states. Self-attention is the same math applied within one sequence — queries, keys, and values all come from the same tokens. You'll formalize it with Q/K/V matrices at #128; here, build the intuition that it's "every token gathering context from every token, at once."

Token "it" attends over its own sentence; the heavy edge to "tank" is coreference, learned, not programmed.
Example 
import numpy as np

def softmax(x):
    e = np.exp(x - x.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    return e / e.sum(-1, keepdims=True)

X = np.random.randn(6, 64)         # 6 tokens, 64-dim embeddings

scores = X @ X.T / np.sqrt(64)     # every token scores every token
A      = softmax(scores)           # each row sums to 1
out    = A @ X                     # each token = blend of all tokens

print(A.shape, out.shape)          # (6, 6) (6, 64) — same shape in, same out
print(A[2].round(2))               # token 2's attention over all six
Real scenario — the O(n²) bill for long logs

Embedding an 8,000-token Apollo mission log costs 64,000,000 pairwise scores per attention layer; a 16k log costs 4× that, not 2×. This quadratic curve is why your Mission Control RAG chunks documents at all instead of embedding them whole, and why "just increase the context window" is never a free answer when the FastAPI service's GPU latency budget is 300 ms.

121

NLTK

Concept

NLTK (Natural Language Toolkit, 2001) is the classic teaching library: corpora, tokenizers, stemmers, POS taggers, parsers, and WordNet, all in pure Python with an academic flavor. It's slow and dated for production — spaCy or a transformer beats it on almost every axis — but it remains ubiquitous in tutorials, courses, and legacy code, and its bundled corpora (Brown, Gutenberg, movie reviews) are still handy sandboxes. Know your way around it; don't build on it.

  • Downloads are separate: nltk.download(...) fetches models/corpora on first use — the classic "LookupError" gotcha.
  • Its Porter/Snowball stemmers (#112) and POS tagger are the reference implementations you'll see cited.
  • Interview trivia lives here: tokenize → tag → chunk is the classical pipeline vocabulary.
nltk.corpus

Ready-made corpora: Gutenberg, Brown, stopword lists — instant sandbox text.

nltk.tokenize

Sentence + word splitters (punkt) — the pre-subword tokenizers.

nltk.tag

POS taggers: label each token NN, VB, JJ… fuel for rule-based extraction.

nltk.stem / wordnet

Stemmers, the WordNet lemmatizer, synonym graphs.

Example 
import nltk
nltk.download("punkt_tab"); nltk.download("averaged_perceptron_tagger_eng")

para = ("Flight director Gene Kranz polled the controllers. "
        "Guidance reported the trajectory was stable after the burn.")

sents = nltk.sent_tokenize(para)
tags  = nltk.pos_tag(nltk.word_tokenize(para))

nouns = [w for w, t in tags if t.startswith("NN")]
print(len(sents), "sentences |", nouns)
# 2 sentences | ['director', 'Gene', 'Kranz', 'controllers', 'trajectory', 'burn']
Real scenario — a ten-minute corpus probe

Before designing metadata for Mission Control RAG you spend ten notebook minutes with NLTK on a sample of mission logs: sentence lengths, noun frequency, stopword ratios. The histogram shows transcripts average 9-word sentences while engineering reports average 31 — evidence that the two document types need different chunk sizes. NLTK's job here is exactly this: quick, disposable corpus archaeology, not production code.

122

spaCy

Concept

spaCy is industrial-strength classical NLP: a fast, Cython-powered pipeline that takes raw text through tokenization, POS tagging, dependency parsing, lemmatization, and named-entity recognition in one pass, returning a rich Doc object. One design choice defines it: opinionated defaults over academic flexibility — you load a pretrained pipeline (en_core_web_sm) and it just works.

The reason it still matters in the LLM era is economics: extracting every organization, date, and location from a million documents costs pennies of CPU with spaCy versus real money and latency with an LLM. For high-volume, well-defined extraction, spaCy remains the pragmatic choice — save the LLM for what actually needs reasoning.

One call to nlp(text) runs the whole pipeline; every stage annotates the same Doc object.
Example 
import spacy
from collections import defaultdict

nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm")
doc = nlp("NASA and SpaceX confirmed the Crew-9 launch from Kennedy "
          "Space Center on September 28, after the FAA cleared the pad.")

ents = defaultdict(list)
for e in doc.ents:
    ents[e.label_].append(e.text)
print(dict(ents))
# {'ORG': ['NASA', 'SpaceX', 'FAA'], 'DATE': ['September 28'],
#  'FAC': ['Kennedy Space Center'], ...}
Real scenario — metadata tagging 40k chunks for filtered retrieval

Mission Control RAG improves sharply when retrieval can filter by metadata ("only chunks mentioning JPL, dated 1970"). Running spaCy NER over all 40,000 chunks to extract ORG/DATE/GPE tags takes about twenty minutes on one CPU and costs nothing. The same job through an LLM at ~500 tokens a chunk is tens of dollars and hours of rate-limited calls — for entity extraction this shallow, spaCy wins on every axis.

123

Hugging Face (library basics)

Concept

Hugging Face is two things fused together: the Hub — hundreds of thousands of pretrained models, datasets, and model cards behind a git-like API — and the transformers library that loads and runs them. Learn it at two levels. Level one: pipeline() wraps preprocessing, model, and postprocessing into one line — perfect for prototyping. Level two: AutoTokenizer + AutoModel* expose the raw pieces — tokenize yourself, run the forward pass, handle the logits — which you need for batching, custom heads, calibration, and serving.

  • Tokenizer and checkpoint must match: always load both from the same model name.
  • AutoModelForSequenceClassification, ...ForCausalLM, etc. pick the right head for the task.
  • Model cards document training data, eval scores, and licenses — read them before you ship someone's weights.
pipeline() is a convenience wrapper around the Auto* chain — same tokenizer, same model, same math.
Example 
import torch
from transformers import (pipeline, AutoTokenizer,
                          AutoModelForSequenceClassification)

clf = pipeline("sentiment-analysis")               # level 1
print(clf("Telemetry restored. Crew morale is high."))
# [{'label': 'POSITIVE', 'score': 0.9998}]

name  = "distilbert-base-uncased-finetuned-sst-2-english"
tok   = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)          # level 2
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(name)
logits = model(**tok("Telemetry restored. Crew morale is high.",
                     return_tensors="pt")).logits
print(torch.softmax(logits, -1))      # same numbers, full control
Real scenario — from notebook demo to FastAPI endpoint

You prototype anomaly-note triage with pipeline() in an afternoon. Moving it into the FastAPI telemetry service, you switch to the Auto* level: load tokenizer and model once at startup, batch 32 notes per forward pass, and keep the raw logits so you can route anything with max-softmax below 0.7 to human review instead of trusting the argmax. That confidence gate is impossible to build from pipeline()'s prettified output alone.

— Transformer Anatomy —
124

Encoder

Concept

A transformer encoder is a stack of identical layers — each one self-attention followed by a feed-forward network, wrapped in residual connections and normalization — where every token attends to every other token bidirectionally. Token 5 sees tokens 1 through N, left and right, all at once. After N layers of this mixing, the output is one contextual vector per token: the same word gets a different vector in every sentence it appears in, because its neighbors shaped it.

That output shape tells you what encoders are for: understanding, not generating. Classification (pool the vectors, add a small head), embeddings for semantic search, token labeling (NER), and reranking all consume "a good vector per token." An encoder cannot write text — it has no notion of "next word" — and that is by design.

Encoder: tokens in at the bottom, N rounds of attention + FFN, one context-aware vector per token out the top.
Example 
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModel

tok   = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")
model = AutoModel.from_pretrained("bert-base-uncased")

def vec(sent, word):
    ids = tok(sent, return_tensors="pt")
    i   = ids.input_ids[0].tolist().index(tok.vocab[word])
    return model(**ids).last_hidden_state[0, i]   # (768,) for that token

a = vec("the capsule will dock with the station", "dock")
b = vec("the crew walked along the dock at the harbor", "dock")
print(torch.cosine_similarity(a, b, dim=0))  # well below 1.0 — same word,
# different sense: context reshaped the vector. Word2Vec can't do this.
Real scenario — the embedder inside Mission Control RAG

Your embedding model (a sentence-transformers checkpoint) is a transformer encoder with mean-pooling on top: every mission-log chunk goes in, one 768-dim vector comes out, and that vector is what sits in your vector DB. When retrieval confuses "docking port" with "port thruster", you now know exactly which component to swap — the encoder — and why a domain-fine-tuned one might separate those senses better.

125

Decoder

Concept

A decoder is the same stack of attention + feed-forward layers with one change that changes everything: a causal mask. Each token may only attend to tokens before it — the future is hidden. That restriction is what makes generation possible: because token 12's representation never depends on token 13, the model can be trained to predict token 13 from tokens 1–12, then at inference generate left to right, appending its own output and predicting again.

GPT, Claude, Llama, Mistral — every chat model you use is a decoder-only transformer. The causal structure also enables the KV cache (previous tokens' computations never change, so cache them), which is why generating token 2,000 isn't 2,000× slower than token 1.

Key distinction

Encoder = one parallel pass, sees everything, outputs vectors → understand. Decoder = causal, sees only the past, outputs a next-token distribution → generate. When an interviewer asks "why can't BERT chat?", this is the answer: bidirectional attention leaks the future, so there is no honest "next word" to predict.

Same architecture, one mask apart: bidirectional attention understands; causal attention can honestly predict what comes next.
Example 
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

tok   = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")

ids = tok("Mission control reported the oxygen", return_tensors="pt").input_ids
for _ in range(4):
    logits = model(ids).logits[0, -1]          # scores for the NEXT token
    top = torch.topk(torch.softmax(logits, -1), 5)
    print([(tok.decode(i), round(p.item(), 3)) for p, i in zip(top.values, top.indices)])
    ids = torch.cat([ids, top.indices[:1].view(1, 1)], dim=1)  # greedy append
# watch the distribution shift as each chosen token becomes context
Real scenario — streaming answers over SSE

Your FastAPI endpoint streams the RAG answer token by token over server-sent events. That UX exists because of the decoder's causal structure: each new token depends only on what's already written, so the model can emit as it goes, and the KV cache means each additional token costs one forward step, not a re-read of the whole prompt. Encoder models could never stream — they compute everything about everything at once.

126

Multi-head attention

Concept

One attention operation forces one compromise pattern of who-looks-at-whom. Multi-head attention runs h attention operations in parallel, each with its own learned Q/K/V projections operating in a smaller subspace (dimension d/h each), then concatenates the results and mixes them with an output matrix W_O. Different heads are free to specialize: in trained models researchers find heads tracking syntax, coreference, adjacent-token copying, rare-token lookups.

  • Cost is the same as one full-width head: 8 heads × 64 dims = 512 dims of total attention either way.
  • Implementation is pure reshape + transpose — no loops. Master that tensor shuffle; it's a favorite interview whiteboard task.
  • Modern variants (GQA, MQA — see #135) share K/V across heads to shrink the KV cache.
Four parallel attention lanes, each with private projections; concatenation stitches their findings back into one vector per token.
Example 
import numpy as np
n, d, h = 6, 64, 4                # 6 tokens, 64-dim, 4 heads
X = np.random.randn(n, d)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (np.random.randn(d, d) * 0.1 for _ in range(3))

def split_heads(M):                # (n, d) → (h, n, d/h)
    return M.reshape(n, h, d // h).transpose(1, 0, 2)

Q, K, V = split_heads(X @ Wq), split_heads(X @ Wk), split_heads(X @ Wv)
A = softmax(Q @ K.transpose(0, 2, 1) / np.sqrt(d // h))  # softmax from #120
out = (A @ V).transpose(1, 0, 2).reshape(n, d)          # concat the heads
print(A.shape, out.shape)          # (4, 6, 6) (6, 64) — 4 maps, one output
Real scenario — debugging the reranker's judgment

Your cross-encoder reranker demotes a clearly relevant mission-log chunk, so you dump its attention maps. Head 7 — which usually links query terms to their document matches — never fires on "EVA" because the chunk spells it "extravehicular activity". Seeing per-head maps turns "the model is being weird" into a concrete fix: add abbreviation expansion to the indexing pipeline.

127

Positional encoding

Concept

Attention is a set operation — it scores pairs of vectors with no idea of order. Without help, "dog bites man" and "man bites dog" are literally identical to a transformer. Positional encoding injects order: give each position a signature the model can read from the token vectors themselves.

Three generations to know. Sinusoidal (the 2017 paper): add sine/cosine waves of geometrically increasing wavelength to each embedding — every position gets a unique fingerprint of phases, and relative offsets are simple transformations of it. Learned (GPT-2, BERT): just train an embedding per position — flexible, but positions beyond training length don't exist. RoPE (rotary, used by Llama/Mistral/Qwen): rotate Q and K by a position-dependent angle so attention scores depend on relative distance by construction — this is the one that context-extension tricks (rope scaling, YaRN) manipulate.

Sinusoidal encoding: many wavelengths at once. Reading down any vertical line gives that position a fingerprint no other position shares.
Example 
import numpy as np, matplotlib.pyplot as plt

def pos_encoding(n_pos, d):
    pos = np.arange(n_pos)[:, None]
    i   = np.arange(d)[None, :]
    angle = pos / 10000 ** (2 * (i // 2) / d)
    return np.where(i % 2 == 0, np.sin(angle), np.cos(angle))

pe = pos_encoding(100, 128)
plt.imshow(pe, cmap="RdBu", aspect="auto")
plt.xlabel("dimension"); plt.ylabel("position"); plt.show()
# every row is unique — and without adding pe to X, shuffling your input
# tokens produces the exact same self-attention output (try it on #120)
Real scenario — why order matters in anomaly reports

"Thruster fired after the leak was sealed" and "leak was sealed after the thruster fired" contain identical tokens and opposite failure narratives. When Mission Control RAG's generator gets causality right, positional information is doing it. It's also why you check rope_theta in a model's config before feeding 30-page incident reports: models extended past their trained positions degrade quietly, scrambling exactly this kind of before/after reasoning.

128

Self-attention (transformer-specific)

Concept

The formal version of #120, and the whiteboard question of the decade. Each token's vector is projected three ways: a Query ("what am I looking for?"), a Key ("what can I be found by?"), and a Value ("what do I contribute if chosen?"). Score every Q against every K with dot products, scale by √d (without it, large dimensions produce huge dots that saturate softmax into near one-hot — gradients die), softmax into weights, and output the weighted sum of V's: Attention(Q,K,V) = softmax(QKᵀ/√d)·V.

Decoders add the causal mask: set every score where a query would look at a future key to −∞ before the softmax, which turns those weights to exactly zero. Separating K from V is the subtle brilliance: how a token advertises itself (K) is decoupled from what it actually hands over (V).

Left: the full Q/K/V recipe. Right: the causal mask — each row (query) may only touch columns (keys) at or before itself.
Example 
import numpy as np
np.random.seed(0)
n, d = 8, 32
X = np.random.randn(n, d)
Wq, Wk, Wv = (np.random.randn(d, d) * 0.1 for _ in range(3))

def attend(X):
    Q, K, V = X @ Wq, X @ Wk, X @ Wv
    S = Q @ K.T / np.sqrt(d)
    S += np.triu(np.full((n, n), -np.inf), k=1)   # causal mask
    A = np.exp(S - S.max(-1, keepdims=True))
    return (A / A.sum(-1, keepdims=True)) @ V

out1 = attend(X)
X2 = X.copy(); X2[7] += 100.0          # vandalize token 7 (the future)
print(np.allclose(out1[3], attend(X2)[3]))  # True — token 3 never saw it
Real scenario — the interview whiteboard, and the KV cache

Two payoffs. First: "implement scaled dot-product attention with a causal mask in NumPy" is a literal interview question for AI-engineer roles — the twelve lines above are the answer. Second: the property your test just proved (past tokens' outputs never change when the future changes) is exactly what makes the KV cache valid, which is why your self-hosted mission-log assistant doesn't recompute 4,000 tokens of context for every generated word.

129

Cross-attention

Concept

Cross-attention is attention between two different sequences: queries come from one, keys and values from the other. In an encoder–decoder model like T5, every decoder layer contains a cross-attention sublayer where the half-written output asks questions of the fully-encoded input — "I'm writing the summary's next word; which part of the source log answers it?" This is the modern, formalized descendant of the original 2014 attention (#119).

The same wiring shows up wherever two modalities or streams must talk: multimodal models let text queries attend over image-patch keys/values ("what's in the upper-left of this satellite image?"), and diffusion models inject the text prompt into image generation through cross-attention layers.

Cross-attention: the decoder's queries reach across into the encoder's keys and values at every generation step.
Example 
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM

tok   = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("t5-small")
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained("t5-small")

inp = tok("summarize: Oxygen tank two exploded 56 hours into the "
          "flight, forcing the crew into the lunar module lifeboat.",
          return_tensors="pt")
out = model.generate(**inp, max_new_tokens=12, output_attentions=True,
                     return_dict_in_generate=True)

step0 = out.cross_attentions[0][-1]        # first step, last layer
top   = step0.mean(1)[0, -1].argmax()      # avg heads → strongest source token
print("decoder step 0 looked at:", tok.decode(inp.input_ids[0, top]))
Real scenario — grounded captions for satellite imagery

Your Orbital Research Agent captions EONET wildfire satellite images with a vision-language model. Inside it, text queries cross-attend over image-patch keys/values — when the caption says "smoke plume in the northeast quadrant", the cross-attention map over patches shows which pixels justified the phrase. You use exactly those maps in review tooling to catch captions the model wrote without actually looking.

— The Model Families —
130

BERT

Concept

BERT (2018) is an encoder-only transformer pretrained with masked language modeling: hide 15% of the tokens, make the model predict them from both sides. That bidirectional pretraining produces spectacular representations for understanding tasks, and BERT ushered in the fine-tune era: download the pretrained weights, add a small head, train briefly on your labels.

Don't file BERT under history. Its descendants are alive inside every RAG pipeline you'll build: sentence-transformers embedding models are BERT-family encoders with pooling, and cross-encoder rerankers are literally a BERT with a one-score head reading query and document together. When your job description says "embeddings" or "reranking", it's saying BERT.

Masked language modeling: context flows in from left and right to fill the blank — great vectors, no generation.
Example 
from transformers import pipeline

fill = pipeline("fill-mask", model="bert-base-uncased")
for p in fill("the crew reported a sudden [MASK] in tank two pressure."):
    print(f"{p['token_str']:10s} {p['score']:.3f}")
# drop       0.4x
# increase   0.2x
# spike      0.0x   ← the pretraining objective, live

# next step (the real exercise): fine-tune distilbert with the HF Trainer
# on a labeled sentiment set and report held-out F1
Real scenario — the reranker is a BERT

Mission Control RAG's second stage feeds each of the 50 retrieved chunks through a cross-encoder — query and chunk concatenated into one sequence, a BERT-family encoder reading both together, one relevance score out. It's slower than the vector lookup (that's why it only sees 50 candidates, not 40,000) but it catches what bi-encoders miss: the chunk that mentions every query term yet answers a different question.

131

RoBERTa

Concept

RoBERTa (2019) is BERT with the training done right — same architecture, better recipe: 10× more data, much longer training with bigger batches, dynamic masking (new random masks each epoch instead of one frozen pattern), and the next-sentence-prediction objective dropped after it proved useless. Result: it beat BERT everywhere without changing a single layer.

Memorize the lesson more than the model: training recipe matters as much as architecture. It's why "we trained longer on better data" keeps beating clever new designs, why model cards detail data and schedules, and why you should be suspicious of any comparison that changes both architecture and recipe at once.

  • Data: 16GB → 160GB of text.
  • Masking: static (one pattern, reused) → dynamic (fresh pattern every pass).
  • Objectives: MLM + NSP → MLM only.
  • Practical note: roberta-base is still a top default for encoder fine-tunes and reranker backbones.
Example 
# the entire experiment is one changed line:
name = "distilbert-base-uncased"   # run 1 → F1 0.89 on anomaly triage
name = "roberta-base"              # run 2 → F1 0.92 — nothing else touched

from transformers import (AutoTokenizer,
    AutoModelForSequenceClassification, Trainer)

tok   = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(name)
model = AutoModelForSequenceClassification.from_pretrained(
            name, num_labels=3)     # nominal / warning / critical
# ...same Trainer, same data, same epochs. The Auto* classes make
# checkpoint swaps free — always benchmark 2–3 backbones before committing.
Real scenario — picking the triage backbone honestly

For the telemetry anomaly-report classifier, you run the identical fine-tune over distilbert, bert-base, and roberta-base and log all three F1 scores in the experiment tracker. RoBERTa wins by three points — worth it for the batch triage job, not worth it for the latency-critical path where distilbert is 2× faster. The RoBERTa lesson also guards your own fine-tunes: before redesigning anything, ask whether more epochs, better data, or better masking of your inputs closes the gap.

132

T5

Concept

T5 ("Text-to-Text Transfer Transformer", 2019) unified NLP with one framing: every task is a string in, string out. Translation, summarization, classification, even regression — all become "input text → output text" through the same encoder–decoder: the encoder reads the input bidirectionally, the decoder generates the answer through cross-attention (#129). Which task to perform is stated inside the input ("summarize:", "translate English to German:").

Recognize what that foreshadowed: if the task lives in the input string, then changing behavior means changing text, not weights — prompting, two years early. Its instruction-tuned descendant Flan-T5 remains a genuinely useful small workhorse for summarize/classify/extract on CPU.

Text-to-text: three different "tasks", zero different models. Prompting before prompting had a name.
Example 
from transformers import pipeline

t5 = pipeline("text2text-generation", model="google/flan-t5-base")

log = "Crew reports O2 tank 2 pressure dropped 40 psi in 3 minutes."

print(t5(f"summarize: {log}")[0]["generated_text"])
print(t5(f"translate English to German: {log}")[0]["generated_text"])
print(t5(f"Is this alert routine or critical? {log}")[0]["generated_text"])
# same weights, zero fine-tuning — only the wording of the input changed
Real scenario — the cheap tier before the LLM

Not every DONKI alert deserves a frontier-model call. Your alert pipeline runs Flan-T5 on CPU as tier one: one-line summary plus routine/critical triage for every incoming space-weather notice, sub-second and effectively free. Only alerts scored "critical" escalate to the expensive LLM for full analysis and operator-ready writeups — a two-tier pattern that cuts the API bill by an order of magnitude.

133

GPT

Concept

GPT is the decoder-only lineage trained on one deceptively simple objective: predict the next token. No labels, no tasks — just trillions of tokens of text and the pressure to continue them well. The 2020s' central empirical surprise is that scaling this up makes capabilities emerge: translation, arithmetic, code, reasoning-like behavior — none explicitly trained, all appearing as the loss drops. The lineage runs from GPT-2 through every frontier model you call today.

At inference the loop is: forward pass → probability distribution over the vocabulary → sample a token (temperature, top-k, top-p shape this) → append → repeat. Every generation parameter you'll ever tune in production lives inside that loop. The single most instructive project on this ladder is building a tiny one — nanoGPT-style, ~300 lines — and watching generations improve epoch by epoch.

The autoregressive loop: predict, sample, append, repeat. Temperature and top-k/p live at the "sample" step.
Example 
import torch
from transformers import AutoTokenizer, AutoModelForCausalLM

tok   = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained("gpt2")
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained("gpt2")
ids   = tok("Flight, we see a pressure", return_tensors="pt").input_ids

for _ in range(10):                       # the whole trick, as a loop
    logits = model(ids).logits[0, -1]
    probs  = torch.softmax(logits / 0.8, -1)   # temperature 0.8
    nxt    = torch.multinomial(probs, 1)       # sample — don't argmax
    ids    = torch.cat([ids, nxt.view(1, 1)], -1)
print(tok.decode(ids[0]))
# rerun with temperature 0.1 vs 1.5 and watch determinism vs chaos
Real scenario — sampling parameters are production knobs

Mission Control RAG sets temperature=0.1 for answer generation (factual, grounded in retrieved chunks) but the Orbital Research Agent uses 0.7 when brainstorming which NASA APIs to query for an open-ended question. Both numbers configure the same multinomial-sampling step you just wrote by hand — after building the loop yourself, "temperature" stops being folklore and becomes a division you performed on logits.

134

LLaMA

Concept

LLaMA is Meta's open-weight family and the foundation of most industry fine-tuning work: when a company adapts a model on private data, the base is more often a Llama than anything else. Its architectural refinements over GPT-2 are now the standard recipe that nearly every open model copies: RMSNorm applied before each sublayer (simpler and cheaper than LayerNorm), RoPE rotary positions (#127), SwiGLU gated activations in the FFN (instead of GELU), no bias terms, and in later versions grouped-query attention to shrink the KV cache.

Learn to read these choices in a config.json — it's how you identify any open model's true anatomy in ten seconds, and it's the vocabulary of every fine-tuning conversation.

The LLaMA block: GPT-2's skeleton with four upgrades — RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, no biases. Now the default recipe everywhere.
Example 
# run one locally, then read its anatomy off the config:
$ ollama run llama3.2:3b "One line: what is a Hohmann transfer?"

$ python - <<'EOF'
from huggingface_hub import hf_hub_download
import json
cfg = json.load(open(hf_hub_download(
    "meta-llama/Llama-3.2-3B", "config.json")))
print({k: cfg[k] for k in
    ["hidden_act", "rms_norm_eps", "rope_theta", "num_key_value_heads"]})
EOF
# {'hidden_act': 'silu', 'rms_norm_eps': 1e-05,
#  'rope_theta': 500000.0, 'num_key_value_heads': 8}  ← name each choice
Real scenario — the base for your private fine-tune

Mission telemetry annotations can't leave your VPC, so the mission-log assistant is a LoRA fine-tune of a Llama base served on your own A10 GPU. Every downstream decision — which quantization works, how big the KV cache grows with 20 concurrent controllers, whether rope scaling can stretch context for full incident reports — is read straight off those config.json fields you just learned to name.

135

Mistral

Concept

Mistral is the efficiency-focused French lab whose 7B model famously beat larger models at release, on the back of two tricks. Sliding-window attention: each layer attends only to the last w tokens (4096) instead of everything — cost drops from O(n²) toward O(n·w), and because layer 2 sees layer 1's outputs, information still propagates further than the window (receptive field grows w per layer). Grouped-query attention (GQA): 32 query heads share 8 key/value heads, shrinking the KV cache ~4× — directly more concurrent users per GPU.

Their Mixtral models brought mixture-of-experts to open weights: 8 expert FFNs per layer with a router activating 2 per token — large-model quality at a fraction of the per-token compute. Mistral's lesson mirrors RoBERTa's from the other side: architecture efficiency is a product feature, paid out in tokens/sec and GPU bills.

Sliding-window attention: only a diagonal band of the causal matrix is computed. Depth restores the long reach.
Example 
# benchmark it against your Llama run on the same 5 fixed prompts:
$ ollama run mistral:7b --verbose "Define apogee and perigee in one line."
# ...answer...
# eval rate:  61.4 tokens/s     ← log this next to llama's number

$ python -c "
from transformers import AutoConfig
c = AutoConfig.from_pretrained('mistralai/Mistral-7B-v0.1')
print(c.sliding_window, c.num_attention_heads, c.num_key_value_heads)"
# 4096 32 8   ← window=4096; 32 query heads share 8 KV heads (GQA)
Real scenario — more controllers per GPU

Your self-hosted mission Q&A service runs on a single A10 with 24 GB. With a standard-attention 7B, KV cache for 20 concurrent 4k-token sessions blows past memory; a GQA model's cache is a quarter the size, so the same card serves the whole flight-control room. When you choose a base model for deployment, num_key_value_heads is a capacity-planning number, not trivia.

136

Qwen

Concept

Qwen is Alibaba's open-weight family, and as of 2026 the most-fine-tuned open lineage after Llama. Three things distinguish it: genuinely strong multilingual performance (trained heavily beyond English — its calling card in Indic and East Asian languages), consistently strong coding and math, and an unusually complete size ladder — from 0.5B models that run on a Raspberry Pi to frontier-scale flagships, plus Coder, VL (vision), and embedding variants. Licensing is largely permissive (Apache-2.0 for most sizes), which matters the moment your fine-tune ships in a product.

Practical takeaway: when a task involves non-English text or you need one architecture family across wildly different deployment sizes, Qwen is usually the first checkpoint to benchmark.

0.5B–3B

Edge and laptop class — drafting, routing, embedded assistants.

7B–14B

The fine-tuning workhorses — one GPU, production quality.

32B–72B+

Near-frontier open flagships for self-hosted reasoning.

Variants

Qwen-Coder, Qwen-VL, embedding/reranker models — one family, every slot.

Example 
from transformers import pipeline

qwen = pipeline("text-generation", model="Qwen/Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct")

# Tamil: "What is a meteor? In one line."
msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "விண்கல் என்றால் என்ன? ஒரே வரியில்."}]
print(qwen(msgs, max_new_tokens=60)[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])

# Hindi: "What is the difference between a satellite and a meteor?"
msgs = [{"role": "user", "content": "उपग्रह और उल्का में क्या अंतर है?"}]
print(qwen(msgs, max_new_tokens=60)[0]["generated_text"][-1]["content"])
# run the same prompts through llama3.2:3b — the gap is the point
Real scenario — multilingual ground-station reports

Your satellite-telemetry operation ingests observer reports and station notes in Hindi and Tamil alongside English. The triage fine-tune built on a Llama base mangles the Indic-script inputs; the same LoRA recipe on a Qwen base handles them natively — no translation layer, no extra latency. Model-family choice, decided by one afternoon of side-by-side prompting, saved an entire preprocessing service.

137

Gemma

Concept

Gemma is Google's open-weight family, distilled from Gemini technology — the third major open lineage to know alongside Llama and Qwen. Its niche is small models that punch above their weight: because distillation transfers ability from a much larger teacher, Gemma's 2B–27B checkpoints often outperform same-size peers, which is exactly what you want at the resource-constrained edge.

Close this volume with the habit that makes all these families useful: a personal eval harness. Five fixed prompts you know cold — one factual, one multilingual, one structured-output, one code, one refusal-bait — run against every candidate model, forever. Leaderboards measure someone else's task; your harness measures yours, and it converts every new model release from hype into a five-minute measurement.

Your permanent model-comparison harness: fixed prompts, candidate models, a score grid you own.
Example 
import subprocess, json

PROMPTS = [l.strip() for l in open("my_eval.txt")]   # your 5 fixed prompts
MODELS  = ["gemma3:4b", "qwen2.5:3b", "llama3.2:3b"]

for m in MODELS:
    for p in PROMPTS:
        out = subprocess.run(["ollama", "run", m, p],
                             capture_output=True, text=True).stdout
        print(json.dumps({"model": m, "prompt": p[:40],
                          "answer": out.strip()[:80]}))
# score by hand first; automate with an LLM judge when you reach the
# evaluation rungs later in the ladder — the prompt file never changes
Real scenario — choosing the ground-station edge model

A remote ground station needs an offline assistant on a fanless mini-PC: 8 GB RAM, no GPU, no uplink. You run your 5-prompt harness over gemma, qwen, and llama small models plus a latency column. Gemma's 4B wins your factual and code prompts, Qwen takes multilingual; since this station's traffic is English-only telemetry queries, Gemma ships. The decision took one evening and is defensible in front of any review board — because the harness file is in git, next to the results.
