— The Core Loop —
173

Agent architecture (perceive-plan-act)

Concept

Strip away the hype and an agent is an LLM inside a while-loop. Each iteration: perceive (read the current state — conversation so far, tool results, task progress), plan (the model decides one thing: emit a final answer, or request a tool call), act (your code executes the tool and appends the result back into the state). Repeat until the model stops asking for tools or you hit a step limit. Every framework in this volume — LangGraph, CrewAI, AutoGen, all of them — is exactly this loop with opinions layered on top.

The division of labor is the part people miss: the model only emits decisions as text/JSON; your code owns everything that actually happens. Execution, validation, retries, termination — all deterministic code you can test. Understand this and no framework will ever feel magical again.

  • Perceive: the message list is the agent's entire world-state.
  • Plan: one model call per iteration — answer or act, never both.
  • Act: your code runs the tool; the result becomes the next perception.
  • Terminate: on a final answer, a max-step cap, or an explicit stop condition.
The whole agent: a cycle. The model decides; your loop executes and feeds back. Exit only when the model answers instead of acting.
Example 
# the ~10 lines every framework is hiding from you
tools = {"calc": lambda expr: str(eval(expr))}
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": task}]

while True:
    reply = llm(messages, tools=tools)         # PLAN: model decides
    if not reply.tool_calls:                   # no action wanted ->
        print(reply.text); break               #   final answer, exit
    for call in reply.tool_calls:              # ACT
        result = tools[call.name](**call.args)
        messages.append(tool_result(call.id, result))  # PERCEIVE next turn
Real scenario — the reference implementation

Before the Orbital Research Agent touches LangGraph, you build this bare loop with one tool: neo_feed over NASA's NEO API. Ask "any hazardous asteroids this week?" and watch it plan (call the tool), act (hit the API), perceive (read the JSON), then answer. Keep this 30-line file forever — when a framework misbehaves in topics 192–197, you'll debug it by mapping it back onto this loop.

174

ReAct pattern

Concept

ReAct (Reason + Act) interleaves explicit reasoning with actions: Thought (what do I know, what do I still need?) → Action (a tool call) → Observation (the result), repeated until a Final Answer. The insight from the original paper still holds: making the model verbalize its reasoning before each action measurably improves tool selection and argument quality — the thought token stream is scratch computation the model gets to condition on.

Modern APIs bake the Action/Observation halves into native tool calling, but the pattern survives as the mental model for reading traces. When an agent misbehaves, you don't guess — you read the Thought lines and see exactly where its world-model went wrong. That readable trail is ReAct's lasting gift.

The ReAct ladder: each rung conditions on everything above it. Thoughts steer actions; observations correct thoughts.
Example 
# an actual trace from a hand-rolled ReAct loop (formatted prompt style)
Thought: I need this week's NEO feed before I can count hazards.
Action:  neo_feed{"start": "2026-08-17", "end": "2026-08-23"}
Observation: {"element_count": 61, "potentially_hazardous": 3, ...}
Thought: 3 hazardous. The largest matters most — fetch its details.
Action:  neo_lookup{"id": "3542519"}
Observation: {"name": "2010 PK9", "est_diameter_m": 160, ...}
Thought: I have enough to answer precisely.
Final Answer: 3 potentially hazardous NEOs this week; largest ~160 m (2010 PK9).
Real scenario — the trace that caught a routing bug

A user asks the Orbital Research Agent about "storms this week" and it calls EONET (terrestrial events) instead of DONKI (space weather). The Thought line tells you why: "storms are natural events → EONET". The fix isn't more prompting — it's rewriting DONKI's tool description to say "geomagnetic storms, solar flares, CMEs". Without ReAct-style traces you'd never have seen the misinterpretation.

175

Tool calling

Concept

Tool calling is how the model reaches outside its weights: you expose typed functions, and each step the model picks a tool and fills in arguments as JSON. The crucial realization: the model chooses tools by reading their names, descriptions, and schemas — nothing else. A tool description is prompt engineering with consequences. Vague description, wrong tool picked; missing constraint ("max 7 days"), invalid arguments generated.

  • Tight schemas: enums, formats, required fields — constrain what the model can emit.
  • Honest descriptions: say what the tool is for and when not to use it.
  • Validate inputs: the model's JSON is a suggestion, not a guarantee.
  • Safe execution: timeouts, allow-lists, read-only by default.
Tool selection is a reading-comprehension task over your descriptions. Write them like documentation for a sharp intern.
Example 
# a tool definition the model can actually route correctly
tools = [{
  "name": "neo_feed",
  "description": ("List near-Earth asteroids approaching between two "
                  "dates (span <= 7 days). Use for close-approach or "
                  "hazard questions. NOT for solar activity — use donki_events."),
  "input_schema": {
    "type": "object",
    "properties": {
      "start_date": {"type": "string", "format": "date"},
      "end_date":   {"type": "string", "format": "date"}},
    "required": ["start_date", "end_date"]}
}]
Real scenario — three NASA tools, five test queries

You give the Orbital Research Agent neo_feed, donki_events, and eonet_events, then fire five varied queries: asteroids, solar flares, wildfires, "anything dangerous near Earth?", "aurora forecast?". The first version misroutes two of five — because all three descriptions started with "Get NASA data about…". Renaming and rewriting descriptions (front-load the differences) takes routing to 5/5. Tool descriptions are the cheapest accuracy lever you own.

176

Function calling (agent context)

Concept

Topic 175 was the happy path. Production tool calling is about everything else: parallel calls (the model may request three tools in one turn — execute them concurrently, return all results with matching IDs), malformed arguments (hallucinated fields, wrong date formats, ranges the API rejects), and — the big one — error feedback. When a tool fails, you don't crash and you don't silently swallow it. You return the error as the tool's observation, written so the model can act on it.

That last point deserves a rule: write error messages for the model, not for humans. "Error 400" teaches it nothing. "Dates must be YYYY-MM-DD and span ≤ 7 days; you sent 30 days" lets it repair its own call on the next iteration — the loop from 173 becomes self-healing for free.

Failures don't exit the loop — they re-enter it as information. The error message IS the repair prompt.
Example 
try:
    args = NeoFeedArgs(**raw_args)            # pydantic gate
    result = neo_feed(args.start_date, args.end_date)
except ValidationError as e:
    result = (f"INVALID_ARGS: {e}. Dates must be YYYY-MM-DD "
              "and span <= 7 days. Fix the arguments and retry.")
except requests.HTTPError as e:
    result = (f"TOOL_ERROR: NEO API returned {e.response.status_code}. "
              "Try a shorter date range or a different tool.")
# either way: back into the loop, never a crash
messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": result})
Real scenario — the 30-day request that fixed itself

Asked for "close approaches this month," the Orbital Research Agent calls neo_feed with a 30-day span. NASA's API 400s — the feed caps at 7 days. Because your error string states the limit explicitly, the model's next turn splits the month into four weekly calls and merges the results. One deliberate error message turned a crash into a capability.

177

Planning

Concept

Two ways to run a multi-step task. Plan-and-execute: the model drafts all steps upfront, then a (cheaper) executor runs them one by one. Reactive (your ReAct loop): decide each step only after seeing the last observation. Planning keeps long tasks on track and can be dramatically cheaper — the big model plans once, small calls execute. Its weakness is staleness: if step 2's result invalidates the plan, steps 3–5 execute confidently into a wall.

The production answer is the hybrid: plan, execute, replan on surprise. Check each step's result against its expected outcome; when reality diverges, regenerate the remaining plan with what you've learned. You get planning's discipline with reactive's adaptability.

Upfront plans are cheap and disciplined but go stale; reactive steps adapt but wander. Production hybrids replan when a step's result surprises.
Example 
plan = llm(f"""Break into numbered steps with done-criteria:
{task}
Return JSON: [{{"step": ..., "tool": ..., "done_when": ...}}]""")

for step in json.loads(plan):
    result = run_step(step)                  # cheap executor call
    if not meets(step["done_when"], result):
        # assumptions went stale — regenerate the remaining plan
        plan = replan(task, completed=done, surprise=result)
Real scenario — the weekly space report, two ways

Run "compile the weekly space report" through both agents. The planner drafts: fetch NEO → fetch DONKI → fetch EONET → synthesize, and burns ~40% fewer tokens. Then DONKI goes down mid-run (it does that). The pure planner executes "synthesize" with a hole in its data; your ReAct agent notices and works around it. The hybrid replans: proceed without DONKI, flag the gap in the report. Compare token cost, steps, and success on all three — that table is an interview answer.

178

Task decomposition

Concept

Task decomposition is turning a fuzzy goal ("research this and write a brief") into concrete subtasks — each with a verifiable done-criterion and explicit dependencies. This single skill decides whether long-horizon agents finish or wander: an agent can't tell it's making progress unless "progress" is checkable, and it can't parallelize or recover unless it knows which subtasks depend on which.

  • Verifiable: "done_when: diameter, miss distance, velocity all present" — a condition code can check, not a vibe.
  • Dependency-aware: independent subtasks run in parallel; dependent ones wait.
  • Failure-isolating: when subtask 2 of 4 fails, you know exactly what's missing.
Decomposition = a DAG of checkable subtasks. Done-criteria make progress measurable; dependencies make failure local.
Example 
# ask the model for a machine-checkable task list, then execute it
{"goal": "brief on asteroid 99942 Apophis' close approach",
 "tasks": [
  {"id": 1, "task": "fetch orbital data", "tool": "neo_lookup",
   "done_when": "diameter, miss_distance, velocity present", "needs": []},
  {"id": 2, "task": "fetch 2029 approach coverage", "tool": "search",
   "done_when": ">=2 sources dated 2025 or later", "needs": []},
  {"id": 3, "task": "write 200-word brief", "tool": null,
   "done_when": "cites outputs of tasks 1 and 2", "needs": [1, 2]}]}
Real scenario — "is Earth having a bad week?"

That question is maximally fuzzy. The Orbital Research Agent decomposes it into three checkable pulls — NEO hazards, DONKI storm activity, EONET disasters — each with a done_when, plus a synthesis task needing all three. When DONKI fails, the task list shows exactly which box is unticked, so the final answer honestly says "space weather data unavailable" instead of pretending completeness. Wandering agents don't have that map.

— Memory —
179

Short-term memory (context-based)

Concept

An agent's short-term memory is the context window: the conversation history plus scratch state you keep re-sending every model call. It's perfect recall — until it isn't. As history grows you pay twice: cost (every token, every call) and attention quality (models get measurably worse at using facts buried in the middle of long contexts). So you manage working memory deliberately: window it (keep the last N turns), summarize it (compress old turns into a running summary), or structure it (a compact scratchpad of facts instead of raw transcripts).

It helps to see all three memory types of this section as one architecture before diving in — short-term is just the top layer:

The three memory layers (topics 179–181): volatile working memory, durable facts, and recorded experience. Different stores, different write policies.
Example 
def compact(messages, budget=6000):
    """Rolling summarization: compress oldest turns when over budget."""
    while count_tokens(messages) > budget:
        old, messages = messages[:6], messages[6:]
        summary = llm(f"Summarize for future turns. Keep IDs, "
                      f"dates, numbers verbatim:\n{old}")
        messages.insert(0, {"role": "system",
                            "content": f"Earlier context: {summary}"})
    return messages
Real scenario — 40 tool calls of asteroid JSON

A long Orbital Research Agent session accumulates 40 NEO API observations — tens of thousands of tokens of raw JSON, most of it never needed again. Rolling compaction replaces the oldest ones with "checked 14 asteroids; 2 hazardous: 2010 PK9 (160 m), 2005 YU55 (360 m)". Cost drops ~70%, and answers actually improve — the model stops losing key facts in the middle of a bloated context.

180

Long-term memory (vector-store-based)

Concept

Long-term memory persists important facts outside the context window — typically in a vector store — and retrieves them back in by relevance at session start or per turn. The read side is just RAG over your own past. The genuinely hard design problem is the write policy: what's worth keeping? Store everything and retrieval drowns in noise; store too little and the agent forgets what mattered. Good systems extract a few durable, atomic facts per session ("user tracks Apophis", not a transcript), deduplicate against what's already stored, and update or expire stale facts rather than piling contradictions.

Two phases, one store. Reads are easy RAG; the write policy — what deserves to be remembered — is the real design work.
Example 
# WRITE — end of session: extract, don't dump
facts = llm(f"Extract <=3 durable facts worth remembering about "
            f"this user or their ongoing work:\n{history}").splitlines()
memory.add(documents=facts,
           metadatas=[{"ts": now()}] * len(facts))   # Chroma collection

# READ — start of the next session
hits = memory.query(query_texts=[user_msg], n_results=3)
system += "\nKnown from past sessions:\n" + "\n".join(hits["documents"][0])
Real scenario — the agent that remembers you across restarts

After a week of use, the Orbital Research Agent's memory holds "user tracks 99942 Apophis", "prefers miss distances in lunar distances", "cares about CMEs only above X-class". Kill the process, restart, ask "anything new on my asteroid?" — retrieval pulls the Apophis fact into the system prompt and the agent answers without being re-told. That restart demo is the proof the memory is real and not just a long chat.

181

Episodic memory

Concept

Episodic memory stores complete past execution traces — task, steps taken, outcome — and recalls similar episodes when a new task arrives. Where long-term memory stores facts ("the user likes X"), episodic memory stores experience ("last time I faced a task like this, this sequence worked"). Injected as an in-context worked example, a retrieved episode teaches the model your environment's quirks: which tool sequences succeed, which failure modes have known workarounds.

  • Log everything: one JSONL line per run — task, trace, outcome, step count.
  • Recall by similarity: embed the new task, retrieve the nearest past episode.
  • Failures are gold: episodes recording a recovery teach more than clean successes.
Every run gets logged; the most similar past run gets recalled. The agent equivalent of "I've seen this one before."
Example 
# after every run: append the episode
episode = {"task": task, "steps": trace,
           "outcome": outcome, "n_steps": len(trace)}
log.write(json.dumps(episode) + "\n")
store.add(documents=[task], metadatas=[episode])

# before a new run: recall the closest episode
past = store.query(query_texts=[new_task], n_results=1)
prompt += ("\nA similar past task and how it was solved:\n"
           + json.dumps(past["metadatas"][0][0]))
Real scenario — Tuesday's DONKI outage pays off on Friday

Tuesday: DONKI times out mid-run; the agent flails for six steps before falling back to its cached CME table. That whole trajectory — including the successful fallback — lands in episodes.jsonl. Friday: a new space-weather question arrives, the Tuesday episode is retrieved as an example, and the agent goes to the cache fallback in two steps instead of six. Experience, operationalized.

— Many Agents —
182

Multi-agent systems

Concept

A multi-agent system is multiple specialized agents passing messages — a researcher that gathers, a writer that composes, an analyst that checks. The pitch is division of labor: each agent gets a focused prompt, focused tools, a cleaner context. The reality check is the costs, and you should be able to recite them: coordination overhead (handoff logic, shared-state plumbing), error compounding (each hop can garble the previous agent's output), and token multiplication (context gets re-sent per agent, per turn).

The professional stance: reach for multi-agent only when a single agent measurably fails at the combined job — usually because one prompt can't hold two conflicting personas, or one context can't hold both workloads. Always build the single-agent baseline first and compare honestly.

Two specialists sharing a scratchpad. Elegant — and roughly twice the tokens. Earn the split with a measured failure, not a vibe.
Example 
# the honest experiment: pair vs single, same task
research = researcher.run("Gather this week's NEO + DONKI highlights",
                          scratchpad="shared.md")
draft    = writer.run("Write the weekly ops brief from shared.md")

solo     = single_agent.run("Gather this week's NEO + DONKI highlights "
                            "and write the weekly ops brief")

print("pair:", tokens(research) + tokens(draft), "tokens")
print("solo:", tokens(solo), "tokens")   # then blind-grade both briefs
Real scenario — the split that half-earned its keep

You split the Orbital Research Agent into fetcher + analyst + writer, then run the weekly-report task against the single-agent baseline. Result: the trio costs 2.3× the tokens; the solo agent's brief is factually equal but structurally worse — it buries the hazard summary. Verdict: keep the researcher/writer pair for the weekly report only, stay single-agent everywhere else. That measured, partial adoption is exactly the judgment interviewers probe for.

183

Agent orchestration

Concept

Orchestration is the control layer above your agents: routing each request to the right one, managing shared state, handling handoffs, timeouts, and failures. The design principle that separates production systems from demos: deterministic code owns the flow; the LLM owns the judgment calls. A model call may classify a query ("asteroid vs space-weather"), but the dispatch table, the retry policy, the timeout, the fallback — those are plain code you can unit-test. Never ask a model to "please retry twice with backoff"; write a for-loop.

The model fills in one word (the route); everything that moves is deterministic, testable code.
Example 
route = llm(f"Classify as exactly one of "
            f"asteroid|space_weather|earth_events: {q}").strip()

agent = {"asteroid": neo_agent,          # dispatch: plain dict
         "space_weather": donki_agent,
         "earth_events": eonet_agent}[route]
try:
    answer = agent.run(q, timeout=60)     # failure policy: plain code
except AgentTimeout:
    answer = fallback_agent.run(q)
Real scenario — the front door of the Orbital Research Agent

Your FastAPI endpoint doesn't hand raw user queries to one giant agent. A one-token classifier call routes each query to the NEO, DONKI, or EONET specialist; a dict does the dispatch; retries and the 60-second timeout live in code. When DONKI's agent times out (again), the fallback path answers from cache — and the router's unit tests still pass without a single LLM call, because the flow was never inside a prompt.

184

Supervisor/hierarchical patterns

Concept

The supervisor pattern puts one agent in charge of others: it assigns work, reviews outputs against explicit criteria, and demands retries with specific critique when a criterion fails. You're trading extra tokens for reliability — a worker's output ships only after passing review. This is the pattern behind most production multi-agent deployments because it converts "hope the model did it right" into a checkable gate.

  • Criteria, not vibes: the supervisor checks a concrete list ("cites a NEO ID", "units present"), not "is this good?".
  • Specific critique: on failure the worker is re-prompted with which check failed and why — that's what makes retry #2 better than retry #1.
  • Bounded loops: cap retries; escalate to a human past the cap.
A hierarchy with a checklist at the top. The supervisor's power is the specific critique it sends back down.
Example 
for attempt in range(3):
    draft = worker.run(task)
    verdict = supervisor.check(draft, criteria=[
        "cites at least one specific NEO ID",
        "distances given in km AND lunar distances",
        "no numbers absent from the tool outputs"])
    if verdict.passed:
        break
    task = f"{task}\nRevise. Fix specifically: {verdict.failures}"
else:
    escalate_to_human(draft, verdict)   # bounded, never infinite
Real scenario — the invented CME speed that never shipped

Your weekly space report's writer once stated a CME travelled "at 3,100 km/s" — a number appearing nowhere in the DONKI output. The supervisor's third criterion ("no numbers absent from tool outputs") catches it, re-prompts with that exact failure, and the revision cites the real 1,240 km/s. Cost: two extra model calls. Value: zero fabricated numbers in front of stakeholders, ever.

185

Reflection

Concept

Reflection is a second pass where the model critiques its own draft before finalizing: draft → critique → revise. It's one of the cheapest quality lifts in the agent toolbox — two extra calls, no new tools, no new data. It works because critiquing is an easier task than generating: reading a draft for flaws requires less simultaneous constraint-juggling than writing it, so the same model performs better as its own reviewer than as a one-shot author. Keep the roles in separate calls with separate prompts; asking for "a great answer, self-checked" in one call loses most of the benefit.

Three calls, three roles. The critique call's only job is to find flaws — which is why it finds them.
Example 
draft = llm(f"Answer: {q}")

critique = llm("List concrete flaws in this answer — missing data, "
               "vague claims, unit errors, uncited numbers. Be harsh:\n"
               + draft)

final = llm(f"Rewrite the answer fixing every flaw.\n"
            f"Answer:\n{draft}\nFlaws:\n{critique}")
# score 10 outputs with and without — the delta is the point
Real scenario — the hazard summary that stopped hand-waving

The Orbital Research Agent's one-shot hazard summaries kept saying "a close approach will occur soon" — no date, mixed km/miles. Adding a reflection pass, the critique call reliably flags "'soon' is not a date" and "units inconsistent," and revisions fix both. You score 10 summaries with and without reflection against a checklist: 4/10 clean become 9/10 clean. Two extra calls per report; the cheapest quality lift you'll find all volume.

186

Self-correction

Concept

Self-correction wires failure signals — tool errors, failed validations, judge scores — back into the loop so the agent retries differently instead of repeating the mistake. The distinction from a blind retry loop is everything: retrying the same call twice against a deterministic failure yields the same failure. Self-correction means the error enters the context, the model reasons over it, and attempt N+1 is materially different from attempt N.

Key distinction

Retry = same action again (right for transient faults like network blips). Self-correction = new action informed by the failure (right for wrong arguments, bad code, failed checks). Production agents need both — exponential backoff for the transient, error-in-context for the systematic — and a cap with human escalation after N distinct attempts.

The failure signal re-enters the loop as context, so each retry is a different attempt — bounded, then escalated.
Example 
# a code-writing agent that debugs itself
last_err = ""
for attempt in range(3):
    code = llm(f"Write Python to {task}."
               f"\nPrevious attempt's error:\n{last_err}")
    try:
        result = run_sandboxed(code)
        break
    except Exception:
        last_err = traceback.format_exc()[-800:]   # the signal, into the loop
else:
    result = "Failed 3 distinct attempts — needs a human."
Real scenario — DONKI, the gift that keeps on failing

DONKI is your flakiest dependency: roughly a third of calls time out or return an empty body. The Orbital Research Agent's self-correction path reads the error observation and changes strategy — shorter date range on a timeout, the cached CME table on an empty body, EONET cross-check when data looks stale — escalating only after three distinct attempts. This is your signature interview story: point at the trace where attempt 2 differs from attempt 1, because the error text is sitting right there in the context.

187

Human-in-the-loop checkpoints

Concept

Some actions are too consequential to let an agent take alone: sending, deleting, paying, posting. Human-in-the-loop (HITL) checkpoints pause the agent at those steps, show the human exactly what's about to happen, and resume cleanly with possibly-edited state. Three responses, not two: approve (execute as-is), edit (execute with modified arguments), reject (feed the refusal back as an observation so the agent re-plans). This is non-negotiable for agents touching real systems.

The engineering requirement people miss: the pause may last hours, so agent state must be persisted at the checkpoint — you can't hold a Python process hostage waiting for a manager's click. This is exactly what LangGraph's checkpointer + interrupt() (topic 193) give you natively.

Approve / edit / reject — and a rejection is an observation the agent learns from, not a dead end.
Example 
call = agent.next_tool_call()
if call.name in RISKY:      # {"send_email", "delete_rows", "post_alert"}
    print(f"About to run {call.name} with:\n{json.dumps(call.args, indent=2)}")
    choice = input("[y]es / [e]dit / [n]o: ")
    if choice == "n":
        agent.observe("User rejected this action. Propose an alternative.")
        return
    if choice == "e":
        call.args = json.loads(input("edited args (JSON): "))
execute(call)                # runs approved or edited version only
Real scenario — the alert that needed a sign-off

The Orbital Research Agent's post_hazard_alert tool posts to the ops Slack channel — visible to real people, so it's gated. When the agent drafts an alert for a 160 m asteroid at 4.6 lunar distances, the checkpoint shows the exact message; the reviewer edits the severity from "warning" to "advisory" and approves. The edited version posts, the agent's state records the edit, and nothing ever reaches Slack un-reviewed. In topic 193 you'll rebuild this gate as a LangGraph interrupt().

— The Protocols: MCP & A2A —
188

MCP (Model Context Protocol)

Concept

MCP is Anthropic's open standard for connecting AI to tools and data. An MCP server exposes three kinds of things — tools (functions the model can call), resources (data it can read), and prompts (reusable templates) — over a uniform JSON-RPC protocol (stdio for local servers, HTTP for remote). Any MCP client — Claude Desktop, Claude Code, an IDE, your own app — plugs into any server with zero custom glue.

The USB-C analogy is earned, and here's the math behind it: without a standard, M applications × N data sources means M×N bespoke integrations. With MCP, each app implements the client once and each source implements the server once: M+N. That economics is why the ecosystem snowballed — and why MCP experience is flagged as the scarcest, highest-demand skill in this entire volume. The session starts with an initialize handshake (version + capability negotiation), then the client discovers what's on offer via tools/list and calls via tools/call.

One protocol in the middle: every client speaks to every server. Implement your side once, inherit the whole ecosystem.
Example 
# what actually happens when a client connects (JSON-RPC, simplified)
→ {"method": "initialize",
   "params": {"protocolVersion": "2025-06-18", "capabilities": {...}}}
← {"result": {"capabilities": {"tools": {}, "resources": {}}}}

→ {"method": "tools/list"}
← {"result": {"tools": [{"name": "close_approaches",
                          "inputSchema": {"type": "object", ...}}]}}

→ {"method": "tools/call",
   "params": {"name": "close_approaches", "arguments": {"min_diameter_m": 140}}}
← {"result": {"content": [{"type": "text", "text": "[...rows...]"}]}}
Real scenario — explain what happened underneath

Install any existing MCP server into Claude Code, then narrate the invisible part: on startup the client spawned the server process, ran the initialize handshake, called tools/list, and folded those schemas into the model's tool set — which is why the tools "just appeared". Being able to explain that handshake, not just consume it, is precisely the low-supply/high-demand skill this ladder flags. Next topic: you build the server side over your own mission database.

189

Building an MCP server

Concept

With FastMCP, a decorated Python function becomes a protocol-compliant MCP tool: the type hints generate the input schema, the docstring becomes the description the model reads (topic 175's lesson applies with full force), and the framework handles the JSON-RPC plumbing, handshake included. Your entire job collapses to: write good functions, write honest docstrings.

Wrapping a real production system — your database, your CRM, your internal API — as an MCP server is the single highest-leverage portfolio project on this ladder: it's concrete, it's demo-able inside Claude in thirty seconds, and almost nobody interviewing next to you has done it. Start read-only (parameterized SELECTs, never string-built SQL), add write tools only behind HITL gates from topic 187.

Example 
from fastmcp import FastMCP
import asyncpg

mcp = FastMCP("mission-db")

@mcp.tool()
async def close_approaches(min_diameter_m: float = 100) -> list[dict]:
    """Asteroid close approaches from the mission DB, largest first.
    Use for hazard questions; diameters in meters, distances in km."""
    conn = await asyncpg.connect(DSN)
    rows = await conn.fetch(
        "SELECT name, diameter_m, miss_km, approach_date "
        "FROM neo_approaches WHERE diameter_m >= $1 "
        "ORDER BY diameter_m DESC LIMIT 20", min_diameter_m)
    return [dict(r) for r in rows]

mcp.run()   # stdio transport — ready for any MCP client
Real scenario — your mission DB, live inside Claude

The Orbital Research Agent already persists NEO snapshots, DONKI events, and run logs into Postgres. You wrap it as an MCP server with three read-only tools — close_approaches, storm_history, agent_run_stats — register it in Claude Desktop's config, and ask: "which asteroid in our DB had the closest approach this quarter?" Claude calls your server, your SQL runs, the answer cites your rows. That thirty-second demo — "I connected Claude to a production database via MCP" — is the portfolio moment this whole volume builds toward.

190

Connecting an MCP client

Concept

The other side of the wire: your own application acts as the MCP client. It spawns (or connects to) a server, runs the initialize handshake, calls list_tools() to discover what's available, and routes your agent's tool calls through call_tool(). The payoff is enormous: the hardcoded tools dict from topic 173 becomes dynamic — your agent inherits every MCP server you plug in, yours or anyone's, without a line of integration code per tool.

  • Session lifecycle: connect → initialize → list_tools → call_tool → close.
  • Schema bridging: MCP tool schemas map almost 1:1 onto LLM tool-calling formats — a thin adapter converts them.
  • Trust boundary: third-party servers run their code on your box — vet what you plug in.
Your bare loop grows a protocol arm: tools are discovered at runtime, not hardcoded at write time.
Example 
from mcp import ClientSession, StdioServerParameters
from mcp.client.stdio import stdio_client

params = StdioServerParameters(command="uv",
                                args=["run", "mission_mcp.py"])
async with stdio_client(params) as (read, write):
    async with ClientSession(read, write) as session:
        await session.initialize()
        tools = await session.list_tools()      # → your LLM's tool set
        result = await session.call_tool(
            "close_approaches", {"min_diameter_m": 140})
Real scenario — the loop that stopped hardcoding tools

You upgrade the topic-173 reference loop: instead of a hardcoded dict, it opens sessions to two MCP servers at startup — your mission-db server and a community filesystem server — converts their list_tools() schemas into the LLM tool format, and routes each tool call to the owning session. Adding a third integration is now a config line, not code. You've closed the full circle: server author (189), client author (190), protocol literate (188).

191

A2A (Agent2Agent Protocol)

Concept

A2A is the Google-initiated open standard for agent-to-agent communication. Each agent publishes an agent card — a JSON capability manifest, conventionally served at /.well-known/agent.json — that other agents fetch to discover what it can do. Agents then exchange tasks (with lifecycle states: submitted, working, completed, failed) and return artifacts, delegating work across teams, companies, and vendors without bespoke API contracts.

Key distinction

MCP connects an agent to tools (vertical: one brain, many capabilities). A2A connects agents to each other (horizontal: many brains, negotiating work). They're complementary, not competing — a mature system uses MCP inside each agent and A2A between them. Interviewers love this one-liner because most candidates conflate the two.

Discovery by card, delegation by task, results as artifacts — across vendors, with no bespoke contract negotiated.
Example 
# the agent card describing your #189-powered agent to the world
{"name": "orbital-research-agent",
 "description": "Answers questions on NEOs, space weather, and Earth events using live NASA data.",
 "url": "https://agents.example.com/orbital",
 "capabilities": {"streaming": true},
 "skills": [
   {"id": "neo-hazard-scan",
    "description": "Scan a date range for hazardous close approaches"},
   {"id": "space-weather-brief",
    "description": "Summarize solar activity from DONKI"}]}
Real scenario — a stranger's agent hires yours

A partner team's launch-planning agent needs space-weather clearance for an August 30 window. It fetches your agent card, sees the space-weather-brief skill, and delegates the task over A2A — receiving a structured brief as an artifact. Neither team wrote an integration; both implemented the standard once. Write your Orbital agent's card today even if nothing consumes it yet: it forces you to define your agent's capabilities crisply, and it future-proofs the demo.

— The Frameworks —
192

LangChain

Concept

LangChain is the most famous LLM framework: chains (composable pipelines, now written in the LCEL pipe syntax), document loaders for a hundred file formats and APIs, and a vast integration catalog — every vector DB, every model provider, every reranker has a LangChain wrapper. You learn it for two honest reasons: job posts list it, and its loaders/integrations genuinely save time when you need to talk to five backends in a week.

You should also know its standard criticism from experience, not hearsay: abstraction bloat. Simple things route through many wrapper layers, stack traces tunnel through Runnable machinery, and debugging means reading framework source. The professional position isn't "LangChain bad" — it's "I've built the same pipeline with and without it, and here's where each wins." That answer requires doing the exercise.

Example 
from langchain_core.prompts import ChatPromptTemplate
from langchain_core.runnables import RunnablePassthrough
from langchain_core.output_parsers import StrOutputParser

prompt = ChatPromptTemplate.from_template(
    "Answer strictly from context:\n{context}\n\nQ: {question}")

chain = ({"context": retriever, "question": RunnablePassthrough()}
         | prompt | llm | StrOutputParser())    # LCEL: | composes steps

chain.invoke("What damped the lander's oscillation during descent?")
Real scenario — the two-column comparison you'll cite in interviews

You rebuild Mission Control RAG's retrieval-QA in LangChain (loader → splitter → Chroma retriever → LCEL chain, ~25 lines) and keep your raw-Python version (~60 lines) beside it. LangChain wins on the PDF loader and retriever swap; raw Python wins the day a mission-log query fails and the stack trace is 5 frames instead of 30. Now "LangChain: abstraction bloat or lifesaver?" gets a measured answer with line counts — experience, not a hot take.

193

LangGraph

Concept

LangGraph models an agent as an explicit state graph: nodes do work (call the model, run tools), edges route between them — including conditional edges (branch on state) and cycles (the agent loop itself) — over a shared, typed state that each node reads and updates. Two features make it the current production standard for stateful agents: checkpointers persist the full state after every step (crash recovery, time-travel debugging, resumable runs), and interrupts pause the graph at a node for human-in-the-loop approval — exactly the persistence requirement from topic 187, solved natively.

Look at the diagram and you'll recognize topic 173: the conditional edge is "answer or act?", the cycle is the loop. LangGraph didn't invent anything — it made your reference implementation explicit, persistent, and inspectable.

Nodes, a conditional edge, a cycle back to the agent, and a checkpointer under it all — the 173 loop made explicit and persistent.
Example 
from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, MessagesState, START, END
from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver

g = StateGraph(MessagesState)
g.add_node("agent", call_model)          # decides: answer or tools
g.add_node("tools", run_tools)
g.add_edge(START, "agent")
g.add_conditional_edges("agent",          # branch on state
    lambda s: "tools" if s["messages"][-1].tool_calls else END)
g.add_edge("tools", "agent")             # the cycle — this IS the loop

app = g.compile(checkpointer=MemorySaver())
app.invoke({"messages": [q]},
           config={"configurable": {"thread_id": "run-42"}})  # resumable
Real scenario — the Orbital Research Agent's real skeleton

This graph, with run_tools wrapping NEO/DONKI/EONET, is the production Orbital Research Agent. The checkpointer earns its keep the first time DONKI stalls a 9-step run at step 6: the process restarts, you re-invoke with the same thread_id, and the run resumes from the checkpoint instead of re-paying for six steps. The post_hazard_alert gate from topic 187 becomes interrupt() before the tools node — approve from another process, hours later, state intact.

194

CrewAI

Concept

CrewAI is a role-based multi-agent framework: you define each agent by role, goal, and backstory, compose them into a crew, and pick a process — sequential (tasks run in order, output feeding forward) or hierarchical (a manager LLM delegates, topic 184 as a config flag). It's the fastest framework here for getting a multi-agent demo running, and deliberately opinionated about structure.

Demystify the magic once: role, goal, and backstory are prompt text — CrewAI interpolates them into each agent's system prompt. Knowing that tells you exactly what a backstory can and cannot fix, and keeps you from cargo-culting "personas" when the real problem is a missing tool or a bad task description.

Example 
from crewai import Agent, Task, Crew, Process

researcher = Agent(role="Space-weather researcher",
    goal="Collect this week's verified solar activity facts",
    backstory="Meticulous DONKI analyst; never invents numbers.")
writer = Agent(role="Mission brief writer",
    goal="Turn research notes into a 150-word ops brief",
    backstory="Writes for flight controllers: terse, unit-exact.")

crew = Crew(agents=[researcher, writer],
    tasks=[Task(description="Research CME activity this week",
                expected_output="bullet list with dates + speeds",
                agent=researcher),
           Task(description="Write the ops brief from the research",
                expected_output="150-word brief", agent=writer)],
    process=Process.sequential, verbose=True)
result = crew.kickoff()
Real scenario — reading the handoff in the logs

You rebuild topic 182's researcher + writer pair as a crew and run it with verbose=True on the weekly brief. The logs show exactly what the framework does for you: the researcher's final answer is injected verbatim into the writer's task context — the handoff you previously plumbed through shared.md, now free. Then compare token bills: the crew costs ~15% more than your hand-rolled pair for the same output. That's the trade — convenience for control — and now you've measured it.

195

AutoGen

Concept

AutoGen (Microsoft) treats conversation as computation: agents talk to each other in two-party chats or group chats, and the work gets done inside the dialogue. Built-in code execution lets an agent write Python that another agent (or a sandboxed executor) runs, with results flowing back into the chat; termination conditions — a keyword like TERMINATE, a max round count — decide when the discussion is over.

Contrast the mental models: LangGraph makes control flow explicit (you draw the edges); AutoGen makes it emergent (whoever speaks next, per the chat manager, steers). Emergent conversation shines for open-ended collaboration like debate and code-review loops — and is precisely what you don't want when compliance asks "show me the exact path a request takes."

Example 
from autogen import AssistantAgent, GroupChat, GroupChatManager

analyst = AssistantAgent("analyst", llm_config=cfg,
    system_message="Estimate quantitatively; show your math.")
skeptic = AssistantAgent("skeptic", llm_config=cfg,
    system_message="Attack weak assumptions. Say TERMINATE when convinced.")

chat = GroupChat(agents=[analyst, skeptic], messages=[], max_round=8)
mgr = GroupChatManager(groupchat=chat, llm_config=cfg,
    is_termination_msg=lambda m: "TERMINATE" in m.get("content", ""))

analyst.initiate_chat(mgr,
    message="Impact energy of a 160 m stony asteroid at 19 km/s?")
Real scenario — the debate that caught a bad assumption

You give the analyst/skeptic pair a real question from your NEO data: impact energy for 2010 PK9. Round 2, the skeptic attacks the density assumption (3,000 kg/m³ for a possibly porous body) and demands a range instead of a point estimate; round 4 they converge on 30–70 megatons and TERMINATE fires. Reading where convergence happened — and noticing the run cost 8 model calls where topic 185's reflection would've cost 3 — is exactly the framework judgment this volume is building.

196

OpenAI Agents SDK

Concept

The OpenAI Agents SDK is deliberately lightweight — notable as OpenAI's official opinion on how simple agent code should be. Five primitives, nothing else: agents (a model + instructions + tools), handoffs (one agent transfers the whole conversation to another — routing as a first-class verb), guardrails (validators on inputs/outputs that can halt a run before tokens are wasted), sessions (conversation memory), and built-in tracing for every run.

Compare it to your own topic-183 router: triage-by-handoff is the same pattern, but the transfer, the memory, and the trace viewer come free. The cost of the convenience: it's opinionated about staying inside its ecosystem.

Guardrail gates the door, triage hands off the whole conversation, specialists answer — five primitives, no ceremony.
Example 
from agents import Agent, Runner, InputGuardrail

neo_agent   = Agent(name="NEO specialist",
    instructions="Answer asteroid close-approach questions precisely.")
donki_agent = Agent(name="Space-weather specialist",
    instructions="Answer solar-activity questions from DONKI data.")

triage = Agent(name="Triage",
    instructions="Hand off to the right specialist.",
    handoffs=[neo_agent, donki_agent],
    input_guardrails=[InputGuardrail(guardrail_function=on_topic_check)])

result = Runner.run_sync(triage, "Any big CMEs expected this week?")
Real scenario — the router you already built, minus the plumbing

You port topic 183's front door: triage hands off to NEO or DONKI specialists, and the on_topic_check guardrail rejects "write my homework" before a specialist ever sees it. The trace viewer shows the handoff chain per request — the observability you'd otherwise wire yourself. Keep both versions in the repo: "here's the pattern raw, here's it in the SDK" is a portfolio artifact that proves you understand the layer beneath the framework.

197

PydanticAI

Concept

PydanticAI, from the team behind Pydantic itself, makes agents feel like well-engineered Python instead of prompt glue. Three signatures: typed dependencies (a deps object — DB pool, API client — injected into every tool through RunContext, so tools are testable functions, not closures over globals), validated structured results (the agent's output must parse into your Pydantic model), and automatic retries on validation failure — a bad output is sent back to the model with the validation error, which is topic 186's self-correction built into the return type.

  • Output as contract: downstream code consumes result.output.verdict, never regex over prose.
  • Dependency injection: swap the real DB for a fake in tests — agent tools become unit-testable.
  • Type-checker friendly: mypy catches wiring mistakes before any tokens are spent.
Example 
from pydantic import BaseModel, Field
from pydantic_ai import Agent, RunContext

class HazardReport(BaseModel):
    neo_id: str
    diameter_m: float = Field(gt=0)          # "unknown" → retry
    verdict: Literal["safe", "monitor", "alert"]

agent = Agent("anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-5",
              deps_type=Database, output_type=HazardReport)

@agent.tool
async def lookup(ctx: RunContext[Database], neo_id: str) -> dict:
    """Fetch one NEO's orbital record from the mission DB."""
    return await ctx.deps.fetch_neo(neo_id)

report = agent.run_sync("Assess NEO 3542519", deps=db).output
print(report.verdict)          # typed, validated — or it retried
Real scenario — the endpoint that trusts its agent

Your FastAPI route /assess/{neo_id} returns HazardReport directly — because PydanticAI guarantees the agent's output parses or retries. You force the failure once to watch it work: prompt the model into answering diameter_m: "unknown", and the validation error goes back as a retry prompt; attempt two returns a proper float. The FastAPI layer never sees the mess. Contrast this with the JSON-parsing try/except pyramid in your early prototypes: that's the pitch.

— Proving It Works —
198

Agent evaluation

Concept

Chatbot evaluation grades the answer. Agent evaluation grades the trajectory — the whole sequence of decisions — because an agent can reach a right answer by wasteful or lucky paths that will betray you in production. The three core metrics: tool-call accuracy (right tool and right arguments at each step), step efficiency (steps taken vs. the minimal path), and task completion rate (did the final state satisfy the task's rubric?). Hand-label a small suite first — 20 tasks with expected calls — so you know your ground truth; automate with an LLM judge only after your labels exist to calibrate it against.

This is the discipline that turns agent demos into agent products: every change to a prompt, a tool description, or a framework gets run against the suite, and "it feels better" becomes three numbers moving.

Grade every step, then aggregate over a fixed suite. A completed task with a wasteful trajectory is a warning, not a win.
Example 
correct = total = completed = steps = 0
for task in test_set:                       # 20 hand-labeled tasks
    traj = agent.run(task.q, log_trajectory=True)
    for step in traj.tool_calls:
        total += 1
        correct += (step.name, frozenset(step.args.items())) \
                   in task.expected_calls  # right tool AND right args
    completed += grade(traj.final, task.rubric)
    steps += traj.n_steps

print(f"tool acc {correct/total:.0%} · "
      f"completion {completed}/{len(test_set)} · "
      f"avg steps {steps/len(test_set):.1f}")
Real scenario — the numbers that closed the volume

You build the Orbital Research Agent's suite: 20 tasks mixing NEO, DONKI, EONET, and deliberately ambiguous queries, each with expected tool calls hand-labeled. First run: completion 18/20 — looks great — but tool-call accuracy is 71% and average steps are 4.2 against a 3.0 minimum. The agent is getting right answers through wasteful detours (that redundant second neo_feed shows up constantly). You tighten two tool descriptions from topic 175, rerun: 87% accuracy, 3.4 steps, same completion. That before/after table — trajectory metrics, not vibes — is what separates "I built an agent demo" from "I ship agent products," and it's the last thing this volume asks you to prove.
