— The RL Formalism —
199

Markov Decision Process (MDP)

Concept

Reinforcement learning has one job: choose good actions in an environment that answers back. The Markov Decision Process is the formalism that makes that job precise. An agent observes a state, picks an action, and the environment responds with a next state — drawn from transition probabilities — and a scalar reward. Then the loop repeats. Five ingredients define the whole game:

S — states

Every situation the agent can be in (each cell of a grid).

A — actions

The menu of choices available in each state.

P(s′|s,a)

Transition probabilities: where an action can land you.

R(s,a)

The reward signal — the only definition of "good".

γ — discount

How much future reward is worth: γⁿ per step of delay.

The discount factor γ (typically 0.9–0.99) says a reward n steps away is worth γⁿ today — it makes infinite futures sum to a finite number and encodes impatience. The payoff of the formalism: if you can write your problem as an MDP, every algorithm in this volume applies to it verbatim. Framing the problem is usually the hard part; the machinery is reusable.

The canonical MDP loop, flavored as a probe on a grid: the policy acts, the world answers with state and reward, and γ decides how much tomorrow's reward counts today.
Example 
# a 4x4 gridworld as a plain MDP — no library, just dicts and a function
STATES  = [(r, c) for r in range(4) for c in range(4)]
ACTIONS = ["N", "S", "E", "W"]
GOAL, CRATER = (3, 3), (1, 2)
MOVES = {"N": (-1, 0), "S": (1, 0), "E": (0, 1), "W": (0, -1)}

def step(s, a):                          # the transition function P(s'|s,a)
    dr, dc = MOVES[a]
    s2 = (min(max(s[0] + dr, 0), 3), min(max(s[1] + dc, 0), 3))
    if s2 == GOAL:   return s2, +1.0, True   # reached the lander
    if s2 == CRATER: return s2, -1.0, True   # drove into a crater
    return s2, -0.01, False                   # small cost per step; γ lives in the learner
Real scenario — a rover route as an MDP

Picture a rover on a Mars grid: cells are states, drive commands are actions, craters pay −1, the lander pays +1, and each step burns a little battery (−0.01). Written this way, the exact Q-learning loop from topic 205 solves it with zero changes — and the same framing exercise is how DeepMind turned Atari, data-center cooling, and LLM alignment into RL problems.

200

State

Concept

The state is everything the agent knows about the current situation — the input to its policy. The load-bearing assumption is the Markov property: given the present state, the past adds nothing. Formally, P(s′|s,a) depends only on the current state and action, not on the whole history. Real problems are rarely perfectly Markov; your job as the designer is to build states that make it approximately true.

  • Position alone is not Markov for a moving probe — the same (x, y) can precede many futures. Add velocity, and the present suddenly summarizes the past.
  • Frame stacking is the classic fix: DQN on Atari feeds 4 consecutive frames so motion is visible in a single "state".
  • When important information is fundamentally hidden (sensor can't see it), you have a POMDP — partially observable — and life gets harder: agents need memory (RNNs, transformers) to reconstruct state.
The Markov test: does the present state alone predict what comes next? Position fails it; position + velocity passes it.
Example 
# position alone is NOT Markov for a drifting probe
s_bad  = {"x": 4.0, "y": 2.0}                    # same state → many possible futures

# add velocity → the present now carries what the past mattered for
s_good = {"x": 4.0, "y": 2.0, "vx": 0.3, "vy": -0.1}

def next_x(s, dt=1.0):
    return s["x"] + s["vx"] * dt              # predictable from s alone — Markov restored
Real scenario — designing telemetry states

Suppose you train an RL agent to manage a satellite's battery from telemetry. A state of just charge_pct is not Markov — 60% charging and 60% discharging demand opposite actions. Add charge_rate and sunlight_flag from the same Kafka telemetry stream and the state passes the Markov test; the agent stops thrashing. State design, not algorithm choice, is what fixed it.

201

Action

Concept

The action space is the agent's menu of choices in each state. It comes in two flavors, and the flavor decides which algorithms you can use: discrete (a finite menu — up/down/left/right, buy/hold/sell) suits Q-tables and DQN, which need a max over actions; continuous (real-valued — a steering angle, a thrust vector) breaks that max and demands policy-gradient methods like PPO or SAC that output distributions over actions.

Action-space design shapes what's learnable. Too coarse and the best behavior isn't expressible; too fine and exploration takes forever — a probe with 360 discrete headings explores 90× slower than one with 4. Even edge behavior is a design decision you must make explicitly: what happens when the agent drives into a wall — stay put? bounce? pay a penalty? The learner will faithfully learn whatever you chose.

Discrete menu vs continuous knob. The dashed circle is the point: infinitely many actions, so "take the max over actions" stops being an option.
Example 
# edge behavior is YOUR design decision — here: stay put + small penalty
def step(s, a):
    dr, dc = MOVES[a]
    r2, c2 = s[0] + dr, s[1] + dc
    if not (0 <= r2 < 4 and 0 <= c2 < 4):   # drove into the crater wall
        return s, -0.05, False                  # bump: stay, pay extra
    return (r2, c2), -0.01, False

# same world, two action-space designs:
#   Discrete(4)  — N/S/E/W        → tabular Q-learning solves it in seconds
#   Box(-1, 1)   — thrust (dx,dy) → you now need PPO and 100x the samples
Real scenario — choosing the thruster menu

For a toy attitude-control sim of a tumbling cubesat, you get to pick: three discrete actions (fire left thruster / right / coast) trains with DQN in minutes on a laptop; a continuous torque vector needs PPO and hours. Start discrete to prove the pipeline works end to end, then graduate to continuous only if the coarse menu can't hold the spin steady enough.

202

Reward

Concept

The reward is the scalar signal that defines the goal — and it is the only thing the agent optimizes. Not your intent, not the documentation, not what you meant: the number. The agent will exploit any loophole you leave, a failure mode called reward hacking — the RL ancestor of an LLM reward model being gamed into sycophancy. This is why practitioners say reward design is where RL projects live or die.

  • Sparse rewards (+1 only at the goal) are honest but slow — the agent may never stumble onto the signal.
  • Shaping (a small −0.01 per step, partial credit for progress) speeds learning but every shaping term is a new loophole to audit.
  • A tiny change transforms behavior: per-step reward 0 → the agent wanders indefinitely; per-step −0.01 → every wasted move hurts, and the policy becomes a beeline.
Same goal reward, one line changed. The agent optimizes exactly what you wrote — nothing more, nothing less.
Example 
# the entire "spec" of the agent's behavior lives in this function
def reward(s2, step_cost):
    if s2 == GOAL:   return +1.0
    if s2 == CRATER: return -1.0
    return step_cost

# step_cost =  0.00 → any eventual path pays +1; agent wanders forever
# step_cost = -0.01 → every wasted step hurts;  agent beelines
# step_cost = -0.20 → detours cost more than a crater; agent SUICIDES into it
#                     ...a reward bug, not an agent bug
Real scenario — the probe that learned to spin

You reward a survey probe +0.1 whenever its solar panels are charging, hoping it stays powered while mapping terrain. It learns to park facing the sun and spin gently forever — maximum reward, zero mapping. That's reward hacking, and it's the exact failure RLHF (item 141) fights at LLM scale: models learn to please the reward model (confident tone, flattery) rather than be correct. Same disease, bigger patient.

203

Policy

Concept

The policy π is the mapping from state to action — it is the agent. Everything else in RL — value functions, replay buffers, critics — is machinery for improving the policy. It comes in two forms: deterministic, π(s) = a (one fixed answer per state), and stochastic, π(a|s) (a probability distribution over actions). Stochastic policies matter more than they first appear: they explore naturally, they're differentiable (which is what policy-gradient methods like PPO need), and an LLM generating tokens is one — a distribution over next actions given the state (the context).

A clarifying question for any RL system: what ships? The answer is always just the policy — a small table or network mapping observations to actions. The training machinery stays home.

A policy, visualized: a lookup from cell to arrow. The highlighted cell keeps a little randomness — exploration lives in the policy itself.
Example 
import random

def pi_random(s):  return random.choice(ACTIONS)                    # baseline
def pi_greedy(s):  return max(ACTIONS, key=lambda a: Q[(s, a)])     # exploit a Q-table

def avg_return(pi, episodes=100):
    total = 0.0
    for _ in range(episodes):
        s, done = (0, 0), False
        while not done:
            s, r, done = step(s, pi(s))
            total += r
    return total / episodes

print(avg_return(pi_random), avg_return(pi_greedy))   # ≈ -0.4 vs ≈ +0.94
Real scenario — what actually flies

When your rover agent is "done training", the artifact you'd upload to the vehicle is the policy alone — for the gridworld, a 16-row lookup table; for the cubesat, a 20 KB network. No replay buffer, no optimizer, no reward function on board. Exactly like shipping an LLM: the served model is a frozen policy, and RLHF's training rig never leaves the datacenter.

204

Value function

Concept

A value function answers "how good is it to be here?" — as a number. V(s) is the expected total discounted future reward starting from state s and following policy π; Q(s,a) is the same but committing to action a first, then following π. Values are the concept that makes lookahead unnecessary: the agent doesn't simulate the future, because the future's worth is already baked into the number on each state.

The math engine behind everything is the Bellman equation: V(s) = E[ r + γ·V(s′) ] — a state's value is the immediate reward plus the discounted value of where you land. It's recursive bookkeeping: value flows backward from rewards, shrinking by γ per step. Every algorithm in the next section is a scheme for making estimates obey this equation.

Value radiates backward from reward, fading by one factor of γ per step of distance. Brightness = how much future the cell already "contains".
Example 
# hand-compute V along the last row, policy = "always go East", γ = 0.9
GAMMA = 0.9
V = {}
V[(3, 3)] = 0.0                        # terminal: no future after arrival
V[(3, 2)] = 1.0 + GAMMA * V[(3, 3)]   # stepping in pays +1 now      → 1.00
V[(3, 1)] = 0.0 + GAMMA * V[(3, 2)]   # the +1 is one step away      → 0.90
V[(3, 0)] = 0.0 + GAMMA * V[(3, 1)]   # two steps away               → 0.81

# verify by simulation: roll out from (3,0), sum discounted rewards,
# average over episodes — it converges to 0.81. the number IS the future.
Real scenario — valuing orbital positions

An agent scheduling downlinks for your telemetry constellation doesn't get rewarded until data lands at the ground station. Value functions are what let it prefer "buffer 80% full, ground pass in 2 minutes" over "buffer empty, no pass for an hour" — neither state pays anything now, but their V(s) differ enormously. Without values, only immediate payoffs would steer.

— Learning Algorithms —
205

Q-Learning

Concept

Q-learning learns Q(s,a) directly from experience with the Bellman update: after each step, nudge the estimate toward what actually happened plus the best you believe you can do next — Q(s,a) += α·(r + γ·max Q(s′,·) − Q(s,a)). The term in parentheses is the TD error: the gap between the promise and the evidence. Do this enough times and the table converges to the true values of the optimal policy.

Two words carry the exam weight: it's off-policy — the update bootstraps from the best next action, so it learns about the greedy policy even while behaving ε-greedy (explore randomly with probability ε, exploit otherwise). A lookup table suffices for small worlds, and this exact algorithm — table swapped for a network — is DQN (topic 207).

The trained Q-table as a heat grid: rows are states, columns are actions, brightness is learned value. Read a row's brightest cell and you're reading the policy.
Example 
import random
Q = {(s, a): 0.0 for s in STATES for a in ACTIONS}
alpha, gamma, eps = 0.1, 0.9, 0.1

for ep in range(2000):
    s, done = (0, 0), False
    while not done:
        a = random.choice(ACTIONS) if random.random() < eps \
            else max(ACTIONS, key=lambda a: Q[(s, a)])          # ε-greedy behavior
        s2, r, done = step(s, a)
        best_next = 0.0 if done else max(Q[(s2, a2)] for a2 in ACTIONS)
        Q[(s, a)] += alpha * (r + gamma * best_next - Q[(s, a)])  # the Bellman nudge
        s = s2
Real scenario — the rover learns the craters

Run this on the Mars grid from topic 199: 2,000 episodes finish in under a second, and if you log reward-per-episode you'll watch the curve climb from −1 (falling into the crater constantly) to +0.94 (clean beeline). Plot the Q-table as the heat grid above at episodes 0, 100, 500 — you can literally watch value flow backward from the lander cell. That animation is the best RL intuition you'll ever build.

206

SARSA

Concept

SARSA (State, Action, Reward, State′, Action′ — the quintuple it updates from) is Q-learning's on-policy sibling. One term changes: instead of bootstrapping from the best next action, it bootstraps from the action it will actually take — exploratory stumbles included. So SARSA learns the value of the policy it is really running (ε-greedy, with its 10% random lurches), while Q-learning learns the value of the ideal greedy policy it isn't actually following during training.

The consequence is behavioral, and the classic demonstration is cliff walking: Q-learning learns the reward-optimal path hugging the cliff edge — and keeps falling off during training, because its ε-greedy behavior stumbles. SARSA's values include the cost of its own stumbles, so it learns a detour with a safety margin. Neither is "better": Q-learning finds the optimum, SARSA respects the risks of exploring.

Cliff walking: same world, same reward, different bootstrap. Off-policy learns the optimum; on-policy learns what's safe to actually execute while exploring.
Key distinction

Off-policy (Q-learning): learn about a different policy than the one generating behavior — enables replay buffers and learning from logged data. On-policy (SARSA, PPO): learn about the policy you are actually running — fresher, safer, but every sample is single-use. This axis reappears in topic 212's deadly triad.

Example 
# the entire difference is the bootstrap target
# Q-learning: from the BEST next action (off-policy)
target = r + gamma * max(Q[(s2, a2)] for a2 in ACTIONS)

# SARSA: from the action you will ACTUALLY take (on-policy)
a2 = eps_greedy(s2)
target = r + gamma * Q[(s2, a2)]

Q[(s, a)] += alpha * (target - Q[(s, a)])
s, a = s2, a2          # SARSA carries the chosen action forward — hence S,A,R,S',A'
Real scenario — training near a real cliff

Your rover grid has a crater rim along the shortest route. If exploration happens on real (or expensively simulated) hardware, SARSA's caution is a feature: with ε = 0.1, the Q-learning agent loses ~5% of training rovers to the rim, the SARSA agent almost none. Interviewers love this question in disguise: "your agent behaves recklessly during training — why, and what would you change?"

207

DQN

Concept

A Q-table needs one row per state — hopeless when the state is an image (Atari: 210×160 pixels) or anything continuous. DQN (Deep Q-Network) replaces the table with a neural network Q(s,a;θ) that generalizes across states. But naive "Q-learning with a net" diverges, because two assumptions of supervised learning break at once: samples arrive correlated (consecutive frames), and the training target contains the very network you're updating — the estimate chases its own tail. DeepMind's 2013–2015 Atari papers fixed both, and those two fixes are the whole exam:

  • Replay buffer: store transitions (s, a, r, s′) in a large ring buffer and train on random minibatches — decorrelates samples and reuses each experience many times.
  • Target network: compute bootstrap targets with a frozen copy θ⁻, synced every N steps — the target holds still long enough to be learned.
DQN's two stabilizers: the buffer decorrelates the data; the frozen target stops the estimate from chasing itself.
Example 
import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import DQN

env = gym.make("CartPole-v1")
model = DQN("MlpPolicy", env,
            buffer_size=50_000,             # replay buffer → decorrelated minibatches
            target_update_interval=1_000,   # frozen target net → stable bootstrap
            learning_rate=1e-3, verbose=1)
model.learn(total_timesteps=100_000)        # solved ≈ eval reward 500

# ablate either trick (buffer_size=1 or target_update_interval=1)
# and watch the reward curve collapse — see topic 212
Real scenario — CartPole as flight-control rehearsal

CartPole — keep a pole balanced by nudging a cart — is the "hello world" with the same shape as attitude control: continuous state (angle, velocity), discrete corrective actions, instability if you do nothing. Solve it with DQN, log both q-value estimates and reward to your tracking server (topic 217), and you have a template: the cubesat detumbling sim from topic 201 trains with the identical script, only the env swapped.

208

PPO

Concept

Policy-gradient methods skip value tables and adjust the policy's weights directly in the direction that makes good actions more probable. Their curse: one oversized update can wreck the policy — and since the (now broken) policy collects the next batch of data, it may never recover. PPO (Proximal Policy Optimization) fixes this with one elegant move: compute the probability ratio r = π_new(a|s) / π_old(a|s) and clip it to [1−ε, 1+ε] (ε ≈ 0.2) inside the objective. Beyond the clip, the gradient dies — so however loudly the advantage screams, the new policy can only drift a bounded distance from the old one per update. Trust regions, made simple.

Two reasons this is the single most important algorithm in the volume: it's the default for continuous control and robotics, and it is the engine of RLHF (item 141) — when an LLM is aligned with human feedback, the "PO" doing the optimizing is exactly this clipped objective, with the LLM as policy, tokens as actions, and a reward model standing in for the environment.

PPO's clip: each update is a bounded step. No single batch — however extreme — can move the policy outside the trust band around its old self.
Example 
import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import PPO

model = PPO("MlpPolicy", gym.make("LunarLander-v3"),
            clip_range=0.2,          # the ε: ratio clipped to [0.8, 1.2]
            n_steps=2048, verbose=1)
model.learn(total_timesteps=300_000)

# in the training logs, find:
#   clip_fraction  — share of samples where the clip actually engaged
#   approx_kl      — how far the new policy drifted from the old
# healthy runs: clip_fraction ~ 0.1–0.3, approx_kl small and steady
Real scenario — the same clip that aligned your chatbot

When you diagrammed RLHF's four models back in item 141 — policy, reference, reward, value — the optimizer holding it together was this exact algorithm: the clip keeps the LLM near its reference so it doesn't collapse into reward-hacked gibberish, the KL penalty backs it up. Land LunarLander with PPO first: watching clip_fraction on a 2D lander gives you real intuition for what those RLHF training curves mean.

209

A2C

Concept

A2C — Advantage Actor-Critic, synchronous — is the clean baseline PPO improved on. N environment copies step in lockstep; their experience is pooled into one batch; the actor updates along the advantage (topic 211) with a single, unclipped gradient step; repeat. Nothing protects against an oversized step — that protection is precisely what PPO added.

Why keep A2C in your vocabulary? Because it isolates the ingredients: A2C = actor-critic + parallel envs; PPO = A2C + clipped updates + multiple epochs per batch. Run both on the same environment for the same timesteps and the learning curves teach you exactly what clipping buys: PPO's curve is smoother, A2C's has cliffs where a bad batch knocked the policy over. One comparison run, permanent intuition.

Example 
import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import A2C, PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.evaluation import evaluate_policy

for Algo in (A2C, PPO):                       # same env, same budget, same seed
    model = Algo("MlpPolicy", gym.make("CartPole-v1"), seed=42, verbose=0)
    model.learn(total_timesteps=100_000)
    mean_r, std = evaluate_policy(model, model.get_env(), n_eval_episodes=20)
    print(f"{Algo.__name__}: {mean_r:.0f} ± {std:.0f}")

# typical: A2C reaches ~380 with wobble; PPO sits at 500 flat.
# the difference IS the clip.
Real scenario — the honest baseline row

When you propose PPO for the cubesat detumbling sim, a good reviewer asks "compared to what?". The A2C run is your answer: same budget, same seeds, logged side by side in MLflow (topic 217). It's cheap insurance against the classic RL embarrassment — a fancy algorithm "winning" only because nobody ran the simpler one.

210

A3C

Concept

A3C — Asynchronous Advantage Actor-Critic (DeepMind, 2016) — is a history lesson worth knowing cold. The problem: on-policy methods can't use DQN's replay buffer, but consecutive samples from one environment are hopelessly correlated. A3C's answer: run many parallel workers, each with its own environment copy, each computing gradients and pushing them to shared parameters asynchronously — no locks, no waiting. Parallelism replaced replay as the decorrelator, and slightly-stale gradients turned out to be harmless noise. It matched GPU-trained DQN on Atari using 16 CPU cores.

Why it faded: the follow-up finding that synchronous A2C works just as well and is far simpler to reason about, and PPO's clipping attacked the stability problem directly rather than statistically. Know the story, skip the implementation — "why did A3C matter and why don't we use it?" is a real interview question.

A3C's bet: many desynchronized workers make the data stream look i.i.d. — parallelism as the replay buffer for on-policy learning.
Example 
# A3C in pseudocode — know the shape, don't build it
shared_theta = init_params()

def worker():
    while not done:
        local = copy(shared_theta)          # may already be stale — that's fine
        batch = rollout(local, n_steps=20)   # own env copy
        grads = backprop(local, batch)
        apply_async(shared_theta, grads)    # push without locking

# 2016: 16 CPU workers ≈ GPU DQN on Atari
# today: sync A2C is as good and simpler; PPO is more stable — use PPO
Real scenario — the one-paragraph answer

Write this from memory and you own the topic: "A3C solved on-policy sample correlation with asynchronous parallel workers instead of a replay buffer, proving deep RL on commodity CPUs. It faded because synchronous A2C matched it with less complexity, and PPO's clipped objective fixed stability at the source. Its real legacy is the parallel-rollout pattern every modern library uses — including the RLlib workers in topic 215."

211

Actor-Critic

Concept

Actor-critic is not one algorithm but the two-part template under A2C, A3C, PPO, and SAC. The actor is the policy π(a|s) — it decides. The critic estimates values V(s) — it judges. Why bother with the critic? Raw policy gradients (REINFORCE) learn from total episode returns, which are astronomically noisy: a good action in a doomed episode gets punished. The critic supplies a baseline: the advantage A = r + γ·V(s′) − V(s) asks "was that action better than expected from here?" — subtracting expectations cancels most of the noise, and learning accelerates dramatically.

  • Actor update: push probability toward actions with A > 0, away from A < 0.
  • Critic update: plain regression of V(s) toward observed returns.
  • In RLHF fine-tuning, the "value head" bolted onto the LLM is the critic — same template, 70B-parameter actor.
The actor decides, the critic judges: their difference — the advantage — is the low-variance signal that makes policy gradients practical.
Example 
import torch.nn as nn

class ActorCritic(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, obs_dim, n_actions):
        super().__init__()
        self.body   = nn.Sequential(nn.Linear(obs_dim, 64), nn.Tanh())
        self.actor  = nn.Linear(64, n_actions)   # → action logits (the policy)
        self.critic = nn.Linear(64, 1)           # → V(s)         (the judge)

    def forward(self, obs):
        h = self.body(obs)
        return self.actor(h), self.critic(h)     # shared trunk, two heads

# advantage = r + gamma * V(s2) - V(s)   ← the critic's whole purpose
Real scenario — annotate it once, own it forever

Open Stable Baselines3's policies.py and find action_net and value_net — the actor and critic heads, sharing a feature extractor exactly like the snippet above. Annotate where the advantage is computed in ppo.py, and you'll never again blank on "walk me through actor-critic" — you'll be describing code you've read, from the library you actually train the lander with.

212

Deep RL (general)

Concept

Deep RL is what happens when function approximation meets a moving target, and the honest summary is: it breaks in characteristic ways, and knowing them is a skill. The centerpiece is Sutton's deadly triad — combine (1) bootstrapping (targets built from your own estimates), (2) off-policy data (replay from old behavior), and (3) function approximation (networks that generalize errors across states) and value estimates can spiral to infinity. DQN sits squarely on all three; its replay buffer and target network are engineering duct tape holding the triad together.

  • Sample inefficiency: millions of environment steps for tasks a human learns in minutes — fine in simulators, brutal on hardware.
  • Reward hacking (topic 202): the agent optimizes the letter of the reward, never its spirit.
  • Seed sensitivity: the same code and hyperparameters can succeed or fail on different random seeds. A single learning curve is an anecdote, not a result.

Healthy skepticism is the professional posture: prefer the simplest algorithm that works, run 5+ seeds, and ask "what loophole did it find?" before celebrating a high score.

Each corner is standard practice alone; together they can make value estimates explode. Every DQN stabilizer exists because of this triangle.
Example 
# meet the triad personally: remove DQN's anchor
model = DQN("MlpPolicy", env, target_update_interval=1)   # target = online net
model.learn(100_000)   # watch the logs: q-values balloon, reward collapses

# and never trust one seed:
for seed in (0, 1, 2, 3, 4):
    DQN("MlpPolicy", env, seed=seed).learn(50_000)
# 5 curves, 5 different stories — report mean ± std, or you're publishing luck
Real scenario — reading RL claims like a reviewer

A vendor demo claims RL "optimizes satellite downlink scheduling 40% better than heuristics" — one environment, one learning curve, no seeds, no baseline. You now know the three questions that puncture or validate it: how many seeds? what does the simple baseline (topic 209's lesson) score? what loophole might the reward have? Skepticism here isn't cynicism — it's literacy.

— RL in Practice —
213

Stable Baselines3

Concept

Stable Baselines3 (SB3) is the sane default for applying RL rather than researching it: reliable, tested PyTorch implementations of the standard algorithms — PPO, A2C, DQN, SAC, TD3 — behind a scikit-learn-feeling API: construct, .learn(), .save(), .load(), evaluate. This matters more in RL than anywhere else, because RL implementations are notoriously easy to get subtly wrong — the famous "37 implementation details of PPO" blog post exists for a reason. SB3's versions are verified against reference results, so when your run fails you can suspect your environment and reward, not the algorithm's plumbing.

  • One-line algorithm swaps make honest baselines (topic 209) nearly free.
  • Built-in evaluate_policy, checkpointing callbacks, vectorized envs, TensorBoard logging.
  • Its boundary: single-machine training and standard algorithms. Beyond that, RLlib (topic 215).
Example 
import gymnasium as gym
from stable_baselines3 import PPO
from stable_baselines3.common.evaluation import evaluate_policy

env = gym.make("LunarLander-v3")
model = PPO("MlpPolicy", env, seed=7, verbose=1)
model.learn(total_timesteps=200_000)
model.save("lander_ppo")                          # train once...

loaded = PPO.load("lander_ppo")                   # ...reload anywhere
mean_r, std = evaluate_policy(loaded, env, n_eval_episodes=20)
print(f"reward {mean_r:.0f} ± {std:.0f}")

# swap the algorithm: PPO → A2C. one word. that's the whole point.
Real scenario — twenty lines to a landed probe

LunarLander is the closest gym env to your space world: thrust, gravity, a landing pad, fuel penalties. The script above — train, save, reload, evaluate — is your permanent SB3 template; the custom telemetry env you'll write in topic 214 drops into the same five lines. Keep the saved lander_ppo.zip: in topic 218 it becomes your first registered model version.

214

Gymnasium

Concept

Gymnasium (the maintained fork of OpenAI Gym) is the standard contract between environments and algorithms: reset() returns (obs, info); step(action) returns (obs, reward, terminated, truncated, info); and the env declares its observation_space and action_space up front so libraries can build matching networks automatically. Two endings are deliberately distinct: terminated means the MDP itself ended (crashed, reached goal — bootstrap value 0), while truncated means a time limit cut the episode (the state still has future value). Confusing the two silently corrupts value estimates.

The practical superpower: wrapping your own problem as a Gymnasium env is how you make it RL-ready. Implement four methods, and every algorithm in SB3 and RLlib plugs in unchanged.

The Gymnasium contract: two functions, two declared spaces, two distinct endings. Anything that speaks it can be trained by any RL library.
Example 
import gymnasium as gym
import numpy as np

class RoverGrid(gym.Env):
    def __init__(self):
        self.observation_space = gym.spaces.Box(0, 3, shape=(2,), dtype=np.int64)
        self.action_space      = gym.spaces.Discrete(4)      # N/S/E/W

    def reset(self, seed=None, options=None):
        super().reset(seed=seed)
        self.pos = np.array([0, 0])
        return self.pos.copy(), {}

    def step(self, a):
        self.pos = move(self.pos, a)                          # topic 199's dynamics
        done = bool((self.pos == GOAL).all())
        r = 1.0 if done else -0.01
        return self.pos.copy(), r, done, False, {}            # terminated, truncated

PPO("MlpPolicy", RoverGrid()).learn(50_000)                 # it just plugs in
Real scenario — making your telemetry sim RL-ready

You already have a Python simulator of satellite battery dynamics fed by historical Kafka telemetry. Wrap it in the four-method class above — observations: charge, rate, sunlight; actions: heater on/off/eco — and it instantly becomes trainable by every algorithm in this volume. The env wrapper, not the algorithm, is the actual engineering work of applied RL.

215

RLlib

Concept

RLlib is Ray's distributed RL library — the tool for when training outgrows one machine. Its architecture separates the learner (gradient updates, usually on GPU) from rollout workers (environment simulation, fanned out across a cluster's CPUs), with Ray handling scheduling, fault tolerance, and data movement. It adds cluster-scale extras SB3 doesn't attempt: population-based training, multi-agent environments, and tight integration with Ray Tune for hyperparameter search.

The honest trade-off: RLlib's configuration surface is an order of magnitude larger than SB3's, and you inherit a distributed system's operational weight. Rule of thumb — SB3 until a single machine of simulators is the bottleneck; RLlib when you need hundreds of parallel rollouts or PBT. Knowing where the line sits is the interview answer.

RLlib's split: one learner, many rollout workers across a Ray cluster. SB3 fills a machine; RLlib fills a datacenter.
Example 
from ray.rllib.algorithms.ppo import PPOConfig

config = (
    PPOConfig()
    .environment("LunarLander-v3")
    .env_runners(num_env_runners=8)          # 8 parallel rollout workers
    .training(train_batch_size=32_000)       # big batches from pooled rollouts
)
algo = config.build()
for i in range(20):
    result = algo.train()
    print(i, result["env_runners"]["episode_return_mean"])

# same PPO math as SB3 — the difference is where the rollouts run
Real scenario — when the sim farm outgrows your laptop

Your cubesat detumbling env from topic 214 runs at 300 steps/second — PPO needs 50M steps for the hard config, which is two days on one machine. Point RLlib at your existing EKS cluster with num_env_runners=200 and the same training finishes over lunch. That's the whole pitch: not better math, just the rollout loop spread across the Kubernetes cluster you already operate.

— The ML Lifecycle —
216

ML lifecycle (concept)

Concept

Here begins MLOps, and its founding insight is one mindset shift: the ML lifecycle is a loop, not a line. Data → train → evaluate → deploy → monitor → retrain → back to data. In classic software, shipping is the finish line because code doesn't rot by itself. A model is different: it froze a snapshot of the world into weights, and the world keeps changing underneath it — sensors get recalibrated, user behavior shifts, upstream schemas evolve. Shipping is the midpoint.

Every tool in the rest of this volume is a station on this loop: DVC versions the data, MLflow/W&B track training and evaluation, the registry and CI/CD gate deployment, monitoring and drift detection watch production, and their alarms trigger the next lap. Hold the loop in your head and every MLOps conversation becomes "which station are we talking about?"

The lifecycle as it actually is: a loop. Every station has a tool, and every deploy schedules the investigation that leads to the next retrain.
Example 
# the loop, written down as pipeline stages (dvc.yaml style)
stages:
  ingest:    { cmd: python ingest.py,  outs: [data/lightcurves] }
  train:     { cmd: python train.py,   deps: [data/lightcurves], outs: [model.pt] }
  evaluate:  { cmd: python eval.py,    deps: [model.pt], metrics: [metrics.json] }
  deploy:    { cmd: python deploy.py,  deps: [metrics.json] }

# monitoring runs in prod, outside the DAG —
# when drift fires (topic 221), the loop re-enters at ingest
Real scenario — the exoplanet classifier's year in production

Your exoplanet classifier shipped in January. February: TESS releases a new sector — data station. March: a retrain, tracked as runs — train station. April: the eval gate blocks a regression — evaluate. May: v3 promoted — deploy. August: drift alarm on a telemetry feature after a pipeline change upstream — monitor — and the loop starts again. One model, twelve months, three full laps. That's the job.

217

Experiment tracking

Concept

Experiment tracking means logging, automatically and for every run: the parameters (hyperparameters, config), the metrics (loss curves, eval scores), the code version (git commit), the data version, and the artifacts (model weights, plots). The alternative is the folder graveyard — results_final_v2/, model_best_REAL.pt — which makes the most important question in applied ML, "which model was that and how do I reproduce it?", unanswerable within a month.

The discipline: a run is the atomic unit. Anything that influenced the result gets attached to the run, by code, not by memory. Tracked runs become a queryable table — sort by metric, diff two configs, hand a colleague the exact run ID. Interviewers probe this hard because it's the habit that separates notebook science from engineering.

"Which model was that?" — with tracking, the answer is a query. Without it, archaeology.
Example 
import mlflow

mlflow.set_experiment("exoplanet-cnn")
for lr in (1e-2, 1e-3, 1e-4):
    with mlflow.start_run():
        mlflow.log_params({"lr": lr, "layers": 4, "data": "tess_q1_q4@v3"})
        model, auc = train(lr=lr)
        mlflow.log_metric("val_auc", auc)
        mlflow.log_artifact("confusion_matrix.png")

# $ mlflow ui  →  three runs side by side, sortable by val_auc,
#                each pinned to its git commit and data version
Real scenario — the quarterly retrain audit

Your exoplanet classifier retrains every time TESS drops a sector. Six months in, a teammate asks why March's model outperforms June's. Because every retrain was a tracked run, the answer takes three minutes: same code commit, same hyperparameters — but June's run logged data: tess_q1_q6@v5, and v5 silently included a sector with a known noisy detector. Without tracking, that's a week of forensic guessing.

218

Model registry

Concept

A model registry is a versioned store for trained models with two superpowers experiment tracking alone doesn't give you: stage transitions (a version moves through none → staging → production → archived, with review baked into the promotion) and lineage (every version links back to the exact run — code, data, params — that produced it). It exists to answer the two questions that get asked at 2 a.m.: "exactly what is running in prod?" and "can we roll back, right now?"

The operational trick that makes it work: serving code loads by name and stage, not by file path — models:/exoplanet-clf@production. Promotion and rollback become moving a pointer, with zero changes to deployment code.

Key distinction

Tracking (topic 217) records everything you tried — hundreds of runs, most disposable. The registry holds the few graduates — versions worthy of a stage. Runs are the lab notebook; the registry is the pharmacy shelf.

Versions, stages, lineage. Prod code asks for "@production" — so rollback is a pointer move, not a rebuild-and-redeploy scramble.
Example 
import mlflow

# graduate a tracked run's model into the registry → version 3
mlflow.register_model("runs:/47a3f9/model", "exoplanet-clf")

client = mlflow.MlflowClient()
client.set_registered_model_alias("exoplanet-clf", "production", version=3)

# serving code — no paths, no 'model_best_REAL.pt', ever:
model = mlflow.pyfunc.load_model("models:/exoplanet-clf@production")
Real scenario — the 2 a.m. rollback

Friday's promotion of v3 starts misclassifying eclipsing binaries as planets over the weekend. On-call fix: set_registered_model_alias("exoplanet-clf", "production", version=2), restart the FastAPI pods — ninety seconds, no rebuild. Monday's postmortem opens v3's lineage link and finds the run that produced it trained on the noisy-detector data version from topic 217. Registry plus tracking turned an outage into a query.

219

CI/CD for models

Concept

CI/CD for models applies software delivery discipline to ML, with one twist: datasets and metrics become first-class citizens of the pipeline. A model PR can be "broken" without a single line of code changing — new data, same code, worse model — so the pipeline gates on evidence: validate the data (schema, ranges, nulls), retrain, run the evaluation suite, and block the release if metrics regress. The eval suite plays the role unit tests play in software: an executable definition of "still works".

  • CI: every PR triggers data validation + eval; a metric below threshold is a red X, same as a failing test.
  • CD: merged changes deploy to staging automatically; production promotion goes through the registry (topic 218).
  • CT (continuous training): the pipeline can also be triggered by data — a drift alarm or a scheduled retrain, no human PR involved.
Model CI: the gate is a metric on an eval suite, not a compile. Evidence, or no deploy.
Example 
# .github/workflows/model-ci.yml
on: pull_request
jobs:
  eval-gate:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt
      - run: python eval.py --out metrics.json
      - run: |
          python -c "import json, sys; \
            m = json.load(open('metrics.json')); \
            sys.exit(0 if m['auc'] >= 0.91 else 1)"   # red X if regressed
Real scenario — the gate that caught a silent regression

A teammate's PR to Mission Control RAG swaps the embedding model "for speed". Code review looks fine — it's three lines. But your CI runs the RAGAS eval suite on every PR, and faithfulness drops from 0.88 to 0.79: red X, merge blocked, with the metric diff right in the check output. Nobody had to notice the regression; the pipeline is the noticing.

220

Monitoring

Concept

Model monitoring watches two layers, and the trap is stopping at the first. Layer one is the serving system — latency, error rate, throughput — standard SRE fare, covered by your existing Prometheus/Grafana stack. Layer two is the predictions themselves — output distribution, confidence histograms, class balance, feature statistics. The uncomfortable truth that justifies layer two: a model can be perfectly healthy as a service while being completely wrong as a model — 200 OK, 40 ms, nonsense predictions, forever.

  • Log every prediction (inputs, output, confidence, model version) — it's the raw material for drift detection (topic 221) and future retraining.
  • Alert on distribution changes, not just errors: "planet rate jumped from 3% to 31%" should page someone even though nothing threw.
Two dashboards or you're blind in one eye: the left one says the service is up; only the right one says the model has lost its mind.
Example 
from fastapi import FastAPI
import time, logging, collections

app = FastAPI()
pred_counts = collections.Counter()               # rolling class balance

@app.post("/classify")
def classify(curve: LightCurve):
    t0 = time.perf_counter()
    label, conf = model.predict(curve.values)
    pred_counts[label] += 1                       # layer 2: the model view
    logging.info("pred", extra={
        "label": label, "conf": round(conf, 3),
        "model_version": "v3",
        "latency_ms": (time.perf_counter() - t0) * 1000,   # layer 1: the service view
    })
    return {"label": label, "confidence": conf}
Real scenario — 200 OK, wrong for six weeks

A ground-station firmware update rescales one telemetry channel by a factor of 10. Your FastAPI anomaly endpoint keeps serving: latency perfect, zero errors — and every prediction subtly wrong, because the model never saw values in that range. The service dashboard stayed green for six weeks. The prediction-distribution log above would have flagged it in an hour: anomaly rate tripled overnight, nothing else changed. That log line is your smoke detector — and topic 221 is the alarm.

221

Drift detection

Concept

Drift is the reason the lifecycle is a loop, and it comes in two species. Data drift: the input distribution P(x) changes — inputs no longer look like the training data (a sensor recalibrated, a new customer segment arrives). Concept drift: the input→output relationship P(y|x) itself changes — the same inputs now mean something different (fraud tactics evolve, an instrument ages). Both degrade the model silently: no exception, no 500, just accuracy quietly rotting.

The smoke alarm is statistical: keep a reference window (training-era data) and compare it to a live window feature by feature — a KS test per numeric feature, PSI or chi-squared for categoricals. A drift alarm is a trigger to investigate, not proof the model is wrong — but ignored alarms are how six-week silent failures happen.

Key distinction

Data drift is visible in inputs alone — you can detect it with no labels. Concept drift needs ground truth (or a labeled sample) to catch, because the inputs may look perfectly normal while their meaning shifts. That asymmetry drives real monitoring architecture: input tests run continuously; label-based checks run whenever truth arrives.

Data drift: this month's feature distribution has walked away from the training era's. Nothing crashed — that's exactly the problem.
Example 
from scipy import stats

# same feature, two time windows
train_win = telemetry["battery_temp"]["2026-05"]     # reference (training era)
live_win  = telemetry["battery_temp"]["2026-08"]     # current month

ks, p = stats.ks_2samp(train_win, live_win)
if p < 0.01:
    alert(f"drift in battery_temp: KS={ks:.3f}, p={p:.1e}")

# run per feature, on a schedule. the alarm is a trigger to investigate —
# and usually the entry point back into the lifecycle loop (topic 216)
Real scenario — drift in the telemetry features

After a satellite firmware update, the heater duty-cycle feature your anomaly classifier relies on shifts its whole distribution — new power-management logic, same physics. Your nightly KS-test job flags it within a day: heater_duty: KS=0.42. Investigation confirms the model was trained on pre-update behavior; you retrain on a post-update window and the loop closes. Without the test, this is topic 220's six-week silent failure.

222

A/B testing

Concept

Offline evaluation says the new model is better on old data. A/B testing is the honest final exam: route a fraction of live traffic to the challenger, measure a business metric (not AUC — acceptance rate, click-through, resolution time), and promote only if the difference is statistically significant. Your stats topics (#54–56) cash in here: hypothesis test for the verdict, and — the step everyone skips — a power analysis before starting, because detecting a 1% lift needs far more samples than intuition suggests. An underpowered test that "showed no difference" showed nothing at all.

  • Randomize per user/session, not per request — one user seeing both models contaminates the metric.
  • One primary metric, declared in advance; peeking at twenty metrics until one is significant is p-hacking.
  • Variants: canary release (tiny fraction, watching for breakage) and shadow mode (challenger scores traffic but its answers aren't shown) — cheaper, weaker evidence.
The challenger earns production on a live business metric with significance — not on an offline score.
Example 
import numpy as np
from scipy import stats

# 2,400 sessions per arm: did the analyst accept the answer?
rng = np.random.default_rng(0)
a = rng.binomial(1, 0.118, 2400)          # champion   ~11.8%
b = rng.binomial(1, 0.131, 2400)          # challenger ~13.1%

_, p = stats.ttest_ind(a, b)
print(f"p = {p:.3f}")                       # < 0.05 → promote challenger

# BEFORE running: power analysis for a +1% absolute lift at 80% power
# → ~14,000 sessions per arm. most "quick A/B tests" are underpowered.
Real scenario — two rerankers, one honest verdict

Offline, your new cross-encoder reranker beats the old one on RAGAS. But Mission Control RAG's users are the real metric, so you route 10% of analysts to it and track answer-acceptance for two weeks. Result: +1.3 points, p = 0.03 — promote, via the registry alias from topic 218. Had you shipped on the offline score alone and been wrong, you'd never have known: prod has no RAGAS, only users.

— The MLOps Toolbelt —
223

MLflow

Concept

MLflow is the open-source default of MLOps: tracking (topic 217), the model registry (topic 218), and model packaging in one self-hostable tool — a Python package, a UI server, and a database, no vendor required. Its killer convenience is mlflow.autolog(): one line that instruments sklearn, PyTorch, XGBoost, LightGBM and friends to log params, metrics, and the trained model automatically — the lowest-friction on-ramp to tracked experiments that exists.

  • Tracking: runs, params, metrics, artifacts, the comparison UI.
  • Registry: versions, aliases/stages, lineage back to runs.
  • Models: a packaging format (pyfunc) that makes any model loadable and servable the same way, whatever framework trained it.
Three lifecycle stations in one self-hostable tool: scripts log in, serving loads out.
Example 
import mlflow
mlflow.autolog()                              # one line: params, metrics, model, env

from sklearn.ensemble import GradientBoostingClassifier
clf = GradientBoostingClassifier(learning_rate=0.05, max_depth=3)
clf.fit(X_train, y_train)
print(clf.score(X_test, y_test))              # logged automatically too

# run it twice with different params, then:
#   $ mlflow ui        → compare both runs at localhost:5000
# nothing about the training code had to change
Real scenario — one server for the whole space stack

You run MLflow on a small EC2 instance with S3 as the artifact store and Postgres as the backend — one docker-compose file. Every project in your portfolio logs to it: exoplanet-classifier retrains, the RL lander runs from topic 213, even RAGAS eval scores from Mission Control RAG logged as run metrics. When a recruiter asks "how do you manage experiments?", you screen-share one UI with a year of evidence.

224

Weights & Biases

Concept

Weights & Biases (W&B) is the hosted tracker deep-learning teams tend to prefer: live dashboards that stream during training (watch loss curves update mid-epoch from any browser), team reports, artifact versioning — and its standout feature, sweeps: a managed hyperparameter search service. You declare a search space and strategy (grid, random, Bayesian) in a config; any machine running wandb.agent pulls the next suggested config; results flow into a parallel-coordinates plot that shows at a glance which hyperparameters actually matter.

Trade-off vs MLflow in one line: W&B is hosted polish — zero setup, your metrics on their servers; MLflow is self-host control — your infra, your data. Teams doing heavy DL often run W&B for research velocity and MLflow for the production registry.

Example 
import wandb

sweep_cfg = {
    "method": "bayes",                                  # or grid / random
    "metric": {"name": "val_auc", "goal": "maximize"},
    "parameters": {
        "lr":         {"distribution": "log_uniform_values",
                       "min": 1e-4, "max": 1e-1},
        "batch_size": {"values": [32, 64, 128]},
    },
}
sweep_id = wandb.sweep(sweep_cfg, project="lightcurve-cnn")
wandb.agent(sweep_id, function=train, count=30)         # 30 runs, live dashboard
Real scenario — the sweep that ended a week of guessing

Your CNN on TESS light curves plateaus at 0.89 AUC and you've been hand-tuning learning rates for days. A 30-run Bayesian sweep overnight produces the parallel-coordinates plot that settles it: every run above 0.91 has lr between 2e-4 and 8e-4, and batch size barely matters. Two insights, one plot, zero further debate — and the plot itself goes straight into your project write-up.

225

DVC

Concept

DVC (Data Version Control) gives git-like versioning to what git can't hold: multi-gigabyte datasets and model files. The mechanism is elegant: dvc add data.parquet hashes the file, moves the bytes to a remote store (S3, GCS, a shared drive), and leaves behind a tiny .dvc pointer file containing the hash — and that is what git commits. git checkout any historical commit, run dvc checkout, and the matching data bytes are restored: code and data travel together through history.

Its second act: pipelines. dvc.yaml declares stages with dependencies and outputs (like the one in topic 216), and dvc repro re-runs only the stages whose inputs actually changed — make for ML, with data-aware caching.

Two commits share one blob (data unchanged); the third points at a new hash. Checkout any commit and dvc restores its exact bytes.
Example 
# track a 2 GB dataset the git way
$ dvc init && dvc remote add -d store s3://brain-ml-data
$ dvc add data/lightcurves.parquet            # bytes → S3, pointer stays
$ git add data/lightcurves.parquet.dvc .gitignore
$ git commit -m "track TESS Q1–Q4 lightcurves (v1)"

# dataset updated and committed as v2 … now roll the DATA back:
$ git checkout HEAD~1 -- data/lightcurves.parquet.dvc
$ dvc checkout                                # bytes restored to v1, from the hash
Real scenario — "which dataset trained prod?"

The topic 218 postmortem asked exactly this. Because your training repo tracks lightcurves.parquet with DVC, the tagged release commit for model v2 contains a pointer with one specific hash — check it out, dvc checkout, and you are holding byte-identical training data from four months ago. Reproducibility stops being a slide-deck word and becomes two commands.

226

Kubeflow

Concept

Kubeflow is ML pipelines as Kubernetes-native workflows: every pipeline step is a container, the pipeline is a DAG, and K8s schedules the whole thing — GPU steps on GPU nodes, parallel branches fanned out, retries and artifacts handled by the platform. Around the pipeline engine sits a platform suite: Katib (hyperparameter tuning), KServe (model serving), notebook servers, and multi-tenant namespaces.

It is deliberately heavyweight, enterprise-scale machinery, and knowing when it's justified is the actual skill: a good fit when your organization already runs Kubernetes seriously and many teams need shared, governed ML infrastructure with per-step GPU scheduling. Overkill for a small team with a handful of models — a simpler orchestrator (Airflow, Prefect) plus MLflow covers that at a tenth of the operational cost. Airflow orchestrates any tasks; Kubeflow is opinionated about ML on K8s — that contrast is a favorite interview question.

Kubeflow: the ML pipeline compiled down to Kubernetes primitives — powerful at platform scale, heavy for one small team.
Example 
from kfp import dsl

@dsl.component(base_image="python:3.12")
def train(data_path: str) -> str:
    ...                                        # runs as its own container

@dsl.pipeline(name="exoplanet-retrain")
def pipeline(data_path: str = "s3://tess/q1-q4"):
    v = validate(data_path=data_path)
    t = train(data_path=v.output)              # each step → a pod on the cluster
    evaluate(model=t.output)

# compile → upload → the DAG runs on K8s, GPU steps on GPU nodes
Real scenario — knowing when to say no

Your solo exoplanet project does not need Kubeflow: a GitHub Action (topic 219) plus MLflow covers its whole loop. But when you interview at an org running 40 models across six teams on EKS — retrains needing GPU scheduling, per-team quotas, audited pipelines — you can explain exactly why Kubeflow earns its overhead there and where the Airflow-vs-Kubeflow line sits. Knowing when a tool is too much is what "architect" means on your title.
