— SQL Mastery · items 227–232 —
227

SQL fundamentals

Concept

SQL is declarative set logic: you describe the result you want, and the engine's planner decides how to compute it. You never write loops; you describe shapes of data. Fluency here is assumed, silently, in every data conversation — nobody will ever say "we need someone who knows SELECT," they simply expect it the way they expect typing.

The single fact that unlocks the whole language: clauses execute in a fixed logical order that is not the order you write them — FROM → WHERE → GROUP BY → HAVING → SELECT → ORDER BY. Every classic confusion dissolves once you see this.

  • WHERE filters rows before grouping — cheap, do as much here as possible.
  • HAVING filters groups after aggregation — it can see COUNT(*), WHERE cannot.
  • SELECT aliases don't exist yet in WHERE (it runs earlier) but do exist in ORDER BY (it runs last).
  • GROUP BY collapses each group to exactly one row — anything you SELECT must be grouped or aggregated.
The pipeline every SELECT statement actually runs. Memorize this order and half of SQL's "weird rules" become obvious.
Example 
-- which satellites had 3+ weak-signal passes this week?
SELECT sat_id,
       COUNT(*)                AS weak_passes,
       ROUND(AVG(snr_db), 1)   AS avg_snr
FROM   passes
WHERE  started_at >= now() - interval '7 days'  -- rows filtered BEFORE grouping
  AND  snr_db < 12
GROUP BY sat_id
HAVING COUNT(*) >= 3                            -- groups filtered AFTER aggregation
ORDER BY weak_passes DESC;
Real scenario — nightly telemetry triage

Your satellite-telemetry Postgres holds every ground-station pass. Ops asks: "which birds are degrading?" That's one GROUP BY + HAVING, answered in seconds — no pandas, no notebook, no export. The exercise in the ladder is exactly right: load a CSV into SQLite and answer five real analytics questions with SQL only, until reaching for pandas first feels like the detour it is.

228

SQL joins

Concept

A join matches rows from two tables on a key. INNER keeps only rows that match on both sides. LEFT keeps everything on the left, filling the right side with NULLs where no match exists. FULL keeps both sides, NULL-padding whichever is missing. The choice is never cosmetic — it decides which rows silently vanish from your report.

The trap that bites everyone, eventually, in production: duplicate join keys multiply rows. If a key appears twice on the right, every matching left row appears twice in the output — and every SUM and COUNT downstream is silently inflated. When an aggregate looks "about double what it should be," suspect the join before the data.

  • Anti-join idiom: LEFT JOIN … WHERE right.id IS NULL — "rows on the left with no partner." Interview staple.
  • Filters on the right table of a LEFT JOIN belong in the ON clause — putting them in WHERE quietly turns your LEFT into an INNER.
Three join types as overlapping row-sets. Shaded = rows that survive into the result. NULLs fill the unmatched side.
Example 
-- every satellite, with its pass count — INCLUDING the silent ones
SELECT s.sat_id, s.name, COUNT(p.pass_id) AS passes_24h
FROM   satellites s
LEFT JOIN passes p
       ON  p.sat_id = s.sat_id
       AND p.started_at >= now() - interval '24 hours'  -- filter in ON, not WHERE
GROUP BY s.sat_id, s.name;

-- INNER JOIN would drop satellites with zero passes —
-- which are exactly the ones ops needs to see
Real scenario — the doubled downlink report

Your telemetry warehouse joins fact_downlinks to a ground-station table. Svalbard station was decommissioned and re-added, so its key appears twice — and total downlinked gigabytes exactly doubles for every pass through that station. Do the ladder's exercise for real: build the duplicate-key case on purpose, predict the row count, and watch the multiplication happen. You'll never un-see it.

229

SQL window functions

Concept

Window functions are aggregates that don't collapse rows. GROUP BY squashes each group into one row; a window function computes over a group — the window — but writes the answer onto every row, keeping the original grain intact. The OVER (…) clause defines the window: PARTITION BY splits rows into groups, ORDER BY sequences them, and an optional frame (ROWS 2 PRECEDING) slides a boundary within the partition.

This is the line between basic SQL and interview-passing SQL. Three patterns cover most of what you'll be asked:

  • Top-N per group: ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY g ORDER BY x DESC), then filter rn <= N in an outer query.
  • Deltas over time: LAG(x) OVER (…) pulls the previous row's value onto this row — subtraction gives the change.
  • Running totals: SUM(x) OVER (ORDER BY ts) accumulates as it walks the ordering.
Key distinction

GROUP BY answers "what is the average per satellite?" — one row per satellite. A window answers "how does this reading compare to its satellite's average?" — every reading keeps its row, now enriched with context. If the question contains "per X, compared to…", it's a window.

A 3-row frame slides over battery-voltage telemetry: row t5's moving average is computed from t3–t5, and every row keeps its own answer.
Example 
-- latest 2 readings per satellite, each with its delta vs the previous reading
SELECT * FROM (
  SELECT sat_id, ts, battery_v,
         battery_v - LAG(battery_v) OVER w                AS delta_v,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY sat_id
                            ORDER BY ts DESC)            AS rn
  FROM   telemetry
  WINDOW w AS (PARTITION BY sat_id ORDER BY ts)
) t
WHERE rn <= 2;   -- top-N-per-group: filter the ROW_NUMBER in an outer query
Real scenario — battery discharge slope

Anomaly detection on your telemetry stream starts life as SQL: LAG(battery_v) per satellite gives the discharge delta per reading, and any bird whose rolling 3-reading average drops faster than 0.2 V/orbit gets flagged before the exoplanet-observation window opens. Do the ladder's exercise verbatim too — top-2-products-per-category and month-over-month revenue with LAG — because that exact pair shows up in interviews constantly.

230

Query optimization

Concept

The database is honest with you if you ask: EXPLAIN shows the plan the engine chose; EXPLAIN ANALYZE runs it and shows real timings. The pattern to hunt for is a Seq Scan — reading every row of a big table — where an Index Scan should be. An index is a sorted B-tree over chosen columns; the fix is almost always an index that matches the query's filter and join columns, in the right order.

  • Sargable predicates: the index is on ts, so ts >= '2026-08-01' can use it — but date(ts) = '2026-08-01' cannot, because wrapping the column in a function hides it from the index. Rewrite as a range.
  • Avoid SELECT *: fewer columns means smaller rows over the wire and, when the index covers everything you asked for, an index-only scan that never touches the table.
  • Indexes aren't free — every write must maintain them. Index what you filter and join on, not everything.
The plan flip you're engineering for: sequential scan over a million rows becomes a B-tree descent to exactly the rows that match.
Example 
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT sat_id, ts, snr_db FROM passes
WHERE  sat_id = 'NOAA-19' AND ts >= '2026-08-01';
--> Seq Scan on passes (actual time=0.4..941.8 rows=42) ... 942 ms

CREATE INDEX idx_passes_sat_ts ON passes (sat_id, ts);

--> rerun: Index Scan using idx_passes_sat_ts ... 0.8 ms
-- sargable:      ts >= '2026-08-01'      (range on the raw column — index used)
-- NOT sargable:  date(ts) = '2026-08-01' (function hides the column — full scan)
Real scenario — the RAG metadata filter that got slow

Mission Control RAG filters chunks by mission_id and date range before the vector search. At 40k chunks nobody noticed; at 4M the pre-filter alone takes 1.2 s per query. One EXPLAIN ANALYZE, one composite index on (mission_id, published_at), and retrieval latency drops under 10 ms — the single highest-leverage 15 minutes in the whole system.

231

PostgreSQL

Concept

PostgreSQL is the default serious open-source database — and, quietly, an AI platform. Three extensions of plain relational storage matter for your work: JSONB stores documents as binary JSON you can index and query inside; built-in full-text search (tsvector) gives ranked keyword retrieval; and pgvector adds an embedding column type with distance operators, so cosine similarity becomes an ORDER BY.

The strategic consequence: one database can serve your whole RAG stack — document metadata, keyword search, and vector search in a single system, joined in a single query, backed up by a single process. Before reaching for a dedicated vector DB, ask whether Postgres already does the job.

One Postgres instance serving all three retrieval modes of a RAG system — documents, keywords, and vectors — joinable in one SQL statement.
Example 
CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector;

CREATE TABLE chunks (
  id      bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  doc     jsonb,            -- raw mission-log metadata, queryable in place
  body_ts tsvector,         -- full-text search column
  emb     vector(1536)      -- the embedding
);

SELECT id, doc->>'mission' AS mission
FROM   chunks
WHERE  doc->>'source' = 'apollo_reports'       -- filter inside the JSON
ORDER BY emb <=> '[0.02, -0.11, ...]'::vector  -- cosine distance, plain SQL
LIMIT  5;
Real scenario — collapsing the RAG stack

Version 1 of Mission Control RAG ran Postgres for metadata plus a separate vector DB, with sync bugs between them (deleted reports whose embeddings lived on as ghosts). Version 2 is one Postgres with pgvector: the chunk row, its JSONB metadata, and its embedding are the same row, so a DELETE is a delete everywhere. Fewer moving parts, one backup, and metadata filters + vector search happen in a single query plan.

232

MySQL (deepen)

Concept

MySQL is the other giant — everywhere in existing companies, and you will inherit it far more often than you choose it. The part worth knowing deeply is InnoDB, the default storage engine: it provides row-level locking, crash recovery, and — its most distinctive trait — a clustered primary-key index, meaning the table itself is physically stored in primary-key order and every secondary index carries the PK to reach the row. MySQL has had a real JSON type since 5.7, so "MySQL can't do documents" is folklore.

The professional habit: know where the two engines genuinely differ because you verified it, not because you read a listicle. The ladder's exercise is exactly this — five differences you personally ran on both engines.

Upsert syntax

PG: ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE · MySQL: ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE

FULL OUTER JOIN

PG has it; MySQL doesn't — you emulate with LEFT ∪ RIGHT via UNION.

Transactional DDL

PG rolls back a failed CREATE TABLE inside a transaction; MySQL auto-commits DDL.

Default isolation

PG: READ COMMITTED · InnoDB: REPEATABLE READ. Different phantom behavior.

RETURNING

PG returns changed rows inline from INSERT/UPDATE/DELETE; MySQL needs a second SELECT.

Identifier quoting

PG: "double quotes" · MySQL: `backticks`. Bites every cross-dialect migration.

Example 
-- the same upsert, two dialects — run both; that's the whole exercise
-- PostgreSQL
INSERT INTO stations (id, name) VALUES (7, 'Svalbard')
ON CONFLICT (id) DO UPDATE SET name = EXCLUDED.name;

-- MySQL (InnoDB)
INSERT INTO stations (id, name) VALUES (7, 'Svalbard')
ON DUPLICATE KEY UPDATE name = VALUES(name);

-- and the one that bites in migrations: MySQL auto-commits DDL, so a failed
-- migration can leave you HALF-migrated. Postgres rolls the whole thing back.
Real scenario — inheriting the client's database

A field-service client wants your ticket-summarization LLM wired into their existing stack — which is MySQL 8 on InnoDB, non-negotiable. Your Postgres-flavored migration scripts fail on ON CONFLICT and a rolled-back DDL that didn't roll back. The engineer who knows the real differences ships that week; the one who knows folklore spends it reading stack traces.

— Warehouses & Pipelines · items 233–239 —
233

Data warehouse concepts

Concept

Your Postgres is built for transactions: fetch a few rows fast, by index. A data warehouse (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift) is built for the opposite: scan millions of rows and aggregate. The trick is column orientation — data is stored column-by-column instead of row-by-row, so SUM(parts_cost) reads only the parts_cost column, and same-typed values sitting together compress brutally well.

Warehouse data is organized as a star schema: a central fact table of events (one row per ticket, per pass, per download — with numeric measures), surrounded by dimension tables of context (who, where, when — the things you filter and group by). Facts are long and skinny; dimensions are short and wide. Every analytics query is the same shape: join fact to a few dimensions, filter on dimension attributes, aggregate the measures.

Star schema: one long, skinny fact table of events in the middle; short, wide dimension tables as the spokes you filter and group by.
Example 
-- the canonical warehouse query shape: fact + two dimensions
CREATE TABLE fact_tickets (
  ticket_id      bigint,
  technician_id  int,       -- spoke to dim_technician
  date_id        int,       -- spoke to dim_date
  minutes_spent  int,
  parts_cost     numeric
);

SELECT d.month, t.region, SUM(f.parts_cost) AS cost
FROM   fact_tickets f
JOIN   dim_date d       USING (date_id)
JOIN   dim_technician t USING (technician_id)
GROUP BY d.month, t.region;
Real scenario — the telemetry mart

Ops wants "downlink volume by station, by satellite, by week" dashboards. You model fact_downlinks (one row per pass: bytes, duration, snr) with spokes to dim_station, dim_satellite, and dim_date. Every dashboard tile — and every question ops will invent next quarter — is now the same join-filter-aggregate query with different GROUP BY columns. That's the point of the star: you model once, then every question is cheap.

234

ETL

Concept

ETL — Extract, Transform, Load — cleans and shapes data before it lands in the destination. Extract pulls from the source (an API, a production DB, a file drop); Transform runs in a middle tier (usually Python or Spark) — parsing, filtering, renaming, joining; Load writes the finished rows into the warehouse. Only clean data ever touches the destination.

This is the classic pattern from the era when destination compute was precious — you couldn't afford to transform inside the warehouse, so you did the work outside. Its cost: the raw data is gone. If your transform had a bug, or next quarter someone needs a field you dropped, you re-extract — if the source still has it.

ETL: the transform sits between source and destination, so only finished rows ever reach the warehouse.
Example 
import requests, psycopg2

url  = "https://api.nasa.gov/neo/rest/v1/feed"
feed = requests.get(url, params={"api_key": KEY}).json()      # E: extract

clean = [(o["id"], o["name"], float(o["absolute_magnitude_h"]))
         for day in feed["near_earth_objects"].values() for o in day
         if o.get("absolute_magnitude_h") is not None]        # T: in Python

with psycopg2.connect(DSN) as conn, conn.cursor() as cur:      # L: clean rows only
    cur.executemany("INSERT INTO neo (id, name, h_mag) VALUES (%s, %s, %s)", clean)
Real scenario — the asteroid cache

Your Orbital Research Agent hits the NEO API on every question about asteroids — slow, rate-limited, and the same data every time. A nightly ETL job pulls the feed, flattens the nested per-day JSON into typed rows, and loads them into Postgres. The agent now queries its own warm cache in milliseconds. Then a week later you need a field you dropped in the transform… which is exactly the pain the next topic exists to fix.

235

ELT

Concept

ELT swaps the last two letters: load the raw data first, untouched, then transform inside the warehouse using SQL. Modern warehouses have cheap, elastic compute, so the old reason to transform outside is gone. This is the dbt pattern: raw tables at the bottom, layers of versioned SQL views/models on top.

Why it wins: the raw data is preserved forever — a transform bug means rebuilding a view, not re-extracting from a source that may no longer have the data. And transformations become versionable SQL that anyone can audit: a data analyst can read, review, and fix the logic in a pull request, no Python required.

Key distinction

ETL: transform code owns the truth, raw data is discarded. ELT: raw data owns the truth, transforms are re-runnable views on top. When history matters — and in analytics it always ends up mattering — ELT is the safer default.

The order swap: in ELT the transform moves inside the warehouse, and the raw table stays as the permanent source of truth.
Example 
-- 1. land the payload raw, untouched
CREATE TABLE raw_neo (payload jsonb, loaded_at timestamptz DEFAULT now());

-- 2. transform INSIDE the warehouse — versionable SQL (the dbt pattern)
CREATE VIEW stg_neo AS
SELECT payload->>'id'                               AS neo_id,
       payload->>'name'                             AS name,
       (payload->>'absolute_magnitude_h')::numeric  AS h_mag
FROM   raw_neo
WHERE  payload ? 'absolute_magnitude_h';
-- bug in the view? fix the SQL, rebuild — the raw rows never moved
Real scenario — DONKI's flaky payloads

The DONKI space-weather API is known to be flaky: fields appear, vanish, and change shape between events. With ETL, every schema surprise crashed the nightly job and lost that night's data. As ELT, the raw JSONB always lands — parsing bugs become a view fix plus a rebuild over all history. Do the ladder's exercise: redo #234's pipeline as ELT and write three honest sentences on which one you'd rather maintain at 2 a.m.

236

Spark

Concept

Spark is distributed dataframes: the same filter/group/aggregate mental model as pandas, but the data is split across a cluster and the work is shipped to it. The API is lazy — every transformation (filter, groupBy, select) just adds a node to a DAG of operations; nothing computes. Only an action (.collect(), .count(), .write) makes the driver optimize the whole DAG and dispatch tasks to executors.

Laziness is the feature, not a quirk: because Spark sees the whole plan before running any of it, it can push filters down to the file scan, prune unread columns, and skip work you never asked to materialize. Spark is the standard answer when data outgrows one machine — and knowing exactly which line triggers execution is the difference between using it and merely importing it.

The driver accumulates a lazy DAG; the first action optimizes it end-to-end and fans the work out across executors.
Example 
from pyspark.sql import SparkSession, functions as F

spark = SparkSession.builder.master("local[4]").getOrCreate()

df  = spark.read.csv("telemetry_2026.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
hot = (df.filter(F.col("panel_temp_c") > 80)      # lazy — adds a DAG node
         .groupBy("sat_id")                        # lazy
         .agg(F.count("*").alias("hot_readings")))# still lazy

top = hot.orderBy(F.desc("hot_readings")).collect()
# ^^^ THE line — .collect() is an action: the DAG executes here, not before
Real scenario — reprocessing three years of light curves

Your exoplanet classifier needs features recomputed over three years of raw light-curve files — 400 GB, far past pandas territory. A local local[4] PySpark session proves the logic on one month; the identical script then runs on a cluster over the full archive, because the DAG doesn't care how many executors exist. The ladder's exercise — pinpoint the exact line where execution happens — is the one that makes the laziness real in your head.

237

Hadoop

Concept

Hadoop (2006) is two ideas welded together. HDFS solved storage: files too big for any one machine are split into blocks, replicated across cheap nodes, with a namenode tracking where everything lives — lose a disk, lose nothing. MapReduce solved compute: ship the code to the data — a map step transforms records where they sit, a shuffle groups by key across the cluster, a reduce step aggregates each group.

MapReduce wrote every intermediate result to disk between stages — durable, but brutally slow for anything iterative. Spark's in-memory model displaced it for exactly that reason. Hadoop is legacy now, but its vocabulary survives everywhere: "data lake," block storage on object stores, partitioned directory layouts, and the map/shuffle/reduce shape that lives on inside every distributed engine — including Spark itself.

HDFS replicates blocks across nodes; MapReduce writes to disk between every stage — the exact cost Spark's in-memory DAG removed.
Example 
# the vocabulary in action — HDFS commands you may still meet in the wild
$ hdfs dfs -put telemetry_2019.log /data/telemetry/
$ hdfs dfs -ls /data/telemetry/          # 128 MB blocks, replicated 3x
$ hadoop jar wordcount.jar /data/telemetry /out

# what that job did, conceptually:
#   map:    (log line)            -> (station, 1)
#   shuffle: group pairs by key across the cluster   [writes to disk]
#   reduce: (station, [1,1,...])  -> (station, count) [writes to disk]
Real scenario — the legacy mission archive

A space-agency partner keeps a decade of pre-2018 mission logs on an on-prem Hadoop cluster your Mission Control RAG must ingest from. You'll never write MapReduce — but you must read HDFS paths, reason about block sizes and replication when estimating the pull, and answer the inevitable interview question "why did Spark replace Hadoop?" in one crisp sentence: same map/shuffle/reduce shape, minus the disk writes between stages.

238

Kafka

Concept

Kafka is a distributed append-only log. Producers append messages to named topics; messages are never updated or deleted on read, only appended and (much later) expired. Each topic splits into partitions — independent ordered logs — which is where parallelism comes from: messages with the same key always land in the same partition, preserving per-key order while different partitions are consumed in parallel.

The crucial inversion vs. a classic message queue: consumers track their own position, called the offset. The broker doesn't push and forget; each consumer group reads at its own pace and commits how far it got. Kill a consumer, restart it tomorrow — it resumes at its committed offset. Rewind the offset and you replay history. That property makes Kafka the backbone of event-driven architectures and real-time pipelines: one stream of truth, many independent readers.

One topic, three partitions: the producer appends to the head, while two consumers read the same log at completely different offsets.
Example 
from kafka import KafkaProducer, KafkaConsumer
import json

prod = KafkaProducer(bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092",
                     value_serializer=lambda v: json.dumps(v).encode())
prod.send("sat.telemetry", key=b"NOAA-19",        # same key -> same partition
          value={"ts": "2026-08-19T10:02:11Z", "battery_v": 27.4})

cons = KafkaConsumer("sat.telemetry", group_id="anomaly-detector",
                     bootstrap_servers="localhost:9092")
for msg in cons:                                  # offset advances as you commit
    print(msg.partition, msg.offset, msg.value)
Real scenario — the crashed anomaly detector

Your satellite-telemetry stream feeds two consumer groups: the anomaly detector and the warehouse loader. The detector crashes Friday night; the loader keeps running untouched. Monday, the detector restarts, reads its committed offset, and chews through the weekend's backlog in order — zero messages lost, zero coordination with the loader. Run the ladder's exercise (kill, restart, explain the offset) and the design clicks permanently.

239

Airflow

Concept

Airflow is the standard pipeline scheduler: you declare workflows as Python DAGs — tasks plus dependency edges — and Airflow runs them on a schedule, retries failures with backoff, alerts on breakage, and shows everything in an ops-friendly UI grid of runs × tasks. The killer feature nobody appreciates until they need it: backfills — because each run is parameterized by its logical date, you can re-run last week's pipeline for last week's data, task by task.

  • DAG = the workflow; task = one node; >> = the dependency edge.
  • Retries are declared, not hand-coded — a flaky API becomes a config line.
  • Seeing "Airflow" in a JD translates directly to: "we have scheduled data pipelines, and they break."
A four-task DAG: fetch feeds clean, which fans out to two independent downstream tasks. Edges are the >> operators in code.
Example 
from airflow import DAG
from airflow.operators.python import PythonOperator
from datetime import datetime, timedelta

with DAG("neo_daily", start_date=datetime(2026, 8, 1),
         schedule="@daily", catchup=True,          # catchup=True enables backfill
         default_args={"retries": 2,
                       "retry_delay": timedelta(minutes=5)}) as dag:
    fetch = PythonOperator(task_id="fetch_neo", python_callable=fetch_neo)
    clean = PythonOperator(task_id="clean",     python_callable=clean_rows)
    load  = PythonOperator(task_id="load_pg",   python_callable=load_postgres)

    fetch >> clean >> load        # the DAG edges — dependencies, not a pipeline of calls
Real scenario — re-embedding after the model swap

Mission Control RAG's nightly DAG is fetch_reports → chunk → embed → upsert_vectors. You upgrade the embedding model, which invalidates three weeks of vectors. Instead of a hand-rolled script, you clear the embed task for those dates and let Airflow backfill: it re-runs embed and upsert for 21 logical dates, in order, with retries — while fetch and chunk stay untouched because their outputs were fine. That grid view is why Airflow is in every data JD.

— The Three Clouds · items 240–247 —
240

AWS core services (EC2, Lambda, ECS)

Concept

AWS compute comes in three shapes, and choosing between them is a cost/latency/ops-burden decision you should be able to argue out loud. EC2 is a raw virtual machine: full control, always on, always billed, yours to patch and scale. Lambda is a function: it scales to zero (idle costs nothing), scales out instantly, but caps at 15 minutes per invocation and pays a cold-start tax when it hasn't run recently. ECS runs containers with managed orchestration — and with the Fargate launch type, no servers to see at all.

  • Spiky, low volume (10 requests/day): Lambda — you pay pennies; an idle EC2 box costs real money for nothing.
  • Steady, high volume (100 requests/second): ECS or EC2 — per-invocation Lambda pricing turns brutal, and cold starts hurt tail latency.
  • Weird dependencies, GPUs, long jobs: EC2 — the escape hatch when the managed shapes don't fit.
The three compute shapes on one axis: every AWS compute decision is a point on this control-vs-ops-burden line.
Example 
# the same hello API, three ways — and the cost argument in comments
$ aws lambda invoke --function-name hello out.json
#   10 req/day  -> Lambda: ~free tier. EC2 t3.small: ~$15/mo doing nothing.
#   100 req/s   -> Lambda: per-invocation $$$ + cold starts. Containers win.

$ aws ecs update-service --service api --desired-count 4
#   ECS: containers scale by count; Fargate bills per vCPU-second, no hosts

$ ssh ec2-user@3.110.x.x
#   EC2: it's a computer. Yours. Including the patching. Forever.
Real scenario — placing the FastAPI backend

Your FastAPI service fronts Mission Control RAG. The demo phase sees ~50 requests/day — Lambda behind API Gateway, effectively free. Launch week hits 40 requests/second sustained, and Lambda's cold starts push p99 past 3 s while the bill climbs — so it moves to ECS Fargate with two always-warm tasks. Being able to narrate that migration, with numbers, is the interview answer.

241

AWS S3

Concept

S3 is object storage — the universal data substrate. Datasets, model weights, logs, backups: if it's a file in the cloud, odds are it lives in S3. The model is simple: a bucket (globally unique name) holds objects addressed by key. The namespace is flat — exoplanet/v3/model.pkl is one string; the "folders" are an illusion drawn by prefix.

  • Storage classes trade cost for access speed: Standard → Infrequent Access → Glacier. Colder is cheaper per GB and slower/costlier to read.
  • Presigned URLs grant temporary access without credentials: your backend signs a URL that works for anyone, for exactly as long as you say — the standard way to hand a browser a private file.
  • Objects are immutable — you overwrite whole objects, you don't edit bytes in place.
A bucket of flat keys, and a presigned URL handing a browser 60 seconds of access to one private object — no credentials involved.
Example 
import boto3
s3 = boto3.client("s3")

s3.upload_file("model.pkl", "mission-artifacts", "exoplanet/v3/model.pkl")
s3.download_file("mission-artifacts", "exoplanet/v3/model.pkl",
                 "/tmp/model.pkl")

url = s3.generate_presigned_url("get_object",
        Params={"Bucket": "mission-artifacts",
                "Key": "exoplanet/v3/model.pkl"},
        ExpiresIn=60)   # works in any browser, dies in 60 seconds
print(url)
Real scenario — everything lands in the bucket

Count what your stack already keeps in S3: exoplanet training datasets, each classifier version's weights, raw DONKI payloads from the ELT pipeline, RAGAS eval reports, and Langfuse trace exports. When a mission scientist asks for last month's eval report, your FastAPI endpoint doesn't proxy the file — it returns a 60-second presigned URL and lets S3 serve the bytes. That pattern removes your server from the download path entirely.

242

AWS networking basics (VPC)

Concept

A VPC is your private slice of the AWS network. Inside it, subnets divide the address space: a public subnet has a route to the internet gateway (things in it can be reached from outside); a private subnet has no such route — the internet literally cannot open a connection in. A NAT gateway gives private things outbound-only access, so your DB can fetch patches without ever being reachable.

Security groups are instance-level stateful firewalls, and their best trick is referencing each other: instead of allowing an IP range, the database's group allows port 5432 from the API's security group. Instances come and go, IPs change, the rule stays correct. This — not a password — is the first reason your database isn't on the front page of Shodan.

Two-tier app in a VPC: the internet reaches the API through the gateway; the DB sits in a private subnet, reachable only via the sg-api → sg-db rule. A NAT gateway would give the DB outbound-only access for patches.
Example 
# THE rule of the whole diagram: sg-db admits only traffic from sg-api
$ aws ec2 authorize-security-group-ingress \
    --group-id sg-db \
    --protocol tcp --port 5432 \
    --source-group sg-api      # a security group, not an IP range

# note what is ABSENT: no rule from 0.0.0.0/0 to sg-db.
# the internet cannot connect to Postgres. not "shouldn't" — CAN'T.

$ aws ec2 create-nat-gateway --subnet-id subnet-public --allocation-id eipalloc-1
# private subnet's outbound-only door: patches out, connections never in
Real scenario — the pgvector store goes dark

Your Postgres+pgvector instance holds every Mission Control RAG embedding — proprietary chunked NASA-report derivatives you don't want scraped. It lives in a private subnet; only sg-api can open 5432. When a pentest report comes back with "database not reachable from any external vantage point," that's not luck — it's this exact diagram, and you should be able to draw it from memory and point at the one rule that makes it true.

243

SageMaker

Concept

SageMaker is AWS's managed ML platform, covering the lifecycle: hosted notebooks for exploration, training jobs that spin up (and crucially, tear down) GPU instances on demand, and model endpoints — your model behind an HTTPS URL with autoscaling, no server babysitting. You bring a script and a model artifact; AWS brings the iron.

Its sibling Bedrock serves foundation models behind one API — Claude, Llama, and friends — with enterprise IAM, billing, and no GPUs to manage. Together they're the two answers to "how does an AWS shop run models?": SageMaker for models you train, Bedrock for foundation models you call.

The SageMaker lifecycle: notebook to training job to S3 artifact to autoscaling endpoint — with Bedrock alongside for foundation models you call rather than train.
Example 
from sagemaker.sklearn import SKLearnModel

model = SKLearnModel(
    model_data="s3://mission-artifacts/exoplanet/v3/model.tar.gz",
    role=ROLE, entry_point="inference.py")
endpoint = model.deploy(instance_type="ml.m5.large",
                        initial_instance_count=1)
print(endpoint.predict(light_curve_features))   # HTTPS behind the scenes

# and the Bedrock side — a foundation model with zero infrastructure:
import boto3
bedrock = boto3.client("bedrock-runtime")
resp = bedrock.converse(modelId="anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-5",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Summarize this pass log…"}]}])
Real scenario — one platform, both model kinds

Your exoplanet classifier trains as a SageMaker job (GPU spins up, trains on the S3 light-curve set, writes model.tar.gz, spins down — you pay for 40 minutes) and serves from an endpoint that autoscales during transit-survey release weeks. Meanwhile the Orbital Research Agent's LLM calls go through Bedrock under the same AWS account and IAM story. Do the ladder's comparison — deploy sklearn, then call Bedrock — and you'll feel exactly where "your model" ends and "their model" begins.

244

GCP core services

Concept

Map GCP by analogy from AWS, then note where it genuinely shines. Compute Engine = EC2 (VMs). Cloud Run runs containers that scale to zero — genuinely excellent: give it an image, get an HTTPS URL, pay nothing while idle. GKE is widely considered the strongest managed Kubernetes (Google wrote Kubernetes). And BigQuery is the serverless warehouse: no cluster to size, you pay per query over data scanned.

GCP's data tooling is its calling card — BigQuery plus the analytics stack around it is the reason many data-heavy teams choose GCP even when everything else lives on AWS.

Cloud Run's whole pitch in one line: zero instances until traffic arrives (one cold start), scale out under load, back to zero — and $0 — after.
Example 
# container to public HTTPS URL in one command — then measure the cold start
$ gcloud run deploy exoplanet-api --source . --region asia-south1 \
    --min-instances 0                # scale to zero: pay nothing while idle

$ time curl https://exoplanet-api-xyz.a.run.app/health
# first hit after idle: ~1.8 s (cold start) — warm hits after: ~40 ms

$ bq query 'SELECT disposition, COUNT(*) FROM `sky.exoplanet_archive.koi`
            GROUP BY disposition'     # BigQuery: no cluster, pay per scan
Real scenario — the free-tier demo that survives launch

Your public exoplanet-classifier demo goes on Cloud Run: weeks of near-zero traffic cost near-zero rupees, and the Hacker News spike scales itself. Meanwhile you load the full Exoplanet Archive into BigQuery and run population analytics — no warehouse cluster to size or babysit. Do the ladder's exercise and measure the cold start yourself; "about two seconds, then 40 ms warm" is an answer that lands very differently from "it's serverless."

245

Vertex AI

Concept

Vertex AI is GCP's ML platform — the analogue of SageMaker — and the front door to Gemini. Its three faces: the Model Garden (a catalog of foundation and open models you can deploy or call), Pipelines (managed, versioned training workflows), and Endpoints (deploy-and-autoscale serving, for your models or tuned foundation ones). If your employer is a GCP shop, this is where their AI workloads live — the JD will literally say "Vertex."

For LLM work, the day-one skill is calling Gemini with a structured-output schema: pass a response schema, get back JSON that parses into a typed object instead of prose you have to regex.

Model Garden

Catalog of foundation + open models: browse, deploy, or call — Gemini included.

Pipelines

Managed, versioned training workflows — the Airflow-shaped piece, but for ML steps.

Endpoints

Your model behind an autoscaling URL — the SageMaker-endpoint analogue.

Example 
from google import genai
from pydantic import BaseModel

class EventSummary(BaseModel):
    event_type: str          # "CME", "flare", ...
    severity:   int          # 1–5

client = genai.Client(vertexai=True, project="mission-ctl",
                      location="us-central1")
resp = client.models.generate_content(
    model="gemini-2.5-flash",
    contents=donki_report_text,
    config={"response_mime_type": "application/json",
            "response_schema": EventSummary})
event = EventSummary.model_validate_json(resp.text)   # typed, guaranteed shape
Real scenario — the GCP-shop interview

A prospective employer runs everything on GCP; their "LLM feature" is Gemini via Vertex. Your portfolio move: port one Orbital Research Agent tool — the DONKI space-weather summarizer — to Vertex with the response schema above. Same agent, different front door, and in the interview you can compare Bedrock's converse() and Vertex's generate_content() from experience rather than from blog posts.

246

Azure core services

Concept

Azure is the enterprise default wherever Microsoft contracts already exist — which, in India's services sector, is very often. You rarely choose Azure; you arrive at it, because the client's Active Directory, Office licensing, and procurement already live there. The efficient way in: map your AWS knowledge by analogy, then learn the deltas on the job.

  • The concepts transfer one-to-one: VMs, managed Kubernetes, functions, blob storage — same shapes, different names and portal.
  • Azure's organizing quirk: everything lives inside a resource group — a named container for related resources you can tag, secure, and delete as a unit.
EC2 → Virtual Machines

Raw VMs. Same trade-offs, different portal.

Lambda → Functions

Event-driven, scale-to-zero compute.

S3 → Blob Storage

Objects in containers under a storage account.

EKS → AKS

Managed Kubernetes — the enterprise workhorse.

RDS → Azure Database

Managed Postgres/MySQL flavors.

Example 
# the same muscle memory, new verbs — note the resource group everywhere
$ az group create -n mission-rg -l centralindia
$ az storage account create -n missionblobs -g mission-rg
$ az storage blob upload --account-name missionblobs \
    -c artifacts -f model.pkl -n exoplanet/v3/model.pkl
# S3 bucket/key  →  storage account + container + blob name

$ az aks create -n mission-aks -g mission-rg --node-count 2   # ≈ EKS
$ az functionapp create -n neo-fetcher -g mission-rg ...      # ≈ Lambda
Real scenario — the client who was always Azure

A large services client wants your ticket-triage LLM system deployed "on our cloud" — Azure, decided years ago by a Microsoft enterprise agreement, not by architecture review. Your K8s manifests move to AKS nearly unchanged; S3 calls become Blob Storage calls; the FastAPI container doesn't care. Do the ladder's exercise from memory — map five AWS services to Azure, then verify — because that mapping is the onboarding.

247

Azure AI

Concept

Azure OpenAI Service is OpenAI models wrapped in enterprise controls — and it's the reason many banks' "GPT" is actually Azure. The controls are the product: regional data residency (prompts and completions processed in the region you choose), configurable content filters, private networking, and Microsoft-grade compliance paperwork that procurement departments already trust.

The API's telling difference: you don't call a model name, you call your deployment name. You first deploy a specific model version into your Azure resource — choosing region, capacity, and filter policy — and give that deployment a name. Your code targets the name; the enterprise controls ride along with it. One sentence for the ladder's exercise: the deployment name points at your pinned, governed instance of the model, not at the vendor's moving target.

The request targets your named deployment, which pins the model version, applies your content filters, and keeps processing inside your chosen region.
Example 
from openai import AzureOpenAI

client = AzureOpenAI(
    azure_endpoint="https://mission-ctl.openai.azure.com",
    api_key=KEY,
    api_version="2024-10-21")

resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="ticket-triage-gpt4o",   # ← YOUR deployment name, not "gpt-4o"
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize ticket #4812"}])
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)
# the deployment pins model version, region, capacity, and filter policy
Real scenario — the residency clause

A banking client loves your ticket-triage demo but their compliance team has one non-negotiable line: customer data must not leave India. Public OpenAI API — no. Azure OpenAI with a GPT-4o deployment in Central India — yes, with the content-filter policy attached to the deployment and the audit trail procurement expects. Nothing about your prompt engineering changes; the deployment, not the model, is what made the deal signable. That's Azure AI's entire value proposition in one meeting.
