— The LLM API Stack —
248

FastAPI

Concept

FastAPI is the modern Python API framework and the default chassis for LLM services — most example code you will read from here on simply assumes it. Its trick is making your type hints do triple duty: the same annotations that document your code also validate every incoming request (via Pydantic, #249) and generate an interactive OpenAPI docs page at /docs for free. Under the hood it's an ASGI app (built on Starlette) served by uvicorn, which is what makes it async-native — critical when every request spends seconds awaiting an LLM provider.

  • Declare, don't check: annotate the request model and FastAPI rejects bad input with a precise 422 before your code runs.
  • response_model: the output contract — extra fields are stripped, wrong types are caught on your side, not the client's.
  • /docs: a live, clickable API console generated from the very same annotations — nothing to keep in sync.
One set of type hints drives validation, serialization, and the interactive /docs page.
Example 
from fastapi import FastAPI
from pydantic import BaseModel

app = FastAPI(title="Mission Control RAG")

class ChatRequest(BaseModel):
    question: str
    top_k: int = 5

class ChatResponse(BaseModel):
    answer: str
    sources: list[str]

@app.post("/chat", response_model=ChatResponse)
async def chat(req: ChatRequest):
    chunks = await retriever.search(req.question, k=req.top_k)
    answer = await llm.answer(req.question, chunks)
    return ChatResponse(answer=answer, sources=[c.doc_id for c in chunks])
# uvicorn main:app --reload  →  open /docs and click "Try it out"
Real scenario — the RAG gets a front door

Your Mission Control RAG has lived in notebooks for nine volumes. This endpoint is its public face: /chat takes a question about NASA mission logs, runs retrieval + generation, and returns an answer with source chunk IDs. When a teammate asks "how do I call it?", you don't write docs — you send them the /docs URL, where they can fire test questions from the browser.

249

Pydantic models

Concept

Pydantic turns type annotations into runtime validation and serialization: define the shape of your data once as a class, and you get parsing, coercion ("5" becomes 5 where sensible), crystal-clear errors, and a JSON schema — all from the same declaration. The killer feature is error paths: when nested data is wrong, the error names exactly where — observations.0.magnitude — instead of a vague "invalid input" somewhere in a 2 KB payload.

It also doubles as the contract layer for LLM structured outputs (#156): you hand the model's JSON schema to the LLM, then model_validate whatever comes back. If the LLM hallucinated a field or returned a string where a float belongs, you get a machine-readable error you can feed straight back into a retry prompt.

  • Validate at the boundary: the moment data enters your system — API request, LLM output, external API response — never deep inside business logic.
  • field_validator: custom rules beyond types — ranges, formats, cross-field checks.
  • model_dump() / model_dump_json(): the reverse trip, typed object → dict/JSON.
One declared shape → either a typed object or an error naming the exact failing field.
Example 
from pydantic import BaseModel, field_validator

class Observation(BaseModel):
    magnitude: float
    band: str

class NeoReport(BaseModel):
    neo_id: str
    hazardous: bool
    observations: list[Observation]

    @field_validator("neo_id")
    @classmethod
    def looks_like_spk(cls, v: str) -> str:
        if not v.isdigit(): raise ValueError("SPK-ID must be numeric")
        return v

bad = {"neo_id": "3542519", "hazardous": "yes",   # "yes" → True, coerced
       "observations": [{"magnitude": "bright", "band": "V"}]}
NeoReport.model_validate(bad)
# ValidationError: observations.0.magnitude — 'bright' is not a valid float
Real scenario — the structured-output retry loop

Your Orbital Research Agent asks the LLM to extract NeoReport objects from free-text asteroid bulletins. One response in twenty has "magnitude": "approximately 22". Instead of that string poisoning your database, model_validate raises, your code appends the error message — which names the exact field — to the conversation, and the LLM fixes it on the retry. Validation errors become self-healing prompts.

250

Async endpoints

Concept

An async def endpoint can serve other requests while it awaits IO — and an LLM call is the purest IO wait there is: 5–30 seconds of doing nothing but listening to a socket. One worker process can hold hundreds of in-flight LLM requests open concurrently, because await hands control back to the event loop at every wait point.

The fatal mistake: a blocking call inside an async route. requests.get(...), time.sleep(...), or a heavyweight pandas crunch inside async def never yields — it freezes the entire event loop, so every other user's request stalls behind it. The rule: inside async def, all IO must be awaitable (httpx.AsyncClient, asyncio.sleep). Genuinely blocking work goes in a plain def route — FastAPI runs those in a threadpool — or behind a task queue.

Three concurrent requests: one blocking call serializes everyone; awaiting overlaps the waits.
Example 
import asyncio, time
from fastapi import FastAPI
app = FastAPI()

@app.get("/frozen")
async def frozen():
    time.sleep(3)            # blocks THE WHOLE event loop
    return {"ok": True}

@app.get("/fine")
async def fine():
    await asyncio.sleep(3)   # yields; other requests proceed
    return {"ok": True}

# hammer each with 20 concurrent requests:
#   /frozen → ~60s wall time      /fine → ~3s wall time
Real scenario — the demo that died at 12 users

First version of your Mission Control /chat used the synchronous requests library to call the LLM inside an async def route. Solo testing: perfect. Demo day, 12 people ask questions at once: request twelve waits ~90 seconds and times out, because each 8-second LLM call froze the loop for everyone behind it. The fix was one dependency swap — httpx.AsyncClient and an await — and the same box now holds 200 concurrent chats.

251

Dependency injection

Concept

FastAPI's Depends flips construction inside-out: instead of each route building what it needs (a DB session, the authenticated user, an LLM client), the route declares what it needs in its signature and the framework constructs and shares it per request. Dependencies can depend on other dependencies, forming a graph FastAPI resolves for you; yield-style dependencies even handle cleanup (close the session after the response).

The real payoff is testability: app.dependency_overrides lets a test swap any dependency for a fake — a canned-response LLM, an in-memory DB — without touching route code. That one dict is the difference between a test suite that needs API keys and network access, and one that runs offline in two seconds.

Routes declare what they need; the framework builds it — and tests can swap any piece.
Example 
from fastapi import Depends, FastAPI
from fastapi.testclient import TestClient
app = FastAPI()

def get_llm():
    return AnthropicClient()          # real client, needs API key

@app.post("/chat")
async def chat(req: ChatRequest, llm=Depends(get_llm)):
    return {"answer": await llm.answer(req.question)}

# --- in tests: no network, no key, runs in milliseconds ---
class FakeLLM:
    async def answer(self, q): return "canned answer"

app.dependency_overrides[get_llm] = lambda: FakeLLM()
assert TestClient(app).post("/chat", json={"question": "hi"}).status_code == 200
Real scenario — CI without API keys

Your Mission Control test suite runs on every push (#270). With Depends(get_llm) and Depends(get_vector_db) injected everywhere, CI overrides both with fakes: a canned-answer LLM and a five-chunk in-memory retriever. Forty endpoint tests run offline in three seconds, cost zero tokens, and never flake because DONKI is down — while the route code being tested is byte-for-byte what runs in production.

252

Streaming responses (SSE)

Concept

Server-Sent Events push tokens to the client as they generate, over plain HTTP with content type text/event-stream — each message is just a data: ... line followed by a blank line. It is the difference between staring at a spinner for 20 seconds and reading the first words in half a second, and it is the standard transport for LLM streaming: the Anthropic and OpenAI APIs both speak SSE to you, and your product API speaks SSE to the browser.

  • One-way: server → client only. For two-way traffic you'd reach for WebSockets (#257) — but LLM chat rarely needs that.
  • TTFT (time to first token) becomes your headline latency metric instead of total time.
  • Browser-native: EventSource handles parsing and auto-reconnect with zero libraries; curl -N debugs it from the terminal.
Same 12-second generation — streaming turns perceived latency into half a second.
Example 
from fastapi.responses import StreamingResponse

@app.post("/chat/stream")
async def chat_stream(req: ChatRequest):
    async def gen():
        async for token in llm.stream(req.question):
            yield f"data: {token}\n\n"      # one SSE event per token
        yield "data: [DONE]\n\n"
    return StreamingResponse(gen(), media_type="text/event-stream")

# terminal:  curl -N -X POST localhost:8000/chat/stream -d '{"question":"..."}'
# browser:   new EventSource(url).onmessage = e => out.append(e.data)
Real scenario — the 15-second answer that feels instant

Mission Control answers about Apollo-era failure reports run long — retrieval plus a 900-token answer takes ~15s end to end. After switching /chat to SSE, the first tokens land while the model is still writing, and your Langfuse traces now track TTFT (0.6s) separately from total generation. Same compute, same cost — but in user testing, "slow" complaints disappeared entirely.

— Frameworks & API Styles —
253

Flask

Concept

Flask is the minimal, synchronous predecessor to FastAPI — a routing layer, a request object, and almost nothing else. It has a huge installed base: a decade of internal tools, ML demo servers, and production APIs are written in it, so you learn Flask primarily to read it — and to articulate, in an interview or a migration proposal, exactly what FastAPI adds. Flask is WSGI (one worker thread per in-flight request), validation is whatever if statements you write by hand, and documentation is whatever you keep updated by hand.

Flask

WSGI, synchronous. Manual validation, manual docs, mature ecosystem, tiny surface — everything is explicit.

FastAPI

ASGI, async-native. Pydantic validation, auto /docs, DI built in — the boilerplate Flask makes you write is generated.

Example 
from flask import Flask, request, jsonify
app = Flask(__name__)

@app.route("/chat", methods=["POST"])
def chat():
    data = request.get_json(silent=True) or {}
    q = data.get("question", "")
    if not q:                                  # validation by hand
        return jsonify(error="question required"), 400
    answer = rag_answer(q)                     # sync — blocks this worker
    return jsonify(answer=answer)

# what you lost vs #248: typed contracts, async concurrency, free /docs
Real scenario — the inherited telemetry tool

The company you join runs an internal satellite-telemetry viewer written in Flask in 2019. Before proposing a rewrite, you read it fluently: where routes live, how request.get_json() replaces typed models, why it needs 16 gunicorn workers to survive load your FastAPI service handles with two. Your migration memo names precisely what the port buys — types, async LLM calls, auto docs — which is what makes it land.

254

Django

Concept

Django is the batteries-included framework: an ORM (define tables as Python classes), migrations (schema changes generated and versioned automatically), a full auth system, and the famous admin panel — a complete CRUD web UI over your models, generated from one line of registration. Django is for building products — dashboards, portals, internal tools with users and forms — not model servers; you would not serve an LLM through it, but you might build everything around the LLM with it.

  • The admin alone can replace a week of hand-built internal-tool work — search, filters, edit forms, permissions, all free.
  • Convention over configuration: apps, models, views, templates in prescribed places — big teams stay consistent by default.
One model class fans out to versioned schema migrations and a working admin UI.
Example 
# missions/models.py
from django.db import models

class MissionLog(models.Model):
    mission  = models.CharField(max_length=80)
    ts       = models.DateTimeField(auto_now_add=True)
    severity = models.IntegerField(choices=[(1,"info"),(2,"warn"),(3,"crit")])
    note     = models.TextField()

# missions/admin.py
from django.contrib import admin
admin.site.register(MissionLog)   # search, filters, edit forms — free

# python manage.py makemigrations && python manage.py migrate && runserver
Real scenario — a labeling tool in one afternoon

Your RAGAS evals (#281) need humans to grade 500 Mission Control answers as correct/partial/wrong. Instead of building a labeling UI, you scaffold a Django project, define an AnswerReview model, register it in the admin, and add two reviewer accounts — done in an afternoon. The reviewers get search, filtering by mission, and an edit form; you get graded data in Postgres by Friday.

255

REST APIs

Concept

REST is a design discipline, not a library: model your domain as resources named by nouns (/missions/42/logs, never /getMissionLogs), use HTTP verbs as the actions, and return correct status codes so clients can react programmatically. The deepest idea is idempotency — whether retrying a request is safe. GET, PUT, DELETE are idempotent (doing them twice equals doing them once); POST is not (retry a timed-out POST and you may create a duplicate). Every retry policy, load balancer, and client SDK leans on these guarantees.

API design is permanent: once clients depend on your endpoints, mistakes ship to them forever. Ten minutes of design beats ten months of versioned regret.

Verbs carry the semantics — idempotency decides what a client may safely retry.
Example 
# the REST surface of a mission-log service — designed, not accreted
GET    /missions/42/logs?severity=crit      # → 200, filtered list
POST   /missions/42/logs                    # → 201, Location: /logs/917
PUT    /logs/917                            # full replace  → 200
PATCH  /logs/917   {"severity": 2}          # partial edit  → 200
DELETE /logs/917                            # → 204 (repeatable: still 204/404)

# the POST-retry trap, and its standard fix:
POST /missions/42/logs
  Idempotency-Key: "a3f9c2…"   # server dedupes retries of the same key
Real scenario — the endpoint you can never rename

You expose the exoplanet classifier as POST /predictions returning 201 with the stored result's URL. Six months later three teams' dashboards call it. When a colleague suggests "let's rename it /classify and return 200 with the body inline", you now have the vocabulary to push back: that's a breaking change to a shipped contract — it needs /v2, deprecation headers, and a migration window, not a rename.

256

GraphQL

Concept

GraphQL inverts REST's shape: one endpoint, and the client sends a query describing exactly the fields it wants — including nested relations — in a single round trip. It solves REST's twin annoyances: over-fetching (the endpoint returns 40 fields, you need 3) and under-fetching (you need repo → issues → authors, which is three sequential REST calls). The response mirrors the query's shape exactly.

The costs are real: the server must implement resolvers for every field (naive ones trigger N+1 database queries), HTTP caching mostly breaks because every query is a unique POST, and you must guard against maliciously deep queries. Rule of thumb: GraphQL earns its keep when many different UIs consume the same rich data graph; a service with three consumers and flat data wants REST.

Three sequential REST round trips versus one query shaped exactly like the UI that needs it.
Example 
# GitHub's GraphQL API — repo → issues → authors in ONE request
query {
  repository(owner: "nasa", name: "fprime") {
    stargazerCount
    issues(last: 3, states: OPEN) {
      nodes { title author { login } }
    }
  }
}
# curl -H "Authorization: bearer $TOKEN" \
#      -d '{"query":"…"}' https://api.github.com/graphql
Real scenario — one paint, one round trip

Your mission dashboard's home screen shows mission → latest telemetry alerts → the instrument behind each alert. Over REST that's three sequential fetches and a visible loading stagger on the ops floor's wall display. Behind a GraphQL layer, the dashboard asks for exactly that tree in one query and paints once — and when the mobile version needs two fewer fields, it just asks for two fewer fields, with zero backend changes.

257

WebSockets

Concept

A WebSocket upgrades an HTTP connection into a persistent, two-way channel: either side can send a message at any time, for the life of the connection. That's what chat between users, live dashboards with client interaction, and collaborative state need — cases where SSE's one-way push (#252) isn't enough because the client talks back on the same channel.

The costs are what the persistence buys you: the server now holds per-connection state (memory, file descriptors), clients need reconnect-and-resync logic you write yourself (SSE reconnects for free), and horizontal scaling gets harder — two users on different replicas can only "see" each other through a shared pub/sub backbone like Redis. Decision rule: server-push only → SSE; genuine two-way → WebSocket.

SSE pushes one way over HTTP; a WebSocket keeps one socket open for traffic in both directions.
Example 
from fastapi import FastAPI, WebSocket
app = FastAPI()
clients: set[WebSocket] = set()

@app.websocket("/ws/telemetry")
async def telemetry(ws: WebSocket):
    await ws.accept()
    clients.add(ws)
    try:
        while True:
            msg = await ws.receive_text()      # client → server
            for c in clients:                   # server → every tab
                await c.send_text(f"echo: {msg}")
    finally:
        clients.discard(ws)   # open two tabs — both see every message
Real scenario — when the dashboard talks back

Your satellite telemetry dashboard started as SSE — the Kafka consumer pushed frames one way, perfect. Then operators asked to acknowledge alerts and adjust alarm thresholds from the same screen, with every other operator seeing the change instantly. That's two-way, multi-client shared state: you switched the feed to a WebSocket and fanned messages across replicas via Redis pub/sub. The decision rule did the design for you.

— Identity & Access —
258

Authentication (general)

Key distinction

Authentication answers who are you? — fail it and the correct response is 401 Unauthorized. Authorization answers what may you do? — a known user touching something above their pay grade gets 403 Forbidden. Mixing these up in an API is a small tell; getting them right is free.

Concept

Two session-keeping strategies dominate: server-side sessions (a random ID in a cookie, user data looked up server-side — easy to revoke, needs shared storage) and tokens (state carried by the client, e.g. JWT #260 — no lookup, harder to revoke). And one iron rule for credentials: passwords are stored only as salted, deliberately slow hashes — bcrypt or argon2 — never encrypted, never plain. Encryption is reversible; a leaked key un-hides every password. A slow salted hash means even a full database leak forces attackers to grind each password individually, and identical passwords still hash differently.

  • Salt defeats rainbow tables (precomputed hash lookups); slowness (cost factor) defeats brute force at scale.
  • Verify, don't decrypt: login re-hashes the attempt and compares — the original password is never recoverable, even by you.
Two gates, two different questions, two different status codes.
Example 
from passlib.context import CryptContext
from fastapi import Depends, HTTPException

pwd = CryptContext(schemes=["argon2"])
stored = pwd.hash("correct horse battery staple")  # salted + slow, by design
pwd.verify("guess", stored)                          # False — no decryption ever

def current_user(token: str = Depends(oauth2_scheme)):
    user = lookup_session(token)
    if not user:
        raise HTTPException(status_code=401)   # authn: who are you?
    return user

@app.post("/admin/reindex")
def reindex(user=Depends(current_user)):
    if user.role != "admin":
        raise HTTPException(status_code=403)   # authz: not allowed
Real scenario — locking down /admin/reindex

Mission Control's /admin/reindex endpoint rebuilds the entire vector index — 40 minutes of compute. Once three teams share the app, you gate it: any anonymous call gets 401; a logged-in analyst gets 403; only the two admin-role users reach it. Because the check lives in a Depends (#251), every future admin endpoint gets the same gate with one function parameter.

259

OAuth

Concept

OAuth is delegated authorization: your app obtains scoped tokens to act on a user's behalf at another service — without ever seeing their password. It's the machinery behind every "Sign in with Google" button, and behind every MCP server that touches a SaaS API on a user's behalf. Three parties dance: the user (resource owner), your app (client), and the provider's authorization server.

The authorization-code flow is the one to internalize: (1) your app redirects the browser to the provider, naming its client_id and the scopes it wants; (2) the user logs in and consents on the provider's page — the password is typed only there; (3) the provider redirects back with a short-lived, one-time authorization code; (4) your server exchanges code + client_secret for tokens, server-to-server. The access token is scoped and expiring; a refresh token mints new ones without re-consent.

The authorization-code handshake: your app ends up with a scoped token — never the password.
Example 
# ① send the user's browser to consent
https://accounts.google.com/o/oauth2/v2/auth
    ?client_id=…&response_type=code
    &scope=openid email&redirect_uri=https://app/callback

# ③ Google redirects back:  https://app/callback?code=4/xyz…

# ④ exchange the one-time code, server-to-server
resp = httpx.post("https://oauth2.googleapis.com/token", data={
    "code": code, "client_id": CID, "client_secret": SECRET,
    "redirect_uri": "https://app/callback",
    "grant_type": "authorization_code"})
tokens = resp.json()   # access_token (scoped), id_token, refresh_token
Real scenario — the agent that files calendar events

You give the Orbital Research Agent an MCP tool that adds asteroid close-approach dates to a user's Google Calendar. OAuth is exactly why this is shippable: the user consents once to a calendar.events scope, your server stores the refresh token, and the agent acts with a token that can do only that — it couldn't read their email if the LLM tried. Scoped delegation is what makes "agent with access to my accounts" sane.

260

JWT

Concept

A JSON Web Token is a signed, self-contained token: three base64url segments — header.payload.signature — where the payload carries claims (sub who, exp until when, plus roles or scopes). Because the signature covers header + payload, any service holding the key can verify it locally — no database hit, no session store. That's stateless auth, and it's why JWTs rule microservice architectures.

The iron rule: the payload is readable by anyone — signed does not mean secret. Base64 is encoding, not encryption; never put secrets in claims. And self-containment cuts both ways: a JWT can't easily be revoked before its exp, so keep access tokens short-lived (minutes) and pair them with refresh tokens.

  • Tamper-evident: flip one character anywhere and signature verification fails.
  • Verify properly: check the signature and pin the expected algorithms=[...] — the classic attacks exploit sloppy verification, not the crypto.
header.payload.signature — signed means tamper-evident, not secret.
Example 
import jwt, time, base64

token = jwt.encode({"sub": "a.rivera", "role": "operator",
                    "exp": time.time() + 900},        # 15-minute life
                   "SECRET_KEY", algorithm="HS256")

jwt.decode(token, "SECRET_KEY", algorithms=["HS256"])  # → claims dict

tampered = token[:-2] + "xx"
jwt.decode(tampered, "SECRET_KEY", algorithms=["HS256"])
# InvalidSignatureError — one flipped character kills it

# …but the payload was never hidden:
print(base64.urlsafe_b64decode(token.split(".")[1] + "=="))
# b'{"sub":"a.rivera","role":"operator","exp":…}'
Real scenario — three services, zero session store

Your platform grew into three FastAPI services: the RAG API, the telemetry API, and the exoplanet classifier. Users log in once and get a 15-minute JWT with role and missions claims; each service verifies the signature locally with the shared key — no auth-service round trip on every request, no Redis session cluster. When a security review asks "what if a token leaks?", your answer is ready: 15-minute expiry plus refresh rotation bounds the blast radius.

— The Delivery Machine —
261

Linux fundamentals

Concept

Every server your code will ever run on is Linux — every Docker container, every K8s node, every EC2 box. The working set is small: the filesystem tree (/etc config, /var/log logs, /proc live process info), permissions (chmod/chown, the rwx triplets for owner/group/other), processes and ports (ps, kill, lsof -i), pipes and redirection (compose small tools over text streams), and enough systemd to start, stop, and read logs for a service.

  • Everything is a file: devices, sockets, process info — the same read/write tools work on all of it.
  • Pipes are the superpower: | chains single-purpose tools into one-off analyses faster than writing a script.
  • kill is a request: -15 (TERM) asks politely and lets cleanup run; -9 (KILL) is the last resort.
Small tools composed over pipes — each stage transforms a stream of text and passes it on.
Example 
lsof -i :8000                    # which process holds port 8000?
kill -15 41217                   # polite TERM; -9 only if it's ignored

# top-5 error messages from the API log, one pipeline:
grep " ERROR " api.log | awk -F"ERROR " '{print $2}' \
  | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -5

chmod 600 ~/.ssh/id_ed25519      # rw for you, nothing for anyone else
systemctl status mission-api     # service up?
journalctl -u mission-api -f     # tail its logs live
Real scenario — the API that "won't start"

The staging deploy of Mission Control fails with address already in use. You ssh in: lsof -i :8000 shows a zombie uvicorn from last week's manual test; kill -15 clears it; journalctl -u mission-api confirms clean startup. Then the on-call question "what's actually erroring?" takes one grep-awk-sort pipeline instead of downloading 2 GB of logs into pandas. Total time: four minutes, all muscle memory.

262

Git

Concept

Git's mental model in one line: commits are immutable snapshots of the whole tree (not diffs), linked into a graph, and branches are just movable pointers to commits — creating one costs nothing. Merge vs rebase is two philosophies of history: merge preserves the fork-and-join truthfully (extra merge commit, non-linear graph); rebase replays your commits on top of the target, producing a clean linear story at the cost of rewriting them. Convention in most teams: rebase your private branch to keep it current, never rebase shared history.

And the safety net that changes how brave you can be: reflog records every place HEAD has pointed. A "deleted" branch or a hard-reset commit is almost never gone — it's just unpointed-at, and git reflog finds it.

Branches are pointers into a snapshot graph — merge and rebase are two shapes of the same history.
Example 
git switch -c fix/reranker
git commit -am "rerank: guard empty chunk list"
git rebase main                # replay my work on the latest main

# disaster drill — make it, then unmake it:
git reset --hard HEAD~1        # "no wait, I needed that commit"
git reflog                     # 41c9f2e HEAD@{1}: commit: rerank: guard…
git reset --hard HEAD@{1}      # back from the dead

git log --oneline --graph --all  # always look at the graph, not the list
Real scenario — the lost light-curve fix

Friday, 6pm: you git reset --hard the exoplanet-classifier repo to test a clean baseline — and realize the un-pushed fix for the light-curve normalization bug went with it. Old you re-derives it from memory over the weekend. New you runs git reflog, spots the commit at HEAD@{2}, cherry-picks it back, and is at dinner by 6:15. Snapshots are never gone; pointers just moved.

263

GitHub (branching, PRs, rebasing)

Concept

GitHub is the collaboration layer on top of Git: feature branches isolate work, pull requests put a diff in front of a reviewer before it lands, branch protection makes review + green CI (#270) mandatory on main, and squash merges collapse a branch's fix-up noise into one clean commit. The PR is also where CI hangs its checks — nothing broken can land, mechanically.

PR habits are visible seniority signals — hiring managers really do read them: small diffs (one concern per PR — a 200-line PR gets reviewed in hours, a 2000-line one rots for a week), descriptions that state what changed, why, and how it was tested, and review comments addressed rather than argued into silence.

  • The solo loop still applies: branch → PR → self-review → squash-merge builds the habit and a readable history recruiters can browse.
  • Squash vs merge vs rebase on the merge button = the #262 philosophies, applied at the team boundary.
Example 
git switch -c feat/sse-streaming
git push -u origin feat/sse-streaming

gh pr create \
  --title "Stream /chat over SSE" \
  --body "TTFT 12s → 0.4s. Tested: curl -N + EventSource page. Rollback: revert."

gh pr view --comments        # respond to every review thread
gh pr checks                 # CI must be green (branch protection)
gh pr merge --squash         # one clean commit lands on main
Real scenario — the portfolio a recruiter actually opens

A hiring manager spends 90 seconds on your Mission Control repo before the interview. What they see: a protected main where every change arrived as a small PR — "Add reranker (#31)", "Stream /chat over SSE (#38)" — each with a crisp description and green checks. That reads as has worked on a real team even for a solo project, and it's a habit that costs you five extra minutes per change.

264

Docker basics

Concept

An image is an immutable, layered snapshot of a filesystem — base OS, dependencies, your code — built from a Dockerfile. A container is a running instance of an image with a thin writable layer on top; kill it and the image is untouched. "Works on my machine" dies here: the image is the machine.

The daily-life skill is layer caching: each Dockerfile instruction creates a layer, and a layer rebuilds only if it — or any layer beneath it — changed. So instruction order matters enormously: copy requirements.txt and install dependencies before copying your source code, and a code-only change rebuilds in 3 seconds instead of re-installing everything for 3 minutes.

Layers cache bottom-up: put what changes most often (your code) on top.
Example 
# Dockerfile — ordered for cache hits
FROM python:3.12-slim
WORKDIR /app
COPY requirements.txt .          # deps change rarely → cached layer
RUN pip install --no-cache-dir -r requirements.txt
COPY src/ ./src                  # code changes daily → top layer only
EXPOSE 8000
CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0", "--port", "8000"]

# docker build -t mission-api .      then:  docker run -p 8000:8000 mission-api
# edit src/, rebuild → "CACHED" on every layer except COPY src/
Real scenario — demo-day hotfixes in seconds

During the Mission Control demo you're fixing prompt wording live between sessions. With the naive Dockerfile (code copied first), every one-line tweak re-installed torch and sentence-transformers: 3-minute rebuilds, sweating visibly. With deps installed before COPY src/, each rebuild hits cache down the stack and finishes in 3 seconds. Same image, same result — the order of two lines is the whole difference.

265

Docker multi-stage builds

Concept

A multi-stage build uses two (or more) FROM blocks in one Dockerfile: a fat build stage with compilers, headers, and dev dependencies does the heavy lifting, then a slim runtime stage starts from a clean minimal base and COPY --from=build pulls in only the finished artifacts. Everything else — gcc, build caches, test tooling — is discarded with the build stage.

  • Smaller images: 1.4 GB → 240 MB is a typical drop for a Python API with compiled wheels.
  • Faster pulls: every K8s node scale-up and cold start downloads the image — size is latency.
  • Less attack surface: no compiler or package tooling in production means fewer CVEs on the scanner report and fewer tools for an intruder.
Build with everything, ship almost nothing — the runtime stage never sees a compiler.
Example 
FROM python:3.12 AS build            # fat: toolchain for native wheels
COPY requirements.txt .
RUN pip install --prefix=/install -r requirements.txt

FROM python:3.12-slim                # slim runtime: no gcc, no pip cache
COPY --from=build /install /usr/local
COPY src/ /app/src
WORKDIR /app
CMD ["uvicorn", "src.main:app", "--host", "0.0.0.0"]

# docker images:  mission-api (single-stage) 1.42GB → (multi-stage) 238MB
Real scenario — the autoscaler that stopped lagging

Traffic to Mission Control spikes whenever a NASA announcement trends. Your K8s autoscaler (#267) adds pods — but each new node pulled a 1.4 GB image first, so capacity arrived 90 seconds late, exactly when users piled in. After the multi-stage rewrite the image is 238 MB, pulls take seconds, and the security team's Trivy scan flags 60% fewer CVEs because the compiler toolchain no longer ships to prod.

266

Docker Compose

Concept

Docker Compose declares your whole dev stack — API, Postgres, Redis — in one YAML file and starts it with one command. Its quiet superpower is networking by service name: Compose puts all services on a private network with DNS, so your API connects to postgres:5432 and redis:6379 — the service names from the YAML — no IP addresses, no localhost port juggling.

  • The "clone and run" standard: git clone → docker compose up → a working stack — the developer experience good repos are judged by.
  • depends_on orders startup; healthchecks make it wait for ready, not just started.
  • Dev-only tool: production orchestration is Kubernetes (#267) — Compose is its single-machine rehearsal.
One YAML: three services, one private network, addressable by name.
Example 
# docker-compose.yml
services:
  api:
    build: .
    ports: ["8000:8000"]
    environment:
      DATABASE_URL: postgresql://mc:mc@postgres:5432/missions  # ← name!
      REDIS_URL: redis://redis:6379
    depends_on: [postgres, redis]
  postgres:
    image: postgres:16
    environment: { POSTGRES_USER: mc, POSTGRES_PASSWORD: mc, POSTGRES_DB: missions }
  redis:
    image: redis:7
# docker compose up --build   → the whole stack, one command
Real scenario — onboarding in four minutes

A collaborator joins the Mission Control project. Old world: half a day installing Postgres, fixing pgvector versions, exporting env vars. New world: git clone, docker compose up, and four minutes later they have the API on :8000, Postgres seeded by the init script, and Redis caching — identical to your machine, byte for byte. Every "works for me" argument the project could have had is deleted by one YAML file.

267

Kubernetes basics (pods, deployments, services)

Concept

Kubernetes is built on one big idea: declarative desired state. You never say "start a container" — you declare "three replicas of this image behind this address" in YAML, and controllers run a reconciliation loop forever: observe reality, diff it against the spec, act to close the gap. A pod crashes at 2am? The diff says 2 ≠ 3, so a replacement starts. Self-healing isn't a feature — it's the loop's normal operation.

  • Pod: the smallest unit — one or more containers sharing network and storage. Ephemeral by design; never point at a pod.
  • Deployment: manages a replica set of identical pods — scaling, rolling updates, self-healing.
  • Service: a stable name and virtual IP that load-balances across whatever pods currently match its label selector.
You declare the end state; controllers keep diffing and correcting until reality matches.
Example 
# deploy.yaml (trimmed to the load-bearing lines)
kind: Deployment
spec:
  replicas: 3
  selector: { matchLabels: { app: mission-api } }
  template:
    metadata: { labels: { app: mission-api } }
    spec:
      containers:
      - name: api
        image: acme/mission-api:1.4.2

# kubectl apply -f deploy.yaml
# kubectl delete pod mission-api-7d9f…   ← sabotage one on purpose
# kubectl get pods -w                    ← watch its replacement appear
Real scenario — the 2am crash nobody noticed

A memory leak in a reranking dependency OOM-kills one Mission Control pod most nights around 2am. Pre-K8s, that was a pager alert and a groggy ssh session. Now the deployment's controller sees 2 ≠ 3 and starts a replacement in seconds; the service pulls the dead pod from rotation so no request ever lands on it. You find out from the restart counter in the morning — fix the leak calmly over coffee, having slept through its symptoms.

268

Nginx

Concept

Nginx is the front door: a reverse proxy that receives every client request and forwards it to your backends. At that choke point it does the jobs you don't want in Python: TLS termination (HTTPS ends at Nginx; backends speak plain HTTP internally), load balancing across replicas (round-robin by default, least_conn when requests vary wildly in duration — like LLM calls), static file serving, and header hygiene like X-Forwarded-For so backends still see the real client IP.

Whatever fancier gateway a company runs — ALB, Traefik, K8s ingress — the concepts are Nginx concepts: upstreams, proxy headers, health-checked rotation. Learn them here, recognize them everywhere.

One front door: terminate TLS, then fan requests out across identical replicas.
Example 
upstream mission_api {
    least_conn;                    # LLM requests vary 1s–30s: don't round-robin blindly
    server api-1:8000;
    server api-2:8000;
}
server {
    listen 443 ssl;
    ssl_certificate /etc/ssl/mc.pem;   # TLS ends here
    location /static/ { root /var/www; }
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://mission_api;
        proxy_set_header X-Forwarded-For $remote_addr;
        proxy_buffering off;           # or your SSE stream (#252) arrives in one lump
    }
}
Real scenario — the stream that arrived as a lump

You put Nginx in front of two Mission Control replicas. Load balancing works — returning the hostname from each backend proves the alternation — but suddenly SSE "streaming" delivers the whole answer at once at the end. The culprit is Nginx's default proxy_buffering, which collects the response before forwarding. One directive — proxy_buffering off for the streaming location — and tokens flow again. A classic interview story: the proxy is part of your streaming path.

269

CI/CD concept

Concept

Continuous Integration: every push is built and tested automatically — broken code is caught in minutes, at the PR boundary, not discovered in production. Continuous Delivery: deploys are automated, reversible, and so routine they're boring. The goal-state is cultural as much as technical: shipping is a non-event. Teams that deploy 20 times a day have small, low-risk changes and instant rollback; teams that deploy quarterly have giant, terrifying ones.

  • A pipeline is ordered gates: each stage must pass before the next runs — and every stage needs a defined failure behavior.
  • Reversibility beats perfection: knowing any deploy can be rolled back in one command changes how boldly you can ship.
  • Delivery vs deployment: delivery = every change can ship automatically; deployment = every change does. Most teams gate the last step on a human click.
Example 
# the Mission Control pipeline — stages, and what failure does
1 lint     ruff + mypy          # fail → block merge; fix is a commit
2 test     pytest w/ fakes #251 # fail → block merge; no retry-until-green
3 build    docker build         # fail → block; no "works on my machine"
4 scan     pip-audit + trivy    # fail → block on critical CVEs
5 deploy   staging → prod       # fail → auto-rollback to last good image
6 verify   smoke-test /healthz  # fail → page a human (the only time)
Real scenario — from Friday ritual to non-event

Early Mission Control deploys were a Friday-evening ritual: ssh to the box, git pull, restart uvicorn, pray, and once — memorably — ship a broken retriever that nobody noticed until Monday. After wiring the six-stage pipeline, a deploy is: merge the PR. The broken-retriever class of incident now dies at stage 2, in CI, three minutes after push — and you've deployed on a Friday at 5pm without a second thought, because rollback is stage 5's automatic reflex.

270

GitHub Actions

Concept

GitHub Actions is CI/CD as YAML living in your repo under .github/workflows/. A workflow names its triggers (on: push, tags, PRs, cron), its jobs (each on a fresh runner VM, ordered with needs:), and its steps — shell commands plus prebuilt marketplace actions (actions/checkout, docker/build-push-action) so you compose rather than script. Secrets are injected from repo settings, never committed; a matrix fans one job out across versions or platforms.

Because it's the default CI for anything on GitHub, the workflow file itself has become a lingua franca — being able to read and write one is assumed.

Push triggers the pipeline; each job gates the next; tags alone reach the registry.
Example 
# .github/workflows/ci.yml
name: ci
on:
  push: { branches: [main], tags: ["v*"] }
jobs:
  test:
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: actions/checkout@v4
      - uses: actions/setup-python@v5
        with: { python-version: "3.12" }
      - run: pip install -r requirements.txt && ruff check . && pytest
  image:
    needs: test
    if: startsWith(github.ref, 'refs/tags/v')
    runs-on: ubuntu-latest
    steps:
      - uses: docker/build-push-action@v6
        with: { push: true, tags: acme/mission-api:${{ github.ref_name }} }
Real scenario — the eval gate

Your Mission Control workflow grows a third job: after unit tests pass, it runs RAGAS (#281) over a 40-question golden set using the fake-LLM overrides from #251 for routing and a small real model for judging. If faithfulness drops below 0.85, the job fails and the PR can't merge — a retrieval regression is now caught by CI like any other bug. "Evals as a merge gate" is precisely the habit the market calls senior right now.

271

Terraform

Concept

Terraform is infrastructure as code, declaratively: you describe resources — buckets, clusters, IAM roles — in HCL files, and Terraform makes reality match. The workflow is the whole point: plan computes a diff between your code and the state file (Terraform's record of what actually exists) and shows exactly what would be created, changed, or destroyed; apply executes precisely that diff and updates state. Infrastructure changes become reviewable (the plan goes in the PR), repeatable (rebuild an identical environment from the repo), and auditable (git blame for your cloud) — instead of unrecorded console clicking.

  • Read the plan like a diff: + create, ~ change in place, -/+ destroy and recreate — that last one is where outages hide.
  • State is sacred: shared remote state with locking (e.g. S3 + DynamoDB) or teammates corrupt each other's view of reality.
plan is a reviewable diff between code and tracked reality — apply executes exactly that diff.
Example 
# main.tf
resource "aws_s3_bucket" "mission_logs" {
  bucket = "mission-control-raw-logs"
  tags   = { project = "mission-control", env = "prod" }
}

resource "aws_s3_bucket_versioning" "v" {
  bucket = aws_s3_bucket.mission_logs.id
  versioning_configuration { status = "Enabled" }
}

# $ terraform plan    →  Plan: 2 to add, 0 to change, 0 to destroy
# $ terraform apply   →  reality changes; state now tracks both resources
# edit one tag, re-plan →  ~ update in-place: tags.env "prod" → "staging"
Real scenario — the environment you can rebuild

Mission Control's AWS footprint — EKS cluster, S3 buckets for NASA report dumps, IAM roles, the ECR registry — lives in a Terraform repo. When a reviewer questions a new IAM permission, the plan output in the PR shows exactly the one policy line changing. And when you need a staging environment, it's terraform apply with a different variables file — an identical stack in 20 minutes, not a week of archaeology into what someone once clicked in the console.
