272

Scalability principles

Concept

Two ways to handle more load: vertical scaling (a bigger box — more CPU, more RAM) and horizontal scaling (more boxes behind a load balancer). Vertical is simple but hits a ceiling and a price wall; horizontal scales almost forever but demands one discipline: statelessness. If any app instance keeps user state in its own memory — a sessions dict, a per-process cache of conversation history — then request two must land on the same instance as request one, and you can no longer add or kill replicas freely. So state moves down a layer: into databases, Redis, object storage. The app tier becomes disposable.

The other half of the skill is bottleneck thinking. A system scales exactly as far as its narrowest component: find the current bottleneck, fix it, and the bottleneck moves — it never disappears. For LLM apps the first bottleneck is rarely your code; it's the provider's rate limit, then the vector DB, then your own connection pool.

  • Vertical: zero code changes, hard ceiling, single point of failure.
  • Horizontal: needs statelessness + a load balancer, near-unlimited headroom.
  • The loop: measure → find bottleneck → fix → measure again. Never guess.
Horizontal scaling works only because no app instance owns any state — replicas become interchangeable.
Example 
# BAD: state in app memory — dies with the pod, breaks at 2 replicas
sessions = {}                                  # module-level dict

# GOOD: state in Redis — any replica can serve any request
import redis, json
r = redis.Redis()

@app.post("/chat/{sid}")
async def chat(sid: str, msg: Message):
    history = json.loads(r.get(f"chat:{sid}") or "[]")
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": msg.text})
    answer = await llm(history)
    r.setex(f"chat:{sid}", 3600, json.dumps(history + [answer]))
    return answer
Real scenario — 1 user to 10,000 concurrent

Sketch scaling the Mission Control RAG chat API from 1 user to 10,000 concurrent. The bottlenecks arrive in this order: (1) the LLM provider's tokens-per-minute limit — long before your CPU sweats; (2) the vector DB's query throughput once retrieval fan-out grows; (3) your FastAPI workers' open-connection count while they hold streaming responses. Each fix is different — request queuing + caching for (1), read replicas for (2), more stateless replicas for (3) — which is exactly why you find the bottleneck before reaching for a fix.

273

Caching strategies

Concept

Cache-aside is the workhorse pattern: check the cache first; on a miss, compute the real answer, write it into the cache with a TTL (time-to-live), and return it. Simple — and haunted by two hard problems. Invalidation: when the underlying data changes, cached copies are silently wrong until the TTL saves you. Stampedes: when a popular key expires, a thousand concurrent requests all miss at once and hammer the backend together (fix: lock so one request recomputes while the rest wait, or refresh hot keys before expiry).

LLM systems add three cache layers of their own, and they attack your largest cost line — tokens:

  • Exact-match response cache: key = hash of (model + prompt + params). Identical request → zero tokens spent.
  • Provider prompt caching: keep the stable prefix (system prompt, tool schemas, few-shot examples) byte-identical across calls and the provider bills cached prefix tokens at a steep discount.
  • Semantic caching: embed the query; if a past query sits within a cosine threshold, serve its cached answer. Catches paraphrases that exact-match misses — but tune the threshold, or "sol 121" answers get served for "sol 122" questions.
Cache-aside: check first, compute on miss, write back with a TTL. The cache is beside the path, not in it.
Example 
import hashlib, json

def cached_llm(prompt: str, model: str = "gpt-4o-mini"):
    key = "llm:" + hashlib.sha256(f"{model}|{prompt}".encode()).hexdigest()
    if (hit := r.get(key)) is not None:      # 1. check cache
        return json.loads(hit)                #    hit → free + instant
    answer = call_llm(model, prompt)          # 2. miss → pay for tokens
    r.setex(key, 86_400, json.dumps(answer))  # 3. write back, 24h TTL
    return answer
Real scenario — semantic cache in front of Mission Control RAG

Your Mission Control RAG gets "what caused the Apollo 13 failure?" phrased forty different ways a day. You put a Redis semantic cache in front of the whole pipeline: embed each incoming query, search a small vector index of past queries, and if the nearest one scores cosine ≥ 0.95, return its cached answer — skipping retrieval, reranking, and generation. Cache hit rate settles at 31%, token spend drops by a third, and P50 latency for hits falls from 3.2s to 40ms. One incident teaches you the threshold lesson: at 0.90 the cache served a "tank 2" answer to a "tank 1" question.

274

Redis

Concept

Redis is in-memory data structures served over the network: strings, hashes, lists, sets, sorted sets, pub/sub channels — each with atomic operations and optional TTLs. Because commands execute one at a time on a single thread, operations like INCR are race-free without locks: two replicas incrementing the same counter can never lose an update. That combination — microsecond latency, rich structures, atomicity — is why one Redis instance so often plays four roles at once: cache, rate limiter, task queue broker, and session store.

  • Strings + TTL: SETEX — caching (topic 273).
  • Atomic counters: INCR + EXPIRE — quotas and rate limits.
  • Sorted sets: ZADD/ZRANGE — leaderboards, priority queues, sliding windows.
  • Lists & pub/sub: LPUSH/BRPOP, PUBLISH/SUBSCRIBE — queues and events.
The Swiss-army layer: the same Redis often backs caching, limiting, queuing, and sessions simultaneously.
Example 
r = redis.Redis(decode_responses=True)

# per-user daily quota: atomic counter + TTL
def under_quota(user: str, limit: int = 100) -> bool:
    key = f"quota:{user}:{date.today()}"
    n = r.incr(key)                 # atomic — race-free across replicas
    if n == 1:
        r.expire(key, 86_400)       # first hit starts the 24h clock
    return n <= limit

# leaderboard of hottest queries: sorted set
r.zincrby("top-queries", 1, "solar flare forecast")
print(r.zrange("top-queries", 0, 2, desc=True, withscores=True))
Real scenario — one Redis, four jobs

The Mission Control stack runs a single Redis (with a replica) wearing four hats: the semantic answer cache from topic 273, per-user daily token quotas via INCR+EXPIRE, the Celery broker for background summarization jobs, and a ZADD sliding-window limiter guarding the NASA DONKI API. In the architecture interview, being able to say which structure backs which job — and that INCR is atomic because Redis executes commands single-threaded — is the difference between "used Redis" and "knows Redis".

275

Message queues

Concept

A message queue decouples the code that produces work from the code that consumes it. The producer drops a job on the queue and returns immediately; consumers pull jobs at whatever rate they can sustain. That buys you three things: spike absorption (a burst of 400 jobs/s piles up in the queue while workers drain at a steady 50/s), retry on failure (a crashed worker's job goes back on the queue), and load smoothing (workers never see the spike, so they never fall over).

The fine print that separates seniors from juniors: the standard delivery guarantee is at-least-once. Exactly-once delivery is (practically) a myth across process boundaries — so the same job will occasionally arrive twice, and making the consumer idempotent (processing a duplicate changes nothing) is your responsibility, not the queue's.

The queue absorbs the spike; consumers drain at their own sustainable rate. Depth is the shock absorber.
Example 
# worker.py — at-least-once delivery means THIS must be idempotent
while True:
    _, raw = r.brpop("jobs:embed")           # blocks until a job arrives
    job = json.loads(raw)
    if not r.set(f"done:{job['id']}", 1, nx=True, ex=86_400):
        continue                             # duplicate delivery → skip
    try:
        embed_and_store(job["chunk"])        # the actual work
    except Exception:
        r.delete(f"done:{job['id']}")        # release the claim…
        r.lpush("jobs:embed", raw)           # …and requeue for retry
Real scenario — the solar-storm ingest spike

A big solar storm hits and NASA publishes 300 new DONKI reports in an hour. Your ingest pipeline doesn't embed them inline — it drops 300 jobs:embed messages on the queue, and four workers drain them at the pace your embedding API's rate limit allows. Kill a worker mid-job to test: the job is redelivered to another worker, and because each job claims done:<id> with SET NX first, the chunk is embedded exactly once even though it was delivered twice. That kill-test is the "prove it" moment for this whole topic.

276

Celery

Concept

Celery is Python's classic task-queue framework: decorate a function with @app.task and it becomes a job you can run on any worker machine, with retries, scheduling (run nightly at 03:00), and result tracking built in. It sits on top of a broker (Redis or RabbitMQ carry the messages) and a result backend (where return values land).

Its signature use case is the 90-second request. HTTP clients, load balancers, and users all give up on requests that take minutes — so you don't make them wait. The endpoint enqueues the task, instantly returns a task_id, and the client polls a status endpoint (or gets a webhook) until the result is ready. The slow work happens in the background, on workers you can scale independently of the API tier.

The 90-second request pattern: enqueue, return a task_id immediately, poll for the result.
Example 
# tasks.py
from celery import Celery
app = Celery("mc", broker="redis://localhost", backend="redis://localhost")

@app.task(autoretry_for=(TimeoutError,), retry_backoff=True, max_retries=3)
def summarize_report(report_id: str) -> str:
    return llm_summarize(load_report(report_id))   # ~90 seconds

# api.py — return immediately, let the client poll
@router.post("/summaries")
def start(report_id: str):
    task = summarize_report.delay(report_id)
    return {"task_id": task.id}   # client polls GET /summaries/{task_id}
Real scenario — the 200-page report summary

A user asks Mission Control for a full summary of a 200-page Apollo post-flight report — map-reduce over 60 chunks, roughly 90 seconds of LLM calls. Done inline, the request times out at the load balancer and the user retries, doubling your token bill. As a Celery task, the endpoint answers in 20ms with a task_id, the UI shows "summarizing… (43/60 chunks)", retry_backoff quietly survives two provider timeouts, and the workers scale from 2 to 8 during business hours without the API tier changing at all.

277

Rate limiting

Concept

A rate limiter caps how many requests pass per unit time. The token bucket is the algorithm to know: a bucket holds up to burst tokens and refills at rate tokens/second; each request takes one token; empty bucket → reject with 429 and a Retry-After header. Its virtue is that it allows short bursts (a full bucket) while enforcing the average rate. The sliding window counts timestamped requests in the trailing N seconds (a Redis sorted set does this naturally) — stricter, no burst allowance.

In LLM systems you limit in both directions. Inbound: users (or a runaway script) can't drain your token budget — this is cost protection. Outbound: your own workers stay just under the provider's requests-per-minute and tokens-per-minute caps, so you throttle yourself smoothly instead of drowning in the provider's 429s and tripping retry storms.

Token bucket: steady refill sets the average rate, bucket depth sets the allowed burst.
Example 
# token bucket in Redis (production version wraps this in a Lua script
# so read-compute-write is one atomic step)
def allow(user: str, rate: float = 5.0, burst: int = 10) -> bool:
    now = time.time()
    tokens, ts = r.hmget(f"tb:{user}", "tokens", "ts")
    tokens = min(burst, float(tokens or burst)
                        + (now - float(ts or now)) * rate)
    if tokens < 1:
        return False       # middleware → 429, Retry-After: 1
    r.hset(f"tb:{user}", mapping={"tokens": tokens - 1, "ts": now})
    return True
Real scenario — limiting both directions at once

The Orbital Research Agent needs both limiters the same week. Inbound: a teammate's eval script hammers your FastAPI endpoint in a 20-request burst — requests 1–10 drain the bucket, request 11 gets a clean 429 with Retry-After: 1 instead of a $40 token bill. Outbound: DONKI's API starts returning 429s during a storm, so you put a shared token bucket in Redis in front of every DONKI call across all four workers — now the fleet collectively self-throttles to 28 req/min under the 30 req/min cap, and the provider errors disappear.

278

Load balancing

Concept

A load balancer spreads incoming traffic across your interchangeable (stateless — topic 272) instances. Three strategies cover the interviews: round-robin — take turns, the default; least-connections — send to the instance with the fewest open requests, better when request durations vary wildly (LLM streaming!); consistent hashing — the same key (user, session, cache shard) always lands on the same instance, and adding a node reshuffles only a sliver of keys.

The part that makes it production-grade is health checks: the balancer probes each backend (an HTTP /health ping, or passive failure counting), and pulls dead instances out of rotation automatically — then re-adds them when they recover. Deploys, crashes, and OOM kills become invisible to users.

Health checks make the balancer self-healing: dead backends leave rotation, users never notice.
Example 
# nginx.conf — builds directly on topic 268
upstream rag_api {
    least_conn;                      # LLM streams have wild durations
    server api1:8000 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=10s;
    server api2:8000 max_fails=2 fail_timeout=10s;
}
server {
    listen 80;
    location / {
        proxy_pass http://rag_api;
        # if one backend errors mid-request, retry on the next
        proxy_next_upstream error timeout http_502;
    }
}
Real scenario — the kill test

Two replicas of the Mission Control RAG API sit behind Nginx with least_conn — round-robin was starving one replica because streamed answers hold connections open for 20+ seconds while quick health queries finish in 50ms. The proof: run a 500-request load test, docker kill api-2 halfway through, and watch the numbers — max_fails=2 ejects the dead backend within a second, proxy_next_upstream replays the in-flight failures onto api-1, and the load test finishes with zero failed requests.

279

Distributed systems basics

Concept

The moment your system spans two machines, three uncomfortable truths apply: networks partition (messages get lost — or worse, delivered after you gave up), messages arrive twice or never (hence at-least-once + idempotency, topic 275), and clocks disagree (never order events across machines by timestamp). You can't fix these; you engineer around them with a small, battle-tested toolkit:

  • Timeouts everywhere — an unbounded wait is an outage in disguise; every network call gets a deadline.
  • Retries with exponential backoff + jitter — wait 0.5s, 1s, 2s… with randomness added, so a thousand clients don't retry in lockstep and re-kill the recovering service (the "thundering herd").
  • Idempotency keys — the client sends a unique key per logical operation; the server executes each key once, so a retried request can't double-charge, double-write, or double-alert.
  • CAP intuition — during a partition you choose: refuse writes (consistency) or accept divergence (availability). Know which your system picks and why.
Exponential backoff spreads retries out; jitter (+j) de-synchronizes clients; the idempotency key makes retries safe.
Example 
def retry(tries=4, base=0.5):
    def deco(fn):
        @functools.wraps(fn)
        def wrapper(*a, **kw):
            for attempt in range(tries):
                try:
                    return fn(*a, **kw, timeout=10)      # deadline always
                except TransientError:
                    if attempt == tries - 1: raise
                    delay = base * 2 ** attempt             # 0.5, 1, 2…
                    time.sleep(delay + random.uniform(0, delay))  # jitter
        return wrapper
    return deco
Real scenario — DONKI is flaky, Kafka duplicates

Both failure modes live in your stack already. The Orbital Research Agent's DONKI tool fails ~50% of the time during solar maxima — wrapped in @retry, the agent's success rate goes from coin-flip to 94%, and jitter matters because all four workers hit DONKI at the same cron tick. Meanwhile the satellite-telemetry Kafka consumer occasionally re-reads a batch after a rebalance; because each anomaly alert carries an idempotency key (sat_id + window_start), operators get one page instead of three for the same event.

280

Event-driven architecture

Concept

In a request-driven system, service A calls service B — A must know B exists, wait for B, and handle B's failures. In an event-driven system, A just announces a fact — log.ingested, anomaly.detected — onto a bus (Redis pub/sub, Kafka, SNS), and any interested service reacts on its own schedule. The publisher knows nothing about its subscribers.

The payoff is loose coupling and easy extension: adding a new consumer means deploying a new subscriber, never touching the publisher. The price is eventual consistency — for a moment, the event has been published but not yet processed everywhere, so different parts of the system briefly disagree — and harder debugging, because "what happened after this event?" spans many services. That second problem is exactly what distributed tracing (topic 292) exists to solve.

Publisher announces a fact; subscribers react independently. New consumers bolt on without touching the source.
Example 
# publisher — knows nothing about who listens
r.publish("events", json.dumps(
    {"type": "log.ingested", "doc_id": "apollo13-day3"}))

# subscriber — one of many, each in its own process
sub = r.pubsub()
sub.subscribe("events")
for msg in sub.listen():
    if msg["type"] == "message":
        evt = json.loads(msg["data"])
        if evt["type"] == "log.ingested":
            embed_document(evt["doc_id"])   # Kafka if you need replay
Real scenario — the refactor that proves the point

Originally your ingestor called the embedder directly: ingest() → embed() → notify() — three coupled steps, and adding anything meant editing the ingestor. Refactored, the ingestor publishes log.ingested and stops caring. The embedder and a keyword alerter subscribe. Two months later you want 5% of new documents sampled into the eval set (topic 289): you deploy an eval sampler subscriber and the ingestor's code doesn't change by one line. When someone asks "why did document X take 90s to become searchable?", that's eventual consistency — and the answer lives in a trace, not a stack trace.

— Evals-First Engineering —
281

RAGAS

Concept

RAGAS is the standard framework for evaluating RAG pipelines. You hand it triples of question / contexts / answer (plus ground_truth where you have it), and it computes the four metrics of the next four topics using LLM judges under the hood — no human labeling per run. The four metrics split cleanly along two axes: which stage is being judged (retrieval vs generation) and which failure is being caught (junk got in — precision — vs something is missing or off-target — recall).

The discipline that makes RAGAS valuable isn't the library, it's the habit: run it before and after every pipeline change — new chunk size, new embedding model, new reranker, new prompt. The score diff tells you whether your "improvement" improved anything, and which stage to blame when it didn't.

The four RAGAS metrics as a 2×2: stage (retrieval/generation) × failure type (precision/recall).
Example 
from ragas import evaluate
from ragas.metrics import (context_precision, context_recall,
                           faithfulness, answer_relevancy)
from datasets import Dataset

ds = Dataset.from_dict({
    "question":     ["Why did Mars Climate Orbiter fail?"],
    "contexts":     [[chunk1, chunk2, chunk3]],   # what you retrieved
    "answer":       [rag_answer],                  # what you generated
    "ground_truth": ["A pound-force/newton unit mismatch…"],
})
scores = evaluate(ds, metrics=[context_precision, context_recall,
                               faithfulness, answer_relevancy])
print(scores)   # per-metric, and per-sample via scores.to_pandas()
Real scenario — finding the weakest link

You run RAGAS over 50 Q&A pairs from the Mission Control RAG: context precision 0.52, context recall 0.81, faithfulness 0.88, answer relevancy 0.90. Read the 2×2: generation is fine — retrieval is stuffing the prompt with junk. You add a reranker (topic from volume 9), rerun the same 50 pairs: precision jumps to 0.79 and — the satisfying part — faithfulness rises to 0.94 without touching the prompt, because less noise in the context means less material to hallucinate from. That before/after table goes straight into your portfolio README.

282

Context precision

Concept

Context precision asks: of the chunks retrieval returned, how many were actually relevant to the question? It's the signal-to-noise ratio of your retrieval stage. RAGAS's version is also rank-aware: relevant chunks near the top of the list score better than the same chunks buried at the bottom, because the LLM (and your token budget) weight early context more.

Why it matters more than it sounds: irrelevant chunks aren't just wasted tokens. Every off-topic paragraph in the prompt is raw material for the model to weave into a confident, wrong answer — low precision invites hallucination. If faithfulness drops, check precision first.

Precision = relevant fraction of what you retrieved; rank-aware scoring rewards relevant chunks appearing early.
Example 
# hand-label the top-5 chunks for one query: 1 = relevant, 0 = noise
labels = [1, 1, 0, 1, 0]

precision = sum(labels) / len(labels)              # plain: 0.60

# rank-aware (mean precision@k over relevant ranks — the ragas flavor)
hits = [sum(labels[:k+1]) / (k+1)
        for k, rel in enumerate(labels) if rel]
rank_aware = sum(hits) / sum(labels)               # 0.92 here
print(f"plain={precision:.2f}  rank-aware={rank_aware:.2f}")
# do this for 10 queries by hand ONCE — then trust the automated number
Real scenario — the boilerplate invasion

Context precision on the Mission Control RAG reads a dismal 0.4, and eyeballing the retrieved chunks shows why: every NASA technical report opens with the same export-control notice and distribution boilerplate, those pages got chunked and embedded like everything else, and they're semantically "close" to almost any query. Two fixes, both measurable: filter boilerplate at ingest (precision → 0.62), then add a cross-encoder reranker over the top-50 (precision → 0.83). Same eval set, three runs, one clean story for the interview.

283

Context recall

Concept

Context recall asks the opposite question from precision: did retrieval surface all the information the correct answer needs? To measure it, take the ground-truth answer, split it into individual claims, and check what fraction of those claims is supported somewhere in the retrieved chunks. Missing claims = information the model literally could not have gotten right, no matter how good the prompt.

The dangerous pattern is high precision + low recall: everything retrieved is on-topic, so the model answers fluently and confidently — but a key piece never made it into the context, so the answer is confidently incomplete. Users rarely notice what's missing; your recall metric does. Typical culprits: chunking that split a table from its caption, top-k too small, or the fact living in a document that was never ingested.

Recall checks the ground-truth answer's claims against the retrieved context — uncovered claims are guaranteed gaps.
Example 
truth_claims = [
    "navigation software expected newton-seconds",
    "the vendor's code produced pound-force-seconds",
    "the discrepancy went uncaught for months",
]
covered = [any(claim_supported(c, chunk)      # LLM yes/no check
               for chunk in retrieved_chunks)
           for c in truth_claims]
recall = sum(covered) / len(truth_claims)     # 2/3 → 0.67
print([c for c, ok in zip(truth_claims, covered) if not ok])
# the uncovered claim tells you WHAT to fix: chunking? top-k? ingest?
Real scenario — the split table

"Why did Mars Climate Orbiter fail?" keeps scoring 0.5 recall even at top-k=10. The uncovered claim is always the unit-mismatch detail — and grepping the corpus shows why: the mishap report presents it in a table, and your fixed-size chunker split the table's numbers from the paragraph naming the units. No reranker can retrieve a chunk that doesn't exist. The fix is upstream in chunking (keep tables atomic), and recall jumps to 0.9 — a perfect demonstration of why you need per-stage metrics, not just "does the answer look right".

284

Faithfulness scoring

Concept

Faithfulness asks: is every claim in the generated answer actually supported by the retrieved context? The procedure: decompose the answer into atomic claims, verify each claim against the context (an LLM judge answers "supported: yes/no" per claim), and report the supported fraction. A claim the context doesn't back is — by definition — something the model made up or dragged in from its training data. This is the hallucination check for RAG, and it's the metric enterprise buyers ask about first, because "grounded in our documents" is the whole reason they bought RAG instead of raw ChatGPT.

Note what faithfulness does not check: whether the answer is correct or complete (the context itself could be wrong or thin — that's recall's job), or whether it answers the question (that's relevancy). It checks one thing only: no claim without a source in the context.

Every answer claim must trace back to the context; the unsupported one is, by definition, hallucinated.
Example 
CLAIMS = "List each factual claim in this answer, one per line:\n{ans}"
VERIFY = ("Context:\n{ctx}\n\nClaim: {claim}\n"
          "Is this claim fully supported by the context? yes or no.")

claims  = llm(CLAIMS.format(ans=answer)).splitlines()
support = [llm(VERIFY.format(ctx=context, claim=c)).strip().lower() == "yes"
           for c in claims]
faithfulness = sum(support) / len(claims)
# do this ONCE by hand for one answer — decompose, verify each claim
# yourself — and you will forever trust (and distrust) the automated score
Real scenario — the invented conclusion

A Mission Control answer about the Apollo 13 review board reads beautifully — and faithfulness flags one claim at 0.75: "the panel concluded schedule pressure was a contributing factor." Grep the retrieved chunks: that sentence exists nowhere. The model imported a plausible-sounding conclusion from its pretraining. This is precisely the failure enterprise buyers fear (a compliance customer citing a "finding" that isn't in their documents), and precisely the one faithfulness catches automatically on every eval run.

285

Answer relevancy

Concept

Answer relevancy asks: does the answer actually address the question that was asked? An answer can be 100% faithful to the context and still dodge the question — summarize the wrong report, answer a related-but-different question, or hedge with generic filler. Faithfulness can't see this failure at all, which is why the two metrics are a pair.

RAGAS measures it with a clever trick: ask an LLM to reverse-engineer questions from the answer ("what question does this answer respond to?"), embed those generated questions, and compute their cosine similarity to the actual question. If the answer is on-target, the reverse-engineered questions land right next to the real one; if it dodged, they land somewhere else in embedding space, and the score drops.

Reverse-engineered questions reveal what the answer actually addresses — compared, in embedding space, to what was asked.
Example 
# the ragas trick, hand-rolled
gen_qs = [llm(f"Write the question this answer responds to:\n{answer}")
          for _ in range(3)]

q_vec  = embed(question)
scores = [cosine(q_vec, embed(g)) for g in gen_qs]
answer_relevancy = sum(scores) / len(scores)

# sanity experiment: feed a faithful-but-off-topic answer through —
# faithfulness stays ~0.9 while relevancy craters. Two metrics, two failures.
Real scenario — the sol 121/122 dodge

A user asks the Mission Control RAG "what caused the anomaly on sol 122?" — but retrieval mostly surfaced sol 121 telemetry (the days overlap in one chunk), and the model, grounded and obedient, faithfully summarizes sol 121's power budget. Faithfulness: 0.92. Answer relevancy: 0.41. Without the second metric this failure is invisible in your dashboards — the answer is well-written, cited, and useless. The fix turns out to be metadata filtering on sol number before vector search, and relevancy on date-scoped questions climbs to 0.88.

286

LLM-as-judge pattern

Concept

Human grading doesn't scale to thousands of outputs per day, and string-match metrics can't grade open-ended text. The LLM-as-judge pattern fills the gap: a strong model receives a written rubric (criteria, in priority order, with a fixed output format) plus the output(s) to grade, and returns a score or a pairwise verdict. It's how RAGAS computes its metrics, and how most production eval suites grade free-form answers.

Trust it only after you know its biases — and design around them:

  • Position bias: in A-vs-B comparisons, judges favor whichever answer is shown first. Mitigation: run every pair twice with order swapped; count disagreements as ties.
  • Verbosity bias: longer answers score higher, correctness held constant. Mitigation: put "brevity" in the rubric explicitly and cap lengths.
  • Self-preference: models rate their own family's style higher. Mitigation: judge with a different model family than the one being judged.
The swap test: whichever slot wins both rounds is a real win; a flip is position bias and counts as a tie.
Example 
RUBRIC = """Grade two answers to the same question.
Criteria in priority order: factual accuracy, completeness, brevity.
Reply with exactly one word: FIRST, SECOND, or TIE."""

def pairwise(q, a, b):
    v1 = judge(RUBRIC, q, first=a, second=b)     # a shown first
    v2 = judge(RUBRIC, q, first=b, second=a)     # order swapped
    w1 = {"FIRST": "a", "SECOND": "b"}.get(v1)
    w2 = {"FIRST": "b", "SECOND": "a"}.get(v2)
    return w1 if w1 == w2 else "tie"            # unstable → tie
Real scenario — judging the reranker A/B

You're comparing two reranker configs on 50 Mission Control questions, using an LLM judge for pairwise verdicts. First pass (no swap): config B "wins" 34–16. With the swap test, 11 of those verdicts flip with order and become ties — the honest tally is 25–14–11, still a win for B but a much smaller one. You also judge with a different model family than the one generating, after noticing the same-family judge rated its own house style a suspicious +0.4 higher. The bias-hardened harness is 15 lines of code and the difference between an eval and a rumor.

287

Benchmark creation

Concept

Public benchmarks (MMLU, HumanEval…) are saturated — top models cluster within noise of each other — and contaminated — their test sets leaked into training data long ago. They tell you almost nothing about your workload. A private domain benchmark does: representative inputs from your actual domain, ground truth you verified, and a scoring script that runs unattended. That's the whole recipe — and because no model trained on it, the scores mean something.

What makes a domain benchmark good: representative inputs (drawn from real user queries, covering easy/hard/edge), hard negatives (questions the corpus can't answer — the correct output is "not in the corpus", and models that bluff get caught), and a scoring script (exact match where possible, an LLM judge with a rubric where not). A benchmark you built for a domain you know deeply is a genuine competitive asset — and a portfolio piece nobody else can copy.

Anatomy of a private benchmark: real inputs + verified truth + a script. No model has trained on it — so scores mean something.
Example 
# bench/missionlog_v1.jsonl — one case per line
{"id": "q07", "q": "What alloy lined the LM ascent engine nozzle?",
 "expected": "columbium (niobium) alloy", "type": "factoid"}
{"id": "q21", "q": "Which sol did rover B lose comms?",
 "expected": "NOT_IN_CORPUS", "type": "hard_negative"}

# score.py — runs unattended, prints one number per model
for case in load_jsonl("bench/missionlog_v1.jsonl"):
    got = rag_answer(case["q"])
    results[case["id"]] = grade(got, case["expected"])  # exact/judge
print(f"score: {mean(results.values()):.1%}")
Real scenario — the benchmark nobody can copy

You build a 30-question benchmark over the Mission Control corpus: 18 factoids from real user queries, 6 multi-hop questions ("compare the failure modes of…"), and 6 hard negatives about missions the corpus doesn't cover. Scoring two candidate models: the expensive one wins 83% vs 71% — but on hard negatives specifically it's 6/6 vs 2/6, and those four bluffed answers are exactly what you can't ship to an ops team. Public leaderboards had these models within a point of each other. Your 30 questions disagreed, on the axis that matters to your users.

288

Regression testing (prompts/models)

Concept

In normal software, you don't merge code that fails the tests. Evals-first engineering applies the same discipline to prompts and models: every prompt tweak, every model upgrade, every retrieval change runs the full eval suite before deploy, and the score diff justifies or blocks the change. This replaces "it seems better on the three examples I tried" with evidence — and it catches the silent killer of LLM systems: the change that improves the cases you were looking at while quietly regressing ten you weren't.

Mechanically it's a CI gate: run the benchmark (topic 287) and golden set (topic 289) against the changed pipeline, compare per-metric against the baseline from main, fail the build if any metric drops more than a tolerance ε (scores are noisy — run twice or use a tolerance, never gate on exact equality). The per-question diff matters as much as the aggregate: it names exactly which behaviors you're trading away.

The eval-gated deploy: no prompt or model change ships without a score diff against baseline.
Example 
# .github/workflows/eval-gate.yml
on: pull_request        # every prompt/model change goes through this
jobs:
  eval:
    steps:
      - run: python score.py --bench bench/missionlog_v1.jsonl
                             --out new.json
      - run: python compare.py --baseline baselines/main.json
             --new new.json
             --fail-if "faithfulness < baseline - 0.02"
             --fail-if "answer_relevancy < baseline - 0.02"
# green = merge. red = the PR now needs a very good explanation.
Real scenario — the model upgrade that wasn't

The provider releases a shiny new mini model, 40% cheaper. You bump one config line; the eval gate runs. Aggregate looks fine — faithfulness +0.04 — but the per-question diff shows answer relevancy collapsed from 0.86 to 0.71 specifically on date-scoped questions: the new model ignores your "answer only about the requested sol" instruction. The PR is blocked with a diff naming all nine regressed questions. You fix it with one prompt line, rerun, both metrics green, merge. Total cost of the safety net: 55 eval questions and three minutes of CI.

289

Golden datasets

Concept

A golden dataset is a small, hand-verified, versioned set of input → expected-output pairs that anchors all your other evaluation. "Golden" means every example has been checked by a human against the source of truth — no scraped labels, no model-generated ground truth you didn't verify. The operating principle is quality over quantity: 25 examples you trust completely beat 2,500 you don't, because every automated metric ultimately calibrates against them — if the anchor is wrong, everything downstream measures the wrong thing.

  • In git: versioned like code, reviewed like code — a changed expectation is a diff someone must approve.
  • Provenance per example: where the truth came from, who verified it, when — so a disputed case can be re-checked at the source.
  • Grown deliberately: every interesting production failure becomes a candidate golden example (fix the bug, keep the test).
The golden set anchors everything: regression gates, judge calibration, benchmarks, and RAGAS ground truth all trace to it.
Example 
# golden/golden.jsonl — one verified example (note the provenance)
{"id": "g03",
 "input": "What caused the Apollo 13 oxygen tank failure?",
 "expected": "Damaged Teflon insulation on tank 2 fan wires; a stir
              caused a short and combustion inside the tank.",
 "provenance": "Cortright Report ch.4 — verified 2026-08-02 by A. Rivera",
 "version_added": 3}

# regression tests read ONLY from here — never from ad-hoc examples
GOLDEN = [json.loads(l) for l in open("golden/golden.jsonl")]
assert len(GOLDEN) == 25, "golden set changed — was that reviewed?"
Real scenario — 25 anchors from real traffic

You curate the Mission Control golden set from Langfuse traces (topic 291): the 25 most representative real user questions, each answered by you, by hand, against the primary-source reports — three hours of work, logged in each example's provenance field. Weeks later a teammate "fixes" a chunking bug and two golden expectations start failing; the git diff discussion that follows uncovers that the expectations were right and the fix subtly broke section-header attachment. Without the goldens, that regression ships silently. With them, it was a failed CI run and a five-minute revert.

290

Hallucination measurement

Concept

"It hallucinates sometimes" is a vibe. Engineering needs a number: a hallucination rate you can track across releases. The pipeline: extract the atomic claims from each output, verify each claim against the trusted sources (retrieved context for RAG; reference docs otherwise) using an LLM or NLI model, and report the unsupported fraction. It's faithfulness (topic 284) industrialized — run over a fixed question set, on a schedule, with the failures logged.

Two things make the number actionable. First, fix the denominator: always the same question set, so the rate is comparable across runs. Second, keep the failures: every unsupported claim is a labeled example of how your system fabricates — patterns emerge (dates get invented, causal conclusions get imported) that point at specific fixes. What gets measured gets fixed; what gets logged gets prevented.

Extract → verify → count: the unsupported fraction turns "it hallucinates sometimes" into a trackable rate.
Example 
total, unsupported = 0, 0
for q in eval_questions:                  # same 20 every run
    answer, ctx = rag(q)
    for claim in extract_claims(answer):
        total += 1
        if not supported(claim, ctx):     # LLM / NLI check
            unsupported += 1
            log_failure(q, claim)          # future golden examples
print(f"hallucination rate: {unsupported/total:.1%}")
# change ONE thing (reranker, prompt, k) → rerun → compare the rate
Real scenario — 11% to 3%, with receipts

Baseline measurement on Mission Control: 11% of claims unsupported. Reading the failure log, two patterns pop out: invented launch dates, and causal conclusions imported from pretraining (topic 284's "budget pressure" pattern). Two targeted fixes — a prompt line ("state only what the context supports; say 'not in the retrieved documents' otherwise") and the topic-282 reranker — and the rate drops to 3% on the identical question set. "I reduced the measured hallucination rate from 11% to 3%, here's the methodology" is the single strongest sentence an AI-engineering CV can carry in 2026.

— Observability —
291

Langfuse

Concept

Langfuse is open-source observability built specifically for LLM applications. Every request becomes a trace; every pipeline stage (retrieval, rerank, generation, tool call) becomes a span inside it; generation spans additionally record model, token counts, and cost. On top of raw traces it layers the LLM-specific extras: user feedback attached to traces, prompt versioning and management, and eval scores (RAGAS, judges) stored per-trace — so "which prompt version caused the bad answers users flagged?" is a query, not an archaeology dig.

Being self-hostable (one docker compose up) is a real differentiator: regulated industries that can't ship prompts and user data to a third-party SaaS can still have full LLM observability inside their own VPC.

The trace waterfall: spans laid out on the request timeline — the wide one is where your latency lives.
Example 
from langfuse.decorators import observe

@observe()                        # each call becomes a span
def retrieve(q): ...

@observe()
def rerank(q, chunks): ...

@observe(as_type="generation")    # records model, tokens, cost
def generate(q, chunks): ...

@observe()                        # the parent trace
def rag(q):
    return generate(q, rerank(q, retrieve(q)))
Real scenario — Langfuse on Mission Control

You self-host Langfuse next to the Mission Control RAG and decorate the four pipeline functions. First discovery, within the hour: the reranker is 2.8s of the 3.9s P50 — you were blaming the LLM. Second: sorting traces by cost reveals one power user's agent loop re-asking the same question with growing context, 40× a day (hello, topic 273's semantic cache). Third: you wire the nightly RAGAS run to write scores back onto sampled traces, so thumbs-down + low-faithfulness traces become your triage queue — and your golden-set candidates (topic 289).

292

OpenTelemetry

Concept

OpenTelemetry (OTel) is the vendor-neutral standard for the three observability signals — traces, metrics, logs — with SDKs for every language and exporters for every backend (Jaeger, Grafana, Datadog, Phoenix, Langfuse…). Its core mechanism is context propagation: when service A calls service B, the current trace's ID travels in a traceparent HTTP header, so B's spans attach to A's trace. One user request through five services = one trace, viewable as a single waterfall — which is exactly the debugging tool event-driven systems (topic 280) demand.

For AI systems specifically, the GenAI semantic conventions are standardizing attribute names for LLM calls (gen_ai.request.model, token counts, etc.) — meaning traces from any instrumented library render meaningfully in any OTel backend. Instrument once, choose vendors later.

Context propagation: the trace id rides the traceparent header, so spans from both services join into one waterfall.
Example 
from opentelemetry import trace
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.fastapi import FastAPIInstrumentor
from opentelemetry.instrumentation.httpx import HTTPXClientInstrumentor

FastAPIInstrumentor.instrument_app(app)   # server span per request
HTTPXClientInstrumentor().instrument()    # injects traceparent on every
                                          # outgoing call → same trace id
tracer = trace.get_tracer("rag")
with tracer.start_as_current_span("rerank") as span:
    span.set_attribute("gen_ai.request.model", "rerank-v3")
    top = rerank(query, chunks)
Real scenario — the 3-second mystery, solved in one screen

A user reports the Orbital Research Agent "sometimes takes forever." The agent calls the RAG service, which calls vLLM — three services, three log files, no shared request ID… until you add OTel with auto-instrumentation to all three. The next slow request is one trace: agent span 4.9s → RAG span 4.6s → and inside it, a 3.8s gap before the vLLM span even starts. The culprit is connection-pool exhaustion in the RAG service's HTTP client, invisible in any single service's logs, obvious in the joined waterfall.

293

Arize Phoenix

Concept

Arize Phoenix is open-source evaluation and tracing built OTel-native: it ingests standard OpenTelemetry spans (via the OpenInference conventions), so anything you instrumented for topic 292 flows straight in. Where it stands out from a generic trace viewer is the analysis layer bolted on top: retrieval analysis (which documents each query pulled, with relevance scoring), embedding-drift visualization (projected clusters of queries and documents over time), and eval runs executed inside the same tool.

Its trademark is the near-zero barrier to entry — notebook-launchable: px.launch_app() in a cell gives you a local UI, no docker, no account. It's the "open a debugger" of RAG work; Langfuse is the "run it in production" counterpart, and OTel means you don't have to choose at instrumentation time.

traces

OTel/OpenInference spans: every retrieve, rerank, LLM call.

retrieval analysis

Per-query: documents pulled, scores, relevance — find bad retrievals fast.

embedding drift

Query vs corpus clusters, projected and compared over time.

evals

Run judge-based evals over captured traces, in the same UI.

Example 
import phoenix as px
from openinference.instrumentation.langchain import LangChainInstrumentor

px.launch_app()                       # local UI at localhost:6006
LangChainInstrumentor().instrument()  # RAG traces flow in via OTel

run_my_rag_queries()                  # then open the UI:
#  traces view    → every retrieve/generate span, with latencies
#  retrieval view → which chunks each query pulled, scored
#  embeddings view→ query cluster vs document cluster, drift
Real scenario — drift you can see

Mission Control's retrieval quality quietly degrades over a month, and RAGAS numbers say so — but not why. You launch Phoenix in a notebook, load the last 2,000 traced queries, and open the embeddings view: the corpus cluster sits where it always did, but a new lobe of query embeddings has grown off to the side — users started asking about the brand-new Artemis logs, which were never ingested. Retrieval wasn't broken; the corpus was stale. One picture ended a week of prompt-tweaking in the wrong stage.

— Generative Frontier —
294

Diffusion models

Concept

A diffusion model is trained on a deceptively simple task: given a slightly noised image (and the noise level), predict the noise that was added. That's it. The forward process is fixed and needs no learning — add a little scheduled Gaussian noise, step by step, until any image dissolves into pure static. The reverse process is the learned part: start from pure noise and apply the denoiser step by step, each pass removing a little of what it predicts is noise, until an image crystallizes out.

Why this beat GANs (topic 296): the training objective is a stable regression loss (no adversarial cat-and-mouse), it covers the whole data distribution (no mode collapse), and the step-by-step generation gives natural control hooks — which is where text conditioning (topic 295) plugs in. The same recipe now drives image, video, and audio generation.

Forward: image dissolves into noise on a fixed schedule. Reverse: the trained denoiser walks it back — that walk IS generation.
Example 
from diffusers import DDPMPipeline
import torch

pipe = DDPMPipeline.from_pretrained("google/ddpm-celebahq-256")
img = pipe(num_inference_steps=50).images[0]   # noise → image, 50 steps

# the forward process, hand-rolled: watch structure drown
for t in [0.0, 0.25, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0]:
    noisy = (1 - t) * x0 + t * torch.randn_like(x0)   # (simplified)
    show(noisy, title=f"t={t}")
# training = learning to reverse exactly this, one small step at a time
Real scenario — synthetic light curves for the rare class

Your exoplanet classifier starves on confirmed multi-planet transits — a few hundred real examples. You train a small 1-D diffusion model on transit light-curve segments and sample synthetic curves for the rare class. Because diffusion covers the distribution instead of collapsing to one "typical transit" (the GAN failure you'll meet in topic 296), the augmented training set lifts rare-class recall from 0.61 to 0.74 — and the eval discipline from topics 287–288 is what proves the synthetic data helped rather than polluted.

295

Stable Diffusion

Concept

Stable Diffusion is latent diffusion: instead of denoising in pixel space (a 512×512×3 image = 786k dimensions, brutally expensive), a pretrained VAE (rung 129) compresses the image into a 64×64×4 latent, the diffusion U-Net does all its denoising steps in that ~48× smaller space, and the VAE decoder inflates the final latent back to pixels. That one architectural move is why it runs on consumer GPUs.

Text steers generation via cross-attention: the prompt is encoded (CLIP text encoder, topic 297), and at every denoising step the U-Net's attention layers attend over those text embeddings — the prompt whispers into every step, not just the start. The practical knob is guidance scale (classifier-free guidance): each step runs conditioned and unconditioned predictions and extrapolates toward the prompt. Low (1–3) = imaginative but loosely prompted; ~7.5 = the sweet spot; high (12–15) = literal prompt adherence with fried, oversaturated artifacts.

Latent diffusion: denoise in the VAE's compressed space, with the prompt cross-attending into every U-Net step.
Example 
from diffusers import StableDiffusionPipeline
import torch

pipe = StableDiffusionPipeline.from_pretrained(
    "stabilityai/stable-diffusion-2-1",
    torch_dtype=torch.float16).to("cuda")

for g in [1, 4, 7.5, 12, 15]:          # guidance-scale sweep
    img = pipe("a rover on a dune at dusk, film photo",
               guidance_scale=g, num_inference_steps=30).images[0]
    img.save(f"rover_g{g}.png")
# g=1: dreamy, barely on-prompt · g=7.5: sweet spot · g=15: literal, fried
Real scenario — mission patches and an architecture answer

You generate concept art and mission-patch mockups for each portfolio project with the guidance sweep above, and keep the five-image strip for one interview moment: when asked "how does Stable Diffusion actually run on a laptop?", you answer in one breath — "it doesn't diffuse pixels; a VAE compresses to a 64×64 latent, the U-Net denoises there with the prompt cross-attending into every step, and guidance scale is the literal-versus-creative dial — here's the same seed at five guidance values." The strip is the explanation.

296

GANs

Concept

A GAN (Generative Adversarial Network) trains two networks against each other: the generator forges samples from random noise, the discriminator learns to tell forgeries from real data, and each one's improvement forces the other to improve. At equilibrium the forgeries are indistinguishable from data. Historically huge — GANs owned image generation for years — and famously unstable: the two-player game oscillates, and the classic failure is mode collapse, where the generator finds one output family that reliably fools the discriminator and produces only that, abandoning the rest of the distribution.

Diffusion (topic 294) superseded GANs for image generation precisely by removing the adversarial game — stable loss, full coverage. But the adversarial idea recurs everywhere: GAN-style losses sharpen VAE and codec outputs, adversarial examples probe classifier robustness, and red-teaming LLMs is the same forger-versus-detector loop played with prompts.

The adversarial loop: forger vs detector, each training signal sharpening the other — powerful, and unstable by construction.
Example 
for real in loader:                       # tiny DCGAN loop, MNIST
    z    = torch.randn(bs, 100)
    fake = G(z)
    # 1) discriminator: real → 1, fake → 0
    d_loss = bce(D(real), ones) + bce(D(fake.detach()), zeros)
    step(d_opt, d_loss)
    # 2) generator: make D say 1 on fakes
    g_loss = bce(D(fake), ones)
    step(g_opt, g_loss)
# mode-collapse smell: every G(z) starts looking like the same digit —
# when you see it happen, you'll understand why the field moved on
Real scenario — the collapse you should cause once

Before diffusion (topic 294), you tried a GAN for the same synthetic-telemetry job — and hit mode collapse in epoch 40: every generated orbit trace became the same "typical" sinusoid, because that one shape reliably fooled the discriminator. Diversity across 1,000 samples: near zero. It's the most instructive failure in generative ML — cause it once on MNIST, watch every sample become the digit 1, and you'll never need a flashcard for why diffusion's stable objective won, or why the adversarial idea still shows up in your LLM red-teaming.

297

Multimodal AI

Concept

Multimodal AI means one model working across several modalities — and the unlock is the shared embedding space. CLIP's insight: train an image encoder and a text encoder together on 400M (image, caption) pairs with a contrastive objective — pull each image's embedding toward its own caption's embedding, push it away from every other caption in the batch. After training, "a photo of a dust devil" and an actual photo of a dust devil land at nearly the same point in the same vector space.

Two capabilities fall out for free: zero-shot classification — embed candidate labels as sentences, embed the image, and the nearest label wins, no training on your classes at all — and cross-modal search — text queries retrieving images (or vice versa) by plain nearest-neighbor, the same geometry as topic 31's vectors. CLIP's text encoder is also the prompt-conditioning backbone inside Stable Diffusion (topic 295).

CLIP's dual encoders map images and text into one space — cross-modal search becomes plain nearest-neighbor.
Example 
from transformers import CLIPModel, CLIPProcessor

model = CLIPModel.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")
proc  = CLIPProcessor.from_pretrained("openai/clip-vit-base-patch32")

caps = ["a dust devil on the horizon", "a rover wheel in sand",
        "a solar panel covered in dust"]
inputs = proc(text=caps, images=img, return_tensors="pt", padding=True)
probs = model(**inputs).logits_per_image.softmax(dim=1)
print(dict(zip(caps, probs[0].tolist())))
# zero-shot: no training on these classes, ever
Real scenario — text-searching 5,000 rover photos

You embed 5,000 Mars rover photos with CLIP's image encoder into your vector DB. A geologist types "dust devil on the horizon" — the query goes through the text encoder, nearest-neighbor search runs in the shared space, and the top hits are actual dust-devil frames nobody ever tagged. Zero labels, zero fine-tuning; the same pgvector setup your Mission Control RAG already uses, just with image vectors in the table. Cross-modal search is a weekend project once you have this topic.

298

Vision-Language Models (VLMs)

Concept

A VLM goes beyond CLIP's matching: it lets an LLM reason about images. Architecture: a vision encoder (usually a ViT) turns the image into patch embeddings, a small projector maps them into the LLM's token-embedding space, and those image tokens are spliced into the sequence right alongside the text tokens. From the LLM's perspective, the image is just more context to attend over — so it can describe, compare, extract, and answer questions about what it "sees". GPT-4o, Claude, and open-source LLaVA all follow this recipe.

The practical magic in production: screenshot parsing (UI testing agents), document extraction (scanned PDFs → structured JSON), and chart reading. The equally practical caveat: VLMs interpolate visually — they misread precise values off dense axes, hallucinate table cells, and miscount objects. Knowing the failure modes — and evaluating them (topics 287–290 apply verbatim) — is the skill.

The VLM recipe: vision encoder → projector → image tokens in the LLM's sequence, attended over like any other context.
Example 
resp = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="gpt-4o",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": [
        {"type": "text", "text":
         "Extract this chart's data as JSON: {series:[{x,y}]}"},
        {"type": "image_url",
         "image_url": {"url": f"data:image/png;base64,{b64}"}},
    ]}],
    response_format={"type": "json_object"},
)
# then FIND a chart it misreads — dense axes, log scales, stacked bars —
# because knowing the failure modes is the actual skill
Real scenario — 1970s scans to structured JSON

The Mission Control corpus includes scanned 1970s Apollo reports — tables and charts a text extractor mangles into soup. You route those pages through a VLM: "extract this table as JSON with these column names," then validate with Pydantic (rung from volume 6) before ingest. It nails 90% of pages, so you build a 40-page eval set (topic 287) for the other 10%: the systematic failures are log-scale flux charts (values off by 10×) and merged table cells. Those page types get flagged for human review — a trust boundary you can defend in any interview.

299

Graph Neural Networks

Concept

Some data's structure is the signal: who cites whom, who transacts with whom, which atoms bond. Flatten it into rows and the fraud ring, the research community, the functional group — the pattern that lives in the edges — disappears. A GNN learns directly on the graph via message passing: in each layer, every node gathers its neighbors' current representations, aggregates them (sum/mean/attention), and combines the result with its own vector to produce its updated representation. Stack L layers and each node's embedding summarizes its L-hop neighborhood.

The outputs plug into ordinary heads: classify nodes (is this account fraudulent?), predict links (will these papers be co-cited?), or classify whole graphs (is this molecule toxic?). PyTorch Geometric (PyG) is the standard library; Cora — a citation network of 2,708 papers — is its MNIST.

Message passing: a node updates itself from its neighbors' representations — layer by layer, hop by hop.
Example 
from torch_geometric.nn import GCNConv
from torch_geometric.datasets import Planetoid

data = Planetoid("data", "Cora")[0]     # 2708 papers, cite edges

class GCN(torch.nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        self.c1 = GCNConv(1433, 16)      # 1433 word features in
        self.c2 = GCNConv(16, 7)         # 7 topic classes out
    def forward(self, x, edge_index):
        h = self.c1(x, edge_index).relu()    # hop 1
        return self.c2(h, edge_index)        # hop 2
# beats a graph-blind MLP on the same features by ~15 points
Real scenario — the citation graph the RAG ignores

Your Mission Control corpus has structure the RAG never uses: NASA reports cite each other. You build the citation graph and train a two-layer GCN for node classification (which program does an unlabeled report belong to?) — the GNN hits 84% vs 69% for a text-embedding-only classifier, because a report's neighborhood betrays its program even when its abstract is vague. Bonus use: at retrieval time, chunks from reports one hop from a retrieved report make excellent expansion candidates — graph structure quietly improving context recall (topic 283).

300

Federated learning

Concept

Federated learning trains a shared model across devices or organizations without centralizing the data. The FedAvg loop: a server broadcasts the current global weights → each client trains locally on its own private data for a few epochs → clients send back only weight updates (never data) → the server averages the updates (weighted by client data size) into a new global model → repeat. The data never moves; the model does.

It's the pattern for privacy-constrained ML: hospitals that can't pool patient records, phones training keyboards on your typing, companies whose contracts forbid data sharing. Honest caveats: non-IID data (each client's distribution differs) makes naive averaging drift, communication is the bottleneck, and weight updates can still leak information — which is why real deployments add differential privacy or secure aggregation on top.

FedAvg: the model travels to the data, trains locally, and only weight updates return to be averaged.
Example 
# FedAvg by hand: three clients, disjoint data, no raw data moves
states = [train_locally(copy.deepcopy(model), client_data[i], epochs=2)
          for i in range(3)]

avg = {}
for key in states[0]:
    avg[key] = torch.stack([s[key] for s in states]).mean(dim=0)

model.load_state_dict(avg)          # the new global model
# repeat broadcast → local train → average for several rounds,
# then compare against a model trained on the pooled data
Real scenario — three ground stations, zero shared telemetry

Three ground-station partners each hold satellite telemetry they contractually cannot share — but all three want a better anomaly detector than any could train alone. You simulate it first: split your telemetry dataset three ways (non-IID — each "station" sees different orbital regimes), run five FedAvg rounds, and compare against centralized training. Federated lands within 2 points of centralized and 11 points above any single station's solo model. That simulation notebook is the exact artifact that turns a compliance stalemate into a signed collaboration.

301

Quantum machine learning

Concept

Quantum ML uses parameterized quantum circuits as models: qubits are prepared, rotated by trainable angles (the "weights"), entangled, and measured; the measurement statistics are the model output, and the angles are tuned by gradient descent like any other parameters. On paper, n qubits explore a 2ⁿ-dimensional state space. In practice we live in the NISQ era — noisy, intermediate-scale quantum hardware with tens-to-hundreds of error-prone qubits — and no practical advantage over classical ML has been demonstrated for any real ML workload. Simulators and small circuits are genuinely fun; production impact is, honestly, not there yet.

This rung is deliberately awareness-level: know the vocabulary (qubit, entanglement, variational circuit, barren plateaus — the vanishing-gradient problem of quantum circuits), be able to give the honest status answer, and spend the saved study time on topic 302, which appears in actual job descriptions.

Example 
import pennylane as qml
dev = qml.device("default.qubit", wires=2)   # simulator

@qml.qnode(dev)
def circuit(theta):
    qml.RY(theta[0], wires=0)        # trainable rotation = "weight"
    qml.CNOT(wires=[0, 1])           # entangle the two qubits
    qml.RY(theta[1], wires=1)
    return qml.expval(qml.PauliZ(1))  # measurement = model output

print(circuit([0.54, 0.12]))         # differentiable → trainable
Real scenario — the honest senior answer

A director asks whether the team should "explore quantum ML for trajectory optimization" after reading a vendor deck. Your answer, calibrated by this rung: "Today's hardware is NISQ — noisy, small, no demonstrated ML advantage; trainability itself hits barren plateaus as circuits grow. I'd spend that budget on the GPU serving stack, and revisit quantum when error-corrected machines run circuits deeper than simulators can match." Knowing when a frontier isn't ready — and saying so with the right three terms — is itself a senior signal.

— Serving at Speed —
302

vLLM (serving)

Concept

vLLM is the open-source standard for serving LLMs, and its core trick is PagedAttention: treat the KV cache (every generating sequence's attention memory, rung 137) like an operating system treats RAM — fixed-size blocks, allocated on demand, tracked by a per-sequence block table, physically non-contiguous. Naive serving reserves one contiguous max-length slab per request and wastes 60–80% of it; paging cuts that waste to ~4%, so far more sequences fit on the GPU at once.

More resident sequences enables the second trick: continuous batching. Instead of waiting for a whole batch to finish, finished sequences leave and queued ones join between decode steps — the GPU never idles. Know the metrics vocabulary cold: TTFT (time to first token — how fast it starts), TPOT (time per output token — how fast it streams), and throughput (total tokens/s across all requests — what you provision by).

KV cache managed like paged virtual memory: small blocks + a block table, so many more sequences fit per GPU.
Example 
# serve an OpenAI-compatible endpoint on one GPU
vllm serve ./mistral-mc-summarizer-7b --max-model-len 8192

# client: the plain OpenAI SDK, pointed at your box
client = OpenAI(base_url="http://gpu-node:8000/v1", api_key="-")
out = client.chat.completions.create(
    model="mistral-mc-summarizer-7b",
    messages=[{"role": "user", "content": "Summarize sol 122 anomalies"}])

# benchmark it: concurrency 1 → ~42 tok/s; concurrency 32 → ~1,150 tok/s
# aggregate. that ~27× gap IS continuous batching + PagedAttention.
Real scenario — serving your own fine-tune

The mission-log summarizer you fine-tuned in volume 8 has to actually serve users now. One vllm serve command on an A10G gives you an OpenAI-compatible endpoint — so the Mission Control backend just swaps base_url, and LiteLLM (topic 303) can route to it as a fallback. Your benchmark table goes in the README: concurrency 1 = 42 tok/s, concurrency 32 = 1,150 tok/s aggregate with TTFT still under 400ms. When an interviewer asks "how would you serve a fine-tuned 7B for 200 concurrent users?", this topic is the answer, with your own numbers attached.

303

LiteLLM

Concept

LiteLLM gives you one OpenAI-shaped interface over 100+ providers — OpenAI, Anthropic, Bedrock, Vertex, your own vLLM box — so switching models is a string change, not a rewrite. On top of the unified call it layers the production features every multi-provider system eventually rebuilds badly by hand: fallback routing (primary fails → next in the chain), load balancing across deployments of the same model, budgets and rate limits per key/team/project, plus retries and cooldowns.

It runs two ways: as a library inside your Python process, or as a proxy gateway — a standalone server your whole org points at, where keys, budgets, and routing live in one config instead of in every codebase. The proxy is the standard answer to "how do we do multi-provider resilience and cost control without touching every app?"

One interface, a fallback chain behind it: the primary's outage becomes a routing event, not an incident.
Example 
import litellm

resp = litellm.completion(
    model="openai/gpt-4o-mini",          # primary
    messages=msgs,
    fallbacks=["anthropic/claude-haiku-4-5",
               "hosted_vllm/mistral-mc-summarizer-7b"],
    num_retries=2, timeout=20,
)
print(resp.choices[0].message.content)   # same shape, any provider
# prove it: block api.openai.com in /etc/hosts and watch the call
# succeed anyway — failover as a config line, not an incident
Real scenario — the outage that wasn't

Your primary provider has a 40-minute outage on a demo day. The Orbital Research Agent doesn't notice: LiteLLM's fallback chain fails over to Claude, and when your Anthropic budget cap (set per-key in the proxy config) trips an hour later, to the local vLLM summarizer from topic 302. The Langfuse traces (topic 291) show the model column flipping mid-afternoon — that screenshot, "resilience as configuration," is worth ten minutes of any system-design interview.

304

Ray

Concept

Ray makes a cluster feel like one big Python process. Decorate a function with @ray.remote and calling .remote() ships it to any free worker in the cluster, returning a future immediately; ray.get() collects results. Decorate a class and you get an actor — a stateful worker process (a model held in GPU memory, a counter, a cache) you call methods on remotely. The scheduler handles placement, data movement, and fault tolerance.

On this substrate Ray ships higher-level libraries — Serve (model serving with autoscaling), Train (distributed training), Data (distributed preprocessing), RLlib (reinforcement learning) — and much of the large-scale ML world runs on it: vLLM uses Ray for multi-GPU and multi-node serving, and OpenAI famously trained on Ray-based infrastructure.

@ray.remote turns function calls into cluster tasks; actors are stateful workers — a cluster programmed like one process.
Example 
import ray
ray.init()                              # or ray.init("ray://cluster")

@ray.remote(num_cpus=1)
def embed_batch(chunks: list[str]) -> list[list[float]]:
    return model.encode(chunks).tolist()

futures = [embed_batch.remote(b) for b in batches]   # instant
vectors = ray.get(futures)              # blocks until all done
# serial: 14h on one core → 8 nodes × 16 cores: ~2h, same code shape
Real scenario — re-embedding two million chunks

You upgrade the Mission Control embedding model (volume 9's bake-off won), which means re-embedding 2M chunks. Serial estimate: 14 hours — unacceptable during the migration window. With @ray.remote the loop body doesn't change; batches fan out across an 8-node spot-instance cluster and finish in under 2 hours, with Ray retrying the batches lost when a spot node was reclaimed mid-run. Same mental model scales down, too: on your laptop, ray.init() alone parallelizes across all cores.

305

Triton Inference Server

Concept

Triton Inference Server is NVIDIA's production serving layer for any model framework: point it at a model repository (a directory tree of models, each with numbered versions and a config.pbtxt) and it serves them all — ONNX, TensorRT, PyTorch, TensorFlow, even Python scripts — behind one HTTP/gRPC endpoint with shared GPU scheduling. Don't confuse it with OpenAI's Triton language (a kernel DSL, see topic 308) — same name, different thing.

Its two killer features for classic-ML serving: dynamic batching — hold individual requests for a few milliseconds and merge them into one GPU batch, trading a hair of latency for multiples of throughput — and ensembles — chain preprocessing → model → postprocessing inside the server, so clients send raw inputs and network hops disappear. Where vLLM is specialized for LLM text generation, Triton is the general-purpose workhorse for everything else in your zoo.

A model repository served behind one endpoint; the dynamic batcher merges concurrent requests into single GPU batches.
Example 
# model_repository/exoplanet_cnn/config.pbtxt
name: "exoplanet_cnn"
platform: "onnxruntime_onnx"
max_batch_size: 64
dynamic_batching {
  max_queue_delay_microseconds: 5000   # hold ≤5ms to form batches
}

# run it
docker run --gpus 1 -p 8000:8000 -v $PWD/model_repository:/models \
  nvcr.io/nvidia/tritonserver:24.05-py3 \
  tritonserver --model-repository=/models
Real scenario — telemetry burst scoring

The exoplanet CNN (exported to ONNX in volume 4) moves from a hand-rolled FastAPI wrapper to Triton. During Kafka telemetry bursts, hundreds of light-curve windows arrive within milliseconds — individually they'd each trigger a lonely GPU call at batch size 1. With dynamic_batching and a 5ms queue delay, Triton merges them into batches of 40–60 and throughput more than triples on the same GPU. Version 2 of the model deploys by dropping a folder into the repository — Triton hot-loads it while version 1 keeps serving.

306

TensorRT

Concept

TensorRT is NVIDIA's inference compiler: it takes a trained model (usually via ONNX) and builds a hyper-optimized engine for one specific GPU. Three optimizations do the heavy lifting: operator fusion — conv + bias + ReLU become a single kernel, eliminating the memory round-trips between ops (the real cost, as topic 308 explains); kernel auto-tuning — for each layer shape it benchmarks candidate implementations on your actual GPU and keeps the fastest; and precision calibration — drop weights and activations to FP16 or INT8 (with a calibration dataset to keep accuracy), doubling or quadrupling effective throughput.

The result is often multiples faster than framework inference for latency-critical serving. The trade: engines are compiled per GPU model and per input-shape profile — an A100 engine won't run on a T4 — so TensorRT lives at the end of your deploy pipeline, not in your notebook.

Compilation, not magic: fewer kernels, fewer memory round-trips, lower precision — tuned to the exact GPU serving it.
Example 
# compile: ONNX → TensorRT engine, tuned on this exact GPU
trtexec --onnx=exoplanet_cnn.onnx \
        --saveEngine=exoplanet_cnn_fp16.plan \
        --fp16 \
        --shapes=lightcurve:32x1x2048

# measure it (1000 timed iterations, reports latency percentiles)
trtexec --loadEngine=exoplanet_cnn_fp16.plan --iterations=1000
# typical CNN result: PyTorch eager 23 ms → TensorRT FP16 4 ms.
# no NVIDIA GPU handy? read one benchmark deeply and be able to say
# WHERE the speedup comes from: fusion, tuning, precision.
Real scenario — 23ms to 4ms, and why it matters

Live telemetry scoring gives the exoplanet CNN a 10ms budget per batch — miss it and the Kafka consumer lags behind the stream. PyTorch eager takes 23ms. The TensorRT FP16 engine (built in CI on the same T4 the service runs on, cached as an artifact) takes 4ms, and INT8 with a 500-sample calibration set takes 2.5ms with 0.2% accuracy loss — measured, of course, on the topic-287 benchmark. The chain you should be able to recite: ONNX → Triton for the serving plumbing → TensorRT for the per-GPU speed.

307

Speculative decoding

Concept

LLM generation is sequential — one forward pass per token — and each pass is memory-bandwidth-bound: the GPU spends its time streaming weights, not computing. Speculative decoding exploits the slack: a small, fast draft model proposes the next k tokens (k cheap passes), then the big target model verifies all k in a single forward pass — verifying k tokens costs barely more than generating one, because the bandwidth is already paid. Accept the longest prefix the target agrees with, take the target's own token at the first disagreement, repeat.

The two facts to hold onto: a clever acceptance-sampling rule makes the output distribution provably identical to the target model decoding alone — zero quality loss, not "approximately the same" — and the speedup rides on the acceptance rate: easy, formulaic text (code, summaries, boilerplate) accepts 70–80% of drafts for 2–3× wall-clock gains; adversarially weird text accepts less and gains less. A free lunch bought with clever scheduling.

Draft proposes, target verifies in one pass: keep the agreed prefix, substitute the target's token at the first miss.
Example 
# vLLM: add a draft model to the serve command
vllm serve ./mistral-mc-summarizer-7b \
  --speculative-config \
  '{"model": "./mistral-draft-1b", "num_speculative_tokens": 5}'

# then watch the metrics vLLM logs:
#   draft acceptance rate: 0.74  ← how often the 7B agrees with the 1B
#   speedup ≈ tokens accepted per verify pass — here ~2.4×
# same eval scores (it's the SAME distribution), lower TPOT
Real scenario — free speed on formulaic reports

Mission-log summaries are formulaic — "Sol 122: nominal power, DSN pass at 14:20 UTC…" — exactly the text a small draft model predicts well. You add a 1B draft to the topic-302 vLLM deployment: acceptance rate 0.74, TPOT drops from 24ms to 10ms, users see summaries stream 2.4× faster on the same GPU. And because the acceptance-sampling math preserves the target distribution exactly, your topic-288 regression suite confirms what theory promised: every eval score identical, wall-clock nearly tripled. The rare genuinely free lunch — verify it anyway.

308

CUDA basics

Concept

The GPU programming model, in one breath: you write a kernel — a function executed by thousands of threads in parallel — and launch it over a grid of thread blocks (each block = up to 1,024 threads that can share fast on-chip memory and synchronize; blocks are scheduled independently across the GPU's streaming multiprocessors). Each thread computes its own global index and handles its slice of the data. That's the whole model.

The insight that explains every inference optimization you've met: the memory hierarchy is the wall. Registers and shared memory are fast and tiny; global memory (HBM) is huge but hundreds of cycles away — and for most ML workloads the GPU is bandwidth-bound, idling while data streams in. Now reread this volume: operator fusion (306) exists to skip round-trips to HBM, FlashAttention (rung from volume 5) recomputes rather than re-reads, PagedAttention (302) manages HBM like an OS, speculative decoding (307) amortizes one weight-stream over k tokens. You may never write a kernel at work — but this mental model is why all of those work.

Kernels launch as grids of thread blocks; the memory pyramid — not compute — sets the speed limit for ML workloads.
Example 
from numba import cuda
import numpy as np

@cuda.jit
def vadd(a, b, out):
    i = cuda.grid(1)              # my global thread index
    if i < out.size:              # guard the ragged edge
        out[i] = a[i] + b[i]

n = 10_000_000
threads = 256
blocks  = (n + threads - 1) // threads
vadd[blocks, threads](a_dev, b_dev, out_dev)   # launch the 1-D grid
# 10M floats: GPU wins big. 10K floats: kernel-launch overhead loses
# to NumPy — parallelism has a fixed cost of admission.
Real scenario — the ladder's last rung

Run the vector-add at 10M elements and the GPU crushes NumPy; run it at 10K and it loses to launch overhead — and now you can explain both results in memory-bandwidth terms. That closes the loop on this entire volume: why vLLM pages the KV cache, why TensorRT fuses kernels, why speculative decoding gets k tokens for one weight-stream, why batch size is destiny. From print("hello") on rung 1 to reasoning about GPU memory hierarchies on rung 308 — climb down, look back at the ladder, and celebrate. All 308.

Volume 11 / 11 complete — System Design, Evaluation & the Frontier, items 272–308.

All 308 topics complete. There is no next volume — the ladder is climbed. Go build, and go get the offer.

Study rule: run every example, do every "real scenario" with actual NASA API data, and you'll own these — not just recognize them.
